These are the waters in which the soul is strengthened, purified, redeemed, sanctified, and snatched from the power of demons.

And so, two kinds of water are distinguished. For one knowledge is described as being external, and the more one drinks of it, the more he thirsts; the other, as being internal, of which it is said: "He who believes in Me, as the Scripture says, 'From within Him there shall flow rivers of living water.'" He said this, however, of the Spirit whom they who believed in Him were to receive. And these are the waters from the fountain of salvation, that is, awareness of those graces that sustain souls.

12:4.t: And you will say in that day: Confess to the Lord and call upon his name: make known among the peoples his devices: remember that his name is exalted. Sing to the Lord, for he has done magnificently: proclaim this in all the earth. These things are commanded by the Apostles and the remnant of Israel to those of the nations who have believed: that they confess to the Lord alone, and, forsaking idols, call upon his name, and proclaim all his works to unbelievers; that they may know that he alone is exalted: to whom they must sing that he has done magnificently, and that his mercy may be proclaimed in all the world.

388. And you shall say. Here he foretells that the people shall also sing, after the benefit has been received, and it contains the mutual exhortation of the people to divine praise. Exhortation to three things is set out:

to the confession of divine praise,

to thanksgiving: sing to the Lord (Isa 12:5),

to shared rejoicing: rejoice (Isa 12:6).

Concerning the first, four things are set out:

for we either confess the Lord through faith: confess the Lord: with the heart, we believe unto justice: but, with the mouth, confession is made unto salvation (Rom 10:10);

or we call upon him through prayer: and call upon, below: seek the Lord, while he may be found: call upon him, while he is near (Isa 55:6); […]

12:6.t: Exult and praise, O dwelling of Zion: for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel. First it must be said according to the letter: O dwelling of Zion, exult and praise your God, because he who was formerly seen as your God, and was shut within the narrow bounds of the land of Judea, has now filled all the earth with his knowledge, and, rising from death, reigns among the nations, and the nations beseech and adore him; only so, however, that he sets his hand a second time to possess what is left of his people, and to gather the fugitives of Israel, and to collect the dispersed of Judah from the four quarters of the earth: because the seed-bed of the Gospel went forth from the fountains of Israel through the Apostles, who were of the Jews. […]

13:1.t: The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amos saw. The Hebrew word MESSA (משא) can be understood either as burden or as weight. And wherever it is placed at the head, the things that are said are full of threats. Hence I wonder that the Seventy translators chose to put vision in so grim a matter; but of this elsewhere. Now let us carry through what we have begun. Babylon was the metropolis of the Chaldeans, whose king Nebuchadnezzar, having overcome all the nations as far as Ethiopia, laid waste Judea too among the rest, and in the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah took Jerusalem after a long siege; […]

The burden or vision against Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amos saw. He saw, not with the eyes of the flesh but with those of the mind, how great and heavy a weight was to be laid upon Babylon. And since Babylon, which in Hebrew is called BABEL (בבל), means confusion, because there the speech of those building the tower was confounded, spiritually this world is understood, which is set in wickedness and confounds not only the tongues but also the works and the minds of each person. The king of this Babylon is the true Nebuchadnezzar, who grows proud against the Lord and says in his heart: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the North; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; […]

The burden of Babylon. Here he threatens against the Babylonians, who had captured the two tribes. And this is divided into two parts: in the first, he threatens the destruction of the enemy, in the second, he promises, from this, the comfort of the Jews: her time is near at hand (ch. 14). The first of these is divided into two. First, the title of the threat is set out, and the rebuke: the burden, that is, oppressing misery: if this people, or the prophet, or the priest shall ask you, saying: what is the burden of the Lord? You shall say to them: you are the burden (Jer 23:33). Second, the threat itself is set out: upon the dark mountain (Isa 13:2). […]

13:2.t: Upon a misty mountain lift up a signal, raise the voice, lift up the hand. The misty, or dark, mountain, which in Hebrew is called NESPHE (נשפה), understand as Babylon, on account of its pride. These are the dark mountains, bearing gloom and mist before them, of which Jeremiah says: Give glory to the Lord your God, before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains (Jer 13:16). And a command is given either to the angels or to any ministers whatever, that at God's bidding, and with the hand of the messengers raised, the captivity coming upon Babylon should be proclaimed.

Upon a misty mountain, or a level one, lift up a sign. It is commanded to the Apostles, and to apostolic men and teachers of the Churches, that when they are about to fight against Babylon they should raise the sign of the Lord's cross, not in a low place and in sunken valleys, but on a misty or level mountain. Of these, the one signifies the hidden mysteries of the Church, to see which, and to hear the voice of God, Moses entered into the darkness and the mist. For God made darkness his hiding place, and cloud and mist round about him (Ps 17 [18]). […]

And let the leaders enter the gates: I have commanded my sanctified ones, and have called my mighty ones in my wrath, exulting in my glory. The princes and giants of the Seventy translators Eusebius interprets as angelic powers and the worst demons, who were sent to overthrow Babylon. But we, following the order of the history, say that they are the Medes. Of them Scripture testifies more openly in what follows, saying: Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who will not seek silver, nor want gold. Nor is it surprising if he calls the Medes sanctified for the overthrow of Babylon, since through Jeremiah he called Nebuchadnezzar himself his servant and his dove, because in destroying transgressing Jerusalem he was serving His command. […]

By a mountain is designated the apostate angel, as is said to preachers concerning the ancient enemy under the character of the king of Babylon, Lift ye up a banner upon the gloomy mountain. For holy preachers lift up a banner above the gloomy mountain, when they exalt the virtue of the cross against the pride of Satan, which is frequently concealed under the mist of hypocrisy.
13:2.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 6:33.2

13:2.t: Concerning the first of these, he does two things. First, he sets out the calling together; and he calls them together to attack and besiege: lift up a sign, that is, a banner, upon the mountain, of Babylon, dark, because of the smoke from the fire, when it had been burned. Or, upon the mountain, next to the city, dark, hidden by the clouds or its appearance made dark because of its height. He calls them to cry out: exalt the voice, that the enemy should assemble. To join in battle: lift up the hand, to fight. To capture: and let the rulers go into the gates: upon the walls of Babylon set up the standard (Jer 51:12). […]

13:3.t:
I have commanded my sanctified ones. For which the LXX: I will command, and I will lead them. For he himself sanctifies his ministers, so that both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified may all be of one. He who in another place also says to believers: Be holy, because I also am holy, himself commands and will lead his princes, so that they may do what has been commanded (Lev 19:2).

And I have called my mighty ones in my wrath, exulting in my glory. LXX: Giants come to fulfill my fury, rejoicing together and doing outrage. According to the Hebrew, what is said clings to what precedes: that he who had given command to his sanctified ones himself called his mighty ones, exulting in his glory. […]

Second, he sets out the condition of those who are called as to their suitableness on account of charge of office: my sanctified ones, as if to say: those whom I have sanctified to carry out this office; and as to power: strong; and as to cheerfulness: them that rejoice: the Lord has sanctified those he has called (Zeph 1:7).

13:4.t: The voice of a multitude on the mountains, as of crowded peoples; the voice of the sound of kings of nations gathered together. This passage is taken in three ways. First, that when the sign has been raised on the level mountain, the multitude of the nations comes, itself also set upon the mountains, and it is divided into two, namely into peoples and into kings, into disciples and teachers, of whom the Savior spoke in the Gospel: Many will come from the East and from the West, and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matt 8:11). […]

The sound of a multitude on the mountains, as of many peoples: the sound of the din of the kings of nations gathered together. The Lord of hosts has given command to the army of war, to those coming from a land far off, from the summit of heaven. The Lord and the vessels of his fury, to destroy the whole earth. The onslaught of the Medes and Persians is described: that, having gathered many auxiliaries with them, with their Lord going before the army, they come to lay Babylon waste, to destroy the whole earth; not that they laid waste the whole world, but the whole land of Babylon and of the Chaldeans. For it is an idiom of Holy Scripture that by the whole earth it signifies the whole of that province about which it is speaking; […]

The Lord of hosts has commanded the army of war, coming from a far land, from the height of heaven: the Lord and the vessels of his fury, to destroy the whole earth. LXX: The Lord Sabaoth commanded a most warlike nation to come from a distant land, from the highest ÷ foundation ⁚ of heaven, the Lord and his warriors, to destroy the whole world. Foundation is to be marked beforehand with an obelus. In the volume of Kings and of Chronicles we read (2 Sam 24; 1 Chr 21) that the wrath of God was kindled against Israel when David numbered the people and offended the Lord. […]

The voice of a multitude. Here he describes the coming of those who are called, and first, as to the lowly: the voice of a multitude; second, as to the great, the voice of the sound of kings: their voice shall roar like the sea (Jer 50:42); below: the tumult of crowds shall come (Isa 17:12). The Lord of hosts. Here he decrees the command. And first, he sets out the divine command: the Lord has given charge.

13:5.t: Second, divine help to fulfill the command: from the end of heaven, as though to help; and the instruments of his wrath, that is, all kinds of arms.

13:6.t: Howl, for the day of the Lord is near: like a devastation it will come from the Lord. An apostrophe is made to the people of the Chaldeans, that they should make the coming evils resound with their weeping, and not doubt the ruin of their city, since the Lord is coming as its devastator.

Howl, for the day of the Lord is near; it will come like devastation from the Lord. Therefore all hands will be loosened, and every heart of man will melt and be crushed. Since the warriors of the Lord are to come to destroy the whole earth, howl and do penance, you for whom punishment is coming. For the day of the Lord is near, either of the consummation of the whole world and of the judgment, or of each one's departure from life. For there comes from the Lord a plundering, which we have called devastation in order to keep the metaphor, since he had spoken first of warriors. When the day of judgment or of falling asleep has come, all hands will be loosened, to which it is said in another place: Be strengthened, you loosened hands. […]

Howl. Here he describes the affliction of the punishment. And concerning this he sets out three things: first, the fear of those to be punished; second, the affliction: behold, the day (Isa 13:9); third, the ferocity of the punishers, behold I will stir up (Isa 13:17). And their fear is expressed, first, as to the groaning of the mouth: howl: howl, woe, woe to the day: for the day is near, yea the day of the Lord is near: a cloudy day, it shall be the time of groaning (Ezek 30:2–3).

13:7.t: Therefore all hands will be loosened, and every heart of man will waste away and be crushed. Gripings and pains will seize them: they will be in pain like a woman in labor: each will be astounded at his neighbor: their countenances are scorched faces. This needs no exposition; but it is briefly indicated that so great a weight of evils will press upon them that the hand of Babylon's fighting men will be loosened, and the heart will languish with fear, and pain will wring their bowels after the manner of women in labor, and each will seek the help of another, carrying about a face sallow with pallor; for it is natural that, when evils are imminent, we think others wiser than ourselves.
Second, as to the abatement of work: therefore shall all hands be faint: the king of Babylon has heard the report of them, and his hands are grown feeble (Jer 50:43).

13:8.t: And what has been added according to the Seventy: the envoys will be troubled, and pains will seize them: we can interpret as those envoys whom the citizens had sent against him who had set out into a far country to seek a kingdom for himself (Luke 19:27). Hence he himself says in the Gospel: But those enemies who did not want me to reign over them, bring here and slay before me.

Twistings and pains will seize them; they will be in pain like a woman in labor; each one will be astonished at his neighbor; their faces are burnt countenances. When the warriors of the Lord have come from a distant land, and all hands have been loosened, and the heart is fearful and crushed, then strophomata, which we have translated as twistings of the belly, and pains will seize them, like the pains of women in labor. By this it is shown that they are tortured by their own conscience, and have their faces burnt with that fire which they had kindled for themselves: because they cannot say: The light of your countenance has been signed upon us, O Lord (Ps 4:7); and: We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image (2 Cor 3:18). […]

Third, as to the disturbance of the heart, which is disturbed in three ways. According to its inner state, either as to cheerfulness: and every heart of man shall melt; or as to magnanimity: and shall be broken, as though divided into little pieces; or as to security, by the distress of fear: gripings: there were pains as of a woman in labor (Ps 48:8). Second, it is troubled as to lack of help: every one shall be amazed at his neighbor, as though, because of their amazement, they cannot bring help. As to the outward sign: their countenances shall be as faces burnt, because of the pallor of fear; or literally, because they were killed with such a death: their face is now made blacker than coals (Lam 4:8); the faces of them all are as the blackness of a kettle (Nah 2:10).

13:9.t: Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be moved. And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven, and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn (24, 29—30ᵃ). Since we consider that greater themes here come under discussion than lie within the grasp of human understanding — even of those who have advanced in wisdom far beyond others — let us come and examine the passage: first inquiring into those things which can readily be admitted for an exposition of the Gospel text, as though the Lord Himself were prophesying in it; […]

Concerning that day, hear the prophets, saying, "The day of the Lord is incurable, full of anger and wrath." For there will be none to stand by, none to rescue, nowhere the face of Christ, so mild and calm. But as those who work in the mines are delivered over to certain cruel men, and see none of their friends, but those only that are set over them; so will it be then also: or rather not so, but even far more grievous. For here it is possible to go unto the king, and entreat, and free the condemned person: but there, no longer; for He permits it not, but they continue in the scorching torment, and in so great anguish, as it is not possible for words to tell.
13:9.s: Homily 43 on the Gospel of Matthew

13:9.t: Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, and of wrath and of fury, to make the land a wilderness, and to crush its sinners out of it. He calls the day cruel, not by its own desert, but by that of the people. For he is not cruel who cuts the throats of the cruel; but he seems cruel to those who suffer. For even the robber hanging on the gibbet thinks the judge cruel. And at the same time the desolation and devastation of the Babylonian land is announced, and the cause of the devastation is set forth: that all these things come about because of its inhabitants.

Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, and of wrath and fury, to make the land a wilderness and to crush its sinners out of it. For land the Seventy translated τὴν οἰκουμένην, that is, the world; for cruel, incurable. For when the day either of judgment or of death has come, that will be fulfilled which is read in the sixth psalm: But in hell who will confess to you (Ps 6:6)? For that is not a time of penance, but of punishments. And in another place it is said: How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you! […]

But the day of retribution for all sins is that of which all the prophets write, and above all Isaiah cries aloud: Behold, the incurable day of the Lord is coming, of fury and of wrath, to make the whole world a desert, and to destroy the sinners out of it. This day is rightly called incurable, because when the day of judgment has come there will be no place for repentance; and compared with eternity it is near and not far off.

Behold, the day. Here he describes the punishment of the afflicted. And concerning this, he sets out three things: first, the magnitude of the punishment: full of indignation, as to the removal of mercy; and of wrath, as to the delight of punishment; according to the Philosopher: the angry are saddened, but rejoice in punishing; and fury, as to impetuous vengeance, for fury is wrath inflamed as Gregory says, below: his wrath burns, and is heavy to bear (Isa 30:27).

13:10.t: For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread out their light: the sun has been darkened in its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light. The Hebrew word CHISILE (כסילי) the Seventy translated as ὠρίωνα. The Hebrew whom I used as my teacher interpreted it as Arcturus. We, following Symmachus, have used the general word star. And the sense is this: when the cruel day of the Lord has come and his fury has laid all things waste, through the greatness of their fear everything grows dark for mortals, and the sun itself and the moon and the glowing stars seem to deny their brightness. Hence also heaven is clothed in sackcloth, namely because darkness covers all things, and, under the pressure of evils, men perceive nothing else but what the mind compels them to see.

For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread forth their light; the sun is darkened in its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light. LXX: For the stars of heaven and Orion, and all the adornment of heaven, will not give their light: and they will be darkened when the sun rises, and the moon will not give its light. Where we have translated their splendor, that is, beyond doubt, of the stars, Aquila and Theodotion set down the very Hebrew word CHISILEEM (כסיליהם): for which the Seventy translated Orion, adding of their own and all the adornment of heaven, which is to be marked beforehand with an obelus. […]

It is also expressed in the removal of comfort: for the stars of heaven, and their brightness shall not display their light, either literally as how they are reckoned, for all things seem dark to the afflicted; or the stars, the princes; the sun in his rising, the king; the moon, the queen: the sun became black as sackcloth of hair (Rev 6:12).

13:11.t: You have opened "the eyes of our hearts" so that we realize you alone are "highest among the highest, and ever remain holy among the holy." "You humble the pride of the arrogant, overrule the plans of the nations, raise up the humble and humble the haughty. You make rich and make poor; you slay and bring to life; you alone are the guardian of spirits and the God of all flesh." You see into the depths: you look upon humankind's deeds; you aid those in danger and "save those in despair." You are the Creator of every spirit and watch over them. You multiply the nations on the earth, and from out of them all you have chosen those who love you through Jesus Christ, your beloved Son. Through him you have trained us, made us saints and honored us.

"13. And I will command evils for the whole world, and their sins for the unholy, and I will destroy the pride of the lawless, and will humble the pride of the insolent, 14. and they that are left shall be more precious than gold unsmelted, and a man shall be more precious than the stone of Suphir." And afterwards it adds: "And they that are left shall be as a fleeing fawn, or as a straying sheep."

In this too the Scripture shews most plainly the small number of the saved in the time of the ruin of the wicked, so that it is not possible to expect that absolutely all the circumcised without exception and the whole Jewish race will attain to the promises of God.
13:11.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

13:11.t: And I will visit evils upon the world, and against the wicked their iniquity: and I will make the pride of the unbelievers cease, and will humble the arrogance of the mighty. From this place and from the one above, where it is written that the sun is darkened in its rising, and the moon is filled with gloom, and the stars withdraw their brightness, and the iniquity of the whole world is visited, some think that what is foretold is not the ruin of Babylon but the consummation of the world; whereas, surely, in keeping with what precedes, by the world as well, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל), and in Greek οἰκουμένη, Babylon is to be understood. For οἰκουμένη in our language means inhabited; […]

And I will visit upon the evils of the world, and against the ungodly their iniquities. When God visits and strikes, he strikes for this purpose, that he may amend. Accordingly, when he is vehemently angry with those who do not do penance: I will not visit, he says, upon your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor upon your daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery (Hos 4:14). On the contrary, of those who are to believe in Christ it is said (Ps 88 [89]:33): I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges: but my mercy I will not take away from them.

And I will make the pride of the unbelievers to rest, and I will humble the arrogance of the mighty. […]

Second, he sets out equity, ordaining the punishment for the fault which they committed against themselves: I will visit, I will avenge, the evils of the world, that is, of Babylon, for it was in that monarchy, or because of the multitude of those assembling from all over; and, as to the fault which they also committed against their subjects, through the oppression of the wicked: and against the wicked; or the voiding of covenants: infidels; through the vexation of the better: arrogancy, by which they presumed to subjugate everyone, above: because the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud (Isa 2:12).

13:12.t: A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold. The cause is plain why God visits the οἰκουμένην, that is, the evils of Babylon: so that, deserted by its inhabitants, it may be reduced to a wilderness. Now, everything that is rare is called precious; just as above, too, according to the history, we read that because of the scarcity of men seven women take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach (Isa 4:1). And in the volume of Samuel it is contained: The word of the Lord was precious in those days (1 Sam 3:1), that is, rare. Note that in the Hebrew PHAZ (פז) is written for gold in general, and OPHIR (אופיר) for fine gold.

A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold. LXX: And those who have been left will be more honored than refined gold, and a man will be more honorable than the stone of Sophir. At the consummation of the world, when the world has been reduced to a wilderness, and the sun darkened in its rising, and the moon has not given its splendor, such signs and portents will be wrought by the Antichrist that, as iniquity increases, the love of many will grow cold, so as to deceive, if it be possible, even the elect of God (Matt 24). Then a man will be more precious than gold, which in Hebrew is called PHAZ (פז), and Aquila translated κιῤῥὸν, which is of the finest and blood-red color; […]
That price is most precious. On account of this Isaiah says: "A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold of Ophir." This he says of Christ, who made us precious.

Third, he sets out the moderation of the punishment. And he sets out four things: first, the small number of defenders: more precious, that is, more rare: the word of God was precious (1 Sam 3:1), and a man, who can defend by power, yea a man, who can defend by counsel, the finest of gold, that is, red gold, which is the best, above: they that remain of the trees of his forest shall be so few, that they shall easily be numbered (Isa 10:19).

13:13.t: Upon this I will trouble heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place, because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts, and because of the day of the wrath of his fury. Either take it in the sense in which we expounded above concerning the stars, and the sun, and the moon, and the world; or ὑπερβολικῶς, that because of the indignation of God both heaven is sad and the earth is moved, and all the elements too acknowledge the wrath of the Creator.

Upon this I will shake the heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place. LXX: For the heaven will rage, and the earth will be moved from its foundations. When a man has become more precious than gold, and a human being than pure fine gold, and that has been fulfilled which is written: Do you think, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on the earth (Luke 18:8)? then both the heavens and the earth will be moved. For heaven and earth will pass away, not by their own will and by their own choice, as many suppose, believing them to be living beings; but because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts, and because of the day of his fury, who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble. […]

Second, the commotion of the elements: for this I will trouble the heaven: and the earth shall be moved, as to the literal sense, there could have been a storm in the air and an earthquake in the earth; or this is hyperbole for the magnitude of their evils: I beheld the earth, and lo it was void, and nothing: and the heavens, and there was no light in them (Jer 4:23).

13:14.t:
And it will be like a little doe fleeing, and like a sheep, and there will be none to gather them. He means the Babylonian and Chaldean people: that at the irruption of the Medes and Persians it will flee as fearfully as a little doe and a sheep at the roaring of a lion and the howling of a wolf; and it has no defender or prince whose command it may follow.

Each will turn to his own people, and every one will flee to his own land. After Babylon has been taken and the enemy army has entered through its gates, all the auxiliaries and the troops of the various nations by which the city had formerly been defended will go back to their own provinces.

And it will be like a fleeing fawn, and like a flock of sheep, and there will be none to gather them: they will turn each to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. Everyone who is found will be slain, and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be ravished. When heaven and earth have been shaken, the devil, the crooked serpent, will flee, or every doctrine contrary to the truth, which is divided into teachers and disciples: the former of whom, because of their ὀξυδέρκειαν, are called in the Greek tongue Dorcades, that is, roe-deer; […]

Third, as to the dispersion of those who flee, citizens and warriors as much as captives, a doe, a swift animal: deliver yourself as a doe from the hand (Prov 6:5); my flocks were scattered upon the face of the earth (Ezek 34:6).

13:15.t: Everyone who is found will be slain: and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword. He who has not fled will be struck down by the blade; and he who has chosen either to resist or to come back will be of so little use to the captured city that he too will shed his own blood.

Fourth, as to the oppression of those who remain, which occurred in three things: in the killing of men: every one that shall be found, as to citizens, every one that shall come to their aid, as to foreigners, infants, as to children: with you I will break in pieces the old man and the child (Jer 51:22).

13:16.t: Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes: their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be violated. This is what David prophesies in the spirit: Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you your recompense, which you have paid out to us. Blessed is he who will take and dash your little ones against the rock (Ps 136 [137]:8). So great will be the devastation of the city and the savagery of the victors that not even innocent age will be spared, that all the wealth of the houses will be plundered, and the chastity of wives will be violated before their husbands' eyes.

Then their infants and little ones, who have not yet come to the full age of error, they will dash in pieces before the eyes of the teachers, and will plunder their houses and ravish their wives, depraved wisdom and perverse doctrine. Hence for fathers of this sort, whose little ones are to be slain, we ought to pray and say: Give them, O Lord. What will you give them? A barren womb and dry breasts (Hos 9:14). For they have travailed with iniquity, they have conceived sorrow, and they have brought forth unrighteousness.

Second, in the pillaging of goods: their houses shall be pillaged: our inheritance is turned to aliens: our houses to strangers (Lam 5:2); third, as to the violation of women: their wives shall be ravished: they humiliated the women in Zion (Lam 5:11).

13:17.t: Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who will not seek silver, nor want gold. What lay hidden has been made plain: that the mighty ones and the giants are by no means to be understood as angels and demons, but as the nation of the Medes, whose prince Darius was the first to destroy the empire of the Babylonians, having slain Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, who was the son of Evil-merodach (Dan 5). And he describes the savagery of the Medes and Persians as so great that, in their ardor to shed blood, they despise gold and silver and count the riches offered to them as mud.

Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who do not seek silver nor desire gold: but with arrows they kill the little ones, and on the sucklings of the womb they will have no pity, and their eye will not spare their sons. We find in Genesis (Gen 10) that Madai was the founder of the nation of the Medes, which means measure, or from the mighty one, or from the strong one. Therefore against the Babylonians, who are confused in mind, ministers of strength are stirred up by the mighty and strong God to punish, that they may render to each according to his works. For with the measure with which they have measured, it will be measured back to them. They will return into their bosom a measure shaken down and pressed together and full and running over (Matt 7, and Luke 6). […]
Behold I will stir up the Medes against them. Here he describes the ferocity of the enemy, which is not appeased by tribute: who shall not seek silver.

13:18.t: But with arrows they will kill the little ones, and they will have no pity on the sucklings of the womb, and their eye will not spare the sons. The little ones will be killed, whose wounds will be no smaller than their bodies; and the wombs of pregnant women will be cut open, and the infants dashed out, and the cruel victor will kill the sons pressed to the breasts.

Nor softened by mercy: but with their arrows they shall kill the children, neither on powerless men: the sucklings, nor on little children: their sons: behold, I will bring upon her, and she shall be utterly destroyed (Jer 51:64).

13:19.t: And Babylon, that glorious one among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah: it will not be inhabited unto the end, and it will not be founded unto generation and generation. We have heard of the Medes, we have heard of Babylon, we have heard of her who is renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans: and we refuse to understand what was, and seek to hear what was not. And we say this, not because we condemn the tropological understanding, but because the spiritual interpretation ought to follow the order of the history; and many, ignorant of this, wander about in the Scriptures in a frenzied error. […]

And Babylon, that glorious one among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. It will not be inhabited to the end, and it will not be founded unto generation and generation: nor will the Arab pitch his tents there, nor will shepherds rest there: but wild beasts will rest there, and their houses will be filled with dragons: and ostriches will dwell there, and hairy ones will dance there; and owls will answer there in its dwellings, and sirens in the shrines of pleasure. Its time is near to come, and its days will not be prolonged. LXX: And Babylon, which is called renowned, the glorious one of the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; […]

And that Babylon. Here he describes Babylon's subsequent desolation. And first, the destruction of the city: turned, that is, overturned, as Sodom, about which Revelation 18:10 says: alas! Alas! That great city, Babylon, that mighty city: for in one hour is your judgment come.

13:20.t: Nor will the Arab pitch his tents there; nor will shepherds rest there: but beasts will be there, their houses will be filled with dragons, and ostriches will dwell there, and hairy ones will dance there. And owls will answer in its buildings, and Sirens in the shrines of pleasure. Babylon will be so devastated and deserted that it will not be useful even for the pasturing of herds and flocks. For the Arab and the Saracen will not pitch their tents there, nor will shepherds, weary with toil after the tracks of their flocks, rest there; but among the broken walls and the narrow places of the ancient ruins SIIM (ציים) will dwell: which the Seventy alone translated as beasts; […]

Second, as to its perpetual solitude: it shall no more be inhabited: him that bends his bow shall not live there, and him that is armed with a coat of mail shall not go up (Jer 51:3). Third, as to the horror of its solitude, which is shown by the flight of shepherds: neither shall the Arabian pitch his tents there, who do not have fixed houses, but wander through the desert, nor shall shepherds of sheep.

13:21.t: Wherefore I entreat, let us kill the serpent, let us shut up the wild beasts, let us stifle them, let us slay them, and these wicked thoughts let us give over to the sword of the Spirit, lest the prophet threaten us also with such things as he threatened Judea, that "The wild asses shall dance there, and porcupines, and serpents." For there are, there are even men worse than wild asses, living as it were in the wilderness, and kicking; yea the more part of the youth amongst us is like this. For indeed having wild lusts they thus leap, they kick, going about unbridled, and spend their diligence on no becoming object. […]
13:21.s: Homily 59 on the Gospel of Matthew

13:21.t: As to the inhabitation of beasts and the dead: but wild beasts shall rest there, who love solitude. Dragons, who, according to some, are large winged serpents, according to others, are large fish with wet scales, and according to others, are cubit long serpents that eat other serpents and, because of this, poison with the breath of their mouths. Ostriches, animals which have wings but do not fly, indeed, they walk on their feet: the wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron (Job 39:13). The hairy ones, that is, hairy animals, like foxes, wolves, and suchlike; […]

13:22.t: Its time is near to come, and its days will not be prolonged. He says that the time is at hand when it is to be taken by its enemies. For after the captivity of Jerusalem, with no long time in between, it too was laid waste by the Medes and Persians.

14:1.t: Truly his will shall be fulfilled swiftly and suddenly, as the Scripture testifies.

For the proselytes have no need of a covenant, if, since there is one and the same law imposed on all that are circumcised, the Scripture speaks about them thus: 'And the stranger shall also be joined with them, and shall be joined to the house of Jacob.'

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose from Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil. Of this Zephaniah speaks more fully: Praise, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Israel; be glad and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem: for the Lord has taken away your judgment: he has turned away your enemies (Zeph 3:14-15). And it signifies the time when Cyrus king of the Persians permitted the captive people to return to Jerusalem. Read the book of Ezra (Ezra 1), Haggai (Hag 1) and Zechariah (Zech 1): when, under Zerubbabel, and Joshua the high priest, and Ezra, and Nehemiah, the altar, the Temple, and the walls of the city were built.

The stranger will be joined to them, and will cleave to the house of Jacob, and peoples will take them, and bring them into their own place, and the house of Israel will possess them upon the land of the Lord as menservants and maidservants: and they will take captive those who had taken them captive, and they will subdue their taskmasters. We conjecture that many from various nations came to Jerusalem with the people of the Jews, believing in the God of Israel and abandoning the idols of their errors. And that they were brought back by the king's letters, and received gifts and the expenses of the Temple, there is no doubt. […]

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose out of Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil: the stranger will be joined to them, and will cleave to the house of Jacob. And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel will possess them upon the land of the Lord as menservants and maidservants; and they will take captive those who had taken them captive, and they will subdue their oppressors. And it will be in that day, when God has given you rest from your labor, and from your trouble, and from the hard bondage in which you served before: you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and you will say. For stranger, that is, proselyte, the Seventy translated γηώραν, which in Hebrew is called GER (גר). […]

Her time is near at hand. In this part, he promises liberation to the Jews through the destruction of Babylon, which he threatened above. And this is divided into three parts: in the first, he promises liberation; in the second, he foretells the insults of the liberated against their oppressor: and it shall come to pass in that day (Isa 14:3); in the third, he sets out the confirmation of the insult: the seed of the wicked shall not be named (Isa 14:20).

Concerning the first, he sets out three things: the shortness of time: near at hand is the day of the Lord, to whom all things are present, or after our subjugation, her days, of subjugation: the day of destruction is at hand, and the time makes haste to come (Deut 32:35). […]

14:2.t: As to honorable retention: the people, among whom they were taken captive, shall take them, namely, the Jews, as though to carry them in their arms, below: and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders (Isa 49:22); or otherwise, as to the leading away of those who adhered to them, the people, namely, the Jews, shall take, that is, retain, them, leading those who adhered to them with themselves; as to the subjugation of the enemy or of those who adhered to them: and the house of Israel shall possess them, as they once possessed Israel: I will return your recompense upon your own heads (Joel 3:7).

14:3.t: And it will come to pass in that day, when the Lord has given you rest from your labor, and from your turmoil, and from your hard servitude, because you served before: you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and you will say. The discourse is directed to Israel: that after it has returned to Jerusalem and shaken off the yoke of servitude, it should recall the former power of Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonian summit, and lament him with a pitiful voice, because he has come to such calamity that he seems worthy of pity even to his enemies.

And it shall come to pass. Here the insult of the liberated people against their captor, who has now been destroyed, is set out.

And first, the title or the inscription is set out, containing three things: the time, when God shall give you rest from your labor, by which you have labored in waging war; and from your vexation, of captivity, by which you were kept in prison; and from bondage, by which you were oppressed in the land of your captivity.

14:4.t: According to Isaiah, in which lament is offered on behalf of the king of Babylon, much can be learned about the origin and beginning of evil. Evil derived its existence from some who had lost their wings by following the one who was first to lose his own wings.

How has the oppressor ceased, the tribute come to rest? The Lord has broken the staff of the ungodly, the rod of the rulers, which struck the peoples in indignation with an incurable stroke, which subdued the nations in fury, persecuting cruelly. In the Epistle of Peter we read: It is time for judgment to begin at the house of God (1 Pet 4:17). And in Ezekiel it is said to the tormentors: Begin at my holy ones (Ezek 9:6). For the order of judgment is arranged according to the diversity of sin, so that those who have offended less are purged first. And the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Therefore, when Israel has been freed from hard bondage, he will take up a parable against the king of Babylon, which we ought to understand as a parable. […]

How has the taskmaster ceased, the tribute come to rest? The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers, that struck the peoples in indignation, that subdued the nations in fury with an incurable blow, that persecuted cruelly: it has come to rest and fallen silent: the whole earth has rejoiced and exulted. This is the voice of Israel lamenting and pitying: how one who was once a lord and conqueror of the lands, despoiling everything with tributes, has been crushed and brought to nothing. […]

You shall take up this parable, that is, a sermon of similitudes, which says one thing and signifies another: for the things spoken of in the parable signify the condition of Nabuchodonosor, as to his power, his fault and his punishment, because of which these things could have happened, even if they did not happen: against the king of Babylon; in that day a parable shall be taken up upon you, and a song shall be sung with melody (Mic 2:4); shall not all these take up a parable against him? (Hab 2:6).

The insult itself is set out: and first, of the living; second, of the dead: hell below (Isa 14:9). The insult of the living contains three things: his destruction with the fault which he committed in exacting tributes: how is the exactor come to nothing.

14:5.t: And for this reason the rod and staff of the ungodly, for which the Seventy translated yoke, strikes us, or oppresses us, because we would not bear the lightest yoke, the yoke of the Savior. And with this staff and this rod he struck the nations with incurable fury, and cruelly pursued those who fled: not wishing to amend those handed over to him, but to kill them.

In inflicting punishments on men: the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers, that struck the people in wrath, as though in reply to a preceding question; in attacking kingdoms: that brought nations under: how is the hammer of the whole earth broken, and destroyed (Jer 50:32).

14:6.t: That struck the people in wrath with an incurable wound, that brought nations under in fury, that persecuted in a cruel manner: how is the hammer of the whole earth broken, and destroyed (Jer 50:32).

14:7.t: The whole earth has come to rest and fallen silent; it has rejoiced and exulted; the fir trees too have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon. Since you have fallen asleep, no one comes up to cut us down. Hell beneath was troubled: to meet your coming it stirred up the giants for you. All the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones; all the princes of the nations, all of them will answer and say to you: You too have been wounded as we were, you have become like us? Your pride has been dragged down to hell, your corpse has fallen; beneath you the moth will be spread, decay, and worms will be your covering. […]

Second, it contains the ensuing peace: the whole earth is quiet, ceasing from that tumult, and still, ceasing from weeping, it is glad, in your destruction, and has rejoiced, in its liberation: the just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge (Ps 58:10).

14:8.t: The fir trees too have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon: Since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down. By the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon understand the princes of the nations, who were cut down when Nebuchadnezzar struck them; and they too, breaking out into a voice of joy, say: Since you were led down to the underworld, no one else could be found to cut down the great and the mighty.

Third, it contains the eagerness of the princes: the fir trees also, which signify those elevated in dignity; similar to this is what is found in Ezekiel 31:8: the cedars in the paradise of God were not higher than he. You have slept, with the sleep of the dead; cut us down, that is, kill us.

14:9.t: The underworld beneath you was thrown into confusion, at the meeting of your coming it roused up giants for you: all the princes of the earth have risen from their thrones: all the princes of the nations, every one, will answer and say to you. These things are to be read emphatically and in the manner of a stage scene; not because they happened, but because they could have happened; unless perhaps we believe that the souls of the kings whom he had killed came to meet the Babylonian king, mocking him. For it is a solace in evils when men see their enemies suffer the same things:

Hell too, troubled, or turned to bitterness, to meet the coming of the true Nebuchadnezzar, is the place of punishments and torments, in which the rich man clothed in purple is seen: to which the Lord also descended, to release the bound from prison. We can also call hell, coming to meet him, that angel who is set over the punishments of hell, who stirred up all the giants: for which some have translated Raphaim, others Titans. And they are called giants according to the custom of the heathen, who suppose them earth-born, whom the earth begot. But we, according to the etymology of the Greek word, can call giants those who have served earthly works. […]

Hell below. Here the insult of the dead against Nabuchodonosor is set out, and first, that of the princes and the powerful, second, of the others: they that shall see you (Isa 14:16).

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he sets out the meeting with the lower regions, as to the ministers of punishments or officials: hell, that is, the devil, who is set over hell, below, for hell is below, was in an uproar, that is, turned to tumult, as if this could happen, below (ch. 30). Likewise as to other powers rushing in: it will stir up the giants for you, as though to rise to you with them; giants, as to the strong in body, below: let not the dead live, let not the giants rise again (Isa 26:14).

All the princes of the earth, as to kings, to whom it belongs to sit in thrones; […]

14:10.t: And you too have been wounded as we were, you have become like us: your pride has been dragged down to the underworld: there has fallen your corpse; beneath you the moth will be spread, and worms will be your covering. The speech of the mighty ones and princes of the earth, whom he had called cedars and fir trees above, is addressed to the Babylonian king, now placed in the underworld. We no longer grieve that we were cut down, since you too have fallen by the same axe. All your power, and your pride lifted up to heaven, has been dragged down to the earth. So will your corpse too feed the moth, and a multitude of swarming worms cover it? Through death you will feel the worthlessness of man, you who displayed the power of God in yourself.

All, namely, all the giants of hell, shall answer, as if you had summoned them, or as though crying.

Second, he sets out their reproach. And they reproach him with three things: namely, the punishment which he found, as to his death: you also are wounded, in death, by the force of divine power: you have humbled the proud one, as one that is wounded (Ps 89:10).

14:11.t: Your pride has been dragged down to hell, or your glory, and your corpse has fallen, or, as the Seventy translated, your great gladness, in which you formerly rejoiced when the nations were subject to you. Beneath you decay will be spread, and worms will be your covering. This is the rest of the devil, this the bed of the tempter, who was lifted up into such pride that he dared even to tempt the Lord, saying: All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matt 4:9). The decay and the moth and the covering of worms are understood either as the eternal punishments which one's own conscience begets, or as the material of torments, which is born from one's own sins. […]

Then as to the humiliation of the dead man, both in soul, your pride is brought down to hell, and in body, your carcass of death is fallen down; then also as to the affliction of the dead man in hell: under you shall the moth be strewed; worms, in which all the punishments of hell are designated: he will give fire, and worms into their flesh, that they may burn, and may feel for ever (Jdt 16:21).

14:12.t: It is most clearly proved by these words that he who formerly was Lucifer and who "arose in the morning" has fallen from heaven. For if, as some suppose, he was a being of darkness, why is he said to have formerly been Lucifer or lightbearer? Or how could he "rise in the morning" who had in him no light at all?… So he was light once … when "his glory was turned into dust."

How can we possibly suppose that what is said in many places by Scripture, especially in Isaiah, about Nebuchadnezzar is said about a human being? For no human being is said to have "fallen from heaven" or to have been "Lucifer" or the one who "arose every morning."

SUCH was their position. While those on the side of the opposing rebel power were either daemons, or vile spirits immersed more or less in wickedness, with the cunning ruler of them all the mighty daemon, who first failed of their reverence of the Divinity and fell from their own portion, when envy of man's salvation drew them the contrary way, plotting with all sorts of evil devices against all the nations, and even against the Lord's portion in their jealousy of the good. It is this godless and unholy scheme of the great Daemon, which the prophetic spirit in Isaiah reproves in this way, saying:

"13. I will act in strength, and in the wisdom of understanding I will take away the boundaries of the nations, and will diminish their strength, 14. and I will shake inhabited cities. […]
14:12.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 9

14:12.t: [On why God created the world:] And lest we seem to have passed over the mystery, or rather to have been ignorant why the world was made, we say that the apostasy of the Devil drew many angels, that is, spiritual powers, with him into transgression, when he willed by wicked presumption to defend a kingdom for himself. This the prophet Isaiah signifies, saying, “How are you fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12); that is, you who appeared brighter than the rest. For he was a sort of prince of many, among whom he was more splendid, and with whose company he descended into wicked conflict. […]
14:12.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 2: WHY DID GOD CREATE THE WORLD?

14:12.t: And so the secondary Splendours came into being, as the Ministers of the Primary Splendour; whether we are to conceive of them as intelligent Spirits, or as Fire of an immaterial and incorruptible kind, or as some other nature approaching this as near as may be. I should like to say that they were incapable of movement in the direction of evil, and susceptible only of the movement of good, as being about God, and illumined with the first rays from God—for earthly beings have but the second illumination; but I am obliged to stop short of saying that, and to conceive and speak of them only as difficult to move because of him, who for his splendour was called Lucifer, but became and is called Darkness through his pride; […]

[Daniel 4:4] "I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace." The narrative is clear indeed and requires but little interpretation. Because he displeased God, Nebuchadnezzar was turned into a madman and dwelt for seven years amongst the brute beasts and was fed upon the roots of herbs, Afterwards by the mercy of God he was restored to his throne, and praised and glorified the King of heaven, on the ground that all His works are truth and His ways are justice and He is able to abase those who walk in pride. But there are some who claim to understand by the figure of Nebuchadnezzar the hostile power which the Lord speaks of in the Gospel, saying: "I beheld Satan falling from heaven like lightning" (Luke 10:18). […]
14:12.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

14:12.t: Lucifer fell, Lucifer who used to rise at dawn; and he who was raised in a paradise of delight had the well-earned sentence passed upon him: "Though you exalt yourself as the eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, thence will I bring you down, says the Lord." For he had said in his heart, "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God," and "I will be like the Most High."

How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have crashed to the earth, you who wounded the nations? LXX: How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, who rose in the morning? He who sent to all the nations has been crushed to the earth. For Lucifer, who in Hebrew is called ELIL (הילל), Aquila translated howling son of the dawn. For truly he ought to howl and wail, who because of his pride was cast headlong from heaven to earth and crushed. Hence the Savior too says to the disciples: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). Not, I see now; but I saw before, when he fell. And if he fell from so great a height because of pride, you too ought not to glory because the demons are subject to you, but because your names are written in heaven; […]

How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning: you have crashed to the earth, you who wounded the nations: who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God I will exalt my throne, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the North; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. In place of what we have translated, for ease of understanding, How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning, in the Hebrew, to render it word for word, one reads: How you have fallen from heaven, howl, son of the dawn. Now in other words Lucifer is meant; and he is told that he ought to weep and mourn, he who was once so glorious that he was compared to the brightness of the morning star. […]

A certain one was named Lucifer, who fell; for he was an angel and became a devil; and concerning him the Scripture said, "Lucifer, who did arise in the morning, fell" And why was he Lucifer? Because, being enlightened, he gave forth light. But for what reason did he become dark! Because he abode not in the truth.

And So we are clearly shown that out of that number of them some of the leaders fell, by the lamentations of Ezekiel and Isaiah, in which we know that the prince of Tyre or that Lucifer who rose in the morning is lamented with a doleful plaint: and of him the Lord speaks as follows to Ezekiel: "Son of man, take up a lamentation over the prince of Tyre, and say to him: Thus saith the Lord God: Thou wast the seal of resemblance, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty. Thou wast in the pleasures of the paradise of God: every precious stone was thy covering: the sardius, the topaz and the jasper, the chrysolyte and the onyx and the beryl, the sapphire and the carbuncle and the emerald: gold the work of thy beauty, and thy pipes were prepared in the day that thou wast created. […]
14:12.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 8

14:12.t: And that we may understand the power of its awful tyranny we see that that angel who, for the greatness of his splendour and beauty was termed Lucifer, was cast out of heaven for no other sin but this, and, pierced with the dart of pride, was hurled down from his grand and exalted position as an angel into hell. If then pride of heart alone was enough to cast down from heaven to earth a power that was so great and adorned with the attributes of such might, the very greatness of his fall shows us with what care we who are surrounded by the weakness of the flesh ought to be on our guard. But we can learn how to avoid the most deadly poison of this evil if we trace out the origin and causes of his fall. […]
14:12.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 12, Chapter 4

14:12.t: The first among the Angels, Lucifer, presuming upon his private good, sought private excellence, wishing to be raised above the others; and therefore he fell together with the rest who consented to him. Falling, moreover, he became impenitent, obstinate and blinded and excluded from the contemplation of God and disordered in operation, striving with all his effort to subvert man through manifold temptation. Since through the free choice of the will he could tend toward the supreme good or turn toward his private good, Lucifer, aroused by the consideration of his own beauty and loftiness to love himself and his own private good, presumed upon the loftiness he possessed and sought his own excellence, yet not one that was obtained; […]

Second, they reproach him with the glory he has lost. Both as to the dignity of the king: O Lucifer, beautiful among all other kings, in the morning, monarch before all others; and as to the power of war: how are you fallen to the earth: you, therefore, are the head of gold. And after you shall rise up another kingdom, inferior to you (Dan 2:38-39).

14:13.t: Now Nebuchadnezzar said:—I will ascend to heaven and exalt my throne above the stars of God and sit in the lofty mountains that are in the borders of the North. Isaiah said concerning him:—Because thy heart has thus exalted thee, therefore thou shalt be brought down to Sheol, and all that look upon thee shall be astonished at thee.

WHY WAS THE SON OF GOD SENT, AND NOT ANOTHER? — Although everything that God does must be believed to be done reasonably and providentially, I nevertheless think it better if, after faith, the cause of what is done can also be noticed, so that what is believed is not unknown. Therefore the Lord says: “Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (Jn. 17:3). For first what is said by the Prophet must be believed, and then what is believed must be known; because the Holy Spirit helps the faithful and diligent person in this matter, so that by coming to know he may understand the rationale of faith. Then he enjoys the full joy of his believing, if he understands what he believes. […]
14:13.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 113: WHY WAS THE SON OF GOD SENT, AND NOT ANOTHER?

14:13.t: For what proud enemy can there be against the servants of God, who exalts himself against God and says: I will ascend into heaven, I will place my seat above the stars of heaven: I will sit on a lofty mount, above the high mountains that are from the north: I will ascend above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High? Therefore, it is not surprising if he can burden men, who with obstinate spirit do not yield to God. How then will he preserve the measure of truth and faith in man, who promises himself to be equal to the Almighty Lord with blasphemous and shameless falsehood? How he falsely accuses individuals, who has amazed the whole earth, shaken kings, laid waste the entire world, and destroyed cities: he did not release those who were in captivity. […]

When the Lord Jesus redeemed the human race through obedience and restored justice, the serpent introduced sin through disobedience; we can estimate the extent of this vice, of which the author is the devil, whom the Prophet introduces saying: I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High. Therefore, since he is most wicked, he did not give honor to our Lord God; nevertheless, he educated worse disciples. For he exalted himself in such a way that he wanted to be equal and similar to the Most High: but his disciple, as signified by the Apostle, would be indignant to be considered equal and similar to God. For it is written: When the man of sin and son of perdition is revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god. […]

There were some who dared in the opinion of the multitude to immortalize themselves; and notwithstanding that the very sense of sight bore witness to their mortality, were ambitious to be called gods, and were honoured as such; to what a length of impiety would not many men have proceeded, if death had not gone on teaching all men the mortality and corruptibility of our nature? Hear, for instance, what the prophet says of a barbarian king, when seized with this frenzy. "I will exalt," saith he, "my throne above the stars of heaven; and I will be like unto the Most High." Afterwards, deriding him, and speaking of his death, he says, "Corruption is under thee, and the worm is thy covering;" […]

You who said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God I will exalt my throne: I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North: I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High. He said these things either before he fell from heaven or after he had fallen from heaven. If he was still set in heaven, how does he say, I will ascend into heaven (Ps 113 [115]:16)? But because we read: The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, when he was in heaven, that is, in the firmament, he desired to ascend into the heaven where the throne of the Lord is, not by humility but by pride. […]

It must also be said another way: the north wind is a very harsh wind, which makes very hard the hearts of those who dwell in its land, and from which evils are kindled upon all who dwell on the earth, and toward which, according to this very prophet Zechariah, the black horses go out, to take their stand in its region. He too who in Isaiah had said in his boasting: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, I will sit on a lofty mountain, above the high mountains in the north, vaunts that he holds his kingdom in the coldest place of the earth.

Whence did the devil fall? because he committed theft? because he committed murder? because he committed adultery? These indeed are evils: but the devil did not fall on account of these, but he fell on account of his tongue. For what did he say? 'I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High.' So then let not monks suppose that they ought to be secure, and say, Meanwhile we do not commit great crimes in the monastery: I do not commit adultery, I do not commit theft, I do not commit murder, I do not commit parricide, and the rest of the great vices. In the tongue too there are great vices.

And to go on in the order which we proposed, with our account of the way in which the other passions act (our analysis of which was obliged to be interrupted by this account of gluttony and of the Lord's temptation) vainglory and pride can be consummated even without the slightest assistance from the body. For in what way do those passions need any action of the flesh, which bring ample destruction on the soul they take captive simply by its assent and wish to gain praise and glory from men? Or what act on the part of the body was there in that pride of old in the case of the above mentioned Lucifer; as he only conceived it in his heart and mind, as the prophet tells us: "Who saidst in thine heart: I will ascend into heaven, I will set my throne above the stars of God. […]

So then the devil also in as much as he was created a spirit or an angel and good, had no one as his Father but God his Maker. But when he had become puffed up by pride and had said in his heart: "I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will be like the Most High," he became a liar, and "abode not in the truth;" but brought forth a lie from his own storehouse of wickedness and so became not only a liar, but also the father of the actual lie, by which when he promised Divinity to man and said "Ye shall be as gods," he abode not in the truth, but from the beginning became a murderer, both by bringing Adam into a state of mortality, and by slaying Abel by the hand of his brother at his suggestion.
14:13.s: The Second Conference of Abbot Serenus, Chapter 25

14:13.t: And so God, the Creator and Healer of all, knowing that pride is the cause and fountain head of evils, has been careful to heal opposites with opposites, that those things which were ruined by pride might be restored by humility. For the one says, "I will ascend into heaven;" the other, "My soul was brought low even to the ground." The one says, "And I will be like the most High;" the other, "Though He was in the form of God, yet He emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, and humbled Himself and became obedient unto death." The one says, "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God;" the other, "Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly of heart." The one says, "I know not the Lord and will not let Israel go;" […]
14:13.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 12, Chapter 8

14:13.t:
Third, they reproach him with the pride of heart which he had, as to three things: as to his proud thought; second, as to his perverse intention: I will be like the most high (Isa 14:14); third, as to the frustration of his proposal: but yet you shall be brought down to hell (Isa 14:15).

Now his thought was proud because he thought to usurp what belongs to God, according to the error of the gentiles, who believed that men are turned into gods, and that stars come to be from princes, as it says in 2 Maccabees 11:23: our father being translated amongst the gods; he also thought to usurp the divine place: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of God, as if to say: for as I am above other the princes on earth, so will I be above other the stars in heaven; […]

14:14.t: [Daniel 7:4] "The first beast was like a lioness and possessed the wings of an eagle. I beheld until her wings were torn away, and she was raised upright from the ground and stood on her feet like a human being, and she was given a human heart." The kingdom of the Babylonians was not called a lion but a lioness, on account of its brutality and cruelty, or else because of its luxurious, lust-serving manner of life. For writers upon the natural history of beasts assert that lionesses are fiercer than lions, especially if they are nursing their cubs, and constantly are passionate in their desire for sexual relations. […]
14:14.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER SEVEN

14:14.t: He has so forgotten himself that he wishes to ascend above the clouds, which the Lord commanded not to rain rain upon Israel, and to which the truth of the Lord reaches, to whom Obadiah also says: Though you be exalted like the eagle, and set your nest among the stars of heaven, thence I will drag you down, says the Lord (Obad 4). Unhappy Judas, who like a cloud was sent with the other Apostles to rain rain upon Israel, and was like a star among the other stars, to whom the Lord said: Let your light shine before men (Matt 5:16), by his own fault received the devil as his rider, who, to complete his words of pride, dared even to say this: I will be like the Most High, so that, as Christ has his Prophets and Apostles, so I too may have false apostles. […]

Michael indeed means "Who is like God"; Gabriel, "the strength of God"; and Raphael is called "the medicine of God." And whenever something of wondrous power is accomplished, Michael is said to be sent, so that from the act itself and the name it may be understood that no one can do what God is able to do. Hence that ancient enemy, who through pride desired to be like God, saying: "I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven, I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north, I will ascend above the height of the clouds, I will be like the Most High," when at the end of the world he is left to his own power to be destroyed by the final punishment, is said to be about to fight with the archangel Michael, as it is said through John: […]

Both meditated iniquity, affecting height: the one, of power; the other, of knowledge. For the foolish woman believed him who promised, but who was deceiving: "You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil." Had he not already first deceived himself, he who had persuaded himself that he would be like the Most High? For he who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself.

Therefore the devil was judged in fury, because his iniquity was found to be unto hatred; but man's unto wrath, and therefore he is chastised in wrath. Thus every height has been crushed, both that which puffs up and that which casts down, the Father indeed being zealous for the Son. […]
14:14.s: Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 69

14:14.t: I will be like the most high: here, his perverse intention: will you yet say before them that slay you: I am God? (Ezek 28:9).

14:15.t: But you will be dragged down to the underworld, into the depth of the pit. He who in his pride had said: I will ascend into heaven, I will be like the Most High, is dragged down not only to the underworld but to the lowest underworld. For this is what the depth of the pit signifies, in place of which we read in the Gospel of the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Luke 13:28).

But you will be dragged down to hell, into the depth of the pit. LXX: But now you will go down into hell, and to the foundations of the earth. You will not go down to hell of your own accord, for this belongs to the Lord the Savior, to free the bound from hell, but you will be dragged down to hell against your will, so that you who could have climbed to the heights through virtues are dragged down to punishments through vices. The saints have the wings of an eagle and the wings of a dove, and can say: I will fly away and be at rest (Ps 54 [55]). But the ungodly, like the Egyptians, sank like lead in the mighty waters, and sank into the depth like a stone (Exod 15). Hence also iniquity, or, as it is better in the Hebrew, ungodliness, is seen sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech 5). […]

For as long as vain, transitory, passing good is loved, man is "passing over." And such passing over Wisdom reproves. This passing over is the cause of every evil. In this way Lucifer passed over, to whom it was said: "Down to the nether world you go, to the recesses of the pit!" He was thrown first by sin, then by the judgment. Adam did the same: after he had given up the tree of life, he hid. Indeed, he saw himself denuded of all good habits. Wherefore he was thrown out of Paradise.
But yet: here, the frustration of his intention; into the depth of the pit, that is, into the harshest punishments: they spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell (Job 21:31).

14:16.t: Those who see you will bow down to you, and will look closely at you. Is this the man who troubled the earth? who shook kingdoms? who made the world a desert, and destroyed its cities, and did not open the prison to its prisoners? Or, as the Seventy translated: did not release those who were being led away? Those who see Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, fallen from heaven to hell, with the gaze not of the eyes but of the heart, will bow down in the humility which is contrary to pride, and will look closely at him, saying these things: Is not this the man, or the human being, who troubled, or stirred up the earth? […]

Those who see you will bend down toward you and gaze at you (understand: saying): Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities; who did not open the prison to his captives? This too is the voice of those who mock and marvel, how the devastator of all has himself been devastated. And when he says: Who did not open the prison to his captives?, the greatness of his cruelty and impiety is expressed: that he kept even men in chains in prison, and chains were not enough for the wretches unless the horror of darkness also shut them in.

They that shall see you. Here the insult of the other, common persons, is set out. And first, he describes their meeting: all others that shall see you, being punished, shall bend to you, as if to say: you will be so far below these others that it will be necessary for them to bend down for them to see you: the mighty shall be mightily tormented (Wis 6:7).

Second, he sets out their reproach, and they reproach him with three things. First, the fault which he committed: is this the man that troubled the earth, in wars, that shook the kingdoms, changing dominions.

All this is explained mystically of the devil: he shakes the kingdoms (Isa 14:16), as the minister of punishment, and inciter of sin; […]

14:17.t: There follows: Who made the world a desert, or, as according to the Hebrew all the others besides the Seventy translated, as a desert. For by vices and sins he made the world, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל), a desert, so that it had no virtue, or was subject to the same vices with which the solitude of the nations is filled. He also destroyed the cities of that same world, to make synagogues of the devil out of the Churches of Christ, and to pollute the purity of the true faith with heretical filth. But also to its prisoners, that is, the world's, he did not open the prison. We were all prisoners, and were held shut up in prison, to which prisoners the Savior said, come out, and to those who were in darkness, be uncovered. For the Lord sets free those in fetters. […]

That made the world a wilderness, exiling men, and destroyed the cities, overturning their governments, that opened not the prison to his prisoners, that they might see light: they spread their terror in the land of the living (Ezek 32:25).

14:18.t: All the kings of the nations, all of them, have slept in glory, each one in his own house. But you have been cast out of your tomb like corrupt matter: polluted, wrapped up with the slain and those pierced through by the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit. LXX: All the kings of the nations have slept in honor, a man in his own house. But you will be cast out on the mountains like an untimely birth, abominable, and wrapped up with those slain by the sword who go down to the foundations of the earth. The kings of the nations, to whom, according to the Song of Deuteronomy, God had entrusted the nations to be governed (Deut 32), who were shaken by Nebuchadnezzar and yet not overthrown, in whom sin by no means reigns; […]

All the kings of the nations, every one, have slept in glory, each man in his own house. But you have been cast out of your tomb like a useless shoot, defiled and wrapped up with those who were slain by the sword, and went down to the foundations of the pit; like a rotting corpse you will have no fellowship, not even with them in burial. The Hebrews tell a fable of this kind. Evil-merodach, who had reigned earlier while his father Nebuchadnezzar lived for seven years among the beasts, was kept in chains together with Jehoiachin king of Judah, after his father had been restored to his kingdom, until his father's death; […]

14:19.t: But Nebuchadnezzar has been cast out of his tomb, and not even in death has he rested from torments. And he has been cast out like corrupt matter, which in Hebrew is called NESER (נצר), which Aquila translated ἰχῶρα, namely putrefaction and filth, which Symmachus translated ἔκτρωμα, that is, an untimely birth, the Seventy a dead thing, Theodotion a shoot: although this very word above (Isa 11:1), where we read of Christ: A rod will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise up from its root, the Seventy translated flower, Theodotion shoot, Aquila ἀκρέμονα, that is, sucker. Properly, however, Neser means sucker, which grows at the roots of trees and, torn off by farmers, is thrown away as useless; hence we too translated useless stock. […]

Like a putrid corpse, you will not have fellowship with them even in burial. For you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people.
