LXX: As a garment mixed with blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and have slain my people. Since the Hebrew and the edition of the Seventy differ greatly from each other, let us discuss each separately. Like a putrid corpse, or, as Aquila translated, trampled, you will not have fellowship of burial, not even with those whom you slew. For you are the teacher, they were the disciples: and from him to whom more has been entrusted, more is required. For you have destroyed your land, you have killed your people, namely those who were entrusted to you to govern. […]

Second, they reproach him with the grave he has lost, for he was exhumed by his son, who divided his corpse into two-hundred pieces and bound the pieces to just as many birds gathered from different lands, that he might not rise again: defiled, by the blood of those whom you killed: he shall be buried with the burial of an ass (Jer 22:19).

14:20.t: For you have destroyed your own land, you have slain your own people. According to the Seventy interpreters, who said: Because you have destroyed my land, and slain my people, there is no doubt what they mean. For Nebuchadnezzar slew and destroyed the land of Judea and its people Israel. According to the Hebrew the understanding is difficult: how he destroyed his own land and slew his own people; unless perhaps it is to be taken in this sense: those whom God had given you for chastening, you have utterly destroyed. Or otherwise: the ancient kingdom of the Assyrians, through your great pride and your lifting up your neck against God, has been utterly destroyed. For had you behaved humbly and known your own measure, the Assyrian and the Babylonian would be reigning to this day. […]

The seed of the most wicked will not be named forever. Prepare his sons for slaughter in the iniquity of their fathers: they will not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. All the histories agree that, after Belshazzar the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar was slain and Darius succeeded to the kingdom of the Chaldeans, no one of Nebuchadnezzar's stock reigned thereafter. This, then, is what Scripture foretells: that Babylon will come to such devastation that not even of the royal seed will anyone remain, but on account of the father's impiety all his offspring will be wiped out. […]

Seed of the most wicked, prepare your sons for slaughter for the iniquities of their fathers: they will not rise up nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts: and I will destroy the name of Babylon and its remnant, and its offshoot and offspring, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: Most wicked seed, prepare your sons for slaughter for the sin of your father: that they may not rise up and possess the land, and fill the land with cities. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord Sabaoth: and I will destroy their name and remnant and seed. For most wicked seed, which the Seventy translated, in the Hebrew is written ZERA MRIM (זרע מרעים), which the others translated seed of the most wicked. […]

Third, they reproach him with the damage he inflicted on his own kingdom: you have destroyed your land, for the Chaldeans would have held the kingdom longer had it not been for the sins of Nabuchodonosor; for the people are punished for the fault of their prince, as is evident from Proverbs 31; the reason for this is that the people are accustomed to imitate the fault of their king: a prince that gladly hears lying words, has all his servants wicked (Prov 29:12).

The seed of the wicked shall not be named. Here he confirms the insult, and first, through the prophecy of the prophet; second, through the divine purpose: and I will rise up (Isa 14:22); third, through the support of the divine purpose: the Lord of hosts has decreed (Isa 14:27). […]

14:21.t: And since the victory of men is not perfect: For unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it will keep watch in vain (Ps 126 [127]:1): therefore the Lord himself will rise up against the sons of the most wicked, and will destroy out of confusion their name and remnant, and every offshoot and offspring, so that they may no longer sprout in the cities of the Lord. We read in the Gospel (John 8) that the devil is a liar from the beginning, and his father, that is, of the lie; which many not understanding wish the father of the devil to be the dragon who reigns in the sea, whom the Hebrews call Leviathan. […]

Second, the killing of his sons by the Medes and Persians: prepare his children for slaughter in the iniquity, that is, for the iniquity, of their fathers.

Third, the impossibility of recovery, they shall not rise up; the face of the world, that is, of Babylon, which above (Isa 13:11) was referred to as the world: I am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children (Exod 20:5); from the unlawful iniquity is born (Wis 4:6).

14:22.t: And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts: and I will destroy the name of Babylon, and the remnant, and the offshoot, and the progeny, says the Lord. And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with a broom, grinding it away, says the Lord of hosts. That Babylon was most mighty, and that, set foursquare on the plains, it extended sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner of the wall, that is, sixty-four thousand in all around its circuit, is reported by Herodotus and many others who have written Greek histories. […]

And I will rise up. Here the divine purpose to fulfill the prophecy is set out. And first, to destroy Babylon, as to the destruction of its men: against them, namely, the sons of Nabuchodonosor, I will destroy the name of Babylon, that is, the reputation of its power, the remains, his sons, and the offspring, his nephews and so forth: his seed shall not subsist, nor his offspring among his people (Job 18:19).

14:23.t: And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of waters: and I will sweep it with a broom, grinding it, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: And I will make Babylonia desert, says the Lord, so that hedgehogs dwell in it, and it will come to nothing. And I will make it a gulf of mud, for destruction. When the Lord of hosts has destroyed the name of Babylon, and its remnant, and its offshoot, and all its offspring, he will not be content with its destruction unless he gives it as a possession to the hedgehog, and as pools of waters, and sweeps it, not lightly and casually, but grinding, so that nothing of its old filth remains in it. […]

As to it being inhabited by beasts: I will make it a possession for the hedgehog, below: there has the hedgehog had its hole, and brought up its young ones, and has dug round about (Isa 34:15). As to the destruction of its walls: I will sweep it, so that nothing will remain but pavement, like a house that has been cleansed with a broom.

14:24.t: The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: If it is not so, that as I have thought, so it will be, and as I have pondered in my mind, so it will come to pass, that I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and tread him down upon my mountains: and his yoke will be taken from them, and his burden will be removed from their shoulder. He returns to the present, that is, to Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, who laid waste Samaria and Judea and, Jerusalem excepted, destroyed everything round about; and he joins things near at hand to things that are to come long afterward, so that the fear hanging over them may be removed: because those who heard could say: We are enduring a siege now, and this man promises things that will come many ages later. […]

The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely as I have thought, so shall it be, and as I have purposed in my mind, so shall it come to pass: that I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains I will trample him. And his yoke will be taken from them, and his burden will be removed from their shoulder. After the hedgehog has dwelt in deserted Babylon, and in place of well-watered and fertile fields pools have covered everything, so that nothing of the former seed and abundance remains in Babylon, the oath of the Lord will be fulfilled, and what he purposed in his mind will come to pass: that the Assyrian is crushed in his land and trampled on his mountains. […]

Second, he sets out the divine purpose to destroy the Assyrians, that it might set an example. And first, he sets out the oath: the Lord of hosts has sworn, that is, immovably established, surely as I have thought, that is, established: the Lord has sworn, and he will not repent (Ps 110:4).

14:25.t:
Second, the place of destruction: in my land, for the army of Sennacherib was destroyed near Jerusalem, below: and the Lord of hosts shall make . . . in this mountain, a feast of fat things (Isa 25:6).

Third, he describes the fruit of the punishment, his yoke shall be taken away from them, above: for the yoke of their burden, and the rod of their shoulder, and the scepter of their oppressor you have overcome (Isa 9:4).

14:26.t: This is the counsel which he has purposed upon the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out upon all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who will be able to weaken it? And his hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? For the whole earth the Seventy translated the whole world, at the end of the burden, or vision, against Babylon. What lay hidden is opened: that God purposed his counsel upon the whole earth, that is, the whole world, and not only against the land of the Chaldeans and the Assyrian and Chaldean king; and that his hand is stretched out, or raised, upon all the nations, and not upon the one Babylonian nation. […]

This is the counsel that I have devised upon the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out upon all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who will be able to weaken it? And his hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? In this place some think that the prophecy is general, against the whole world, and that the devastation of Babylon and of the Assyrian city is a type of the consummation of the world. We by no means contradict them, so long as we know that here the whole land of the Assyrians is properly signified, and that all the nations allied with the Assyrian king are pointed out. Whatever has been decreed by the Lord is prevented by no one's power. And his hand, stretched out and ready to strike, no one will be able to hold back.

Third, he places the divine purpose to destroy all peoples: this is the counsel, that I have purposed upon all the earth, to destroy it, as to deliberation; his hand, that is, his power, as to execution: take the cup of wine of this fury at my hand (Jer 25:15). Or the counsel, that I have purposed upon all the earth, to protect it from the Assyrians; and this is the hand that is stretched out, which was destroyed. And thus the fruit of the punishment will be in all nations.

14:27.t: They were ready to expose him [Joseph] to death, or to sorrow, or to slavery—to the uttermost ills. But the overruling God used the wickedness of the conspirators for the trial and approval of him who was sold and betrayed. In order that this result may not be thought to arise from any casual coincidence or accidental revolution of things, God, by means of the very men who opposed it, brought to pass the very result which they opposed, using His enemies for the approval of His servants, in order that you may learn, that what God has willed no one will hinder, and that none will turn aside His high hand; […]
14:27.s: Discourse 4 on Lazarus and the Rich Man

14:27.t: They did not realize that if human hands had put an end to those things, then human hands could get them back for them. But it was God who destroyed their city, and no human power could ever change what God had decreed. "For what God, the Holy One, has planned who shall dissipate? His hand is stretched out; who will turn it back?" What God has reared up and wishes to remain, no man can tear down. In the same way, what he has destroyed and wishes to stay destroyed, no man can rebuild.

And what is said: Who will be able to weaken it, and who will turn it back? we ought to take not as of something difficult, as that is read: Who is wise, and will understand these things (Ps 106 [107]:43)? And: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward (Luke 12:42)? and other things like these; but as of something impossible. For no one will be able to weaken the counsel of the Lord, and to turn back his hand, stretched out or lifted on high, from striking.

For the Lord of hosts. Here he shows the support of the divine purpose, both as to the decree of wisdom: he has decreed, and as to the fulfillment of power: and his hand is stretched out: and who shall turn it away? He is alone, and no man can turn away his thought: and whatsoever his soul has desired, that has he done (Job 23:13).

14:28.t: In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came. We read that four kings of Judea are placed at the head of the Prophet's title: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, each succeeding the other in order and by descent; of whom we read above that Uzziah had died, as Isaiah relates: In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. From this we understand that both the Vision of the Lord seated and the things enjoined upon the Prophet, up to the place where it is written (Isa 6): Like a terebinth and like an oak that spreads out its branches: the holy seed will be its shoot, were prophesied under King Jotham (ibid., 7). […]

In the year in which King Ahaz died, this burden came. Do not rejoice, all you Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken. For out of the root of the serpent will come forth a basilisk, and its seed swallowing the bird. And the firstborn of the poor will be fed, and the poor will rest confidently, and I will make your root perish with famine, and I will slay your remnant. LXX: In the year in which King Ahaz died this word came: Do not rejoice, all you foreigners, for the yoke of him who struck you has been broken. For out of the seed of the serpent will come forth the offspring of asps, and out of their offspring will come forth winged serpents: and the poor will be fed through him, and poor men will rest in peace. […]

In the year. Here he threatens against the enemies who were rejoicing over the affliction of the Jews, and first, against the Philistines, who were rejoicing over their reduction by the death of Ezechias; second, against the Moabites, who were rejoicing over their destruction by the Assyrians or the Chaldeans: the burden of Moab (Isa 15:1).

The first of these is divided into two. In the first, the time of the threat is set out: in the year, in the time when the Philistines had occupied certain cities of the kingdom of Judea, as it says in 2 Chronicles 28, and yet Achaz resisted them, and therefore they were delighted in his death, as though they might more freely attack the Jews. Second, the threat is set out: rejoice not you. […]

14:29.t: Do not rejoice, all you Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken: for out of the root of the serpent will come forth a regulus, and its seed swallowing the bird. What we say is natural: when the king of a hostile nation dies, his enemies always rejoice, expecting from the new state of things civil wars and seditions and inexperience in ruling. When Ahaz the sinner died, therefore, who had walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and had been joined to them by kinship, we understand that the Philistines, from close by, rejoiced and mocked Israel, because, having lost a king of mature years, they were subject to the young Hezekiah. […]

It is commanded, therefore, to the Philistines, whom they now call Palestinians, and whom the Seventy always translate ἀλλόφυλοι, that is, foreigners; and it is said to them that they should not rejoice nor be glad because they have broken the rod, or the yoke, of him who struck them (Heb 12:6). For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. And God instructs us as sons when he visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with scourges, so as not to take away his mercy from us (Ps 88 [89]). This is the rod of which it is written in another Psalm: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps 22 [23]:4). […]

But because this Leviathan is called in another place not merely a serpent, but also a basilisk, because he rules over unclean spirits, or reprobate men, as Isaiah says, Out of the serpent's root shall come forth a basilisk, we must attentively observe how a basilisk destroys, that by the doings of the basilisk, his malice may be more plainly made known to us. For a basilisk does not destroy with its bite, but consumes with its breath. It often also infects the air with its breath, and withers with the mere blast of its nostrils whatever it has touched, even when placed at a distance.
14:29.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 6:33.62

14:29.t:
Concerning the first, he does three things. For first, he excludes foolish joy: rejoice not you, over this, namely, that the rod, that is, the power, of him that struck you, that is, Achaz, is broken in pieces, by death: laughter I counted error (Eccl 2:2).

Second, he threatens an increase of the punishment: for out of the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, as if to say: as the basilisk does more harm than another serpent, for even with its sight and breath it kills not just land animals, but also flying birds, just so, Ezechias, the son of Achaz shall afflict you more than others: my father put a heavy burden upon you, but I will add to your burden (1 Kgs 12:11).

14:30.t:
And the firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will rest in confidence. When the regulus has struck you, and the flying dragon has laid waste your borders, you will by no means lie in wait for Judah, nor terrify my poor little people with your treachery; but, hard pressed by your own straits, you will weep over your calamity. And the humble and the poor, who trusted not in riches and in power but in my name, will rest in secure peace, and will dread the onslaught of no enemy.

And I will make your root perish by famine, and I will slay your remnant. He speaks entirely in figures. And the sense is that, while the people of God rest in confidence, the root of the Philistines is dried up, and all its remnant will be consumed.

But those who have not broken the rod and yoke of him who struck them, but have submitted their neck to the Lord, and are poor in spirit, will be fed, and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing (Ps 22 [23]:1). And they will hear from the Lord: In most rich pastures I will feed them (Ezek 34; John 10); and they will go in and go out and find pasture. And the poor will be fed through him who strikes them in order to amend them: and they will rest in peace, or, with a careful shepherd, they will live confidently and will rest with Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16). […]

Third, he foretells the effect of the punishment, in all things as to the fruitfulness of the land: and the firstborn of the poor shall be fed, that is, the Jews, about which it says in Exodus 4:22: Israel is my firstborn; and as to the security of peace: shall rest with confidence, below: my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence (Isa 32:18); and the effect on the Philistines by the opposite of these, namely, famine, against the first: I will make your root perish with famine, that is, those also who ought to furnish nourishment to others; […]

14:31.t: Howl, O gate, cry out, O city, all Philistia is laid low: for smoke will come from the north, and there is none who escapes its column. He says the gate for those who are in the gate, and the city for the inhabitants of the city. And he directs his speech to the cities of the Palestinians, that they should wail and mourn as Sennacherib comes and lays everything waste like a torrent. For under King Hezekiah the Assyrian came, and among the other nations laid waste the Philistines. To them Jeremiah speaks: Behold, waters will rise up from the north, and they will be like an overflowing torrent: and they will cover the land and all that fills it, the city and its inhabitants (Jer 47:2). […]

Howl, O gate; cry out, O city: all Philistia is laid low. For smoke comes from the North, and there is none who escapes its column. And what will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in him the poor of his people will hope. For messengers, that is, Angels, which Symmachus alone translated, all have translated kings, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, because, except for the one letter ALEPH, which is added in the word for Angels, kings and Angels are called by the same name among the Hebrews, that is, MALACHE (Kings מלכי, Angels מלאכי). In the book of Hebrew Names I have found that Philisthiim means falling by the cup. […]

Howl. Here he threatens destruction by the Assyrians. And first, he threatens their destruction; second, the liberation of the Jews: and what shall be answered? (Isa 14:32).

Concerning the first, he sets out three things. First, he threatens universal destruction: gate, that is, the judges sitting in the gates: a voice was heard in the highways, weeping and howling of the children of Israel (Jer 3:21); and the multitude of the enemy: smoke, stirred up by the multitude of the army on account of the dust, from the north, because of the location of the Assyrians in relation to the Philistines: from the north shall an evil break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land (Jer 1:14); […]

14:32.t: What will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in her the poor of his people will hope. Because he had said, There is none who escapes its column, Judah too seemed to be included in the general statement. If, he says, the messengers of the Assyrian nation ask why Judah alone has escaped, answer them that the Lord has founded Zion, and has himself protected the humble people by his power. For messengers (מלאכי) the Seventy translated kings (מלכי), misled by an error over a single letter, ALEPH.

And when Philistia has fallen, and its smoke has penetrated all things, so that no one can escape it, what will be said to the Angels who preside over the several nations, who wonder and desire to know why Zion alone, set on a watchtower and on the heights, has escaped the bitterness of this smoke? What, then, will be said to them? Surely what follows: That the Lord has founded it, and he himself is its foundation. And he has founded it upon the foundation of prudence, righteousness, fortitude and temperance, under which names Christ is understood, of whom the Apostle also says: For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, Jesus Christ (1 Cor 3:11). […]

And what shall be answered. Here he promises liberation. And first, he sets out the inquiry: messengers, angels placed over the different provinces or asking anxiously of their state; or messengers sent to consult with Isaiah, like we read of in Jeremiah 37:3.

Second, the response is set out: that the Lord has founded Zion, that is, he has strengthened it by his protection, below: behold I will lay your stones in order (Isa 54:11).

15:1.t: The burden of Moab: because in the night Ar was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent: because in the night the wall was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. Let it suffice to have spoken once about burden and weight. I give only this brief reminder: that sad things always follow a burden, whereas a vision is followed either by glad things at once, or by glad things at the end after the sad. Moab is a province of the Arabs, in which was Balak son of Beor (Num 22), who hired the soothsayer Balaam from Mesopotamia to curse Israel; where also the people were initiated into Baal-peor (ibid., 25). Its metropolis is the city AR (ער), which today is called Areopolis, a name compounded from the Hebrew and the Greek tongue; […]

The burden of Moab. LXX: The word against the land of Moab. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Moab. Just as circumcision is both carnal and spiritual, and of the spiritual it is said by the Apostle: For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, and glory in the Lord, and put no confidence in the flesh (Phil 3:3); and again, to distinguish the spiritual Israel, it is said of the carnal: Behold Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor 10:18): and, You Gentiles in the flesh (Eph 2:11); so Moab is to be taken spiritually, which means from the father, or paternal water, conceived of incest and drunkenness, because he would seem to have been begotten in a manner in the absence, or rather without the knowledge, of the father. […]

Because by night Ar has been laid waste, Moab has fallen silent; because by night the wall has been laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. LXX: By night the land of Moab perished, for by night the wall of the land of Moab perished. For AR (ער), which Theodotion alone set down thus, as it is read in the Hebrew, Aquila and Symmachus translated city, not considering that between the Hebrew letters AIN and RES it does not have the letter JOD, which, if it were there, would rightly be read as city. Worldly wisdom, of which the Lord speaks through the Prophet: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject (Obad 8; […]

432. The burden of Moab. In this part, he threatens against the Moabites—who were descended from Moab, the firstborn of Lot (Gen 19:37)—because they rejoiced in the destruction of the sons of Israel by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, by whom nevertheless they themselves were destroyed, although afterwards. And this is divided into two parts:

in the first, he threatens their destruction;

in the second, he sets out the condition of their destruction: send forth the lamb (ch. 16).

The first of these is divided into two:

in the first, he threatens destruction by the Assyrians;

in the second, by the Babylonians: they shall lead them to the torrent (Isa 15:7).

The first of these is divided into three:

in the first, he indicates, from their sorrow, the magnitude of the punishment; […]

15:2.t:
The house has gone up, and Dibon, to the high places to lament over Nebo, and over Medeba Moab will howl. Do not let it be irksome to you that I walk along the road of the history; for you yourself wished me to do this. Now what is understood is the royal house; and the city of Dibon goes up to the idols set on the heights: over Nebo and over Medeba, noble cities, the whole province will howl. For in Nebo was consecrated the idol Chemosh, which by another name is called Baal-peor.

On all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. Among the ancients the shaving of the beard and the head was a sign of mourning. […]

The house has gone up, and Dimon, to the high places, to lament. LXX: Be sorrowful within yourselves, for Dimon will perish, where the altar is: thither you will go up to weep. The whole house of hostile wisdom, and Dibon, which means their flowing, goes up to the high places in which it had grown proud: not to sacrifice victims, but to lament the things in which it had formerly sinned. And truly falsehood passes like a river, and flows by, and can never stand firm in a stable dwelling. But the word of God, which is compacted, is stable. Hence the manna too, which is seen like ice upon the face of the earth, does not flow away, but stands firm. […]

Over Nebo and over Medeba Moab will howl: on all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth: and upon its roofs and in its streets everyone howls: he will go down in weeping. And Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out: their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz: for this the armed men of Moab will howl, his soul will howl to itself. My heart will cry out to Moab: its bars as far as Zoar, a heifer of three years: for by the ascent of Luhith he will go up weeping, and on the way of Horonaim they will raise a cry of crushing: for the waters of Nimrim will be desolate: because the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. […]

434. The house is gone up. Here he shows the magnitude of their punishment from the magnitude of their weeping, and he sets out three things.

First, he foretells their weeping, both as to those who weep: the house, namely, the royal house, and Dibon, a certain noble city; and as to the place: is gone up to mourn, that is, to weep, to the high places, in which they offered sacrifices to idols, that they might seek help in their mourning; and as to the matter: Moab, the entire province, has howled over Nabo and over Medaba, certain cities which had been destroyed: make you mourning as for an only son (Joel 2).

435. […]

15:3.t: In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; on its roofs and in its streets all howling will go down into weeping. The tears will not be private; public laments will resound for a public grief; neither matrons nor virgins, nor the tender age of children, nor the broken steps of old men will be kept within doors: the extremity of captivity will know neither shame nor weakness.

In their crossroads too, that is, in the byways of errors, while each one according to his own will fashions what he wishes, he is girded with the sackcloth of penance; and upon the roofs and housetops, on which at first they believed themselves to be lofty, and in the streets (because they do not enter by the narrow way that leads to life, but by the broad way that leads to death), there will be howling. And they will by no means go up into pride, but will go down into weeping.

436. Third, he excludes any limit to their weeping, both as to diversity of place: for every, that is, in every manner, howling, shall be, on the tops of their houses, which had level places for sitting, and in their streets shall come down weeping, from the high places to which they had ascended weeping, so that there was weeping in the mountains and in the valleys.

15:4.t:
Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out. These are names of cities of the province of Moab, of which Heshbon was once the city of the king of the Amorites, about which the same Jeremiah says: Fire has gone forth from Heshbon, and flame from the midst of Sihon. Now Heshbon means thought, and so Jeremiah, alluding to the name: Against Heshbon, he says, they have thought evil things (Jer 48:2).

Even to Jahaz their voice has been heard. The city of Jahaz overlooks the Dead Sea, where the border of the province of the Moabites lies. This, then, indicates that the howling of the province will resound to its farthest borders. Hence Jeremiah too says: From the cry of Heshbon, up to Elealeh and Jahaz they have uttered their voice (Jer 48:34). […]

Then they will understand all their thoughts to be vain, which is the meaning of Heshbon, and the ascent of pride to be empty, which is what Elealeh sounds, so that their voice is heard as far as the evil works which they have done, and the command which they thought was God's, condemning themselves by their own confession. Therefore the bars, that is, those who have been firm in Moab and have understood their error, will howl, and will begin to have hope of progress, when their soul has howled to itself.

Hesebon shall cry, weeping, and Eleale, which were cities that were, indeed, in the land of the kingdom of Moab; their voice is heard even to Jasa, which is another city of Moab. And as to the diversity of those who weep: for this, evil, shall the well appointed men, namely, well appointed for fighting, not just old men, and together with others but also to itself, when it stands alone; his soul, for mourning proceeds from the innermost of the heart: upon all the housetops of Moab, and in the streets thereof general mourning (Jer 48:3).

15:5.t:
My heart will cry out to Moab. The Prophet speaks with the feeling of one who grieves, either because the enemies too, upon whom so many evils come, are God's creatures, or because they were to be crushed by such great calamities that they become pitiable even to their enemies. Jeremiah says the very same: Therefore my heart will sound for Moab like a flute.

Its bars, as far as Segor, a heifer of three years. And Jeremiah: From Segor, he says, as far as Horonaim, a heifer of three years. Of this city we have spoken in the books of Hebrew Questions as well, and now we note briefly that it is the fifth city after Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which, being small, was preserved at the prayers of Lot. […]

Hence the Prophet, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, speaks to those whose soul was howling to itself, and says: My heart will cry out to Moab, that I may call them to penance. And their bars and all the supports which they seemed to have in their heresies will come as far as Zoar, that is, as far as the little one: and they will be shown to be not strong but fragile. And this Zoar, that is, small penance, if it perseveres, will lead them to perfect salvation: which is what the heifer of three years signifies, according to what we read in Genesis, where Abraham is commanded to offer a heifer, a ram and a goat of three years, namely a perfect sacrifice, so that he might deserve to be the heir of the Lord (Gen 15). […]

440. My heart. Here he shows the magnitude of their punishment from the compassion of their enemies, for the prophet himself suffers with them; to Moab, that is, for the affliction of Moab: I will watch over you (Jer 48:31).

The bars. Here he describes the manner and order of their punishment, and he sets out three things.

First, the destruction of their land, the bars, that is, the strength or the borders, thereof, of Moab, are deserted, unto Segar, one of the five cities that was destroyed, Genesis 10, which was in the land of Moab, a heifer, because of lust, of three years old, when animals are in their vigor and ardor; or of three years old, because it fell by the third tremor of the earthquake, after Lot had left: Egypt is like a fair and beautiful heifer (Jer 46:20). […]

15:6.t:
For the waters of Nimrim will be deserted. This town lies above the Dead Sea, with salt waters, and barren for that very reason. And either he has alluded to the name, or what had not been so before came about after the devastation: that even the waters were turned to bitterness.

For the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. It is not, as some think, that all the grass truly dried up because of the barren waters of Nimrim; rather, Scripture is speaking by metaphor. And the sense is: in all Moab there will be the salt and bitter waters of Nimrim; as no grass springs up there, so drought will overtake the whole province, that is, from Segor to Horonaim, from border to border. […]

And this will come about because the waters of Nimrim, that is, the doctrine of the heretics, which is compared to leopards and transgressors, will be desolate and will be brought to nothing. They are leopards whose varieties and spots, in Jeremiah, are not changed (Jer 13), and apostates, of whom we read in the Psalms: I have counted all the sinners of the earth transgressors (Ps 118 [119]:119). Every grass too, and shoot, and whatever seemed green in their discourse, has withered.

Third, the barrenness of their fields, for the waters, that is, the land of Moab will be so barren it will be like the territory around the town of Nemrim, which is by the sea, because its waters are salty and bitter; not indeed because of the waters, but by the judgment of God, the grass, already arisen, is withered away; the spring, as to what was sprouting; the greenness, of trees already arisen: he has turned rivers into a desert (Ps 106[107]:33).

15:7.t: According to the greatness of the work, so also their visitation: they will lead them to the torrent of the willows. For willows we read in the Hebrew ARABIM (ערבים), which can also be understood as Arabs, and can be read ORBIM (עורבים), that is, a village situated on their borders, whose inhabitants are said by many to have provided food for Elijah on Mount Horeb: a name which, because of its ambiguity, is also translated as ravens, and as the West, and as level places. And the sense is: the visitation will be according to the greatness of the disease. Take visitation here not as a remedy but as a blow. I will visit, he says, their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with stripes (Ps 88 [89]:33). […]

And they have been visited by God according to the greatness of their sins, so that him whom they had not perceived through benefits they might come to know through scourges. Accordingly they will be led to the valley or brook of the willows, so that no fruit may remain in them. For they say this is the nature of the seed of these trees: that whoever drinks it in a cup is without children. Hence the saints too, who because of their sins have come to be in the confusion of this world, hang their instruments on the willows of the rivers of the Babylonians (Ps 136 [137]).

442. According to the greatness. Here the reckoning of the magnitude of their punishment is set out: their work, of sin; their visitation, vengeance: according to the measure of the sin shall the measure also of the stripes be (Deut 25:2).

443. They shall lead them to the torrent. Here he threatens destruction by the Babylonians, where some were held captive, and as to this he says: the Chaldeans shall lead them, Moab, to the torrent, the Euphrates, beside Babylon, of the willows, which thrive by the river: upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept (Ps 136[137]:1).

15:8.t: For the cry will go round the border of Moab, its howling as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim. Jeremiah too writes almost all the same things. And these are cities and places of the Moabites, in which the crying and wailing of the captive people is described.

A cry goes round all the borders of the Moabites, either of those who call them to repentance, or of those who lament for their error: so that through their howling they may be able to offer the calves of the lips, and come as far as the fountain of the Lord's rams, or of the strong: because Elim signifies both.
Some of them were killed, and as to this he says: for the cry is gone round about, of those who weep, or of the Chaldean warriors.

15:9.t:
For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood. Where formerly there was luxuriance because of the watered fields and the ever-flowing springs, there, because of the multitude of the slain, streams of blood will flow.

For I will set additions upon Dibon: for those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land. Lest anyone think it a fault of the scribe and, in wishing to correct an error, make one, the one city is written both with the letter M and with the letter B: of these, Dimon is interpreted as silence, Dibon as flowing. Both names having been given it because of the waters that flow silently, to this day this little town is called indifferently both Dimon and Dibon. […]

And the waters of Dimon, which means sufficient sorrow, or grief, which had polluted many by their sprinkling, will be shown to have been to the deceived peoples not for salvation but for blood. Hence the prophetic word promises that upon the flowing tears, which is the meaning of Dibon, they will redouble not one grief but many additions of grief: so that, after they have done full penance and have fled from Moab, they may have as their prince the lion, God, whom the Seventy called ariel, which means lion of God: whose edition I have forborne to discuss in this place, because it disagrees in very many points with the Hebrew truth, and from what we have translated its sense too can be understood.

For the waters of Dibon, the name of a city, in which they practiced their lusts because of the pleasantness of the place: the Moabites ran into the waters of Dibon (2 Kngs 3). Some remained, afflicted by various persecutions: for I will bring more, punishments, upon Dibon, to which the Jews had fled, upon them that shall flee of Moab, from the Assyrians; and upon the remnant of the land, whom the Assyrians sent away; the lion: literally, beasts that were killing them, or a raging enemy, namely the Chaldeans, above: for all this his indignation is not turned away (Isa 9:12).

16:1.t: Send forth the Lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. What we are interpreting is not history but prophecy. And every prophecy is wrapped in enigmas, and with abrupt sentences passes, while speaking of one thing, to another: lest, if Scripture kept to order, it should be not prophecy but narrative. And the sense is: O Moab, upon whom the lion is about to rage, and from whom not even a remnant will be able to be saved, have this consolation: from you will go forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who will rule over the whole world. […]

Send forth the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert, to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. And as a bird fleeing, and as young ones flying from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. Enter into counsel, call a council: make your shadow like night at midday: hide those who flee, and do not betray the wanderers. My fugitives will dwell with you; Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the destroyer. For the dust is at an end, the wretch is consumed; he has failed who trampled the earth. And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and one will sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. […]

Here he describes the condition of their punishment, and he sets out two conditions: first, equity on the part of the one who judges; second, deception on the part of the one who suffers the punishment: and it shall come to pass, when it is seen (Isa 16:12). Now equity of punishment is disposed from the preceding fault, and therefore it orders the fault. And he sets out a double fault: first, against the contempt of the benefit they were promised; second, against the contempt of wholesome counsel they were given: take counsel (Isa 16:3).

Concerning the first, he does two things. In the first, he promises the benefit of Christ to be born from their people, that they might receive some comfort. […]

16:2.t: Then, as for Job, that pattern of patience, what mysteries are there not contained in his discourses? Commencing in prose the book soon glides into verse and at the end once more reverts to prose. By the way in which it lays down propositions, assumes postulates, adduces proofs and draws inferences, it illustrates all the laws of logic. Single words occurring in the book are full of meaning. To say nothing of other topics, it prophesies the resurrection of humankind's bodies at once with more clearness and with more caution than anyone has yet shown. "I know," Job says, "that my redeemer lives, and that at the last day I shall rise again from the earth; and I shall be clothed again with my skin, and in my flesh shall I see God. […]

And it will be: as a bird fleeing, and young ones flying away from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. He returns to the order he had begun: When I have set, he says, a most savage lion upon those who flee from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land, to break their limbs and bones, then they will fly away in terror, and all the daughters, that is, the villages and cities of the province of Moab, will migrate at the crossing of the Arnon, which is the border of the Amorites and the Moabites. And by putting crossing here too, he signifies captivity.

But he who has fled from the desert of Moab (to return from the prophecy to the anagogy), and, despising falsehood, has stood on the mountain of truth, will be like a bird fleeing; and like young ones flying from the nest, lest they be devoured by the Moabite serpents. Thus, he says, will all the daughters, that is, the Moabite souls, be at the crossing of the Arnon, which means their illumination: when, having abandoned their errors, they have crossed over to the knowledge of the truth.

Second, the punishment of those who hold the promise in contempt is set out: and it shall come to pass, that as a bird fleeing away, whence they fled or were led captive, above: my hand has found the strength of the people as a nest (Isa 10:14).

16:3.t: And as I know of two kinds of fire, so also do I of light. The one is the light of our ruling power directing our steps according to the will of God; the other is a deceitful and meddling one, quite contrary to the true light, though pretending to be that light, that it may cheat us by its appearance. This really is darkness, yet has the appearance of noonday, the high perfection of light. And so I read that passage of those who continually flee in darkness at noonday; for this is really night, and yet is thought to be bright light by those who have been ruined by luxury. For what saith David? "Night was around me and I knew it not, for I thought that my luxury was enlightenment."

It is said therefore to Moab himself, or to him who has escaped from Moab: Do nothing without counsel (Prov 13): and do not be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but follow him who is the Angel of great counsel (Eph 4): and call a council, so that out of the wandering and straying you may make a Church of God. And your shade and tabernacle, in which you formerly thought you were resting, which belonged to night and darkness, set it at midday, that is, in the brightest light, in which you ought to hide those fleeing from error, and no longer betray those who were formerly wanderers.

Take counsel, call a council: make your shade like night at midday, hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My refugees will dwell with you: Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator; for the dust is at an end, the wretched one is finished, he who trampled the land has failed. For wretched one in the Hebrew one reads SOD (סד), which can also be understood as devastator. And he speaks to Moab, that it should find counsel for its safety, and, gathering its elders, convene a council for its salvation. Do you wish, he says, to be saved and to merit the mercy of God? In the clear light and the open flight of my people, be like night and shade; take in the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. […]

Here he ordains the punishment against their contempt of the counsel they were given. And this is divided into three: in the first, he sets out the counsel; in the second, their contempt of the counsel: we have heard of the pride of Moab (Isa 16:6); in the third, the punishment of those who hold it in contempt, where it says, therefore shall Moab howl (Isa 16:7).

Concerning the first, he sets out three things. First, he exhorts them to deliberation: take counsel, as if to say: deliberate over how you might be saved. The counsel is the question itself which is moved among those taking counsel; the council is the congregation of those taking counsel. Gather a council, as though having a strict counsel: there is safety where there is much counsel (Prov 11:14); […]

16:4.t: For, O Moab, my fugitives who had forsaken me, who had gone out of the Church and, abandoning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, were following their own sense; or those who had dwelt with you, when the destroyer, the devil, begins to persecute them, do you, turned with your whole mind to the fear of the Lord, offer them hiding places: and know that after the coming of the Lamb, who arose from the rock of the desert as ruler of the whole earth and came to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, all the power of the devil, which is compared to dust, is at an end. And the wretch is consumed who made many wretched: and he has failed who trampled the whole earth, namely those who were earthly.

He also exhorts them to amicably sustain those they have received: my fugitives shall dwell with you, below: and a man shall be as when one is hid from the wind (Isa 32:2).

Third, he assigns the reason: for the dust is at an end. And first, as to the destruction of the enemy, lest they dismiss the Jews in the fear of them: the dust is at an end, the multitude of the army of Sennacherib; consumed, that is, killed by his sons, is the wretch, Sennacherib, below: he has failed (Isa 37:38), as to power (Isa 14).

16:5.t: And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. The Hebrews interpret this place thus: When the Assyrian has been put to flight, Hezekiah, a righteous man, will reign over Judah and will hold the throne of David, judging in truth the people of God subject to him. Others understand it of Christ: when the dust of the Antichrist is at an end, and the devastator who trampled the whole earth has been taken away, Christ the king will come, who will sit in the tabernacle of David, and in the day of judgment will render to all according to their works. Nor is there any doubt that this passage prophesies of Christ. […]

And when he has been consumed and brought to nothing and has utterly failed, a throne and an everlasting kingdom will be prepared. First in mercy (for we are all (Rom 3) under sin, and need the grace of God); and he will sit in the tabernacle of David, which had fallen and has been raised up, who after mercy will judge, and seek righteousness, and render to each according to his works. Let us consider from the beginning of the Burden, or of the word, of Moab, in which it is said: By night Ar of Moab has been laid waste, and the rest up to this place; […]

Second, as to the restoration of the Jews, that they might do it freely; as to the preparation of the kingdom: a throne, of the kings of the Judah, shall be prepared in mercy, the mercy of God, or of a merciful king; as to the power of the king: one shall sit, as if to say, he shall reign restfully; as to the equity of his judgments: in truth; judging, as to the pronouncing of sentences; seeking, as to the examination of cases; rendering, as to the execution of sentences. And this can be explained as referring to Ezechias or as referring to Christ, above: he shall sit upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom (Isa 9:7).

16:6.t: We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. His pride and his arrogance and his indignation are more than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of him will howl: to those who rejoice over the wall of baked brick, speak of his wounds: for the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted, the vineyard of Sibmah. LXX: We have heard of the insolence of Moab: he is exceedingly insolent: his pride and his insolence and his fury are not like your divination: not so will Moab howl: for in Moab all will howl: but for the inhabitants of Deseth you will meditate, and you will not be confounded: the plains of Heshbon will mourn the vineyard of Sibmah. […]

We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is exceedingly proud: his pride, and his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of it will howl: to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick, tell of its wounds. Again he returns to the present, and accuses Moab of pride, because it was lifted up far more than its strength warranted; and because of this pride Moab will howl to Moab, that is, the people to the city, or the metropolis to the province, and the whole land will resound with howling over the walls of baked brick, of which Jeremiah too says: Therefore I will wail over Moab, and to all Moab I will cry out, to the men of the earthen wall, lamenting (Jer 48:31). […]

Here he sets out contempt of counsel proceeding from their pride. Hence he describes their pride as to three things: first, as to its being made commonly known: we have heard, as if it were public; as to its quantity: he is exceeding proud; as to its exceeding their dignity: his pride, by which he extolls himself as to the gifts he possesses, and his arrogancy, by which he pretends to have gifts that he does not possess, and his indignation, by which he presumptuously proposes vengeance, is more than his strength.

16:7.t: Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, that is, one to another: namely, all the varieties of the heretics and of worldly wisdom will bellow against one another when they are in torments (1 Kgs 6). For this reason, to those who have walls not built of squared stones, of which the Temple was built, and so polished that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of God, O you teachers of the Church, or you who have been saved from the error of Moab, announce their wounds, with which they have been wounded by the darts of the heretics. For all their thoughts, which is what Heshbon signifies, do not belong to the dwelling of the Lord's city, of which it is written: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5); […]

Here he sets out the punishment of those who hold the counsel in contempt. And first, the weeping of those to be punished: shall Moab howl to Moab, that is, to each other, about which enough is said above (ch. 15). Second, he describes the manner of punishment: to them that rejoice; and he sets out three things. First, the announcement of the punishment is proclaimed by prophets or messengers: them that rejoice, they glory and trust in the fortifications of their brick walls: if the watchman see the sword coming (Ezek 33:6).

16:8.t:
For the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted: the vine of Sibmah. Between Heshbon and Sibmah there are scarcely five hundred paces; and by the metaphor of the vine he signifies the devastation of the whole province.

The lords of the nations have cut down its shoots. He keeps the metaphor he had begun, showing that the kings of the nations who had laid Moab waste ravaged all its hamlets and fortresses.

They have reached as far as Jazer: they have wandered in the desert: its offshoots have been left behind: they have crossed the sea. Understand the shoots and offshoots as its people and its fugitives; and the crossing of the sea as the captivity into Babylon, about which we shall read later: The burden of the desert of the sea.

The lords of the nations have cut down its branches: they have reached as far as Jazer. They have wandered in the desert: its shoots have been left: they have crossed the sea. For this I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vineyard of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh: for upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. And gladness and exultation will be taken away from Carmel: and in the vineyards he will not exult nor shout for joy: he who was accustomed to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. […]

Second, the description of the punishment is set out as to the destruction of lands: Hesebon, a city in whose territory wheat abounded; Sabama, a neighboring city, in which wine abounded. As to the strength of their enemies: the lords of the nations, that is, of Assyria or Chaldea, ruling over many nations; the branches, that is, the shoots which are on the top of a vine, which metaphorically signify princes and distinguished persons; destroying, even to Jazer—which is on the farthest border—as to the affliction of men, the lords of the nations have wandered: they wandered in a wilderness, in a place without water (Ps 107:4); […]

16:9.t:
Therefore I will lament with the weeping of Jazer, the vine of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh. This is the voice of the Prophet lamenting, and attesting the greatness of the devastation by the greatness of his tears, and weeping for the vine of Jazer and of Sibmah, and for Heshbon and Elealeh, cities once most strong, cut down as the Assyrian pruned them.

For upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. Understand the treaders of the grapes, gathering in the joy of the vintage, as the armies of the enemies; and that in the very season of joy the season of captivity has come.

And so the prophetic word laments the strength of the heretics, that is, Jazer, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God. And I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon, namely their thoughts, and Elealeh, by which they climb to the heights. And why does he lament Jazer and the vineyard of Sibmah, and drench Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears? So that, while he himself weeps, he may teach them also to weep. For, he says, upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. For the vineyard of the Moabites, because of the nearness of the place, is such as is the vineyard of the Sodomites too, of which it is said: For their vine is of the vineyard of the Sodomites, and their shoot of Gomorrah (Deut 32:31). […]

Third, the compassion of the prophet is set out. And first, his compassion is set out: over this, namely the misfortune of Moab, I will lament with the weeping of Jazer, that is, weeping over that city of Moab, and similarly also the vineyard of Sabama, and Eleale.

16:10.t:
And joy and exultation will be taken away from Carmel. It is an idiom of the Scriptures always to liken Carmel, a rich and wooded mountain which overlooks Ptolemais and on which Elijah prayed, to fertility and abundance; and by this it signifies that all joy and fertility are to be taken away from cities once most fruitful.

And in the vineyards he will not exult, nor shout for joy. What is understood is the former vintager, that is, the husbandman of the province of Moabitis. Accordingly he immediately added:

He who used to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. By no means will the joyful vintager sing the vintage shout at the vintage; but everywhere hostile devastation and the clamor of the victors will arise.

The gladness and exultation of the heretics, in which they had formerly been accustomed to rejoice, will also be taken away: so that, after they have done penance, they may deserve to hear: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). And what he added, from Carmel, signifies this: not that the heretics truly have Carmel, that is, the knowledge of the spiritual circumcision, but that they falsely boast of having it. And when the vineyards have been cut down, and gladness and exultation taken away from the knowledge falsely so called, then there will be none of the former treaders to tread the grapes which he had trodden before: and their voice will be struck dumb in eternal silence.

Second, the reason for his compassion is set out as to attack their enemies: the treaders, that is, of the ravaging Assyrians. And as to the taking away of the joy that they had from abundance of grain: from Carmel, that is, from fertility—for Carmel is not in Moab, but the Jews use proper nouns for appellatives; and the joy that they had in abundance of wine: in the vineyards (cf. Jer 48:33).

16:11.t: Therefore my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inmost parts for the wall of baked brick. Lest anyone should think the Prophet's lament a sign of exultation, by which he rejoiced that the enemies of the people of Israel were captives, he says that it is out of affection, and out of the inmost grief of his heart, that he mourns the overthrow of a city once most mighty.

For this my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick. And it will be, when it has appeared that Moab has labored on his high places, he will enter into his holy places to entreat, and he will not prevail. This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. When the error of Moab has been destroyed, or rather its false gladness changed into mourning and tears, my belly, the prophet's, which is composed with musical art like a harp, and which, conceiving from the fear of God, has begotten many children, so that there is no string that does not give back its sound, will resound with the mourning of Moab doing penance: and all my inward parts for the wall of baked brick: for which Theodotion translated for the scattered wall. […]

Moreover, according to the Seventy, who translated: The inner parts of the prophet, like a wall renewed by God, and that he is put to shame, that is, Moab, and enters to the altars and to the things that are made by hand, we can discuss it thus, saying that the inward parts of the prophet are always renewed and made stronger by God, so that the adversaries are confounded, and understand the things which have been fabricated by human hand to be empty and of no profit for salvation.

Third, the conclusion is inferred as from a proof: over this, misfortune, my bowels, that is, my senses, shall sound like a harp, making a sound for lamentation, or because the harp increases joy in the cheerful and sadness in the sad, or because of the harmony of the virtues of the prophet.

16:12.t: And it will come to pass, when it has become apparent that Moab has labored over its high places, it will enter its sanctuaries to pray, and it will not prevail. It is the last misery not to have help even in those whom it has always worshiped. Deserted, he says, by your own strength, and with all your defenders slain, you will go to the idols, you will venerate the shrines, and you will find no help in those upon whom the devastation will come together with you.

And when Moab has understood that he has labored in vain at the doctrines which he formerly thought lofty, he will enter into his holy places, not those which are holy of themselves, but those which in his error he thought holy, and he will not be able to find help. Or surely, having abandoned the error of falsehood, he will try to enter into the holy places of the Church, to make them his own, and to pray and entreat, but he will not prevail. For we cannot take hold of perfect virtue as soon as we wish.

Here he shows their frustration, concerning both the idols to which they sacrificed in high places and the idols to which they sacrificed in temples when they were in fear: where are their gods, in whom they trusted? (Deut 32:37).

16:13.t: This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. From what time, do you suppose? Clearly from the time when Moab was created. And the Lord says: The Moabites and the Ammonites shall not enter into the Church of God (Deut 23:3). Or we may understand from that time as of ancient time: that these things were decreed long ago by the divine sentence; not that the foreknowledge of God brought about the cause of the devastation, but that the future devastation was known beforehand to the majesty of God.

And what he adds: This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time, let us know that an epilogue has been given back to the proem in which he had said, the word against Moab, or the burden, so that what he had begun there he has completed here. And from that time is to be understood as from when he began to speak to him, so that all that he said is one word of God, that is, one sentence.
In the mystery of prophetical revelation, Christ is symbolized by word, which people heard while they could see no one, as they said: "This is the word that the Lord spoke to Moab."
Here is the epilogue. From that time, from the death of the king Achaz.

16:14.t: And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away, above all its great people, and it will be left small and slight, by no means many. This prophecy, as we said above, is directed against the Moabites after the death of Ahaz, in the reign of Hezekiah, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity by Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. So, just as a hireling waits for the setting of the sun, and day and night looks for the end of his work so as to receive his fixed wage, so too after three years Moab will be destroyed when the Assyrian comes, and scarcely a few will be left in the land to inhabit the overthrown cities and to till the deserted fields. […]

And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, and he will be left small and slight, by no means many. The three years in which the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, or great riches, as the Seventy translated, are to be understood mystically. For just as the mercy of the Lord is in weights and measure, so torments and punishments too have their measure, so that after three years have passed, in which he will be left small and slight and by no means many, he may then cease to be without glory. […]

Here he shows the shortness of the time: in three years, which will be until their destruction and from the death of Achaz—in whose time was the vision of this second word—or in which your persecution or battle will last; the years of a hireling, for after these, the Lord will repay to you the wages for your sins; or those who seem great are hirelings and small to the Lord: the life of man upon earth is a warfare, and his days are like the days of a hireling (Job 7:1).

17:1.t: The burden of Damascus: Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city, and it will be like a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks, and they will rest there, and there will be none to frighten them. And help will cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. After Babylon and the Philistines and Moab, the discourse turns to Damascus, that is, Aram, which itself was once a royal city too, and held the primacy in all Syria: Antioch and Laodicea and Apamea were not yet flourishing, cities which we know to have grown after Alexander and the empire of the Macedonians. […]

The burden of Damascus. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Damascus; the LXX: The word against Damascus, adding something of their own, as they did at the beginning of Moab. We first read the name Damascus in Genesis: he was Abraham's home-born servant before Isaac, and was thought to be his heir, had not the son of Sarah been begotten by promise (Gen 15). Now it means either kiss of blood, or drinking blood, or blood of sackcloth, all of which suit the people of the heathen, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty, and did works worthy of lamentation and of sackcloth. […]

Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city, and shall be as a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer shall be left for flocks, and they shall rest there, and there shall be none to make them afraid; and help shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As was shown in the title, by Damascus is signified the calling of the nations, which loved or drank blood; and once they have believed in Christ, they will cease to be cities of their former way of life, and will be as a heap of stones in ruin. […]

Some think that this prophecy is the same as the one we read in Jeremiah: Damascus is dissolved, it has turned to flight, trembling has seized it, anguish and pains have held it like a woman in labor (Jer 49:24, 27). And again: I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it will devour the ramparts of Ben-hadad. But it must be known that Jeremiah describes the Babylonian captivity of the city of Damascus, that is, of the few whom the king of the Assyrians had left in it; whereas Isaiah announces the captivity by the Assyrians that is close at hand. […]

The burden of Damascus. Here he begins to threaten against those who prepared an occasion of sin for the people of God when, through trust in their help, they cared not to trust in God. And this is divided into two parts: in the first, he threatens against the Syrians, who brought help to the people of the ten tribes; in the second, against the Egyptians, who did so to the two tribes: woe to the land (ch. 18). The first of these is divided into three: in the first, he threatens the destruction of the Syrians who promise help; in the second, the destruction of the ten tribes who trust in that promised help: and it shall come to pass in that day (Isa 17:4); in the third, the destruction of the Assyrians who destroy both of them: woe to the multitude (Isa 17:12). […]

17:2.t: The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks. Aroer means tamarisk, which is properly a tree that grows in the wilderness and in salty soil; and by this the devastation is shown. They will rest there: the flocks is understood; and there will be none to frighten them. For the solitude will be so great that not even a robber lying in wait is to be feared.

The forsaken cities of AROER (ערוער), that is, of the tamarisk, shall also be for the flocks of the Church, so that we may inhabit those which the Jews forsook; or else, idolatry being destroyed, the Gospel shall be built up. This too we see fulfilled in our own times: the Serapeum at Alexandria and the temple of Marnas at Gaza have risen up as churches of the Lord, and the cities of Aroer have been made ready for the flocks of the Gospel. Aroer, that is, tamarisks, grow in desert places, according to what is written in the curse of the man who trusts in man, and whose heart departs from the Lord: He shall be, it says, like the tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see good when it comes; but he shall dwell in dryness, in the desert, in a land of salt and uninhabitable (Jer 17:6). […]

Second, as to the neighboring region: of Aroer, that is, of that region of Syria, in which there are many cities; or Aroer, which is Hebrew for "tamarisk," as if to say: as places where tamarisks abound are barren and abandoned to pasturage for sheep, so will the cities of Syria be; there shall be none to make them afraid, for, because of their solitude, there will not even be thieves there; or because they will not be useful for other fruit, as flocks are frightened by vineyards and farmland, below: nettles shall grow up in its houses (Isa 34:13).

17:3.t: And help will cease from Ephraim: by no means will the ten tribes have help in it against Judah. And the kingdom from Damascus: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [from the common or popular edition] will cease is understood. But when he says that the kingdom ceases and rests, he does not signify a perpetual devastation, but takes away for the present the power by which it formerly reigned in all Syria. And the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As, he says, the ten tribes were destroyed when the Assyrian ravaged them, and all their glory was led into captivity, so the few who remain in Damascus will imitate them, and will have the glory of their allied nation. Take glory as said by irony, for ignominy. […]

Then the help of God shall cease from Ephraim, by whom in this place are understood the Scribes and Pharisees, according to the prophecy of Hosea, who names Ephraim those who are opposed to the people of God (Hos 5 and 8). And the kingdom shall cease from Damascus, so that sin, and the prince of sin, the devil, may no longer reign in Damascus, which formerly loved blood; but the remnant of Syria, that is, those from the nations who have believed, are to be as the children of Israel formerly were, the kingdom of God having been taken from them and given to the nations which bring forth its fruit, as the Lord God of hosts has spoken through all his prophets.

And aid shall cease. Here the effect of the destruction is set out, and first, the effect on the ten tribes: from Ephraim; second, the effect as to the royal city: and the kingdom from Damascus shall cease, and it will no longer be the head of the kingdom; third, as to the entire region: and the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, ironically: that is, they will be ignominious like the children of Israel, above: the Lord shall put down his hand, and the helper shall fall (Isa 31:3).

17:4.t: "4. And there shall be in that day a failing of the glory of Jacob, and the riches of his glory shall be shaken. 5. And it shall be as when one gathers standing corn, and reaps the grain of the ears; 6. And it shall be as when one gathers ears in a rich valley, and stubble is left. Or as the berries of an olive tree are left, two or three on the topmost bough, or four or five on its branches, thus saith the Lord God of Israel. 7. In that day a man shall trust in him that made him, and his eyes shall look on the Holy One of Israel, 8. and they shall not trust in the altars, nor in the work of their hands, which their own fingers have made." […]
17:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

17:4.t: And it will come to pass in that day, the glory of Jacob will be made thin, and the fat of his flesh will waste away. When, he says, Damascus has been taken and has ceased to be a city, and such glory has crowned it as crowned Israel, that is, the ten tribes, then all the defense, and the fattest flesh, and the refuge of Jacob will waste away: for by no means will he have allies to join with him in laying Jerusalem waste. We have read above that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, and that it was announced to the house of David: Syria has rested upon Ephraim; […]

And it shall come to pass in that day that the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh shall waste away. And it shall be as one gathering in the harvest what remains, and his arm shall glean the ears, and it shall be as one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there shall be left in it as a cluster of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five at its summits, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. […]

And it shall come to pass in that day. Here he threatens the destruction of the ten tribes, who trust in the help of the Syrians, and first, as to the oppression of their people; second, as to the destruction of their cities: in that day his strong cities (Isa 17:9); third, as to the barrenness of their fields: therefore shall you plant (Isa 17:10). Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he threatens punishment; second, he shows the fruit of the punishment: in that day man shall bow down (Isa 17:7). He threatens punishment on their people first, against their vainglory: the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, that is, it will be brought to little, and reduced as if to nothing, when that which they gloried in is destroyed. […]

17:5.t: And since it is said of the calling of the nations: The harvest is great, but the labourers are few (Matt 9), those poor ones shall glean the remnants of the harvest, which were saved through the Apostles, and the scantiest ears, not from the mountains and lofty places, but in the valley of Rephaim, that is, in the lowliness of the letter. And consider that Rephaim, which means giants, signifies the Pharisees and Scribes, as Ephraim did above. Indeed, for the valley of Rephaim the Seventy translated the hard valley, to express the hardness of the Jewish heart.

And it will be like one gathering in the harvest what has remained, and his arm will gather the ears: and it will be like one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there will be left in it as it were a cluster, and as at the shaking of an olive tree two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five on its topmost boughs, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. Those who understand the present devastation of Damascus as under the Roman empire maintain that these words signify the Apostles: that just as a few ears and olives are wont to remain in the field or on the trees, so the remnant of Israel is saved; especially since there follows: In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, that is, to Christ. […]

As to the first, he sets out scarcity of ears of corn after the harvest, which are gathered by the harvester himself, and thus, the scarcity of the remnant of the ten tribes, shall be as when someone gathers in the harvest that which remains from the first reaping, and, from those gathered, his arm shall pick out the ears of corn, that is, collect them. And this one who gathers was Ezechias, who called together the remnant of the ten tribes, as is written in 2 Chronicles 30. Or also those which are gathered by someone poor, like it says in Ruth 2:3: I will go into the field to glean the ears of corn; and as to this, he says: it shall be as he that seeks ears in the vale of Raphaim, a certain valley which is very fertile.

17:6.t: Out of their lowliness those who shall be saved are chosen like ears among the stubble and like clusters at the vintage; and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives, or four or five. For when the smiting of the people of the Jews came, that olive tree of the people of Israel, which under Moses had six hundred thousand armed men (Num 26), and under David, when Joab numbered them, a countless people (2 Sam 24), could scarcely offer a few fruits to the Lord the Savior: two olives, Paul and Barnabas; and three olives, Peter and James and John (Acts 13), who both beheld the Lord transfigured on the mountain and were found worthy to go with the Lord to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Matt 17). […]

Against abundance of wine, he sets out scarcity of grapes after the grape harvest: and the fruit thereof that shall be left upon it, shall be as one cluster of grapes: woe is me, for I am become as one that gleans in autumn the grapes of the vintage (Mic 7:1). Against abundance of oil, he sets out scarcity of olives after the shaking of the olive. The olive, as Papias says, is the fruit of the olive tree; but here, according to the explanation of the Gloss, it seems to be used to mean the tree itself on whose top remains a small amount of fruit which the harvesters are not able to reach; concerning this scarcity, see Deuteronomy 28:62: you shall remain few in number.

17:7.t: In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. And he will not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought: and they will not look to the groves and the shrines. They think that this was fulfilled in the times of Christ, when, the kingdom of Damascus having been destroyed, the everlasting empire of the Savior succeeded, and the error of idolatry was diminished. The intention of these interpreters is indeed pious, but it does not keep the order of the history. […]

In that day man shall bow down to his maker, and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel. And he shall not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought; they shall not look to the groves and the shrines.
