At that time, when from the people of Israel, to whom it was formerly said, The Lord your God has called you a fruitful olive tree (Jer 11:16), and of whom we read in the Psalms, Your children like young olive plants round about your table (Ps 127 [128]:3), the Lord in his hunger shall scarcely have found, for the drought of spiritual grace, two olives, and three, or four, or five, the fullness of the nations shall come in, and shall bow down not to idols made with hands but to its God, and looking to the Holy One of Israel they shall […]

In that day. Here he sets out the fruit of the punishment: man, any who fled from the ten tribes to Ezechias, shall bow down himself to his Maker, giving the due service of worship; his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel, expecting some help.

Note on the words, his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel (Isa 17:7), that our eyes ought to be inclined to the Lord, first, through the adherence of faith, below: your eyes shall see your teacher (Isa 30:20); second, because of the expectation of hope: the eyes of all hope in you, O Lord (Ps 144[145]:15); third, because of the contemplation of love: from thence she contemplates the prey, and her eyes behold afar off (Job 39:29); fourth, because of the enjoyment of glory: blessed are your eyes (Matt 13:16).

17:8.t: Temples (delubra), temples in which there were fonts, as though for washing, below: in that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver (Isa 31:7).

17:9.t: In that day the cities of its strength will be abandoned like ploughs, and the crops that were abandoned before the face of the sons of Israel, and it will be deserted. He does not say this against Damascus, but against the ten tribes, which were called Israel: that just as, at the coming of the people of God out of Egypt, all the nations that inhabited the land of promise, struck with sudden terror, abandoned their ploughs and the heaps of grain and their work half done, seeking safety in their feet, so the land of Israel too should remain desolate for a long time. Hence I wonder that for ploughs and heaps of grain Aquila chose to translate potsherd and Emir; Symmachus, forest and Amir; the Seventy, the Amorites and the Hivites. […]

In that day the cities of his strength shall be forsaken like ploughs and standing corn, which were forsaken before the face of the children of Israel. And it shall be desolate, because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. LXX: In that day your cities shall be forsaken, as the Amorites and the Hivites forsook them before the face of the children of Israel. And they shall be desolate, because you have forsaken God your Savior, and have not remembered the Lord your helper. […]

In that day. Here he threatens the desolation of their cities, and first, he threatens the desolation itself: as the ploughs. This touches on what is found in Joshua 6 and 7, how the Amorrhites fled at the coming of the sons of Israel, leaving behind everything in the fields, above: your land is desolate, your cities are burnt with fire (Isa 1:7).

17:10.t:
Because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. These things, he says, you will suffer, O Israel, because you have abandoned God your Savior, who freed you from Egypt, who subjected hostile nations to you: and you have not remembered your helper.

Therefore you will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot. This is to be read more pointedly and as irony. Because, he says, you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper: will you on that account have to plant a faithful planting, and not rather sow a foreign shoot, for the enemy to snatch away? […]

And an apostrophe is made to the land of Judea itself, that is, to those who dwelt in it: You have suffered all these things because you have forgotten God your Savior, which means Jesus, whose coming to you the Law and the Prophets continually announced; and you have not remembered your strong helper, who was always your succour. The cause, then, of the desolate cities of Judea is forgetfulness of the Savior, who had said at the beginning of this Prophet: Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood.

Therefore you shall plant a faithful plantation, and shall sow a strange seed. In the day of your planting wild grapes, and in the morning your seed shall flower: the harvest is taken away in the day of inheritance, and he shall grieve grievously. LXX: Therefore you shall plant an unfaithful plantation and an unfaithful seed, and in the day on which you plant you shall go astray. But if you sow in the morning, it shall flower for harvest in the day of inheritance, when, as the father of a man, he gives an inheritance to his sons. Where we, following Aquila and Symmachus and the Seventy, have translated in the day of inheritance, which in Hebrew is BIOM NEHELA (ביום נחלה), one can read in the Hebrew in the worst day. […]

Second, the reason for the desolation is set out: and you shall be desolate because you have forgotten God your savior: you have forsaken the God that begot you, and have forgotten the Lord that created you (Deut 32:18).

Therefore shall you plant. Here he threatens barrenness of fruit, and concerning this, he does three things. First, he shows the useless labor of cultivation, as to their vineyards: unfaithful plants, for they will not return fruit according to your labor, or faithful, ironically, as if to say: because of the evil which you have done, will your plants be faithful? As to their fields: strange seed, which another will gather, above: ten jugera of vineyard shall yield one little measure (Isa 5:10). […]

17:11.t: In the day of your planting, wild grapes, and in the morning your seed will flower. The harvest has been taken away in the day of inheritance, and it will grieve grievously. These, he says, are the fruits of your works that you will reap: your vine of Sorek will degenerate into wild grapes, your seed will hold out hope in the blade; but when ripeness has come, it will be reaped by another. And then you will grieve grievously, when you lose what you hoped for and almost already held.

Second, as to the ruin of the fruit: in the day of your planting, that is, when you ought to have taken up the fruit from your planting, and this as to the vineyards; as to the fields, in the morning your seed shall flourish, that is, it will be beautiful at first, that you may mourn more, or because it will flower before the proper season and be useless: the inheritance gotten hastily in the beginning, in the end shall be without a blessing (Prov 20:21). The harvest is taken away, by enemies, in the day of inheritance, when it ought to be put away in the barn, like the fruit of their inheritance: they have sown wheat, and reaped thorns (Jer 12:13). Third, he threatens sorrow for the loss: it shall grieve you, who sowed; or you shall grieve.

17:12.t: Woe to the multitude of many peoples; like the multitude of the roaring sea, and the tumult of the crowds, like the sound of many waters, they shall roar. The peoples shall roar like the multitude of overflowing waters; and he shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far off, and he shall be carried away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the tempest. At eventide, behold, trouble; in the morning, and he shall not stand. This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. Above, under the name of Damascus, we read of the calling of the nations, and the casting off of the Jews, and, through the Apostles and in the Apostles, the election of the few of the Jews who believed. […]

Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the multitude of the roaring sea: and the tumult of crowds, like the sound of many waters: the peoples will roar like the sound of flooding waters: and he will rebuke him, and he will flee far off: and he will be snatched away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the storm. At eventide: and behold, confusion in the morning, and he will not endure. This is the portion of those who have laid us waste, and the lot of those who plunder us. Those who suppose that the earlier captivity of Damascus was brought on by the Romans refer this also that is written: Man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, to the times of Christ and of the Apostles. […]

Woe to the multitude. Here he threatens the destruction of the Assyrians, and concerning this he sets out three things. And first, he describes the multitude of the army as to the noise of their marching, woe to the multitude of people, coming with Sennacherib; as to the tumult of their speaking, the tumult, which is confused speech, especially of a multitude.

17:13.t: For the peoples shall roar in the spectacles of theatrical licence, and in the cruelty of the amphitheatre, and in the frenzies of the circus, like the sound of overflowing waters, when with a voice concordant in impiety they blaspheme and cry that the Christians be thrown to the lions and the beasts, and other things of the kind. But while they rage like the sea, the Lord shall rebuke the author of their sedition and drive him away from his people. And as dust stirred up on the mountains is carried off the more violently the higher it is, and as a whirlwind that rises from the earth is borne aloft by a sudden tempest, so he too shall be carried off and separated from the people of God and shall flee, lest he be banished to the abyss.

As to the shout of their fighting, nations shall make a noise, in battle, above: behold the Lord will bring upon them the waters of the river strong and many (Isa 8:7); their voice shall roar like the sea (Jer 6:23); many waters, many peoples (Rev 17).

Second, he threatens destruction. Concerning which he first sets out the destruction itself: but he shall rebuke him, killing his army by an angel, and he shall flee far off, to his own land with only a few men, as it says above (Isa 10:18); you have rebuked the Gentiles (Ps 9:6[5]). Second, a similitude is set out corresponding to the condition of the destruction, for he was proud: he shall be carried away as the dust: like the dust (Ps 1:4), which is driven before the wind; […]

17:14.t: And when the day of consummation comes, which is what evening means, then there shall be trouble for him as he recognizes his own sins. And at morning time, that is, on the day of the resurrection, he shall not stand, which the Seventy translated shall not be. But if he shall not be, what will they answer who grant the devil repentance and, as far as in them lies, promise him the summit of an archangel? This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. These words are spoken either by the Christian people, or by the prophet in the person of the believing people: that their persecutors, who oppressed the saints of God with exiles, prisons and confiscations of goods, shall have eternal destruction and shall possess everlasting punishments.

Third, the completion of the destruction is set out: and he shall not be, for he himself was killed: you are brought to nothing (Ezek 28:19). Fourth, the reason for the destruction is set out: this is the portion of them that have wasted us, our possessions, and the lot of them that spoiled, our moveable goods: fire and brimstone, and storms of winds, shall be the portion of their cup (Ps 10:7[11:6]).

18:1.t: Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. The Hebrew word SELSEL (צלצל), which Symmachus interpreted as sound and Theodotion as birds, we have rendered as cymbal. Aquila translated double shadow. But it must be known that a shadow is called SEL (צל), and here the syllable itself is doubled. From this we can understand the saying thus: Woe to the land that promises help in the shadow of its wings. And whereas Scripture says: He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven (Ps 90 [91]:1), for which in the Hebrew is written, He will abide in the shadow of the Almighty, this land, boasting that it has the very likeness of God, promises, though itself set in dangers, to give support to others. […]

Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by the sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters: go, swift Angels, to a nation torn away and rent asunder, to a terrible people, after which there is no other, to a nation waiting, waiting and trodden down, whose land the rivers have plundered. All you inhabitants of the world, who dwell on the earth, when the sign has been lifted up on the mountains you shall see, and you shall hear the blast of the trumpet. LXX: Woe to the land of the wings of ships beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, you who send hostages by the sea, and letters of papyrus upon the water. […]

But according to the Seventy the wings of the heretics are bewailed, which flit like ships over the sea of this world and surpass the impiety of the heathen, whom the Scripture now calls Ethiopians; and it is said to their teaching and speech: You who send books on the sea of this world, the hostages of your perversity, and letters to deceive those who will read them. Swift messengers go to a lofty nation, and to a foreign and most wicked people. For none of the churchmen has as much zeal for good as the heretics have for evil, and they think they gain a profit if they deceive others, and, being lost themselves, destroy the rest. Now the nation is called lofty on account of its pride, and foreign and most wicked because it is estranged from God. […]

Someone might wonder and say to himself, "Why does the prophetic oracle addressed to Damascus now mention the land that is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia?" At certain times the Israelites foolishly abandoned God the Savior of all and fell into the error of worshiping many gods. Paying no heed whatsoever to the law given by Moses, they were chastised by God, at times through foes who rose up against them and at times by other catastrophes. Although they should have repented and been healed, ceased their wicked way, walked in the commandments and sought help from God, they made alliances with their neighbors, first with the kings in Damascus, then with those in Egypt. Not only this. […]

Woe to the land, the winged cymbal. Here he threatens against the Egyptians. And first, he threatens their punishment through comparison to what merits the punishment; in the second part, he describes the manner of the punishment: the burden of Egypt (ch. 19); in the third part, he designates the time of the punishment: in the year (ch. 20). Concerning the first, he sets out three things: first, he designates the fault, which merits the punishment; second, he threatens the punishment: all you inhabitants (Isa 18:3); third, he shows the fruit of the punishment: at that time (Isa 18:7).

Concerning the first, he does two things. […]

18:2.t: Who sends envoys by sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters. Go, swift messengers, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a terrible people, after whom there is no other, to a nation waiting and trampled down, whose land the rivers have plundered. Among the Hebrews Egypt, and the Egyptian, and the Egyptians are all called by one word, MESRAIM (מצרים). Let this be said lest anyone stick at the word when he finds the masculine in place of the feminine, that is, the man in place of the land; […]

These, then, are beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and they send ambassadors on the sea of this world, that is, their disciples, who, carrying their volumes, are rightly said to carry vessels of papyrus, that is, of paper, upon the waters, which are quickly blotted out. For as books by water and damp are soon dimmed, blotted out and perish, so their speech and teaching, though at the beginning it seemed to possess some strength, passes away and slips by. And so it is said to them ironically: O Angels of the heretics, go swiftly. These the blessed apostle Paul calls false apostles, deceitful workers, who transform themselves into Apostles of Christ (2 Cor 11). And go to a nation torn away and rent asunder: torn away from God and mangled by the bites of the heretics. […]

Second, he describes the help which they promised to the two tribes. And first, he describes the manner of announcing, saying: they that, namely, the Egyptian people, sends ambassadors, that is, messengers, to the two tribes, in the sea, that is, through the sea, and upon the waters, of the river or the sea, in vessels of papyrus, a kind of rush, from which they made small boxes for carrying letters, or reeds so large that they made ships from them, as is written in the history of Alexander: the word comes from pyr, which means "fire."

Second, he sets out the command given to the ambassadors, in which he determines two things. First, the manner of announcing, saying: O angels, that is, O my messengers, go, swift, that is, swiftly. […]

18:3.t: All you inhabitants of the world who dwell on the earth, when the signal has been raised on the mountains, you will see, and you will hear the blast of the trumpet. All you nations round about, he says, when you hear my command like a signal raised on the mountains, and my order like the blast of a trumpet resounding on high, then you will see what I have commanded.

And so all who inhabit and dwell in the world lift up their eyes to the sign of the heretics, which is lifted up as it were on the mountains, and hear the blast of the trumpet, that is, of their teaching. So much according to the Hebrew.

All you inhabitants of the world. Here he threatens the punishment, and concerning this, he does two things. First, he shows the manifestation of the punishment: you shall see, that is, it will be known to you, the sign, the flag of Nabuchodonosor: the nations have heard of your disgrace, and your howling has filled the land (Jer 46:12); or, you shall see the abundance of the enemy, appearing in his army: the strongest of nations, shall be brought to destroy the land (Ezek 3:11).

18:4.t:
For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will consider in my place. What is it that the Lord spoke to the Prophet? What follows: until the things I have commanded come about, I will rest in my seat: as the Jews think, in the Temple; as we think, in the heavens. And I will consider, he says, what end of things is coming.

As the noonday light is clear, and as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest. Just as in the whole day nothing is clearer than noon, when the sun glows from mid-heaven and lights up the whole world alike; […]

For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will consider in my place, as the noonday light is clear, and as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest. For before the harvest it has all blossomed, and an unripe perfection shall bud, and its twigs shall be cut off with sickles; and what is left shall be cut away and shaken off. And they shall be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth, and the birds shall be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon it. […]

Second, he takes away their confidence in divine defense: for thus says the Lord. And first, because he takes away the help of his defense from them: I will take my rest, as though not helping you; and consider, I will see what you can do: I will consider what their last end shall be (Deut 32:20). Second, because he will give help to the enemy in fighting, as to counsel in doubtful things: as the noon light is clear, so clearly will what they should do be shown to them; as to relief in labors, as a cloud: you have set up the right hand of them that oppress him (Ps 88:43[89:42]).

18:5.t: For before the harvest it has wholly blossomed, and an unripe perfection has budded, and its little branches will be cut off with pruning hooks, and what is left will be cut away and shaken off. And they will be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth, and the birds will be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts of the earth will winter upon it. Because he had spoken of noon, and had mentioned beforehand a cloud of dew in summer and harvest, and had taken his metaphor from husbandry, he keeps it in the rest, describing the pride of Egypt and the devastation of its people, and the corpses throughout the whole province which are to be devoured by birds. […]

And before the time of the consummation comes, since now we know in part and prophesy in part, many will be found perfect, of whom the Apostle says: Let as many of us as are perfect be of this mind (1 Cor 13; Phil 3:15). But the twigs that are useless shall be cut off with sickles, as the Savior says in the Gospel: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take it away; and every one that bears fruit he will prune, that it may bear more fruit (John 15:2).

Third, where it says, before the harvest, he describes a metaphor of the punishment, namely through the destruction of fruit in the field, and he sets out three things. First, as to the ruin of the fruit which is ruined in the flower, when it begins to flower too quickly, for before the harvest it was all flourishing; similarly, before Egypt had power, it showed the flower of its glory: concerning which it says below: all the glory thereof as the flower of the field (Isa 40:6). It is also ruined in the bud, when the humor from which the fruit ought to arise is not yet ripe: and it shall bud without perfect ripeness; similarly, Egypt presumed beyond the power which it had. […]

18:6.t: And lest you should think he speaks of a vine and not of men, he turns the metaphor into the truth of history: And they will be left, he says, together to the birds of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth. For birds and beasts devour not the cut branches of trees, but corpses. Let us read Ezekiel more fully, where he prophesies against Pharaoh and against Egypt, and we shall find all these things written most plainly (Ezek 29). And when he says: The birds will be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts will winter upon it, he either truly signifies the multitude of the slain, or shows through the same metaphor that it is to be laid waste by all the nations.

And those that have been cut off shall be left to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth: to the birds which ravage what is sown by the wayside, and to the beasts to which the soul that does not confess God is delivered; so that whoever has been cut off and cast away by the Lord, and separated from his body, which is the Church, becomes, in summer as in winter, that is, in prosperity and adversity, the dwelling of birds and beasts.

Third, he places the abandonment of the field itself: and they shall be left, like an uncultivated field, which signifies the slaughter of men, after there were many beasts in the land of Egypt: these things says the Lord God, say to every fowl, and to all the birds, and to all the beasts of the field: assemble yourselves, make haste, come together from every side to my victim, which I slay for you, a great victim upon the mountains of Israel: to eat flesh, and drink blood (Ezek 39:17).

18:7.t: At that time a gift will be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn away and torn apart, from a terrible people, after whom there has been no other: from a nation waiting, waiting and trampled down, whose land the rivers have plundered, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion. After the devastation of Egypt and the destruction of its empire, Israel will by no means trust in the vanity of its shadow, but will return to the Lord, and will bring its gifts to Mount Zion, that is, to his temple, entreating him alone, whose protection is true and eternal. And we understand this to have been done under Zerubbabel and Joshua, and Ezra and Nehemiah. […]

But as those who are useless and unfruitful in the Church are cut off and cast out, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump, so on the contrary it may come about that those who had been deceived by heretical error, torn away from the Lord and rent, terrible on account of blasphemy, vainly awaiting lies, trodden down by demons, and scattered by the rivers in various directions, when they remember their God and forsake their most wicked masters, may offer a gift to the Lord of hosts nowhere else but on Mount Zion, and in the watchtower, which is interpreted as the Church. We speak more briefly because we have already said much in the book of the historical explanation.

At that time. Here the fruit of the punishment is set out, namely, that the people of the two tribes shall trust in God and shall call on his help with offerings of presents, above: and it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and they that shall escape of the house of Jacob, shall lean no more upon him that strikes them: but they shall lean upon the Lord the Holy One of Israel (Isa 10:20).

Note on the words, shall a present be brought, that the present is manifold: first, that of fervent love: a secret present quenches anger (Prov 21:14); second, of devout prayer: let my prayer rise as incense in your sight (Ps 140[141]:2); third, of perfect action: I will not receive a gift of your hand (Mal 1:10); […]

19:1.t: Egypt is sometimes understood to mean the whole world in [Isaiah], because of superstition and malediction.

Consider also, in the vision of Egypt, Isaiah saying: "behold the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and he will come into Egypt", whether he means this Egypt which is commonly understood, or the whole world. For according to John himself, the place "in which their Lord was crucified" "is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt", whether the whole world or Judea is called Sodom and Egypt. But he who upon a light cloud will come into Egypt, will first make his ascent into Judea (for it is according to reason that, when he comes again, it should first happen there). But it is called "Sodom" "where their Lord was crucified", just as also once it was said to that people and their princes: "hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; attend to the law of God, people of Gomorrah".

[Passage quoted, Isa. xix. 1-4 and the context.]

HERE the prophecy before us states that the Second after the God and Lord of the Universe, I mean the Word of God, will come into Egypt, and will come not imperceptibly nor invisibly, nor without any bodily vesture, but riding on a light cloud, or better "on light thickness": for such is said to be the meaning of the Hebrew word. Let the sons of the Hebrews tell us, then, on what occasion after Isaiah's time the Lord visited Egypt, and what Lord he was. For . the Supreme God is one: let them say how He is said to ride on "light thickness," and to alight locally on any part of the earth. And let them interpret "light thickness," and explain why the Lord is said not to visit Egypt without it. […]
19:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 20

19:1.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xix. 1.]

I SUPPOSE that the reason why it is foretold that the Lord would come to Egypt is this: The Egyptians are said to have been the first to practise the errors of polytheism and the daemons, and to have introduced superstition to the rest of mankind, and to have been concerned more than others with the activities and meddling of the daemons. And Holy Scripture witnesses that they were the enemies of God's people from the very beginning, for it is written that their ancient king confessed that he did not know the Lord, when he said: "I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." […]
19:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 2

19:1.t: Hear, for the flesh of the Lord was a shadow: Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and will come to Egypt. And David says: Protect me under the shadow of your wings. Therefore, he became a shadow emptied for us, whom the sun of iniquity had burned. We saw him in the shadow when faith first advanced. But now he illuminates the whole world: and yet we still see him through the shadow of his body, which is the Church, not yet face to face; for the eyes of the body are unable to receive the brightness of divinity. This shadow also protects the entire world every day. Therefore, the conclusion is beneficial; For God has concluded all in unbelief, that he may have mercy upon all.

What then? He Himself speaks nothing, nor Moses, nor Elias, but He that is greater than all, and more worthy of belief, the Father, uttereth a voice out of the cloud. Wherefore out of the cloud? Thus doth God ever appear. "For a cloud and darkness are round about Him;" and, "He sitteth on a light cloud;" and again, "Who maketh clouds His chariot;" and, "A cloud received Him out of their sight;" and, "As the Son of Man coming in the clouds." In order then that they might believe that the voice proceeds from God, it comes from thence. And the cloud was bright.
19:1.s: Homily 56 on the Gospel of Matthew

19:1.t: That it was Jesus himself [at the ascension] they knew from the fact that he had been conversing with them (for had they seen only from a distance, they could not have recognized him by sight), but that he is taken up into heaven the angels themselves inform them. Observe how it is ordered, that not all is done by the Spirit, but the eyes also do their part. But why did "a cloud receive him"? This too was a sure sign that he went up to heaven. Not fire, as in the case of Elijah, nor fiery chariot, but "a cloud received him"; which was a symbol of heaven, as the prophet says, "Who makes the clouds his chariot"; it is of the Father himself that this is said. Therefore he says, "on a cloud"; […]
19:1.s: Homily 2 on the Acts of the Apostles

19:1.t: The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the images of Egypt will be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt will waste away in its midst. It is the custom of the Scriptures to append plain things to obscure ones, and to bring out in open speech what they had first said in enigmas. Hence in the present place too, because he had threatened Egypt: Woe to the land that overshadows with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and the rest that the prophetic discourse wove together, he now makes the understanding plainer, and speaks with threats to Egypt itself: that not through angels but the Lord himself comes upon a light cloud, that is, a swift one, and enters Egypt, and the idols of Egypt tremble, and the heart of […]

The burden of Egypt. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Egypt. LXX: The vision of Egypt. Where in the Hebrew is written MASSA MESRAIM (משא מצרים), which we have translated The burden or weight of Egypt, for which Aquila rendered ἄρμα Αἰγύπτου, we may say that because the prophet takes up and carries the yoke of the Lord, he proved worthy to behold, or to bear, the prophecy of Egypt. Hence I marvel that the Seventy, both in Babylon translated Vision for Weight, and in Philistia and Moab and Damascus Word, and now in Egypt Vision, when in the Hebrew in all these places what is set down is not Word and Vision but MASSA (משא), that is, Burden and weight. […]

Behold, the Lord shall go up upon a light cloud, and shall enter into Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it. And I will make the Egyptians clash against the Egyptians, and a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, kingdom against kingdom. And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken in its bowels, and I will cast down its counsel; and they shall consult their idols and their diviners, and those with familiar spirits, and the soothsayers. And I will deliver Egypt into the hands of cruel lords, and a strong king shall rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts. Most of the prophecy of Egypt, which Isaiah took up or saw, I touched upon in the historical explanation; […]

And in Isaiah we read that the Lord came into Egypt on a light cloud. Egypt is taken as the world, into which the Lord is recorded to have descended in the flesh, which, brought forth from a virginal womb, was weighed down by no weight of human seed and of sins.

"Behold, the Lord comes into Egypt upon a light cloud." By the light cloud we ought to understand either, properly, the body of the Savior, because it was light and weighed down by no sin; or certainly by the light cloud we ought to understand holy Mary, weighed down by no human seed. Behold, the Lord comes into the Egypt of this world upon a light cloud, the Virgin.

"The Lord comes into Egypt upon a light cloud." See what he says. The Lord comes, the Lord and Savior, into this Egypt, in which we are: into the place of darkness, where Pharaoh is, the Lord comes. He comes only upon a light cloud. What is this light cloud? It seems to me to be holy Mary, weighed down by no human seed. This light cloud came into the world, and carries with it the Creator of the world. And what is said there in Isaiah? "The Lord comes into Egypt upon a light cloud: and the idols of Egypt shall be shattered." The Lord comes, and the idols of Egypt were shaken and struck and destroyed. This cloud destroyed the Serapeum in Alexandria; not the emperor, a mortal man, but this cloud which came into Egypt.
This he says also in Isaiah: "The Lord shall come into Egypt on a light cloud," that is, in holy Mary. On a light cloud, because he was not weighed down by human seed.

It is relevant to recall that holy Isaiah uttered a particular prophecy concerning Egypt: "And the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt within them" and the rest.In the same class with these prophets were those who rejoiced because they knew he had come whom they had been expecting. Such were Simeon and Anna, who recognized Jesus when he was born, and Elizabeth, who, in the Spirit, realized that he had been conceived, and Peter, who, by revelation of the Father, affirmed, "You are the Christ, the son of the living God."

The psalmist spoke of this solemnity [when he said], "God has ascended with a shout of jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet." He ascended with a shout of jubilation, since he sought heaven as the disciples rejoiced in the glory of his being lifted up. He ascended with the sound of the trumpet, since he went up to the throne of his heavenly kingdom as the angels heralded his return to judge the living and the dead.How God, who is present always and everywhere and does not change from place to place, ascended, the same [inspired writer] declares elsewhere, saying, "He who makes a cloud his stairway and walks upon the wings of the winds." […]

Such brief downpours are rightly compared with the shallow, inflated boasting of secular teaching which often seems to pour forth an endless, deep river of eloquence and broad learning but soon dries up entirely, as though it had never existed at all, where the sun of justice and the summer of evangelical radiance shine. The Lord himself laments this state of affairs through the prophet: "They abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns which cannot hold water." Isaiah also says, "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will come to Egypt," and again, "The water of the sea will dry up and the river will be desolate and arid." […]
19:1.s: Commentary on the Song of Songs 3:4.15

19:1.t: The blessed Virgin, being purely human, was unable to receive bodily all the plenitude of divinity. But the power of the Most High overshadowed her, that is, her body received the incorporeal light of divinity. The prophet comments on this beautifully: "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon on a light cloud and will come to Egypt," which is to say, Behold, the coeternal Word of God the Father, the light from light who was born before the ages, will receive at the end of the age a flesh and soul not burdened with any sin, and he will enter the world from a virginal womb, like a bridegroom from his chamber. Therefore, what will be born will be called holy, the Son of God. In distinction from our holiness, Jesus alone is said to be born holy.

But if the entire world is divided against itself with respect to faith in Christ, each home contains both infidels and believers. A good war is waged, therefore, to disrupt an evil peace. Isaiah also announced prophetically under the figure of Egypt: "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will come to Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence and the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them, and I will cause Egyptians to attack Egyptians." Clearly this refers to a struggle between proponents of the faith and its enemies.

Isaiah had said: The Lord is riding on a swift cloud on His way to Egypt; the idols of Egypt tremble before Him. This came about in Christ. Never was any prophet or philosopher found who could do away with idolatry: yet that is what Christ did through His apostles all over the earth.

The burden of Egypt. In this part, he threatens the destruction of the Egyptians, describing the manner and the order. And this is divided into three parts: in the first, the preparation of the punishment is described; in the second, the destruction itself: and I will deliver Egypt (Isa 19:4); in the third, the attainment of advantage, where it says, in that day there shall be five cities (Isa 19:18).

The preparation of the punishment is described as to four things.

First, as to the disposition of the enemy: he will ascend, inspiring, upon a cloud, from which comes a storm, light, because of his agility and promptness: clouds and darkness are round about him (Ps 96[97]:2). […]

19:2.t:
Hence, soon among the Egyptians as among other nations, revolution and civil war arose, between those who gave up polytheistic error and turned to the Word of Christ, and those who warred with them, urged on by their own daemons, so that brothers were parted one from the other, and the dearest fought together because of the Gospel of Christ, for the oracle says, "And Egyptians shall rise against Egyptians, and a man shall fight with his brother, and a man with his neighbour." And our Saviour Himself confirms the prophet's prediction, saying in the Gospels:

"Brother shall deliver brother to death, and father child, and children shall rise up against their parents and slay them."

And again:

"Think not that I came to give peace on earth. I say not so unto you, but division. […]
19:2.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 20

19:2.t: And I will make Egyptians rush against Egyptians, and a man will fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. When the Lord has entered Egypt and destroys a most powerful nation by his presence, the first victory will be that Egyptians fall out with Egyptians and fight one another with rebellious hatred: which, it is clear, came about in the times of the Assyrians and of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, some sitting still and others resisting. And that he foretells these things of the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah is witness, saying: Egypt is a choice and beautiful heifer; a goader will come to her from the North. […]

Then the whole heart of Egypt melted, and Egyptians rose against Egyptians, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth; I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (Matt 10:34ff.). At that time this too was fulfilled: A man's enemies are those of his own household (Mic 7:6). And a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend. […]

Third, as to the dissension of those who resist, as to external contact: and I will set, as to strangers: the Egyptians to fight against the Egyptians; as to kindred, they shall fight brother against brother; as to acquaintances and friends: and friend against friend; as to different peoples, city against city, kingdom against kingdom.

19:3.t:
It is the fact also that all the Egyptian idolaters, and the spirit of idolatry working in them, are even now conscious of their confusion, and though they make many plans against the teaching of Christ, to quench it, and abolish it from among men, yet they are ever scattered by God, as it is said in the prophecy, "And the spirit of the Egyptians shall be disturbed within them, and I will scatter their counsel."

And they who make many inquiries and ask endless questions against us of the oracles and diviners of their gods, and of the daemons that haunt the idols, and the familiar spirits who were of old so powerful among them, get no more profit of them. For Scripture says:

"And they will inquire of their gods, and their idols, and the familiar spirits."
19:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 20

19:3.t: And the spirit of Egypt will be broken in its inward parts, and I will cast down its counsel: and they will consult their images and their diviners, and those with pythonic spirits, and the soothsayers. When sedition has arisen in Egypt, some desiring to serve the Babylonian, others unwilling to submit their necks to his yoke; or else some believing in Christ, and others resisting, the spirit of Egypt will be broken and torn apart, since not all wish the same things, and all their counsel will be brought to nothing. Then they will go to their images; and they will ask the diviners, and the soothsayers, and the seers, and those schooled in the magic arts, why these things have happened.

And the spirit of Egypt was broken in its bowels, so that they were no longer of one mind; but, separated against themselves by the spiritual sword, they came to know that all their counsel had been cast down; and nonetheless, remaining in their former error, those who had refused to receive the truth of the faith consulted their idols and their diviners, and those with familiar spirits, and the soothsayers.

He sets out the diversity of wills: the spirit, that is, the will, shall be broken, that is, divided, in the bowels thereof, that is, in the inhabitants of the land: every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate (Matt 12:25).

Fourth, as to the error of taking counsel from men: and I will cast down their counsel: he catches the wise in their craftiness, and disappoints the counsel of the wicked (Job 5:13); and from demons: and they shall consult, in vain, above: and when they shall say to you: seek of pythons, and of diviners, who mutter in their enchantments (Isa 8:19).

19:4.t: But when they flee, it says, to them that falsely appear to be gods, they will receive no help, for then will God chiefly deliver them to cruel kings and rulers, when under the influence of their daemons, and in their power, they arouse persecutions against the Churches of Christ. And, please, notice the fact, that until the appearance of our Saviour Jesus Christ all Egypt had its own kings, as a separate and responsible state, and the Egyptians were autonomous and free, and their dynasty was great and famous through long ages, and it was after that date, when Augustus, in whose time our Lord was born, being the first Roman to subjugate Egypt, captured Cleopatra the last of the Ptolemies, that they came under the Roman power, laws, and enactments, losing their former autonomy and […]
19:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 20

19:4.t: And I will deliver Egypt into the hand of cruel masters, and a mighty king will rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts. We follow a twofold understanding: either of the Chaldean times, when Egypt was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar; or of the Roman empire, when, after Antony and Cleopatra had been overcome, Augustus Caesar subjugated Egypt. That the Babylonians were cruel all Scripture testifies: they did not spare little ones, and wounded them with their darts, and had no pity on pregnant women. And that the Roman kingdom was most mighty the Scripture of Daniel also testifies (Dan 7), setting forth the fourth beast, which has teeth and claws of iron.

And when they had done this, the Lord delivered them into the hand of cruel lords, according to that saying of the Apostle: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1:20), so that, oppressed by that hardest servitude, they may return to the most merciful Lord. And fittingly he calls the demons cruel lords, for nothing is crueller than they. The strong king also, who is their lord, is plainly understood as the devil, whom the Lord in the Gospel too calls the strong man; and when he is bound and overpowered, the vessels of his house and the spoil are plundered.

And I will deliver Egypt. Here he describes the destruction itself; and first, as to the slavery of the people; second, as to the desolation of the land: and the water of the sea shall be dried up (Isa 19:5); third, as to the stupidity of their wise men: the princes of Tanis are become fools (Isa 19:11).

Into the hand of cruel masters: the Assyrians, the Chaldeans, and the Romans: you shall serve your enemy (Deut 28:48).

19:5.t: And the water shall dry up from the sea, and the river shall be laid waste and dried up, and the rivers shall fail; the streams of the embankments shall be diminished and dried up. The reed and the rush shall wither; the bed of the stream shall be laid bare from its source, and every watered sowing shall be dried up; it shall wither and shall not be. And the fishers shall mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river shall lament, and those who spread a net upon the face of the water, and they shall wither away. And those who work flax shall be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine things, and its watered places shall be drooping, all who made pools to catch fish. Foolish are the princes of Tanis; the wise counsellors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel. […]

And the water will dry up from the sea, and the river will be desolated and dried up, and the streams will fail; the channels of the embankments will be diminished and dried up. The reed and the rush will wither, the bed of the stream will be laid bare from its source, and every watered sowing will be dried up, will wither, and will be no more. It is natural that, when captivity has come through the wrath of God, pestilence should follow upon his indignation, and all the elements together should rage against those who have offended God. Hence it is written in another Prophet (Jer 12) that both the birds in the air and the fish in the waters fail, so that all things are withdrawn from human use. […]

The destruction of the land he designates by the drought of the waters in which Egypt is well-endowed and rich; because the wrath of God goes before so that their waters are dried up and their animals die; or he speaks hyperbolically, as if to say: so great will be the tribulation that it will seem even to dry up the waters.

Therefore, he sets out three things. First, the manner of the drought, the water of the sea shall be dried up: that is, shall be diminished, and the river, the Nile.

19:6.t:
And the rivers, other rivers: I will make the channels of the rivers dry (Ezek 30:12).

Second, he sets out the sign of the drought: the reed and the bulrush, which are raised in the water, below: shall rise up the verdure of the reed and the bulrush (Isa 35:7).

19:7.t: All the streams too, once the head of the streams has dried up, shall be dried up, and whatever was formerly watered by the Egyptian waters shall be dried up and shall not be; so that the fishers of Egypt shall mourn, who are utterly opposed to the fishers of the Lord, and those shall lament who used to cast a hook into the river and spread a net upon the face of the water. Those who deceive people one at a time cast a hook into the turbid waters; but those who deceive many at once, speaking publicly in the synagogues of Satan and leading away whole flocks of the peoples, cast a net upon the Egyptian waters.

Third, he sets out the ruin from the drought, shall be laid bare: first, the ruin of agriculture, from its fountain, that is, from its beginning, or this to the end: he has turned rivers into a wilderness: and the sources of waters into dry ground (Ps 106[107]:33).

19:8.t: And the fishermen will mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river will lament, and those who spread a net upon the face of the water will waste away. And those who work flax will be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine things: and its watered places will be withered: all who made pools for catching fish. Take this too in two ways: that when Egypt has been laid waste and the whole province dried up with drought, the fishermen mourn, and those who used to cast a hook into the river lament, and those who worked nets and dragnets and wove little vessels of various kinds out of rush, that is, the princes and those of royal stock, and the rulers; […]
Second, the ruin of fishers: the fishers also shall mourn: I will cast you forth into the desert, and all the fish of your river (Ezek 29:5).

19:9.t: Those too shall be confounded who used to work flax to make the vestments of the priests, plaiting it and weaving fine things, which belongs properly to the art of the dialecticians. For fine things the Seventy translated byssus, which itself also is woven into the vestments of the priests.
Third, the ruin of various craftsmen, they shall be confounded that wrought in flax, which is raised in wet places. Flaccid, that is, parched, pools, fish ponds.

19:10.t: And what follows, And its watered places shall be drooping, all who made pools to catch fish, signifies that all the snares of the fishers of Egypt shall be destroyed and perish. Where we, following the sense, have translated pools made to catch fish, both in the Hebrew and in all the translators souls are set in place of fish, so that we may be drawn from the history to tropology: namely, that these fishers who made pools and pits made them for this purpose, to ensnare souls in them. It should be noted that for pools the Seventy translated ζύθον, which is a kind of drink made from grain and water, and is commonly called sabaium in the provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia, in the heathen and barbarian speech. […]

19:11.t: And the Father says to him: Return to me, calling him from the earth to heaven, whom he had sent for our salvation. Therefore, raising up his only-begotten Son, he frustrated the plan of the slanderers. Hence, Isaiah also says: The futile plan of your spirit. And the one who had been accusing and directing arrows like a hunter, has disarmed everything: he has crushed the power of those who relied on their own strength and not on God.
19:11.s: On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, 11.49

19:11.t: Then the princes of Tanis shall be foolish, which means a lowly command. For all the heretics teach a lowliness contrary to loftiness, and drag men down to the underworld, and are princes of a lowly and abject command. The counsellors too of Pharaoh, who is the king of Egypt, and is rightly rendered scatterer and divided, and separated into various parts, shall be convicted of having given foolish counsel, when the Lord destroys the wisdom of the wise and rejects the understanding of the prudent (1 Cor 1).

How do you say to Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you, and declare what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools, the princes of Memphis have withered; they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples. The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of giddiness, and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man errs and vomits. And there shall be no work for Egypt which may make the head and the tail, bending and curbing. The heretics are accustomed to say to their king, or Pharaoh: We are sons of the wise, who handed down the Apostolic teaching to us from the beginning; […]

The princes of Tanis are foolish; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel: how will you say to Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where now are your wise men? Let them announce to you and show what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools, the princes of Memphis have withered: they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples. That Tanis was the metropolis of Egypt the Psalmist also declares, because Moses worked there the many signs which are described in Exodus: He set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis (Ps 77 [78]:43). That Memphis too was given over to the magic arts, the traces of its old error show to the present time. […]

The princes of Tanis are become fools. Here he sets out the stupidity of their men; and first, as to error in their counsels; second, as to fear in wars, where it says, in that day Egypt shall be like unto women (Isa 19:16).

Concerning the first, he does three things. First, he mocks the foolishness of their wise men as to deliberation: the princes, that is, the philosophers, of Tanis, where study flourished, are become fools: every man is become foolish by his knowledge (Jer 51:17); as to the promulgation of counsel: wise counselors; […]

19:12.t: These he now asks, or the very king of the heretics, where are his wise men who despised the simplicity of the Church; and he compels them to answer what the Lord Sabaoth has purposed concerning the Egypt of this world, and what he will do at the consummation.

Second, he mocks the confidence of the king: where now, and first, the question, below: there is none that can save you (Isa 47:15); second, the answer: fools have withered away, that is, have failed, as above.

19:13.t: The princes of Tanis, who held the lowly command of the heretics, are proved to be fools. All the princes of Memphis have withered, who were tainted with the boasting of eloquence and of the mouth. For Memphis means mouth or from the mouth, and μεταφορικῶς signifies speech. And what follows: They have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples, or according to the Seventy: they shall deceive Egypt by tribes, signifies that the kingdom of worldly wisdom is shown to be foolish, and the princes of the several doctrines, who are interpreted as the tribes, are convicted of having had foolish teachers.

Third, he mocks the laziness of the deceived people: they have deceived. First, he sets out the deception of the wise: they have deceived the angle, that is, the kingdom, in which many are joined together like walls in an angle, below: your wisdom, and, your knowledge, has deceived you (Isa 47:10).

19:14.t: The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of giddiness: and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man errs and vomits: and Egypt will have no work to do, head and tail, bending and bridling. Let us speak first of the translation, and afterwards we shall discuss what is written. For spirit of giddiness one can also translate spirit of error. In what we have translated, bending and bridling, we can also say bent and wanton, so that we understand the old man and the boy. For we, while translating what is written in haste, misled by its ambiguity, rendered the Hebrew word AGMON (אגמון) as bridling, which Aquila translated more expressively στρεβλοῦντα, that is, one who does nothing rightly but everything perversely, so as to signify a boy. […]

For the Lord has mingled for them a spirit of giddiness, or of errors, according to what is written: And as they did not see fit to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate mind (Rom 1:28). And as he who is holy can say with Isaiah, We shall make the spirit of your salvation upon the earth, so he who is a sinner will make a spirit of error, that is, a spirit of wickedness, according to what we read also in Jeremiah: Your own transgression shall reprove you, and your wickedness shall rebuke you (Jer 2:19). […]

Second, the permission of God: the Lord has mingled, often said metaphorically, the spirit of giddiness, that is, the spirit of error, like one who suffers giddiness: the Lord has given a lying spirit in the mouth of all your prophets (1 Kgs 22:23).

19:15.t: Third, the error of the people themselves: and they have caused Egypt to err. Head, namely, neither with respect to the beginning; tail, nor the end; that bends down, in respect to the old man; that holds back, in respect to the youth, who lacks restraint, or to the lascivious: but evil men and seducers shall grow worse and worse (2 Tim 3:13).

19:16.t: In that day Egypt shall be like women, and shall be amazed, and shall fear before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he shall shake over it. And the land of Judah shall be a festival to Egypt; everyone who remembers it shall tremble before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has purposed concerning it. At that time (for that, as we have often said, is what day signifies), when the Lord has mingled a spirit of error and giddiness, so that Egypt vomits up the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, understanding its error and its former drunkenness, Egypt shall fear like a woman: not with the chance fear that is wont to befall men, whom Egypt does not love but strangles and kills, but with the fear of women, whom alone Pharaoh wishes to live. […]

In that day Egypt will be like women, and they will be astonished and afraid before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he will shake over it. And the land of Judah will be a festival to Egypt: everyone who remembers it will tremble before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has devised against it. I think it better even to censure one's own error than, while blushing to confess one's inexperience, to persist in error. In what I translated, And the land of Judah will be a festival to Egypt, for festival one reads in the Hebrew AGGA (חגה), which can be interpreted both as festival (whence Haggai too is rendered festive) and as fear; […]
In that day. Here he threatens fear of the strong. And first, he places the fear itself, like unto women, feeble and weak: their strength has failed, and they are become as women (Jer 51:30).

19:17.t: Then the land of Judah, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, the Law and the Prophets, the Gospels and the epistles of the Apostles, shall be a festival to Egypt, if it comes to know them; or a fear, if by comparison with their teaching and truth it understands that it has held a lie. Everyone who remembers this land shall tremble with that trembling which leads to life: For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Prov 9:10). And we can take this not only of the consummation of the world, but of the present time as well: that every heretic fears a churchman learned in heavenly teachings, and is terrified at the remembrance of him. And he shall fear and tremble at the counsel of the Lord, which he has purposed concerning the Egypt of this world. […]

Second, the reason for the fear, and the land of Judah shall be a terror to Egypt, namely, the memory of the evils which they did to them, turning them from the worship of God, for which they will know that the wrath of God has befallen them: now I remember the evils that I did in Jerusalem (1 Macc 6:12).

19:18.t: In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan, and swearing by the Lord of hosts: one will be called the city of the sun. For city of the sun the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated asedec, which one of our writers interprets as city of righteousness; and, led astray by error, because according to the Hebrew ARES (חרס) is written, he thinks it means earth, which is written with other letters. Symmachus, then, translated better: one will be called the city of the sun; for ARES, an ambiguous word, means both potsherd and sun, because both are parched and dry. Onias, not understanding this place, built a temple in Egypt in the town of Ἡλιοπόλεως. Read the Histories of Josephus (Josephus, book 12, chapter 9). […]

In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue, and swearing by the Lord of hosts: one shall be called the city of the sun. The hand of the Lord lifted up or shaken over Egypt is of great profit, so that the land of Judah becomes a fear to it, and everyone who remembers it trembles. At that time five cities in the land of Egypt shall speak the tongue of Canaan, which most of our writers understand as the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. When we look on a woman to lust after her, our sight speaks the Egyptian tongue. When we hear a judgment of blood, though the Lord says, You shall not receive a vain report (Exod 23:1, LXX), our hearing speaks the Egyptian tongue. […]

The servant is "faithful in very little" who does not defile the word of God but speaks as though he were speaking from God and with God in Christ. For whatever gifts we receive at present are very little and very poor in comparison with those of the future, since "now we know only partially and prophesy only partially, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away." The ten cities are souls coming to the grace of the gospel through the word of the law. And because he must be glorified, the one who will invest the money of the word worthily for God is placed over them. Hence one successful investor addressed the cities over whom he presided, that is, the souls whose governance he had accepted, asking, "What is our hope or joy or crown of glory? […]

It is fitting that there be a father of fathers, whom we call the Pope, who yet, because of his humility, has four patriarchs: those of Constantinople, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Antioch. And of these Isaias says: "There shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Chanaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts." But Rome is universal, wherefore "one shall be called 'City of the Sun.'" For while the other four sees have full authority over the neighboring churches, yet, like the sun, Rome in its universality has the fullness of power over them all.

In that day. Here the consequence or the consolation is set out, namely their conversion. And first, the threefold sign of their conversion; the first of which is an oath: swearing, below: he shall swear by God, amen: because the former distresses are forgotten (Isa 65:16); the city of the sun, Heliopolis, the language of Chanaan, which is close to the language of the Jews, so that even in language they will agree with the people of God; for some Syrians, who kept their own language, were transplanted in these cities by Nabuchodonosor.

19:19.t:
And Isaiah literally shouts and cries his prophecy to the same effect:

"19. There shall be an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt. . . . And the Lord shall be known to the Egyptians ... 20. And he shall send to them a man who shall save them, . . . 21, and the Egyptians shall know the Lord in that day, and shall offer sacrifice, and vow vows to the Lord and pay (them). And they shall he turned to the Lord, and he shall hear them and heal them."

Do we not say truly then that the prophets were inspired to foretell a change of the Mosaic Law, nay its end and conclusion? Moses lays down that the altar and the sacrifices should be nowhere else on earth but in Judaea, and there only in one city. […]
19:19.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 6

19:19.t: And if they say that they were chosen out to act as priests and to offer worship to God, it can be shewn that the Word promised that He would give to the Gentiles an equal share in His service, when He said: "Render to the Lord, O ye kindreds of the nations, render to the Lord glory and honour: bring sacrifices and come into his courts." To which the oracle in Isaiah may be conjoined, which says: "There shall be an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt . . . and the Egyptians will know the Lord. And they shall do sacrifice, and say prayers to the Lord, and offer." And in this you will understand that it is prophesied that an altar will be built to the Lord away from Jerusalem in Egypt, and that the Egyptians will there offer sacrifice, say prayers and give gifts to the Lord. […]
19:19.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

19:19.t:
[Passages quoted, Isa. xix. 1-3; xix. 19-21.]

THIS is a passage that I have already partly expounded. Now if the Egyptians are not seen in our own time deserting their ancestral gods and calling upon the God of the prophets; if throughout Egypt in every locality, town and country there are not altars erected to the God that was formerly acknowledged only by the Hebrews; if the idols of Egypt have not been shaken, for that the power of the daemons that hung about them is gone, and the ancient superstition driven from the soul of the Egyptians; […]
19:19.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 5

19:19.t: [Daniel 11:13-14] "And the king of the North shall return and shall prepare a much greater multitude than before, and in the end of times and years he shall come in haste with a large army and great resources. And in those times many shall rise up against the king of the South." This indicates that Antiochus the Great, who despised the worthlessness of Ptolemy Philopator (for he had fallen desperately in love with a lute-player named Agathoclea and also her brother, retaining Agatho-cles himself as his concubine and afterwards appointing him as general of Egypt), assembled a huge army from the upper regions of Babylon. And since Ptolemy Philopator was now dead, Antiochus broke his treaty and set his army in motion against Philopator's four-year-old son, who was called Epiphanes. […]
19:19.s: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER ELEVEN

19:19.t: In that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and an inscription to the Lord at its border. And it will be for a sign and for a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they will cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior and a defender to free them. And the Lord will be known by Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day, and will worship him with victims and gifts, and will vow vows to the Lord and pay them. From this place to the end of the Egyptian Vision, or Burden, both the Jews and our writers would have it understood of the coming of Christ; but they put off their hopes into the future, while we hold them as already accomplished. […]

In that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar of the Lord at its border. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he shall send them a Savior and a defender to deliver them; and the Lord shall be known by Egypt. In sequence to what he had said above, In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue, and swearing by the Lord of hosts, there now follows: There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, which Onias, according to Josephus (Antiquities, book 13, ch. 6), misunderstanding it, tried to fulfil. […]

The prophet Isaiah says this about Egypt: "In that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the land of the Egyptians and an inscription to the Lord at its border. It will be a sign forever to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians, for they will cry to the Lord against their assailants, and the Lord will send them a savior who will be determined to save them. And the Lord will be known to the Egyptians, and they will fear the Lord in that day and make sacrifices to him and promise vows to him and fulfill them. And the Lord will strike the Egyptians with plagues and heal them by his mercy, and they will turn to the Lord, and he will listen to them and heal them." What do they [i.e., members of the Donatist sect] say to this? […]
19:19.s: LETTER TO THE CATHOLICS ON THE SECT OF DONATISTS 16:41-42

19:19.t: The second sign is a sacred building: an altar of the Lord; and a monument, for they worshipped many gods, as it says in Acts 17. Some say that this was fulfilled in the time of the Maccabees, when many Jews were fleeing into Egypt, and Onias, wishing to fulfill this prophecy, built an altar against the precept of the law. Which is against Deuteronomy 12: you shall not build an altar to me; and which is denounced in Daniel 11:14, and the children of prevaricators of your people shall lift up themselves to fulfill the vision, and they shall fall; hence it is clear that this can only be understood of the building of altars for Christian worship.

19:20.t: He said, I do not have a man; that is, because through a man is death, and through a man is the resurrection of the dead. He could not descend, he could not be saved, who did not believe that our Lord Jesus had taken flesh from the Virgin. But this one who was waiting for the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, expecting him of whom it was said: And the Lord will send a man to save them; he said: I do not have a man; and therefore he deserved to come to health, because he believed in the one who was coming.

Next he adds: And it will be for a sign and for a testimony, namely of the Lord's passion. Then those who have believed, when Egyptians rush against Egyptians, and a man fights against his brother, and city battles against city, when the time of persecution has broken upon them, will implore the mercy of the Lord, and at once the Savior will come, that is, Jesus, for that is what it means in our language.
The third sign is that they call on the help of God, they shall cry to the Lord; a Savior, Jesus: he shall cry to me, and I will hear him (Ps 90[91]:15).

19:21.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xix. 1.]

I SUPPOSE that the reason why it is foretold that the Lord would come to Egypt is this: The Egyptians are said to have been the first to practise the errors of polytheism and the daemons, and to have introduced superstition to the rest of mankind, and to have been concerned more than others with the activities and meddling of the daemons. And Holy Scripture witnesses that they were the enemies of God's people from the very beginning, for it is written that their ancient king confessed that he did not know the Lord, when he said: "I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." […]
19:21.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 2

19:21.t: And the Lord will be known by the Egyptians, and they will know him, whether the persecutors who have been overcome, or the believers set free by his present help. And they will worship him with victims and gifts, and will vow vows to the Lord and pay them. Let the Jews answer: It is commanded in the Law that no altar be made except in the one place which the Lord God has chosen, and that victims be sacrificed only by priests of the Levitical race (Deut 26). Behold, Isaiah teaches openly that the Egyptians know the Lord and worship him, and offer victims and gifts, and vow vows and pay them. If the Egyptians have a priesthood, the testimony of Paul is fulfilled in them as well, who says: When the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law (Heb 7:12).

And the Egyptians shall know the Lord in that day, and shall worship him with sacrifices and gifts, and they shall vow vows to the Lord and pay them. And the Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague, and shall heal it; and they shall return to the Lord, and he shall be appeased toward them, and shall heal them. After the Egyptians have come to know the Lord, they shall worship him with spiritual sacrifices and gifts; and they shall vow vows to the Lord and pay them, and shall say with David: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit (Ps 50 [51]:19), and: The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice (Ps 140 [141]:2); […]

Second, he sets out the manner of their conversion. And first, as to the undertaking of faith: and the Lord shall be known: all shall know me from the least of them even to the greatest, says the Lord (Jer 31:34); second, as to the offering of sacrifices and vows: and they shall worship: in every place there is offered to my name a clean oblation (Mal 1:11).

19:22.t: And the Lord will strike Egypt with a blow, and will heal it: and they will turn to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them, and will heal them. For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. Persecution serves not for the denial of believers, but for their proving and their crown.

It is asked: if a savior and defender was sent to the Egyptians to deliver them from their straits, how is it now said, The Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague? But let us consider what follows: And he shall heal it. For whom the Lord loves he chastens (Heb 12). And the Savior himself in Psalm 68 (69) says to the Father: For they have persecuted him whom you struck, and they have added to the pain of my wounds (Ps 68 [69]:27). If, then, he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us, that by his bruise and wounds we might be healed (Rom 8), the Lord delivered up the martyrs too to suffering, but he will heal them again in the resurrection, so that by their wounds the faith of believers may be confirmed. […]
Third, as to the remission of sins: and the Lord shall strike, first, through many punishments, and shall heal from sin: he wounds, and cures: he strikes, and his hands shall heal (Job 5:18).

19:23.t: In that day there will be a road from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian will enter Egypt, and the Egyptian the Assyrians: and the Egyptians will serve Assyria. Before the coming of Christ each nation had its own king, and no one could go from one nation to another; but in the Roman empire all things have been made one. Let the learned reader turn over the ancient histories, and he will find that the whole region from the Euphrates to the Tigris, and all between, belonged to the Assyrians. Those, therefore, whom the ancients called Assyrians we now call Syrians, naming the whole from the part. And when it is said: The Egyptians will serve the Syrians, it is to be taken either thus: that Roman legions furnished with Syrian soldiers guard Egypt; […]

In that day there shall be a way from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian shall enter into Egypt, and the Egyptian into the Assyrians; and the Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians. As we have shown that the other things which go before befell the Egyptians in a good sense, namely, five cities in their land speaking the Canaanite tongue and swearing by the Lord, and the altar of the Lord set in the midst of the land of Egypt, and the pillar, and the witness, and the sign, and the savior who should deliver them; and that the Lord should be known by the Egyptians, and they themselves should know him; […]

Third, he sets out the threefold effect of their conversion, namely, peace: in that day there shall be a way, which could not exist before because of the various kingdoms, which, when the Lord was born, were joined under the Romans; they shall serve, each other in trade; or because Syrian soldiers were in the Roman legions that guarded Egypt, above: nation shall not lift up sword against nation (Isa 2:4).

19:24.t: In that day Israel will be the third with the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands to the Assyrian: but my inheritance is Israel. By no means will Israel be crushed in the middle between Egypt and the Assyrian, now with the Antiochi and Demetrii dragging the kingdom of Judah to themselves, now with the Ptolemies claiming its possession for themselves; but it too, established under the Roman empire, and through this under the empire of Christ, will be of the same condition as Egypt and the Assyrians, and will be blessed in all the earth. For out of Zion will go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

In that day Israel shall be the third to the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands the Assyrian; but my inheritance is Israel. Israel shall be the third in Egypt and among the Assyrians, that he may mingle the whole lump with the leaven of his blessing, and that those who formerly were at hostile variance with one another may be joined together by this clasp of blessing; and that Egypt may be the people of God, and the Assyrian the work of his hands, but Israel his inheritance. The Egyptian is blessed by the Lord, because he is blessed through fellowship with Israel. And the Assyrian is the work of his hands, because in him he has shown his clemency. […]

Second, he promises the second effect, the truth of faith: in that day shall Israel be the third to the Egyptian and the Assyrian, at the same time and equally serving the Romans, and in unity of faith: there shall be one fold and one shepherd (John 10:16); there is no distinction of the Jew and the Greek (Rom 10:12).

19:25.t: Then it will be said by the Lord: Blessed is my people of Egypt: when, led not by Moses but by Christ the Lord, countless thousands of men have filled the deserts and, with Pharaoh drowned, have said in the desert: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified: horse and rider he has cast into the sea (Exod 15:1). Then also the work of the hands of the Lord will be among the Assyrians; for these nations above all, Egypt and Mesopotamia, flourish with swarms of monks, and vie with one another in equal piety. And the inheritance of Christ is Israel, that is, the places of his nativity, and of his cross, and of his resurrection and ascension, to which men flock from the whole world.

Third, he sets out the third effect, namely, divine blessing: it, namely, Israel, shall be a blessing, for, through the apostles, the whole world received the blessing of God; Israel is my inheritance, for it was there that he was born and fulfilled the mysteries of our salvation: he has blessed the house of Israel (Ps 113:20[115:12]).

20:1.t: Someone perhaps will say, "Was it not disgraceful for a man to walk naked among the people since he must meet both men and women? Must not his appearance have shocked the gaze of all, but especially that of women? Do we not ourselves generally abhor the sight of naked men? And are not men's private parts covered with clothing that they may not offend the gaze of onlookers by their unsightliness?" I agree, but you must consider what this act represented and what was the reason for this outward show; it was that the young Jewish youths and maidens would be led away into exile and walk naked, "as my servant Isaiah walked," he says, "naked and barefoot." […]

That it may be more fully clear that prophets look not to themselves or what lies at their feet but to heavenly things, Stephen, when he was being stoned, saw the heavens open and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Then he did not feel the blows of the stones, he did not heed the wounds of his body, but, fastening his eyes on Christ, he clung to him.
