Those crossing the sea have filled you; in many waters the seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river is its produce. That Tyre delights in trade and is the emporium of the whole world, both present times prove and Ezekiel describes at length. And that merchants cross the seas in carrying their goods, there is no one who doubts; nor does the city itself have such great wealth from the land of its own region, which is very narrow and hemmed in by the borders of Galilee and of Damascus, as it has from the shipping of goods.

For those who dwell in this isle are like no others than merchants, or carriers, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and pass from one vice to another. And we dwell in an isle as long as we are beaten by the temptations of this world, and on every side our isle and little boat is struck by the waves of the sea. Now the merchants of this isle are from Sidon, which means huntress, and in which dwell very many hunters, of whom it is written: He will deliver you from the snare of the hunters (Ps 90 [91]:3). And in another place the saint rejoices that he has been delivered from their snares, saying: Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (Ps 123 [124]:7).

Second, he sets out their stupor: be silent, adding three things in which they gloried, namely, in the fortification of their position: you that dwell in the island; in the abundance of their merchandise: trade, that is, in which they trade; have filled you, with riches; in abundance of grain: the seed of the river Nile, that is, her harvest, and revenue, namely of Tyre, for much wheat came to them from Egypt, and therefore she is become the mart of the nations: say to Tyre that dwells at the entry of the sea, being the mart of the people for many islands (Ezek 27:3).

23:3.t: The whole Nile and the fertility of Egypt pour into Tyre from close at hand. For Nile, which we read among the Hebrews as SIOR (שיחר), the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted merchants; this word means turbid, and by this signifies the waters of the Nile, as Jeremiah testifies: What have you to do with Egypt, that you should drink the waters of Geon? (Jer 2:18): for which in the Hebrew there is Sior, that is, turbid.

And all the merchants of the nations are compared to crops which quickly wither, or to the harvests of the river, which have their rain not from heaven but from the earth; and therefore they will perish with the nations. Where we read the seed of merchants, in the Hebrew is written the seed of sior, by which the Nile is understood, because it has turbid waters with which the crops of Egypt are watered.

23:4.t: Therefore, after being so often ploughed by returning merchants, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, has said the sea." This is the voice of the fatigued element, as it were, saying, "Be ashamed, Sidon"; that is: Merchant, you accuse my waves although you yourself are more restless than they. Blush indeed for shame since you are not disturbed by peril. More modest are the winds than your desires. They have their rests; never do your cravings for gain take holiday. Even when the weather is quiet, never are your ships quiet. The water is churned under the oar when it is at rest from the blast. "I have not been in labor," it says, "nor have I reared, nor have I nourished up young men." Why do they disquiet me whom I do not know, whom I do not acknowledge?

But this is far from the accepted opinion. As a matter of fact, the farmer cleaves the earth ‘with deep-driven plough’; ‘stripped he ploughs, stripped he sows’; stripped in the glowing ‘heat he thrashes on the floor the parched ears.’ The merchant, impatient when the east winds are blowing, ploughs the sea often when the course is unsafe. Insolent and rash men such as these are condemned by the Prophet, who says: ‘Be thou ashamed, O Sidon, the sea speaketh,’ that is to say, if dangers do not move you, then shame can check and modesty confound you. ‘Be thou ashamed, O Sidon,’ in which there is no place for virtue, no care for safety, no young men exercised in arms and ready to fight in defense of their country. […]

Be ashamed, O Sidon: for the sea has spoken, the strength of the sea, saying: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth, and I have not nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. I said above that Tyre is a colony of the Sidonians. Hear, then, O mother, all the seas crying out together against your daughter, and in a manner uttering a voice, though by nature they cannot speak: In vain have I brought riches together; to no purpose have I gathered wealth from the whole world into Tyre: she that was rich, she that was luxurious, and once rejoiced in a multitude of peoples, in which a throng of mortals was born, a troop of children, swarms of youth, whose streets rang with the games of virgins and infants, of young men and girls, has now been reduced to solitude. […]

Be ashamed, O Sidon, said the sea; and the strength of the sea said: I have not travailed, nor brought forth, nor nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. And when it is heard in Egypt, pain shall seize them over Tyre. The sea of this world, in which dwell small animals with great, and the dragon which God formed to be mocked, seeing that those who had formerly been taken by the demons have been taken by the hunters of Christ, who hunt from every mountain and hill, speaks to the opposing power of the hunters, which Sidon means, and says to it: Be ashamed, O Sidon; for I have not travailed nor brought forth, nor nourished the young men taken by you, nor brought up the virgins whose folly is condemned in the Gospel (Matt 25). […]

Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea, when the life of one who is fortified and supposedly steadfast is reprobated in comparison with the lives of those who are worldly and are being tossed about in this world. For often there are those who, returning to the Lord after their sins of the flesh, evince themselves the more zealous in doing good works, as they realize they were worthy of condemnation for their deeds. And often certain people who persevere in preserving the integrity of the flesh, on perceiving that they have less to deplore, think to themselves that the innocence of their lives is sufficient and do not arouse themselves by zealously striving to be fervent in spirit.

Divine Providence has compassed us about and cut off all excuse. All openings to people's equivocating arts are in every way closed. A Gentile, one without the law, is brought forward to confound the iniquity of those that are under the law; which is well and summarily shown by the prophet, when he says, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea." For in Sidon we have a figure of the steadfastness of those settled upon the foundation of the law, and in the sea of the life of the Gentiles. […]
23:4.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Preface to Book 1, Section 5

23:4.t: Third, he sets out the confusion of their neighbors. And first, of the Sidonians, whose colony Tyre was: the sea, that is, traders of the sea, speaks: be you ashamed, O Sidon, for you did not defend Tyre; for my strength, that is, Tyre, is saying: I have not been in labor, that is: it profited me not to have been in labor, for I was captured. Or otherwise: the sea, that is, the strength of the sea, that is, the traders who were strong on the sea, speaks: be you ashamed, O Sidon, saying: I have not been in labor, in the defense of Tyre. Or otherwise: Sidon speaks: O Sea, even the strength of the sea, that is, Tyre, be ashamed, you, Tyre, saying what follows. […]

23:5.t: When it has been heard in Egypt, they will grieve when they hear of Tyre. This is plain: that the Egyptians, after they have heard that a most mighty and neighboring nation has been destroyed by a long siege, know that destruction is drawing near to them too.

When Egypt hears this, which in Hebrew is called MESRAIM (מצרים), which means ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, afflicting and constraining, it too will be terrified, understanding that it too will suffer the same things that Tyre has suffered. And while this is referred to all vices, it can also be perceived in the diversity of the heresies, when, one heresy being taken, another trembles, and in the confusion of one the other perceives that it is to be taken. And as it is said of Sodom: For if the signs had been done in them which were done in Capernaum, they would have remained until this day; […]
Second, of the Egyptians: when it shall be heard in Egypt: behold I do a thing in Israel: and whosoever shall hear it, both his ears shall tingle (1 Sam 3:11).

23:6.t: Cross the seas, howl, you who dwell in the island. Again, for sea and Tharsis the Seventy translated Carthage. We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, when they saw no hope of escape, embarked on ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Hence too it is said in Ezekiel: No wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29): because all the wealth of the city had been carried away, and all the nobles had left it empty.

Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in this isle. Is not this your disgrace from the beginning, before she was delivered up? Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn. What follows, Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn, has been added from the Hebrew, and is marked beforehand with an asterisk, that is, with shining stars. O Tyrians, you who dwell in distress and abide in an isle, exposed on every side to the waves of temptations, depart from it, and go to Carthage, that is, Tharsis, and hasten to true joy, mourning your old sins and the ancient disgrace which you either inflicted on others or suffered from them. […]

Pass over the seas. Here he foretells the flight of the fearful, as to those who, when Nabuchodonosor was attacking the city, fled into Egypt with their ships. And first, he exhorts them to flight, second, to constancy or haste of flight: pass your land (Isa 23:10). Concerning the first, he does three things. First, the flight of the fearful: pass over, you who flee, howl, you who remain, above: the branches thereof are left, they are gone over the sea (Isa 16:8).

23:7.t:
Is not this yours, which gloried from the days of old in its antiquity? He convicts Tyre of pride, because it gloried in the antiquity of its founding and did not look to God, but, recalling the names of its fathers, thought itself eternal.

Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad. He means those who had remained in the city and were led captive to Babylon.

Second, the ignominy of those who remain: is this not; and concerning this, he does two things. First, he foretells their ignominy, recalling first their former glory: is not this yours, namely, your city? Her feet shall carry her afar off, as to those taken captive: my delicate ones have walked rough ways (Bar 4:26).

23:8.t:
Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned? Read Ezekiel again (Ezek 27), and you will learn from the lament over its prince how great the glory of Tyre was. He calls it crowned because, as a king among a great multitude of men raises his head adorned with a diadem, so Tyre, gleaming and lofty in riches, and shining with gold and gems and silk and purple, was esteemed a queen among all nations.

Whose merchants are princes, its traders the renowned of the earth. We marvel that the envoy of Pyrrhus once said of the city of Rome: I have seen a city of kings. […]

Who has purposed these things against Tyre? Is she less, or does she not prevail? Her merchants are princes of Canaan, the renowned of the earth. The Lord Sabaoth has purposed to dissolve all the insolence of those who glory, and to dishonour all that is renowned upon the earth. The word Canaan has been added from the edition of Theodotion; for it Aquila translated merchants. The Holy Spirit therefore asks, or rather by the question affirms, that the Lord has purposed these things against the princes of Tyre, whose whole industry is to seek wealth by trading. […]

Third, wonder, setting out first the question of the wonderer: who knew this one crowned, as though queen of other cities; whose merchants were princes, because of their excessive luxuries: how are you fallen, that dwell in the sea, renowned city that was strong in the sea, with your inhabitants? (Ezek 26:17).

23:9.t: The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory, and to bring into ignominy all the renowned of the earth. Because above, in the manner of one asking, he had said: Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned?, now he himself answers: It is not that the threads of the fates have been spun thus, as fools think; it is not that the wheel of fortune has run; but it has been accomplished by the judgment of God and by his will, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4); and he reminds the arrogant of their condition, so that through misery they may learn the power of him whose clemency they had refused to feel through his benefits.

The Lord of hosts, then, purposed this counsel: to dissolve the most wicked bonds of the merchants, or rather to scatter the compacted injury through which all who are subject to Tyre grow proud. And as for what he added, and to dishonour all that is glorious upon the earth, the Lord is not the author of dishonour, but shows to be shameful what lies open to shame of itself. This indeed we read in Leviticus also concerning the Priests: With defilement he has defiled him (Lev 21), the priest, no doubt: not that he is the author of the defilement, but that he shows him to be defiled who formerly seemed clean to very many.
And he adds the response: the Lord of hosts has designed it, to pull down the pride of all glory: scatter the proud in your indignation, and behold every arrogant man, and humble him (Job 40:6).

23:10.t: Pass through your land like a river, daughter of the sea: there is no girdle for you any more. As, he says, a river, or, as the Hebrew has it more expressively, a stream, for it is called IOR (יאר), is easily crossed on foot, so you too, led into captivity, will pass through your land, O daughter of the sea, either because you are an island, or because it was written of you above: The sea has spoken, the strength of the sea: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth. And what sense his next words have, there is no girdle for you any more, Symmachus teaches more openly: you will no longer be able to resist, that is, you will not have the strength, nor your loins girded for fighting, so as to be able to go out against your adversaries.

Work your land; for ships no longer come from Carthage, and your hand no longer prevails, which provokes kings on the sea. The edition of the Seventy differs greatly in this place from the other translators and from the Hebrew itself; but let us pursue our purpose. Above he had said: Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in the isle. Now he says the opposite: since ships no longer come from Carthage, work your land. For it profited Tyre that the foreign ships perished, so that she is compelled to work her own land, of which it is said in the Proverbs: He who works his land shall be filled with bread (Prov 12:11): so that she may live not from the uncertain hazard of the waves and of shipwrecks, but from the fruits of her own work, of which it is sung in the psalms to the righteous […]

Pass your land. Here he exhorts them to flee quickly. And first, he sets out the exhortation: pass your land as a river, which is crossed quickly by boat: furnish yourself to go into exile, you daughter inhabitant of Egypt (Jer 46:19). Second, he assigns the reason on their own part: you have a girdle, that is, strength, no more: behold I have made you small among the nations (Obad 1:2). Otherwise, on the part of God: he stretched out his hand over the sea, above: the Lord shall lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt (Isa 11:15).

23:11.t: He has stretched out his hand over the sea, he has troubled kingdoms. Who stretched out his hand? From the very tenor of the discourse there is no doubt that it is God, of whom he said above: The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory. He stretched out his hand, then, over all the seas, signifying the world and the earth, and troubled all the nations, among which you too, O Tyre, were troubled; or else over the sea, in which you are properly situated.

The Lord has given command against Canaan, to crush its strong ones. He shows what the sea is over which the Lord stretched out his hand, saying: He has given command against Canaan. For Tyre was founded in the land of Canaan. Read the Scriptures, and especially the Gospel (Mark 7), where the Syrophoenician woman, pleading for her daughter, comes out of the land of Canaan, and is called a Canaanite woman. And at the same time, because he had said: He has stretched out his hand, lest you should believe that the Lord works with limbs and by bodily function, he added, he has given command, so that for God to have done is to have commanded.

The Lord Sabaoth has commanded concerning Canaan to destroy its strength, and they shall say: You shall no more do injury and iniquity to the virgin daughter of Sidon. That Tyre and Sidon are in the land of Canaan we have shown above also, setting forth the testimony of the Gospel, in which we read that the Canaanite woman, or Syrophoenician, came out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon and met the Lord the Savior. Now every soul that is set amid the waves of the world and is carried about by every wind of doctrine is to be called Canaan, which means as it were a tossing or a shaking. Hence it is said also to the adulterous old man: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you (Dan 13). […]

The Lord has given a charge. Here he threatens destruction. And first, the scourge of persecution; second, he foretells the mourning of compassion: howl (Isa 23:14); third, he designates the time of destruction: and it shall come to pass in that day (Isa 23:15). Concerning the first, he does three things. First, setting out divine indignation, the precept: the Lord has given a charge, to Nabuchodonosor, against Chanaan, in which Tyre is located: the Lord said to me: go up to this land, and destroy it (2 Kgs 18:25).

23:12.t: And he said: You will no more glory, suffering calumny, O virgin daughter of Sidon; rise, cross over to Cethim: there too there will be no rest for you. God, who devised to pull down the pride of all glory, who gave command against Canaan to crush its strong ones, himself says: You will by no means glory any longer, nor trust in your own power. O virgin daughter of Sidon, that is, colony of the Sidonians, you will indeed flee in ships to the islands of the West, or to Cyprus, and the other lands of Macedonia and Greece; but there too, with God against you, you will not be able to find rest. Besides, everyone who is a wanderer and a stranger in the world, and of uncertain abode, is always in straits, continually in grief.

If you go to the Kittim, not even there shall there be rest for you; and if to the land of the Chaldeans, it too has been laid waste by the Assyrians. Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts, they raised its tower: its wall has fallen. What follows has been added from the edition of Theodotion under asterisks: Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts; they raised its tower; and joined without asterisks: its wall has fallen. The Kittim are interpreted a stroke consummated or perfect; the Chaldeans in this place, as it were breasts; the Assyrians, reproving. The etymology of Siim we too have not been able to find, and the other translators rendered it by the very name with which it is written among the Hebrews. […]

And the intended end: and he said: you shall glory no more, O virgin daughter of Sidon, who sustain calumny, accused of pride: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the rich man glory in his riches (Jer 9:23); and he excludes any remedy: arise and sail over to Cethim, there also you shall have no rest: neither shall you be quiet, even in those nations, nor shall there be any rest for the sole of your foot (Deut 28:65).

23:13.t: Behold the land of the Chaldeans, such a people there was not: Assyria founded it for captivity; they carried away its mighty men, they undermined its houses, they made it a ruin. Howl, you ships of the sea, for your strength has been laid waste. Because he had said above: Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad; and again, Pass through your land like a river; and because the people of Tyre was twofold, those who had fled and crossed over to Cethim, and those who had remained in the city, he speaks to both. Of those who had fled he said above: Rise, cross over to Cethim, there too there will be no rest for you. […]

Second, he sets out the strength of the enemy: behold the land of the Chaldeans, there was not such a people, before them; the Assyrians, or Nabuchodonosor, founded it: is not this Babylon, which I have built? (Dan 4:27).

Third, he sets out the destruction as to the subjugation of men: they have led away the strong ones thereof into captivity, above: their strong ones, and their people, and their high and glorious ones shall go down into it (Isa 5:14); as to the destruction of houses: they have destroyed the houses, above: it shall be as a ruinous heap of stones (Isa 17:1).

23:14.t: "Howl," he says—he repeats it—"O you ships of Carthage, for your strength is laid waste. And it shall come to pass in that day, Tyre shall be abandoned;" and below, "but after seventy years, Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot." Behold what words the prophet employs, and how he does not avoid the baseness of words of this kind. We ourselves sometimes avoid them, not because our tongue is more chaste than theirs, but our authority inferior. For very great is the force of words in the vivid exposition of such things, so that they who do not blush at their sins blush at least at the names of their sins. "Tyre shall be," he says, "as the song of a harlot." […]

Furthermore, the Hebrews claim that Tarshish generally represents the sea, as in the psalms: "With a violent wind, you will destroy the ships of Tarshish," that is, the sea, and in Isaiah: "Wail, ships of Tarshish." I recall speaking about this several years ago in a letter to Marcella. The prophet, therefore, was not seeking to flee to a specific place, but he was hastening to continue toward wherever it was the sea would take him. Indeed, a terrified fugitive is rightly more interested in seizing the first opportunity to sail than he is in selecting a place of refuge. […]

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for your strength has perished. The ships of Carthage, that is, of Tharsis, are bidden to howl; for they have not, as above, perished or shall not come, but their strength has perished. For Tharsis, according to another interpretation, is rendered into our tongue consummation of six, or of gladness. Now we read that this world was made in six days, and according to the traditions of the Church it will afterwards be consummated. All the goods of this world, then, and the whole labour of mortals, are compared to the uncertain course of ships, because they will quickly perish, and all the strength of those who sail will be dissolved. […]
Howl. Here he sets out the mourning (Ezek 27:14).

23:15.t: On this account he was the overshadowing Cherub; who destroyed the Prince of Tyre, because he rejoiced over the children of Israel, for that they were carried away captive from their land, and because his heart was exalted. This Tyre also lay waste seventy years like Jerusalem which sat in desolation seventy years. For Isaiah said concerning it:—Tyre shall wander seventy years, as the days of one king, and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms that are upon the face of the earth.

And it will come to pass in that day, you will be in oblivion, O Tyre, for seventy years, like the days of one king. From this place to the end of this prophecy prosperous things are announced to Tyre: that it ought to repent; that it is to be built again; that the overthrow of Tyre is to last only seventy years, the years during which the temple of God too was desolate: so that the city that mocked at the ruins of another should also match the time of that one's ruins. The seventy years of one king many think to be said of Nebuchadnezzar, the years during which the kingdom of the Assyrian nation continued in Jerusalem. Others think it is said in general: that he who has had a long time of reigning cannot go beyond seventy years.

And it shall come to pass in that day that Tyre shall be forsaken seventy years, as the time of one king, as the time of a man. And after seventy years Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about, harlot city given over to forgetfulness. Play well on the harp, sing much, that you may be remembered. And after seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she shall be restored again to her former state; and her trade shall be with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. And her trade and her hire shall be holy to the Lord; but it shall not be gathered for themselves, but for those who dwell before the Lord. All her trade, to eat and drink and be filled in common store, a memorial before the Lord. […]

And it shall come to pass. Here he designates the time: seventy years, according to the days of one king, who rarely even lives so long, below: the Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me (Isa 49:14).

But after seventy years. Here he promises liberation. And first, he sets out the song of the liberated, setting out the time of singing: after seventy years; as the song of a harlot, who, cast aside by a man, throws herself about and moves the hearts of others to mercy through songs in which she remembers her former dignity.

23:16.t: But after seventy years it will be for Tyre like the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about the city, harlot given over to oblivion; sing well, repeat the song, that you may be remembered. Because you have committed fornication with very many nations, and your former lovers have despised you, desolate and naked and filthy with the squalor of captivity, take up the harp now, redouble your songs, go about the city, lament your former brothel, and wash away with tears the traces of your old error, so that you may call forth the mercy of God upon you.

And he sets out the song as to the instrument: take a harp; as to the place: about the city; as to the manner: sing well; as to the number, sing many a song. He also sets out the fruit: that you mayst be remembered: it is commonly said: if a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and marry another man, shall he return to her any more? (Jer 3:1).

Note on the words, take a harp (Isa 23:16), that the harp signifies an upright life: first, as the mortification of the flesh, because of the material of the strings: I will sing to you with the harp, you Holy One of Israel (Ps 70[71]:22); second, as to the connection of the virtues, because of the harmony of the song, above: my bowels shall sound like a harp for Moab (Isa 16:11); […]

23:17.t: And it will come to pass after seventy years, the Lord will visit Tyre, and will bring it back to its wages, and again it will commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth. That all these things were fulfilled according to the history is shown by the concordant writings of the Greeks and Phoenicians: that after seventy years it was restored and returned to its former power, and became the mart of all the nations; and these, I think, are called fornications: so that, as he who commits fornication enters the brothel and pays the wage of debauchery, so the trader, flocking in from the whole world, has filled up the beauty of the city as of a harlot.

Second, he promises the benefit of a liberator: and it shall come to pass after seventy years; that the Lord will visit Tyre, and will bring her back again to her traffic: and she shall commit fornication again, that is, she shall trade: I will glorify them (Jer 30:19).

On the contrary: Ezekiel 27:36 says of Tyre, you are brought to nothing, and you shall never be any more; the Gloss there says, that is, in memory, which is the life of one man, which is seventy years; the days of our years in them are threescore and ten years (Ps 89[90]:10).

23:18.t: And its merchandise and its wages will be sanctified to the Lord: they will not be hidden away nor laid up. For its merchandise will be for those who dwell before the Lord, that they may eat to the full and be clothed even to old age. We find that these things have not yet been done according to the history; unless perhaps it is to be thought that after the building of Jerusalem and the restoration of Tyre the cities were friendly to each other, and Tyre often sent gifts to the temple of God: as we read in Ezra too (Neh 13:16), that he drove off the Tyrians who were selling fish on the sabbath, and did not allow them to enter the city: and from this one item of trade one must judge of the rest as well. […]
Third, he sets out the fruit of liberation: and her merchandise and her hire shall be, below: for brass I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver (Isa 60:17).

24:1.t: Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth, and will lay it bare, and will afflict its face, and will disperse its inhabitants; and as the people is, so will the priest be; and as the servant, so his master; as the handmaid, so her mistress; as the buyer, so he who sells; as the lender, so he who receives the loan; as he who demands repayment, so he who owes. With scattering the earth will be scattered, and with plundering it will be despoiled: for the Lord has spoken this word. […]

565. Behold the Lord. In this part, he threatens the destruction of the entire earth, either that which was carried out in particular kingdoms and different regions, or that which is to come in the day of judgment, according to what is said above, this is the counsel, that I have purposed upon all the earth (Isa 14:26); however, some explain this as pertaining to the land of the Jews, or the land of Babylon, or the land of the Idumeans. And it is divided into two parts: in the first, he threatens against the inhabitants of the land; in the second, against the rulers of the peoples: and it shall come to pass, that in that day (Isa 24:21). Concerning the first, he sets out three things: first, the destruction of men; […]

24:2.t: Then there will be no difference between noble and base, priest and layman, servant and master, handmaid and mistress, rich and poor, the lender and him who is pressed by debt, buyer and seller. For all will stand on equal terms before the judgment seat of Christ, and there will be no respect of persons with God (Rom 14; Col 3). Of this Job too speaks in almost the same words: The small and the great are there, and the servant who does not fear his master (Job 3:19). And the Savior in the Gospel, to whom all judgment has been committed, bears witness in full discourse.

We are put as guards in the vineyards, but we do not cultivate our own. When we are involved with external affairs, we neglect to watch over our own activities. I think that God suffers greater outrage from no one, dearly beloved, than from priests. Those he has placed to reprove others he sees giving an example of wickedness in their own lives. We who ought to have restrained sin, ourselves commit it. More seriously, priests who ought to give of their own possessions frequently plunder the goods of others. If they see others living humbly and chastely, they often make fun of them. Consider what will become of the flocks when wolves become shepherds! They undertake to guard the flock and are not afraid to waylay the Lord's flock.We do not seek to gain souls; […]

And this indeed is what the Lord, in the wrath of just retribution, menaced through the prophet, saying, "And there shall be like people, like priest." For the priest is as the people, when one who bears a spiritual office acts as do others who are still under judgment with regard to their carnal pursuits.

What is written has surely been fulfilled in us: And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest. For the priest does not differ from the people when by no merit of his own does he transcend the common conduct.

567. Second, the universality of destruction as to those punished, making equal those who differ in rank: as with the people, so with the priest; in condition: as with the servant so with his master; in possession of things: as with the buyer, so with the seller: the small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master (Job 3:19).

24:3.t: The earth, therefore, will be scattered, and all earthly works will be reduced to nothing, so that, the image of the χοϊκοῦ having been abolished, the image of the heavenly may remain. For the first man was from the earth, earthly, and the second from heaven, heavenly: as is the earthly, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly; so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear also the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:47-49). Hence the same Apostle says: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God (ibid., 50). Not that, as the heretics say, the nature of bodies perishes, but that this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality. […]

As to the diversity of punishments: with desolation, setting out the loss as to immovable things: the earth shall be laid waste; as to movable things: it shall be spoiled: with desolation is all the land made desolate (Jer 12:11).

24:4.t:
"4 b. The lofty men of the earth mourned, 5. and the earth waxed lawless through her inhabitants. 6b. Therefore, the inhabitants of the earth shall be poor, and few men shall be left."

Here again having rebuked the transgressors of the law of the covenant of God who belong to the people of the circumcision, and threatened them with what was written, he prophesies that some few men of them will be left. And these would be those named of the apostle "the remnant according to the election of grace."
24:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

24:4.t: The earth has mourned and has wasted away, and has been weakened; the world has wasted away, the height of the people of the earth has been weakened, and the earth has been slain by its inhabitants. LXX: The earth has mourned, the world has been corrupted, the lofty of the earth have mourned, but the earth has acted impiously because of its inhabitants. God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Hence the first sentence is against those who are lofty on the earth, that all things which are now strong may be weakened because of those who have mingled blood with blood, and, in the manner of the blood of Abel, have made the gore of the slain cry out to God (Gen 4).

As to the downfall of power, the earth mourned, and faded away, using the past tense for the future, that is, it shall fade away, mourning for its weakness; and this is: is weakened, that this may be said as to the common people; but as to the powerful, the world, that is, leaders of the world, faded away, above: I will visit the evils of the world (Isa 13:11).

24:5.t: Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the ordinance, they have broken the everlasting covenant. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, and its inhabitants will sin; therefore its tillers will go mad, and few men will be left. LXX: Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the precepts, the eternal testament. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, because its inhabitants have sinned; therefore the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, and few men will be left. Let the Jews hear, who boast that they alone have received the law of the Lord, that first all the nations and the whole world received the natural law, and that the law was given afterwards through Moses for this reason, because the first law had been broken. […]

And he sets out the killing of men: and the earth is killed: the land was killed (Ps 106:38).

568. Third, he shows the equity of the punishment: because they have transgressed, and he does this by comparing it to their fault; hence he does two things. First, he sets out their fault: they have transgressed the laws, written or natural; the ordinance, of custom; the covenant, of friendship, everlasting, because it is caused by likeness of kind: they have transgressed my covenant, and have violated my law (Hos 8:1); they have polluted the sanctuary, they have acted unjustly against the law (Zeph 3:4).

24:6.t: And as in the beginning God blessed every creature that he had made (Gen 1), so at the consummation of the world he will curse those who are earthly, and who were not sojourners but inhabitants of the earth, and sinned in it; who, forgetting their condition, have raged against one another in mutual fury. And few will remain who have the heavenly image; or, according to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, because they have lost their spiritual riches.

569. Second, he threatens a fourfold punishment because of this fault: first, a divine curse: a curse: the land has mourned by reason of cursing (Jer 23:10); second, divine desertion: they shall sin, as if the Lord has abandoned them: for this cause, God delivered them up to shameful affections (Rom 1:26); he that is filthy, let him be filthy still (Rev 22:11); third, they shall be made foolish: therefore they shall be mad: they were turned aside into vanities (Ps 78:57); fourth, reduction in numbers: few men shall be left: you shall remain few in number (Deut 28:62).

24:7.t: The vintage has mourned, the vine has been weakened, all who were glad of heart have groaned. The joy of the timbrels has ceased, the sound of those who rejoice has been stilled, the sweetness of the harp has fallen silent; they shall not drink wine with song, the drink will be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity has been crushed, every house has been shut, with no one entering. There will be an outcry over wine in the streets; all gladness has been forsaken, the joy of the earth has been carried away. And desolation has been left in the city, and calamity will overwhelm the gates: for these things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples. At the consummation of the world, the remembrance of past delights will be the matter of torments. […]

570. The vintage has mourned. Here he threatens the removal of joys as to the wicked; and second, he sets out the joys of the good: as if a few olives (Isa 24:13). Concerning the first, he does three things. First, he sets out the ending of joy which came from three things: either in the fertility of things, the vintage has mourned, failing, that is, it was the cause of mourning, above: there shall be no rejoicing nor shouting in the vineyards (Isa 16:10).

24:8.t: Or in the playing of games: the mirth of timbrels has ceased: the voice of harpers, harping on their harps (Rev 14:2).

24:9.t:
Or in the pleasures of feasts: they shall not drink wine with a song, above: the harp, and the lyre, and, the timbrel and the pipe, and wine are in your feasts (Isa 5:12).

571. Second, he sets out the recompense of sadness: the drink shall be bitter, for in their feasts, they will have sadness, against the pleasures of feasts: I will turn your feasts into mourning (Amos 8:10).

581. Note on the words, the drink shall be bitter (Isa 24:9), that the drink of sin is bitter: first, because of the remorse of conscience: her end is bitter (Prov 5:4); second, because of the fear of death: O death, how bitter is the remembrance of you (Sir 41:1); […]

24:10.t: The city of vanity will be crushed, or every city, or the spiritual Babylon, which sits clothed in purple upon seven hills, whose punishments we read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 18). And he did well to say the city of vanity. For if it is said of heaven and earth and of all things that are earthly: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2), how much more must this be said of one city, which is a small part of the whole world! Then the houses whose ceilings are now gilded, and whose walls, while the poor die of cold without roof or hut, are clothed with veneers of marble and shine with the gleam of sawn ivory, will remain empty.
The city of vanity is broken down, against the vanity of games, all things are vanity (Ps 39:5); vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2); the city, of Babylon, any soul.

24:11.t: There will be an outcry in the streets over wine, not in the strait and narrow way that leads to life, but in the broad and spacious one that leads to death (Matt 7): over the wine and drunkenness of the error of those who have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands (Ps 75 [76]). For the joy of the earth has been carried away into heaven, and desolation has been left in the once most crowded city, and the calamity of its inhabitants will overwhelm the gates of the busy streets, through which the throngs of the peoples used to stream in.

There shall be a crying, of those lamenting over the lack of wine, against fertility: in all vineyards there shall be wailing (Amos 5:17).

572. Third, he concludes the exchange: all mirth is forsaken, exchanged for sadness: woe to you that laugh: for you shall weep (Luke 6:25); laughter shall be mingled with sorrow (Prov 14:13).

24:13.t: And that we might know plainly that the destruction of the whole world is being announced, he added: These things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the nations, or of the peoples.

As if a few olives that are left were shaken from the olive tree, and the grape clusters when the vintage is finished. These will lift up their voice and give praise; when the Lord has been glorified, they will neigh from the sea: therefore glorify the Lord in teachings, in the islands of the sea the name of the Lord God of Israel. How far the translation of the Seventy differs in this place from the Hebrew truth, the following words will show. LXX: As if someone were to shake an olive tree, so they will shake them; and if the vintage ceases, these will cry out with clamor. But those who have been left upon the earth will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord; the water of the sea will be troubled; […]

According to the Seventy, all that we have understood of the saints can be referred to the impious: that when the vintage is finished, then they cry out, set in punishments. But those who have escaped the number of the impious rejoice in the glory of the Lord, and the waters of the peoples of this world are troubled.

573. As if. Here he places the joys of the good. And first, he foretells the praise of those to come, whose salvation he foretells: as if a few; few will be saved, in relation to the others, above: the fruit thereof that shall be left upon it, shall be as the shaking of the olive tree, two or three berries in the top of a bough (Isa 17:6).

24:14.t: These, then, who remain, and after the vintage and the pressing of the world have been able to escape the hands of the persecuting Antichrist, or the burning of the impending punishment, will lift up their voices on high and will praise God. When the Lord comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels, and they see him reigning in majesty, then they will neigh in the likeness of horses, exulting in the greatness of their joy, and they will neigh from the sea of this world.

And he places their praise: these shall give praise; they shall whinny, like horses to signify their great joy, below: the voice of your watchmen: they have lifted up their voice, they shall praise together (Isa 52:8).

24:15.t: Therefore you who are now instructed in the Holy Scriptures, and know that such great joy and such great rewards are reserved for you, glorify the Lord in teachings, hearing that which is written: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord (2 Cor 10:17). Not at all in the land of Judea, but in the islands, that is, in the Churches of this sea and world, in which is blessed and praised the name of the Lord God of him who was once Israel, or, of the man who sees God.

By "sea" he means the multitude of nations, and by "coastlands," perhaps, he means cities. All their inhabitants will "raise their voices" when the divine wrath comes upon them. But the majesty of Christ will somehow be in the sea, that is, in all those nations, and they will realize that it is through divine Providence that they are destroyed and annihilated. They are destroyed because their impiety provoked the Almighty God; hence they will reject their gods who are unable to help them. That is how the majesty of the Lord is celebrated. […]

574. Second, he introduces praise in the present: therefore. And first, he places the precept, glorify the Lord in instruction, that is, in teaching others; another translation has: in praises: glorify the Lord as much as ever you can, for he will yet far exceed (Sir 43:30).

24:16.t: From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the Righteous One; and I said: My secret is mine, my secret is mine: woe is me. LXX: From the wings of the earth we have heard portents: hope for the righteous; and they will say ※ my mystery is mine ⁚. This, which is said, my mystery is mine, is not found in the Seventy, but has been added in the Greek from the translation of Theodotion. Again, for what they put as woe, so as to join it to the following verse, in the Hebrew is said OI LI (אוי לי), which properly means woe is me. Also for ends, which we have set down for the sake of explaining the sense more openly, the Hebrew has MECCHENAPH (מכנף), which means wing, not end. […]

The transgressors have transgressed, and with the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed. Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, who are an inhabitant of the earth; and it shall be that he who flees from the voice of terror shall fall into the pit, and he who extricates himself from the pit shall be held by the snare. LXX: Woe to the transgressors who transgress the law. Fear and the pit and the snare are upon you who inhabit the earth. And it shall be that he who flees fear shall fall into the pit, and he who comes out of the pit shall be caught by the snare. […]

Second, he designates the fulfillment of the precept: from the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the just one, that is, Christ, below: behold the Lord has made it to be heard in the ends of the earth (Isa 62:11).

Third, the reward of those who fulfill it: and I said: my secret, of their reward: eye has not seen, nor ear heard: neither has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for them that love him (1 Cor 2:9); to myself, alone. Woe is me, for I cannot tell of it to others: I heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter (2 Cor 12:4). Of the punishments of the damned: woe is me, such great punishments I see; and thus this belongs with the following part.

575. The prevaricators. […]

24:17.t: Second, he threatens a multitude of dangers. And first, he sets out this multitude: fear. He speaks in likeness to those who flee pursuers because of fear, above: they shall fall, and shall be broken in pieces (Isa 8:15); a voice of terror (Jer 30:5).

24:18.t: For the floodgates from on high have been opened, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. With breaking the earth will be broken, with crushing the earth will be crushed, with shaking the earth will be shaken. With tossing the earth will be tossed like a drunken man, and it will be removed like a tent of one night, and its iniquity will weigh it down, and it will fall, and will not add to rise again. Therefore no one will escape the terror and the snare and the pit of the Lord, because the floodgates from on high, or, as the Seventy translated more plainly, the windows of heaven have been opened, so that the Lord might look down upon all the sins of men, which before, because he did not punish them, he seemed to sinners not to know. […]

576. Second, the impossibility of escaping: and it shall come to pass, that he that shall flee from the noise of the fear, shall fall into the pit: as if to say, he will decide upon Scylla, wanting to avoid Charybdis: that which the palmerworm has left, the bruchus has eaten (Joel 1:4). And he assigns the cause: for tribulation will come to them from both heaven and from earth, and this is the flood-gates, that is, hidden channels through which water flows: the floodgates of heaven were opened (Gen 7:11).

24:19.t: Then the earth will be broken and crushed, and shaken and tossed in the likeness of a drunken man: not that the earth itself is reduced to dust and to nothing, but that all earthly things pass away, and another manner of life succeeds. And as a drunken man does not know what he is doing, but, his sinews growing dull with drunkenness, neither foot nor mind stands to its duty: so the whole earth, that is, all men who dwell on the earth, will be drunk with the greatness of the evils and the punishments, and will be stupefied at all that they see. […]

577. Third, he shows the impossibility of reparation under a threefold similitude, namely, of divided things, which are not restored: breaking, as to division into large parts, crushing, as to division into small parts: behold the eyes of the Lord God are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will crush it from the face of the earth (Amos 9:8).

24:20.t: And through the similitude of shaken things, which are not made stable: with trembling shall the earth be moved, from place to place, shaken, as if trembling in its own place, as a drunken man, above: they have caused Egypt to err in all its works, as a drunken man staggers and vomits (Isa 19:14); and through the similitude of a traveler's tent, which is not fixed firmly in the same place: as the tent, below: my generation is at an end, and it is rolled away from me, as a shepherd's tent (Isa 38:12). And he assigns the cause: and the iniquity thereof shall be heavy upon it, like a heavy weight, so that it does not rise again: what is heavier than lead? (Sir 22:14); sin sits on a talent (Zech 5:7); my iniquities are as a heavy burden are become heavy upon me (Ps 38:4).

24:21.t: And this is the sense of the whole passage: The windows of heaven have been opened, so that, as the Lord looked out upon earthly sins, every fashion of earthly works might pass away and fall, and by no means rise again to its former state. In that day, that is, in the day of judgment, the Lord will visit upon the host, or upon the adornment, of heaven on high, so that he may judge not only earthly but also heavenly things. And what the adornment or host of heaven is, let us learn from the writing of Moses: Beware lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon, the stars and all the adornment of heaven, you be deceived and worship them (Deut 4:19). […]

578. And it shall come to pass. Here he threatens against the rulers of the people; and concerning this he sets out three things. First, he sets out their punishment: in that day, of judgment; the Lord shall visit upon the host of heaven on high, that is, the demons, and upon the kings of the earth, these same demons: now shall the prince of this world be cast out (John 12:31); or also the wicked kings. Or, in that day, namely, the day of the destruction of particular kingdoms; the host of heaven on high, the idols, namely, of the sun and moon and the other stars: he adored all the host of heaven (2 Kgs 21:3).

583. […]

24:22.t: These princes, then, who did not keep their rank, the Lord will gather in the day of judgment, bound together as in one bundle, and will cast them into the pit of hell, so that in them too may be fulfilled what is written of the impious: He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the ditch which he made (Ps 7:16). And they will be shut up in prison, according to what the Lord says: Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). But what follows, And after many days they will be visited, seems to applaud my friends who grant repentance to the devil and the demons, in that after long times they are visited by the Lord. […]

And they shall be gathered together, at the same time in hell: which was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41); as in the gathering of one bundle: bind it into bundles to burn (Matt 13:30), that they may be alike in punishment who were alike in sin: I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies, gathered together (Rev 19:19). And they shall be gathered together, through destruction, below: all the host of the heavens shall pine away (Isa 34:4).

579. Second, he designates the measure of the punishment as to time: and after many days they shall be visited, for after however much time of torment, they shall be punished in eternity: go, you cursed, into everlasting fire (Matt 25:41); […]

24:23.t: He [Isaiah] was pricked by the thorn of sin; you are decked with the flowers of virtue. "The moon shall be ashamed, and the sun confounded, when the Lord shall punish the host of heaven on high." This is explained by another passage. "Even the stars are unclean in his sight";21 and again, "He charges his angels with folly." The moon is ashamed, the sun is confounded, and the sky covered with sackcloth. Shall we fearlessly and joyously, as though we were free from all sin, face the majesty of the Judge? After all, the mountains shall melt away, that is, all who are lifted up by pride, and all the host of the heavens, whether they are stars or angelic powers, shall fade away like heavens when the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll.

And it will be in that day: the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven on high, and upon the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. And they will be gathered together in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited. And the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of his elders. For what we have translated, and the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, the Seventy translated, the brick will melt, and the wall will fall; what the cause of the error is, the following words will show. […]

Then the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, according to what the Apostle says: For the creation itself groans and travails (Rom 8:22), seeing that men who enjoyed its light have done nothing worthy of the goodness of God, who makes his sun rise upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matt 5): as if a steward and bailiff, when the master comes, were to see the household subjected to various torments and not having fulfilled his precepts at all. Of this same passage the Savior teaches more fully in the Gospel: The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be moved, when the sign of the Son of man has appeared in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth have beaten their breasts, […]

The stars on the day of judgment will be seen obscurely, not because of a gradual waning of their own light but due to the overwhelming brilliance of the true light, who is the supreme Judge coming in majesty, and the light of the Father and the holy angels. Nevertheless, nothing should prevent us from understanding that the sun, the moon and other stars will be deprived temporarily of their own light, as happened to the sun at the Lord's passion. But because the moon, which should have been full at that time, lay hidden behind the earth, Joel's prophesy remains unfulfilled still today, for after he had said "the sun will be turned to darkness," he added, "and the moon to blood before the great and magnificent day of the Lord comes." […]

580. Third, the glory of him who punishes, and first, of the judge: and the moon shall blush, that is, its splendor shall be thought nothing in comparison to the splendor of the body of Christ: the sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood: before the great and dreadful day of the Lord doth come (Joel 2:31); or, the worshippers of the sun and moon.

Second, of the judge's assessors: when the Lord of hosts shall reign . . . and shall be glorified in the sight of his ancients, above: the Lord will enter into judgment with the senators (Isa 3:14).

25:1.t:
And this very thing the great prophet Isaiah wonderfully foreknew by the Holy Spirit, and foretold. And he therefore says thus:

"O Lord, my God, I will glorify thee, I will hymn thy name, for thou hast done marvellous things."

And he goes on to explain what these things so truly "wonderful" are:

"And the Lord of Sabaoth shall make a feast for all the nations. They shall drink joy, they shall drink wine, they shall be anointed with myrrh (on this mountain). Impart thou all these things to the nations. For this is God's counsel upon all the nations."

These were Isaiah's "wonders."the promise of the anointing with ointment of a good smell, and with myrrh made not to Israel but to all nations. Whence not unnaturally through the chrism of myrrh they gained the name of Christians. […]
25:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

25:1.t: But others, both better and more correctly, understand it as said in the person of the prophet, giving thanks to the Father for the passion of the Lord Savior, because he has done wonders and has fulfilled his ancient designs in truth, when those standing at the right hand will hear: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt 25:34). Understanding this, Paul too said: As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless (Eph 1:4); and, desiring that what he prophesies should come to pass, he adds the Hebrew word AMEN (אמן), for which the Seventy translated so be it. And the Lord in the Gospel often uses this word: Amen, amen, that is, truly, truly I say to you (John 6:54).

O Lord, you are my God: I will exalt you, I will confess to your name, for you have done wonders, ancient faithful designs: amen. For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. Because of this a strong people will praise you, the city of mighty nations will fear you. For you have become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation, a hope from the whirlwind, a shade from the heat: for the spirit of the mighty is like a whirlwind driving against a wall. Like heat in thirst, you will bring low the tumult of strangers; and as with scorching heat under a cloud, you will make the offshoot of the strong wither. LXX: O Lord my God, I will glorify you; […]

O COME, all ye who love the glory of the Saviour, and thereby weave crowns for your heads, come once again, that we may rejoice in Him, and as we extol Him with endless praises, let us say in the words of the prophet Isaiah: "O Lord, my God, I will praise Thee; and I will laud Thy name; for Thou hast wrought wonderful works, even a counsel true from the beginning." What then is the counsel and purpose of God the Father, which was from the beginning, and was true? Plainly that respecting us. […]
25:1.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

25:2.t: And why he praises and confesses to the name of the Lord, and what these wonders are, and the ancient designs which he showed true in deed, follows: For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. The once strong city is understood as Jerusalem, which has become the house of strangers; of whom the Savior says in the psalm: Strange children have lied to me, strange children have grown old and have limped in their paths (Ps 17 [18]:46). This city, when it has been destroyed, will never be built for ever, so that the dreams of a thousand-year kingdom and of a golden and jeweled Jerusalem may be laid to rest.

25:3.t: And when Jerusalem has been destroyed for its impiety, a strong people will praise the Lord. And who the strong people is, the following verse shows: The city of mighty nations will fear you. While those blaspheme, the people of the nations will fear you. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). And a strong people will praise you, and the city of mighty nations will fear you, that is, the Church gathered from the nations.

Israel was called to the knowledge of God through the tutoring of the law and was richly endowed with the things of God. It was delivered [from Egypt] and inherited the Promised Land. Although there were many other peoples living in other parts of the world, all were alien to spiritual matters and heavenly things. They had not tasted the gifts that come from God. They were, as it were, naked and unclothed, enjoying neither divine protection nor shelter from on high, nor the spiritual wealth that comes from virtue nor other things worthy of praise or admiration.When Christ appeared, destroying the arrogance of the devil, he led the nations to God the Father, and they basked in the splendor of the true light and shared in his glory. […]

587. Therefore shall a strong people praise you. Here he sets out the fruit of punishment in the subjection of men to God.

And first, he sets out two signs of subjection:

praise, a strong people shall praise you, strong, as much as they are subject to you, or a gentile people strong in passions;

fear, every city shall fear you, below: the strength of the Gentiles shall come to you (Isa 60:5).

25:4.t: For you have become strength to the poor, to your Christ, of whom we read also in the Psalms: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And in Zechariah, according to the Hebrew truth, the poor man, that is, EBION (אביון), is described as sitting upon the colt of an ass (Zech 9). Strength to the needy, in the tribulation of his passion, a hope from the whirlwind of the cross, and a shade from the heat, when he said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit (Luke 23:46). For as when the wind is dashed against a wall and passes by, so the whirlwind of the blaspheming Jews could not harm him.

Second, he assigns the reason,

which he sets out first: because you have been a strength to the poor, who has little, even if it is sufficient for him, to the needy, who is in need: the Lord is my refuge: and my God the help of my hope (Ps 93[94]:22).

Second, he sets out a similitude: a hope, of defense, from the whirlwind, because of the violence of the persecutor; a shadow, of consolation, from the heat, because of the affliction of persecution, below: a man shall be as when one is hid from the wind, and hides himself from a storm (Isa 32:2).

Third, he sets out the explanation: the spirit, that is, the indignation and pride, above: as whirlwinds come from Africa, it comes from the desert from a terrible land (Isa 21:1).

25:5.t: And to use another comparison: as an offshoot is scorched by most grievous heat and droops, so you will make the tumult and clamor of the strangers, that is, of those who have become strangers to you, wither and perish. According to the Seventy translators, I could not find in this place, I do not say the sense, but the order and sequence of the words. And for that place where we have translated, like heat in thirst, for which in the Hebrew is written BASAION (בציון), which among them means pathless place or thirst: why they turned pathless place and in thirst into in Zion, the error is plain, from the likeness of the words SAION and SION (Both ציון), since it is marked with the same letters.

Perhaps this is what the prophet is referring to, that is, those in Israel who were thirsting for the coming of the Savior. They desired to see the Savior and Redeemer of all. One such person was the righteous Simeon. When he took the infant Jesus in his arms, he said, "Lord, now let your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for mine eyes have seen your salvation which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel."

588. As heat in thirst. Here he sets out the manner of punishment as to affliction: as heat in thirst, afflicts, the tumult, the proud clamor, of strangers; as to barrenness: and as with heat under a burning cloud, united by the south wind, by which fruit of the vine is sometimes destroyed because of its excessive heat: for the sun rose with a burning heat and parched the grass: and the flower thereof fell off (Jas 1:11).

25:6.t: Having been counted worthy of this holy chrism, you are called Christians, verifying the name also by your new birth. For before you were deemed worthy of this grace, you had properly no right to this title but were advancing on your way toward being Christians.Moreover, you shall know that in the old Scripture there lies the symbol of this chrism. For at the time Moses imparted to his brother the command of God and made him high priest, he anointed him after bathing him in water. And Aaron was called Christ or anointed, evidently from the typical anointing. So also the high priest, in advancing Solomon to the kingdom, anointed him after he had bathed in Gihon. To them, however, these things happened in a figure, but to you not in a figure but in truth; […]

After the passion of the Lord, then, when he has freed him from thirst and heat and whirlwind, the Lord will make, not at all for the people of the Jews, but for all nations, on Mount Zion a fat feast, burnt offerings full of marrow, and the wine of a vintage refined from the lees, so that he may cast down and cause to be swallowed up the face of death and of the bond by which all peoples were bound; and he will break the net of death, and the web that had caught all nations. And according to the Apostle, death will be swallowed up for ever (1 Cor 15). […]

Having said that the Lord will reign in Zion and Jerusalem, Isaiah leads us to the mystical meaning of the passage. Thus Zion is interpreted as a high place that is good for surveillance, and Jerusalem is the vision of the world. In fact, the church of Christ combines both: it is high and visible from everywhere, and is, so to speak, located on the mountain. The church may be understood as high also in another way: there is nothing low in it, it is far removed from all the mundane things, as it is written, "I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!" Equally elevated are its orthodox and divine doctrines; thus the doctrine about God or about the holy and consubstantial Trinity is true, pure and without guile. […]

589. And the Lord of hosts shall make. Here he sets out those things that pertain to the exaltation of the good, and this is threefold.

First, as to abundance of honor, which he describes under a metaphor of a feast which is prepared from fat animals and clarified wine; in this mountain, for it was there that Christ suffered, from which all good things come forth to us, or because it is there that he will judge, as it says in Matthew 22:4: behold, I have prepared my dinner: my beeves and fatlings are killed.

594. Note on the words, a feast of fat things (Isa 25:6), that the feast is threefold.

First, the family feast of the Church militant, in which he sets out three things:

first, the bitterness of suffering: you shall eat it with wild lettuce (Exod 12:8); […]

25:7.t: And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a feast of fat things, a feast of the vintage: of fat things full of marrow, of a vintage refined from the lees. And he will cast down on this mountain the face of the bond that was bound upon all peoples, and the web that he wove over all nations. And he will cast down death for ever, and the Lord God will take away the tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth: for the Lord has spoken. LXX: And the Lord Sabaoth will make for all nations upon this mountain: they will drink gladness, they will drink wine. They will be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Deliver all these things to the nations, for this counsel is upon all nations: death, prevailing, has devoured. […]

590. Second, as to the removal of evils: and he shall destroy, as to the punishment of death, which he calls a bond, inasmuch as we are bound to it from sin, and a web inasmuch as it is a just sentence woven by God: death is swallowed up in victory (1 Cor 15:54); O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite (Hos 13:14). The sadness of sorrow: and the Lord God shall wipe away tears from every face: God shall wipe away all tears from the eyes of the saints (Rev 21:4); the ignominy of confusion, and the reproach, above: take away our reproach (Isa 4:1). Some refer this to the judgment carried out in the death of Holofernes, who came against all nations; and similarly concerning the feast.

25:8.t: Now the laws of love summoned Him even as far as Death and the dead themselves, so that He might summon the souls of those who were long time dead. And so because He cared for the salvation of all for ages past, and that "He might bring to naught him that hath the power of death," as Scripture teaches, here again he underwent the dispensation in His mingled Natures: as Man, he left His Body to the usual burial, while as God He departed from it. For He cried with a loud cry, and said to the Father: "I commend my spirit," and departed from the body free, in no wise waiting for death, who was lagging as it were in fear to come to Him; […]
25:8.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 12

25:8.t: In the Old Testament the jaw of death is bitter, since it is said, "Strong death is all devouring." In the New Testament the jaw of death is sweet, for it has swallowed death, as the apostle says: "Death is swallowed up in victory! O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?"

Stricken by the indecency of this act [the golden calf], Moses broke the tablets and shattered the head of the calf and beat it to powder in order to destroy all traces of impiety. The first tablets were broken so that the second ones might be repaired whereon, through the teaching of the gospel, faithlessness, now utterly destroyed, vanished. Thus Moses shattered that Egyptian pride and by the authority of the eternal law checked that loftiness overreaching itself. Therefore David says, "And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and shatter them like the calf of Lebanon. Thus the people swallowed all faithlessness and pride, so that impiety and haughtiness might not swallow them. […]

The apostle said, "With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin," not by giving my members over to committing iniquities but only by feeling lust, without however giving a hand to unlawful lust. So when he said, "With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin," he went on to add, "There is therefore no condemnation now for those who are in Christ Jesus." For those who are in the flesh there is condemnation; for those who are in Christ Jesus no condemnation. […]

It is appropriate and necessary that at the time the "mystery" is handed over, the "resurrection of the dead" is included. For at the time we make the confession of faith at holy baptism, we say that we expect the resurrection of the flesh. And so we believe. Death overcame our forefather Adam on account of his transgression and like a fierce wild animal it pounced on him and carried him off amid lamentation and loud wailing. Men wept and grieved because death ruled over all the earth. But all this came to an end with Christ. Striking down death, he rose up on the third day and became the way by which human nature would rid itself of corruption. […]

It is death that has brought men to old age and corruption: death therefore has made old, that is to say, has corrupted: for "that which is made old, and is growing aged, is near corruption," as Scripture saith: but Christ renews, in that He is "the Life." For He Who in the beginning created, is able again to renew unto incorruption and life. For one may well affirm that it is the office of one and the same energy and power, to effect both the one and the other. As therefore the prophet Isaiah says, "'He hath swallowed up death, having become mighty." And again, "The Lord hath taken away all weeping from every countenance. He hath taken away the reproach of the people from all the earth." […]
25:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

25:8.t: For the prophet Isaiah again assures us that death which entered in because of sin does not retain its power over the dwellers upon earth for ever, but is abolished by the resurrection from the dead of Christ, Who renews the universe, and refashions it to that which it was at the beginning—" for God created all things for incorruption," as it is written; for he says, "He has swallowed up death, having waxed mighty: and God shall again take away all weeping from every countenance; He shall remove the reproach of the people from the whole earth." Now sin is what he calls the reproach of the people, and when this has been taken away, death also is extinguished with it, and corruption departs from the midst: and by having brought it to an end, He removes every one's weeping; […]
25:8.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

25:9.t: And they will say in that day: Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord, we have waited patiently for him; we will exult and be glad in his salvation. For the hand of the Lord will rest on this mountain; and Moab will be threshed under him as straw is crushed in the wagon. And he will stretch out his hands under him, as a swimmer stretches them out to swim, and his glory will be brought low with the dashing of his hands. And the fortifications of your lofty walls will fall, and will be brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust. When death has been swallowed up for ever, the people of God which has been freed from the hand of death will say to the Lord: Behold, this is our God, whom the unbelieving thought only a man; […]

You recognize the one who gives you joy to drink and wine in addition, anointing those in spiritual Zion with myrrh. You recognize that he is true God and Son of God by nature, and although he appeared in the form of a servant, by becoming man he became the source of salvation and life for all, being in all things like those on earth though without sin. The prophet indicates that they are all but pointing [to Christ] with their finger when they say, "Behold our God in whom we have hoped, and we will rejoice in our salvation." I think that this text applies especially to the Israelites who were nurtured in the words of Moses and were not ignorant of the predictions of the holy prophets. They waited for the time of the coming of the Savior and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ. […]

And he sets out the thanksgiving, and they shall say, we have endured for him, patiently waiting: you that fear the Lord, endure for his mercy (Sir 2:7). And he sets out the reason: for the hand of the Lord, with which nothing evil can exist: this is my rest for ever and ever (Ps 131[132]:14).

591. Third, as to the oppression of their enemies, namely, the Moabites, who were most hostile to them because of dreams.

And first, he sets out their affliction: threshed: they have threshed Galaad with iron wains (Amos 1:3).

25:10.t: So the prophetic discourse, although it weaves its prophecy generally about the consummation of the world, yet, so as not to seem to neglect present things entirely, names Moab, which was an enemy of Israel, so much so that it made them commit fornication with the Midianites and be consecrated to the idol Baal-peor, which means Priapus; against which Jeremiah speaks: Chemosh will go forth into captivity, his priests and his princes together (Jer 48:7); and again: Moab will be confounded in Chemosh, as the house of Israel was confounded in Bethel (ibid., 13), and other things like these. And from one idol and the demon who presided over this idol, he indicates that all the adverse powers are to be brought low and led down into Tartarus, and crushed like dust. […]

25:11.t: And as one who swims is wont to stretch out his whole body, so he will be dashed from his power to the ground, and in falling will make a noise.

591. Third, as to the oppression of their enemies, namely, the Moabites, who were most hostile to them because of dreams.

And first, he sets out their affliction: threshed: they have threshed Galaad with iron wains (Amos 1:3); second, their complete subjection: he shall stretch forth his hands, as though prostrate and seeking mercy or help, below: they shall come (49). And the destruction of their fortifications: and the bulwarks, which are mentioned above (Isa 16:7).

25:12.t: And all the fortifications of his lofty men, or of his walls, as is contained in the Hebrew, will fall and be brought low, and will be pulled down to the ground, broken to the dust.
And the destruction of their fortifications: and the bulwarks, which are mentioned above (Isa 16:7).

26:1.t: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. LXX: In that day they will sing this song in the land of Judea: Behold a strong city, and our salvation will set a wall and a surrounding wall. When Moab has been brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust, and all enemies laid beneath the feet of Christ, then this song will be sung in the land of Judah, or Judea, each of which means confession: so that, as we have understood Zion and Jerusalem as the heavenly city, so we may also understand the region of this city as the heavenly confession. Indeed, the saints, unwilling to sing the song of Judea in a foreign land, say: How shall we sing a song to the Lord in a foreign land? […]

This is the wall of which the prophet says: “Our strong city is Zion; the Savior shall be set within it as a wall and fortification” (Isa. 26:1). By this wall, therefore, Christ is signified together with all his members, so that its foundation represents him, while the rest of its structure represents his members.

597. In that day. In this part, he gives thanks for the justification of the people, and it is divided into two parts:

in the first, he foretells the state of the just;

in the second, he shows the fruit of justice: the old error (Isa 26:3).

Concerning the first, he does two things.

For first, he foretells the confidence of the just: in that day, after the return from captivity and the affliction of the Moabites by the Maccabees, or after the coming of Christ; O Zion, the savior, Christ, or Judas Maccabeus, is a city of strength; therein, namely, in protection, a wall and a bulwark shall be set, these only literally in the time of the Maccabees; or a wall, Christ, a bulwark, the prophets. […]

26:2.t: Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, keeping the truth. The old error has gone; you will keep peace: peace, because we have hoped in you.
