You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages. LXX: Open the gates, let the people enter which keeps righteousness, and keeps the truth, laying hold of the truth, and keeping peace: peace, because they have hoped in you, O Lord, for ever. This whole song, which the saints are to sing in the land of confession and praise, suddenly changes persons, and is woven as if by question and answer. The people of God had said: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. […]

After the words of the people and the answer of the Lord, and again the voice of the people, the Prophet speaks to the believers: You have hoped, or hope in the Lord, for everlasting ages, and the rest that follows. According to the Seventy, he enters the gates of the Lord who keeps righteousness in good works, and keeps or embraces the truth in the truth of faith, so that through good works and faith he may come to the peace which surpasses all understanding, and may merit to receive that peace; because he has believed in God, who is the eternal rewarder of good works (Phil 4). Hence also in another place it is written: You have desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you (Sir 1:33).

26:3.t: After the word of God, the people answered in Hebrew JESER SAMUCH (יצרסמך), which Aquila and Symmachus translated alike, πλᾶσμα ἐπηρεισμένον, that is, our error has been taken away, or our thought has been made firm, which before wavered between you and the idols, so that we are by no means carried about by every wind of doctrine, but believe with our whole mind in you, the Lord Savior. For this, so that the sense might be made plainer, we translated, the old error has gone. And because our thought has been made firm, therefore you will keep for us the peace which you promised to the Apostles, saying: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14:27); […]

599. The old error. Here he sets out the fruit of justice, namely, peace; for which is first set out the petition of the people, which contains three things.

For the suitableness of the petitioners is set out: the old error, namely, of idolatry: the old things are passed away (2 Cor 5:17); the benefit of peace is asked for: you will keep peace, of body and soul, below: my people shall sit in the beauty of peace (Isa 32:18); their meriting of peace is alleged: because we have hoped in you: who has hoped in the Lord, and has been confounded? (Sir 2:11).

611. Note also on the word, peace (Isa 26:2), that there are three things that make peace in the present life:

first, contempt for temporal riches, below: but the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest (Isa 57:20); […]

26:4.t: In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever: for he will bow down those who dwell on high; he will bring low the lofty city, he will bring it low even to the ground; he will pull it down even to the dust. The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy. LXX: O great eternal God, who have brought low and pulled down those who dwell on high, you will destroy strong cities, and will bring them down even to the pavement, and the feet of the meek and the lowly will trample them. These things too the Prophet speaks, who answered from that place where he had said above, Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages; and he joins to it what we have now set forth: In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever, and the rest. […]

600. Second, the response of the prophet is set out, who is the mediator between the people and God: you have hoped. And this is divided into three parts:

in the first, the promise of peace is set out;

in the second, the procurement of peace: the way of the just (Isa 26:7);

in the third, the announcement of the procured peace: the inhabitants of the world shall learn justice (Isa 26:9).

601. Concerning the first, he does three things.

First, he concedes their merit: you have hoped in the Lord for eternal ages, that is, forever: in him has my heart confided, and I have been helped (Ps 27[28]:7).

Second, he adds counsel: in the Lord God, that is, hope in the Lord God: he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved (Matt 10:22).

26:5.t: For he will bow down those who dwell on high, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; those who boasted that they had Abraham as their father, and said in insult of the Lord: We were not born of fornication (John 8:41). He will bring low the lofty city: as the Jews think, Rome; as we prove to be more correct, Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to it, and at the last killed the son of the householder, so that, the heir being slain, the inheritance might perish (Luke 13). Nor is it called a city, which in Hebrew is said IR (עיר), but CARIA (כריה), which Aquila translated πολίχνην, which we can call either little city or hamlet or small town; and Jerusalem is frequently called by this name in the Scriptures. […]

And because it is said in the words of the Savior, Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), we can refer this not only to men but also to the adverse powers. According to the Seventy, the Prophet sings praises to God because he brings low all the proud, and razes the fortifications of all cities to the ground, and the feet of the saints, the meek and the lowly trample them.

Third, he promises the benefit of peace for the destruction of enemies: for he shall bring down them that dwell on high, the high city he shall lay low. He shall bring it down even to the ground, he shall pull it down even to the dust. The Jews say this refers to the Romans, but it can refer to any of their enemies, or, mystically, to the Jews themselves, above: the bulwarks of your high walls shall fall (Isa 25:12).

26:6.t: The foot will trample it, and he repeats and joins the feet of the poor, without doubt of Christ, of whom we have said above too: He has become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation. The steps of the needy, namely of the Apostles, who, imitating the poverty of the Lord, obtained also the privilege of his power; who, not being received, shook off upon it the dust of their feet.

And he adds the condition of those who destroy them: the foot shall tread it down, the feet of the poor, the Jews, who have little; the needy, who need to have many things. Or, if taken mystically, he sets out the Jews' meriting of destruction on account of the poor Christ, of whom it says in Psalm 69:6[70:5]: but I am needy and poor, and also: but I am poor and sorrowful (Ps 68:30[69:29]); the needy, the disciples.

26:7.t: The path of the righteous is straight, straight is the track of the righteous for walking; and in the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have waited for you; your name and your memorial are in the desire of the soul: my soul has desired you in the night. LXX: The way of the righteous is straight, the way of the righteous has been made straight, and prepared. For the way of the Lord is judgment; we have hoped in your name, and in the remembrance which our soul desires. The Prophet is still speaking of Christ, of whom he had said above: The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor. The path of this righteous one, then, is straight, or, to coin a new word, straightnesses, which the Greeks call εὐθύτητας, and which we can call more in the Latin manner equities; […]

26:8.t: In this path of the Lord's judgments the saints have waited for him, and have hoped in him, because hope does not confound. And they have had his name and memorial in the desire of their soul, saying: My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times (Ps 118 [119]:20); and again: My soul desires, and has fainted for your salvation (ibid. 81). And he who has the name of the Lord in his desire desires nothing else. And this must be noted, that the desire for the Lord is not in the flesh but in the soul, according to what we read in another psalm: My soul has thirsted for God, the strong, the living (Ps 41 [42]:2). For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal 5). For these are opposed to one another, so that we do not do the things we wish.

26:9.t: But, as I said, at the crowing of the cock their President comes, and gently touching the sleeper with his foot, rouses them all. For there are none sleeping naked. Then as soon as they have arisen they stand up, and sing the prophetic hymns with much harmony, and well composed tunes. And neither harp nor pipe nor other musical instrument utters such sweet melodies, as you hear from the singing of these saints in their deep and quiet solitudes. And the songs themselves too are suitable, and full of the love of God. "In the night," they say, "lift up your hands unto God. With my soul have I desired Thee in the night, yea with my spirit within me will I seek Thee early."

And what follows, In the night, according to the Seventy is joined to the following passage, according to the Hebrew to the former one. And he can say, My soul has desired you in the night, who says confidently with the Psalmist: Every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with tears (Ps 6:7). Night and darkness can also be taken for tribulation and distress. Hence in another psalm too the Prophet sings of the security of the righteous: The sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6), that is, neither in prosperity nor in adversity will you ever be moved from your place.

But also with my spirit within my breast, from the morning I will watch for you. LXX: From the night my spirit rises early to you, O God: for your judgments are a light upon the earth. We wish both to follow the Hebrew and not to pass over the common edition entirely, and by this necessity of things we are compelled to seek different understandings in a different order and wording. So what is said, from the night, is, according to the Seventy, as we said, the beginning of this passage; according to the Hebrew, the end of the preceding one; although even according to the Seventy it can be taken at the end of the preceding testimony, so that the sense is: My soul desires you in the night; and afterwards it begins: in the morning my spirit rises to you, O God. […]

When you have done your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. Let us have mercy on the impious, and he will not learn righteousness; in the land of the saints he has done wickedly, and he will not see the glory of the Lord. LXX: Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth. For the impious has ceased, and he will not learn righteousness upon the earth; he will not do truth; let the impious be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew, and when we have chosen to express the sense of the Prophet, then let us pass to the Seventy translators. […]

According to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth are commanded to learn righteousness. For every man seems righteous to himself; but God knows the hearts of all, who will render to each according to his works (Prov 21). And in another place of the same book it is said: There are ways of a man which seem straight; but their ends look into the depth of hell (Prov 14:12). Hence we ought to learn righteousness, and not trust in our own judgment. For there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl 7); not because he is righteous, but because he seems to himself to be righteous. […]

For "night" is this present life, and as long as we are in it, we are covered with a mist of uncertain imaginations as far as the sight of inward objects is concerned. For the prophet was sensible that he was held by a certain mist in his sight of the Lord, when he says, "My soul longed for you in the night." As if he were to say, I long to behold you in the obscurity of this present life, but I am still surrounded by the mist of infirmity.
26:9.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 23, Section 39

26:9.t: Anyone who has been able to reach out for the truth has been on fire with this love. For this reason David said, "My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" And he counseled us, saying, "Seek his face continually." And for this reason the prophet said, "My soul has desired you in the night, and with my spirit within my breast I will watch for you in the morning." And again the church says to the Lord in the Song of Songs, "I have been wounded with love."It is right that the soul, after bearing in its heart a wound of love brought on by its burning desire, should reach out for healing at the sight of the doctor. And so, again, it says, "My soul melted when he spoke." […]

The constancy of the desire, for day and night, that is, at all times, or in prosperity and adversity, my soul has desired you: in my bed I sought him whom my soul loves (Song 3:1); O God, my God, to you do I watch at break of day (Ps 62:2[63:1]).

Third, he sets out the usefulness of justice: when you shall do your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world shall learn justice: the Lord shall be known when he executes judgments (Ps 9:17[16]).

26:10.t: For our Lord Jesus Christ came, not only that we might behold His glory here, but also that which shall be. For therefore He saith, "I will that these also be with Me where I am, that they may behold My glory." Now if the glory here was so bright and splendid, what can one say of that which shall be? for it shall appear not on this corruptible earth, nor while we are in perishable bodies, but in a creation which is imperishable, and waxes not old, and with such brightness as it is not possible even to represent in words. O blessed, thrice blessed, yea many times so, they who are deemed worthy to be beholders of that glory! It is concerning this that the prophet says, "Let the unrighteous be taken away, that he behold not the glory of the Lord." […]

To which the Lord answered: Let us have mercy on the impious; which all, except the Seventy, translated alike. And the sense is: rather let the impious obtain mercy, and learn my clemency, while he too is saved. And again, to the Lord as he speaks, the Prophet answered in the person of human impatience: And he will not learn righteousness. And the sense is: and how will he be able to know your righteousness, if he has experienced only clemency? And he gives the reasons why he wishes him to learn the righteousness of God: because he has acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and has fought continually against your saints, he ought to feel torments. And again the Lord, tempering the sentence, says: And let him not see, or he will not see the glory of the Lord. […]

O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see: let them see, and let the zeal of the people be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies. LXX: O Lord, your arm is lofty, and they did not know; but knowing they will be confounded: zeal will seize the untaught people, and now fire will eat the adversaries. What he had said above, and he will not see the glory of the Lord, can be understood thus: You ask, O Prophet, that I should not have mercy on the impious, lest, if I have had mercy on him, he who has acted wickedly in the land of the saints should begin not to know righteousness; I answer you: will he then not see the glory of the Lord? Will he then not behold my triumphs, he who rather ought to see me reigning, so that he may know how great a good he lacks? […]

In the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God, except for those who are clean of heart; hence, "Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God." From here on he begins to speak of that world where all who rise again will not see God, but only those who rise to eternal life. The unworthy will not see him, for of them it is said, "Let the wicked be taken away lest he behold the brightness of the Lord." But the worthy will see him, and of such the Lord spoke when, though present, he was not seen, saying, "He that loves me keeps my commandments, and he that loves me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him and will manifest myself to him."

In this human form the good will see him in whom they have believed; the wicked, him whom they have despised. But the wicked will not see him in the form of God in which he is equal to the Father, for as the prophet says, "The wicked shall be taken off that he may not see the glory of the Lord," and, on the other hand, "Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God."

Then, therefore, we shall come and we shall enjoy the one thing; but the one thing will be all things to us. For what was it I said, my brothers, when I began to speak? What is that sufficiency which we shall possess when we shall have no need? What is the sufficiency which we shall possess? I had intended to say, "What will God give to us which he will not give to them?" "Let the wicked be taken away that he may not see the glory of God." Hence God will give his glory to us so that we may enjoy it; and the wicked will be taken away that he may not see the glory of God. God himself will be the entire sufficiency which we shall possess as our own. Greedy one, what did you seek to gain? What does anyone, for whom God is not enough, seek from God?

His coming means his return from the judgment to his kingdom. The Lord comes to us after the judgment, because he lifts us up from his human appearance in the contemplation of his divinity; his coming means that he leads us to the vision of his glory. We see in his divinity after the judgment the one we beheld in his humanity at the judgment. At the judgment he comes in the form of a servant and appears to everyone, since it is written, "They will look on him whom they pierced." When the condemned fall down to their punishment, the righteous are led to the brightness of his glory, as is written: "The wicked is taken away, so that he will [not] see the glory of the Lord."

604. Let us have pity. Here he excludes mercy, and concerning this, he does two things.

First, the Lord proposes mercy interrogatively: let us have pity: the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord (Ps 32[33]:5).

Second, the prophet excludes it, because of its uselessness: but he will not learn: because sentence is not speedily pronounced against the evil, the children of men commit evils without any fear (Eccl 8:11); a horse not broken becomes stubborn, and a child left to himself will become headstrong (Sir 30:8); and because of the gravity of the sin, because it profanes a holy place: in the land of the saints he has done wicked things: O God, the heathens are come into your inheritance, they have defiled your holy temple (Ps 78[79]:1); […]

26:11.t: To which the Prophet answered: O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and be stretched out to strike, so that the impious may not see you, and may not enjoy the light of your glory, not even for repentance. To whom the Lord answered: Let them rather see and be confounded, either the zeal of the people or those zealous for the people, and let fire devour and consume your adversaries, that is, those of the people of the saints. And it is the fire of repentance, which tortures their hearts because they have lost such a Lord. This can also be understood of the Jews, who did not know Christ, the arm of the Lord, and when they have seen and recognized him whom they had fastened to the gibbet, will be confounded. […]

Note that there are two kinds of zeal, one full of love, the other full of hatred. The former is indicated in the words, "The zeal of your house has devoured me"; the latter, in the words, "Zeal has taken hold of the senseless people, and now fire shall devour your opponents."

606. Second, the prophet responds: Lord, let your hand be exalted.

607. Third, the Lord determines the spiritual punishment: let the envious people see, and be confounded: every eye shall see him (Rev 1:7), in the glory of his humanity, not of his divinity; and the bodily punishment: let fire devour your enemies: they were cast alive into the pool of fire (Rev 19:20).

26:12.t: Whenever you see a man living in wickedness, and enjoying great prosperity, and suffering no calamity, on this account lament for him the more, because, being under the power of disease and grievous corruption, he increases his own weakness, becoming worse by luxury and indolence. For punishment is not in itself an evil, but the real evil is sin. The latter separates us from God; the former leads us to God, and mitigates His wrath. How is this shown? Hear the prophet saying, "O priests, comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and say that she has received of the Lord's hand double for her sins." And again: "O Lord our God, give us peace, for thou hast repaid all to us."
26:12.s: HOMILIES ON LAZARUS AND THE RICH MAN 3

26:12.t: But I say all this now, and select all the histories that contain trials and tribulations, and the wrath of kings, and their evil designs, in order that we may fear nothing, save only offending God. For then also was there a furnace burning; yet they derided it, but feared sin. For they knew that if they were consumed in the fire, they should suffer nothing that was to be dreaded; but that if they were guilty of impiety: they should undergo the extremes of misery. It is the greatest punishment to commit sin, though we may remain unpunished; as on the other hand, it is the greatest honour and repose to live virtuously, though we may be punished. For sins separate us from God; as He Himself speaks; "Have not your sins separated between you and Me?" […]

O Lord, you will give us peace: for you have wrought all our works for us. LXX: O Lord our God, give us peace: for you have rendered all things to us. It must be noted that after he has rendered to us our works, he is going to give peace, and how they set out the reasons why they ask for peace. For they say that for all the works which they have wrought upon the earth they have endured torments, and that it is just that after punishments and tortures they should obtain mercy. Or otherwise: Because the consummation of the world has come, and all that you spoke through the Prophets has been fulfilled in deed, and you have rendered all that you promised, grant us peace, which surpasses all understanding.

The time when our external enemy the devil will be under our feet is when the internal enemy, covetousness, has been healed, and we shall be living in peace. What sort of peace? The sort that "eye has not seen nor ear heard." What sort of peace? The sort that no imagination can conceive and no quarreling intrude on. What sort of peace? The sort about which the apostle said, "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts." About this peace the prophet Isaiah says, "O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us everything you promised." You promised Christ; you have given him to us. You promised his cross and the shedding of his blood for the forgiveness of sins; you have given them to us. […]

What's the meaning of "Where, death, is your sting?" It means, "Where is sin?" You ask, and it is nowhere. "For the sting of death is sin." They are the apostle's words, not mine. That is when we will be able to say, "Where, death, is your sting?" Sin will be nowhere, neither to take you captive, nor to assault you nor to tickle your consciousness. That is when we will not say, "Forgive us our debts." But what will we say? "Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us everything."

Through all that we do, therefore, let us return with a careful mind to the fountain of true light. Let us give thanks to our Creator for the good things we receive, and let us humbly say to him with the prophet Isaiah: "All our works you have worked for us." For our good works are the works of him whose heart it did not suffice to raise us up unless he also bowed down himself for us. For if God, coeternal with the Father before the ages, had not become man in time, when would temporal man have tasted eternal things? Therefore the descent of truth became the ascent of our humility.

"A man's steps are directed by the Lord." Whoever walks a straight path composed of human steps does so not by the freedom of human judgment but by the governance of him to whom Isaiah said, "All of our works were accomplished by you." "What man can understand his way?" In this it becomes clear that whatever goodness anyone possesses from himself he does not have except through the grace of God, because no one is able to understand through the freedom of his own judgment either what kind of future he will have or the quality and duration of conquests to come.

All our merits are rooted in the merit of Christ, whether satisfactory for punishment or meritorious of eternal life, because we are worthy neither to be absolved from offense against the highest good, nor to gain the immensity of the eternal reward, which is God, except through the merit of the God-man, to whom we can and ought to say: All our works you have wrought in us, O Lord.

608. Fourth, the prophet consents rejoicing, setting out two good consequences from these punishments: the peace of the people, therefore, Lord, this having been done, you will give us peace, and we hope for this from you: for all our works: it is God who works in you, both to will and to accomplish (Phil 2:13), you have wrought, the works, that is, the punishments, by which you have sufficiently cleansed us, below: she has received of the hand of the Lord double (Isa 40:2).

613. Note also on the word, peace (Isa 26:12), that there are three things that make peace in the future life:

first, the abundance of good things: he has placed peace in your borders (Ps 147:14);

second, freedom from evils, below: and my people shall sit in the tabernacles of confidence (Isa 32:18); […]

26:13.t: For the Son of God indeed, being himself the Word, is Lord of all. But we once were subject from the first to the slavery of corruption and the curse of the law. Then by degrees fashioning for ourselves things that were not, we served, as says the blessed apostle, "them which by nature are no gods." Ignorant of the true God, we preferred things that were not to the truth. But afterwards, as the ancient people when oppressed in Egypt groaned, so when we too had the law "engrafted" in us, according to the unutterable sighings of the Spirit made our intercession, "O Lord our God, take possession of us"; then, as "he became a house of refuge" and a "God and defense," so also he became our Lord. Nor did he then begin to be, but we began to have him for our Lord.

O Lord our God, lords have possessed us without you: only in you may we remember your name. LXX: Lord our God, possess us: O Lord, besides you we know no other, we call upon your name. For this reason we seek mercy and peace, which is to be granted after all things, because lords have possessed us without you, namely the idols, or the demons who sit by the idols; and we ask nothing else but that, after very many errors, we may be worthy to remember your name. According to the Seventy, those who said, Lord God, possess us, pray for this, that after peace has been restored to them they may become the possession of God. […]

Second, the praise of God: O Lord our God, other lords besides you have had dominion over us, and therefore we could not give ourselves to praise of you; only in you, to whom alone we give ourselves, having no other god: servants have ruled over us (Lam 5:8).

26:14.t: Let the dying not live; let the giants not rise again. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have destroyed all memory of them. LXX: For the dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up. Therefore you have brought on, and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs. Symmachus, in his manner, more plainly: The dead will not give life; the giants will not raise up. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have utterly destroyed all memory of them. Let us speak first according to the Seventy. The question seems difficult, how the dead do not see life. It is solved thus: they do not see life so long as they are dead. As if we were to say, a blind man does not see the light so long as he is blind; […]

For hence it is said by the prophet, "The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise up again." For whom does he call "the dead" except sinners, and whom does he designate "giants" except those who over and above take pride in sin. Now the former do "not live," because by sinning they have forfeited the life of righteousness; these latter too "cannot rise up again" after death because after their transgression they are swollen with pride and do not have recourse to the remedies of penitence.
26:14.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 17, Section 30

26:14.t:
614. Let not the dead live. Here the prophet asks that God not free those punished from further punishment.

And first, he sets out the petition: let not the dead, sinners, live, in the life of glory, unless they repent; let not the giants, glorying in their own power, rise again, to glory: the wicked shall not rise again in judgment (Ps 1:5); the ancient giants did not obtain pardon for their sins (Sir 16:8[7]); or he asks that their fallen enemies not rise again further to power.

Second, he places the answer to the petition: therefore have you visited and destroyed them, and have destroyed all their memory: let their memory perish with a noise (Ps 9:7[6]); in the time of their visitation they shall fall (Jer 8:12).

26:15.t: You have been indulgent to the nation, O Lord, you have been indulgent to the nation. Have you been glorified? You have removed far all the ends of the earth. LXX: Add evils to them, O Lord, add evils to the glorious of the earth: you have made far off all the ends of the earth. The evils which the Seventy put twice are not found in the Hebrew; but because he had said above, Therefore you have brought on and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs, following the same sense they added of their own, evils: so that those who are glorious on the earth may be crushed by double evils. Further, according to the Hebrews the sense is far otherwise, and in agreement with the earlier discussion. The Lord had said: Let us have mercy on the impious. […]

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. For when a doctor for the sake of health with good reason either cuts or cauterizes those who are suffering from the inflammation of ulcers, it is considered an evil by those who have to bear it. Nor are the spur and the whip pleasant to a restive horse. […]

615. You have indulged. Here he urges God to the work of justice from experience;

and first, from experience among the gentiles,

second, among to the Jews: as a woman with child (Isa 26:17).

Concerning the first, he does two things.

First, he demonstrates from the experience of the uselessness of mercy, both as to the remission of sins: you have indulged, and as to the multiplication of good things: you have removed all the ends of the land far off: they become great and enriched, and they are grown gross and fat: and have most wickedly transgressed my words (Jer 5:27–28); the prosperity of fools shall destroy them (Prov 1:32).

26:16.t: O Lord, in distress they have sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching was to them. LXX: O Lord, in tribulation I remembered you; in small tribulation your teaching was to us. Because, being indulgent, you have often been despised and not glorified, but on the contrary all have withdrawn from the knowledge of you, therefore, O Lord, strike them, so that in distress they may seek you, and in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching may be to them: when so great a weight of evils presses upon them that they do not even dare to cry out confidently, but swallow their pain in silence. […]

Second, the usefulness of avenging justice: Lord, they have sought after you in distress: in their affliction they will rise early to me (Hos 6:1); in the time of their affliction they will say: arise, and deliver us (Jer 2:27).

26:17.t: As a woman who has conceived, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in pain in her pangs: so have we become before your face, O Lord. We have conceived, and as it were travailed, and have brought forth spirit. LXX: And as a woman in travail, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in her pain: so have we become ÷ to your beloved ⁚ because of fear of you, O Lord; we have received in the womb, and have travailed, and have brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which we have made upon the earth. […]

A time to give birth and a time to die. A time to plant and a time to pluck up what has been planted. No one doubts that both the rising and the passing away of men is known to God and fixed by him, and that to give birth is the same as to plant, and to die the same as to pluck up what has been planted. But since we read in Isaiah: From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and been in labor and given birth, this must be said: that in the perfect man that offspring which was born of fear dies, once he has begun to love God. For perfect indeed love casts out fear.

616. As a woman with child. Here he demonstrates the same thing from the experience among the Jews.

And first, he sets out the scourge of tribulation: as a woman with child: a woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow (John 16:21); there were pains as of a woman in labor (Ps 47:7[48:6]).

Second, the fruit of amendment: so are we become in your presence: now all chastisement for the present indeed seems not to bring with it joy, but sorrow: but afterwards it will yield to them that are exercised by it the most peaceable fruit of justice (Heb 12:11).

26:18.t: That there are also some souls that conceive offspring, the prophet made clear when he said: "from fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and travailed and gave birth to a spirit of salvation which you made upon the earth". For just as in those who are pregnant the seed is formed and shaped, so also in the soul that receives the word, the conception of the word is gradually formed and shaped within it. And this I think is what Paul says to the Galatians: "my children, whom I again bring forth in travail until Christ be formed in you", which is as though he were to say: until the word be formed and made manifest in you. […]

The soul therefore conceives from this seed of the word and forms the conceived word within itself, until it brings forth the spirit of the fear of God. For thus through the prophet the souls of the saints say: "from your fear, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb and have been in labor and have brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth". This is the childbearing of holy souls, this the conception, these are the holy nuptials which are fitting and suited to the great high priest Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

Their cows did not miscarry, therefore, but gave birth, so that their labor would be increased and that they would beget everything they conceived without reverence for God. The righteous, however, take delight in an altogether different way. They glory not in the abundance of their wealth or the fruitfulness of their livestock but in the Lord, saying, "We were impregnated with reverence for you, and we brought forth the spirit of salvation."

Isaiah also, proclaiming the resurrection to the people, says that he is the announcer of the Lord's message, for we read thus: "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken, and they shall speak in that day." And what the mouth of the Lord declared that the people should say is set forth later on, where it is written: "Because of your fear, O Lord, we have been with child and have brought forth the Spirit of your salvation, which you have poured forth upon the earth. They that inhabit the earth shall fall; they shall rise that are in the graves. For the dew which is from you is health for them, but the land of the wicked shall perish. Go, O my people, and enter into your chambers; hide yourselves for a little until the Lord's wrath pass by."

If such, therefore, be our experience in the flesh, let us turn to an examination of what is proper to the soul. There is no question that we have to deal here with something that is without sex, yet it fulfills all the offices of both sexes in that the soul conceives and, as in marriage, gives birth. Nature provides woman with a womb in which a living person is brought to birth in the course of time. Such, too, is that characteristic of the soul which is ready to receive in its womb-like recesses the seeds of our thoughts, to cherish them and to bring them forth as a woman gives birth to a child. This and no other is the meaning of the words of Isaias: We have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation. […]
26:18.s: On Cain and Abel, Book 1, Chapter 10

26:18.t: We, however, who heard the Lord our Savior say that those in Judea should flee to the mountains also lift our own eyes to the mountains, concerning which it was written: "I raise my eyes to the mountains, whence comes my assistance." And in another place [it is written], "Its foundation is in the holy mountains," and "The Lord surrounds his people as the mountains surround them," and "The city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden." We must shed the skin of the letter and, ascending Mount Zion barefoot with Moses, say, "I will cross over and see this great vision." […]

Salvations we have not wrought on the earth; therefore the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. LXX: We shall not fall, but the inhabitants of the earth will fall. A different translation must needs have a different sense too. According to the Hebrew this is said: Because we have done nothing worthy of your mercy, therefore the impious have not fallen, but to this day prevail and possess the earth. But the Seventy assert this: that while the saints make the spirit of salvation upon the earth, those who are inhabitants of the earth fall; although between world, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל) and in Greek οἰκουμένη, and earth there is much difference. […]

For they have crushed, or cut asunder, with iron carts the women with child of Gilead. These are the women with child of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Woe to those who are with child, and to those who give suck in those days. The women with child are the souls of believers, who at the beginning of faith can say: From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived and been in labour; and if they have not been cut up and pierced with iron by the carts and the iron and toothed wheels, of which the psalmist says: The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, they can also say what follows: And we have brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth. […]

I speak to you a wondrous thing, but a true one. Our Zion, in which at times there are foreigners, and Tyre, and the Ethiopian: that watchtower, that harlot, that Rahab, that Babylon, she who spread apart her feet to everyone passing by, according to Ezekiel: that harlot, if she wills, suddenly becomes a virgin. She becomes a virgin, and conceives the Son of God, and gives birth. 'From the fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and were in labor; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.' See, then, that the harlot conceives from God and gives birth, and brings forth the Savior. We brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth. Therefore our soul, that Rahab, that harlot, can conceive and bring forth the Savior.

Even now let us rejoice somehow or other in this hope derived from the promises of one most faithful, until that richest of all possible joys arises, when "we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is," and our joy nobody shall take from us. Of this hope, you see, we have also received already the acceptable and freely given pledge that is the Holy Spirit, who produces in our hearts the unutterable groanings of holy desire. "For we have conceived," as Isaiah says, "and have brought forth the spirit of salvation." And, "when a woman is in labor," the Lord says, "she has sorrow, because her day has come; but when she has brought forth, there is great joy, because a human being has been born into the world." This will be the joy that nobody will take away from us; […]

And what did they? “There pains as of a woman in travail.” What are the pains “as of a woman in travail,” but the pangs of a penitent? See the same conception of pain and travail: “Of Thy fear” (saith Isaiah) “we have conceived, we have travailed of the Spirit of salvation.” So then the kings conceived from the fear of Christ, that by travailing they brought forth salvation by believing on Him whom they had feared. “There pains as of a woman in travail:” when of travail thou hearest, expect a birth. The old man travaileth, but the new man is born.

"When a woman gives birth, she is sorrowful because her hour has come." He refers to holy church as a woman on account of her fruitfulness in good works and because she never ceases to beget spiritual children for God. He says also in another place about this, "The kingdom of heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole [mass] was leavened." A woman took some yeast when the church, by the Lord's generosity, secured the energy of love and faith from on high. She hid this "in three measures of flour until the whole [mass] was leavened" when she performed her ministry of imparting the word of life to parts of Asia [Minor], Europe and Africa, until all the bounds of the world were on fire with love for the heavenly kingdom. […]

617. We have not wrought justice. Here he announces the procured peace, and concerning this, he does three things.

First, the reason for the delay is shown: we have not wrought justice, so that he alludes to what is said in Deuteronomy 28:7: the Lord shall cause your enemies, that rise up against you, to fall down before your face.

26:19.t: Then, too, Isaiah himself has plainly declared that there shall be joy of this nature at the resurrection of the just, when he says: "The dead shall rise again; those, too, who are in the tombs shall arise, and those who are in the earth shall rejoice. For the dew from Thee is health to them."

Unquestionably, if the people were indulging in figurative murmurs that their bones were become dry and that their hope had perished—plaintive at the consequences of their dispersion—then God might fairly enough seem to have consoled their figurative despair with a figurative promise. Since, however, no injury had as yet alighted on the people from their dispersion, although the hope of the resurrection had very frequently failed among them, it is manifest that it was owing to the perishing condition of their bodies that their faith in the resurrection was shaken. God, therefore, was rebuilding the faith that the people were pulling down. […]
26:19.s: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 31

26:19.t: Isaiah the prophet says, "The dead men shall rise again, and those who are in the tombs shall awake." And the prophet Ezekiel, now before us, says most plainly, "Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your graves." And Daniel says, "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame."67And there are many Scriptures that testify of the resurrection of the dead. For there are many other sayings on this matter. But now, by way of remembrance only, we will make a passing mention of the raising of Lazarus on the fourth day and just allude, because of the shortness of the time, to the widow's son also who was raised. […]

Do not listen to those who say that this body is not raised up; for raised it is, as Isaiah witnesses, saying, "The dead shall arise, and they in the tombs shall be raised." Or, as Daniel says, "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame." But while rising again is the common lot of all people, the manner of rising again is not alike for all. For while we all receive everlasting bodies, those bodies are not alike for all. That is to say, the righteous receive such bodies as may enable them to join with the band of angels throughout eternity, while sinners received bodies in which to undergo through the ages the torture of their sins.

Let your dead live, let my slain rise again: awake and give praise, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is a dew of lights, and the land of the giants you will pull down to ruin. LXX: The dead will rise again, and they will rise again from the tombs, and those who are in the earth will rejoice. For your dew is their healing, but the land of the impious will fall. While the saints travail and bring forth the spirit, and the inhabitants of the earth fall, because they have not wrought salvations on the earth, those whom the Apostle calls the dead in Christ, and who have been slain for the name of the Lord, will rise again in glory (1 Thess 4). And because their death is sleep, they are said, not, as according to the Seventy, to rise again, but to awaken and to wake up. […]

But the heavens too shall give their dew, the heavens of which it is written in Psalm 18 (19): The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. Of these heavens it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, O heavens, with him, that is, with the Lord and Savior, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; it is he who speaks with Moses: Let my speech be awaited like the rain, and let my words come down like the dew. For those who were dead in sins shall rise again, and those who lay in whitewashed sepulchres, which are full of dead men's bones, shall be raised up, and those who dwell in the earth shall rejoice. […]

The first part [of the verse] concerns the resurrection of the just, but the last few words may be taken to mean "the bodies of the wicked will fall into the ruin of damnation." In regard to the resurrection of the just, the attentive reader will notice some distinction. "The dead shall rise" refers to the first resurrection; "those in the graves" refers to the second; and in the following words we may not improperly find a reference to the saints whom the Lord will find alive on earth. As for the word "your dew is their health," we are not wrong in taking "health" to mean "immortality," that most perfect health which needs no daily medicine of ordinary food.

Those persons therefore who were restored to life by the power of Christ, we take as a pledge of the hope prepared for us of a resurrection of the dead: and these were, this young man, and Lazarus of Bethany, and the daughter of the chief of the synagogue. And this truth the company of the holy prophets proclaimed before: for the blessed Isaiah said, "The dead shall arise, and those in the graves shall be restored to life: for the dew from Thee is healing to them." And by dew he means the life-giving operation of Christ, which is by the instrumentality of the Holy Ghost.
26:19.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

26:19.t: The prophet Isaiah therefore has said to us, "Your dead men shall arise: and those in the graves shall be raised; and they who are in the earth shall rejoice: for the dew from You is healing to them." And by the dew I imagine he means the life-giving power of the Holy Spirit, and that influence which abolishes death, as being that of God and of life.
26:19.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

26:19.t: Further Isaiah says: The dead shall rise again, and they that are in the graves shall awake. And it is clear that the souls do not lie in the graves, but the bodies.
26:19.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 27

26:19.t:
618. Second, the promise of restoration of the people through resurrection is set out, either bodily resurrection on the last day or resurrection from the misery of captivity. Hence resurrection is promised: your dead men shall live, the voice of the prophet to the Lord (Ezek 37); the thanksgiving of the resurrected is announced: awake, and give praise: many of those that sleep in the dust of the earth, shall awake (Dan 12:2); and the cause, or reason, of the resurrection is assigned: for your dew is the dew of the light, namely, of divine kindness (Hos 6:3).

619. Third, the destruction of their enemies is shown, and first, he sets out the destruction itself: the land of the giants, that is, of the proud and powerful, above: it shall be as a ruinous heap of stones (Isa 17:1).

26:20.t: All the generations from Adam to this day have passed away; but those who were made perfect in charity by the grace of God live among the saints; and they shall be made manifest at the judgment of the kingdom of Christ. For it is written, "Enter into your chamber a little while, until my wrath and anger pass, and I remember the good day and will raise you up out of your graves."

When we read, "Go, my people, enter into your closets for a little while, until my anger passes away," we have in the closets graves, in which they will have to rest for a little while, who shall have at the end of the world departed this life in the last furious onset of the power of Antichrist. Why else did he use the expression closets in preference to some other receptacle, if it were not that the flesh is kept in these closets or cellars salted and reserved for use, to be drawn out thence on a suitable occasion? It is on a similar principle that embalmed corpses are set aside for burial in mausoleums and sepulchers, in order that they may be removed from there when the Master shall order it. […]
26:20.s: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 27

26:20.t: He builds, therefore, the ark and makes in it nests, that is, certain storerooms, in which animals of diverse kinds may be received. Of which the prophet also says: "Go, my people, enter into your storerooms, hide yourself for a little while, until the fury of my wrath passes by." This people, then, which is saved in the Church, is compared to all those, whether men or animals, which were saved in the ark.

But according to the anagogy, the people of God is commanded to enter into its chambers, or storerooms, for ταμεῖα means both: to shut, according to the precept of the Gospel, the door of its chamber (Matt 6), and to say with the Prophet: Set a guard, O Lord, on my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips (Ps 140 [141]:3); and to hide itself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes, so that it does nothing for the sake of glory, but enjoys the good of conscience and awaits God alone as judge. […]

Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your doors upon you: hide yourself a little for a moment, until the indignation passes. For behold, the Lord will come forth from his place, to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him; and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer cover its slain. LXX: Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door: hide yourself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes. For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer hide the slain. Above he had said of the saints, The dead will rise again, and those who are in the tombs will rise again; for the dew from you is their healing; […]

Certainly there are two things that make us hope for the bliss of the just and the end of all suffering: death and the resurrection from the dead. In death is rest, as the prophet says, "My people, enter into your chambers, hide yourself a little until the indignation of the Lord pass away." But in the resurrection there is perfect happiness in the whole person, that is, in flesh and spirit. Consequently we are not to think that both of these are to be marked by the labor of fasting but rather by the rejoicing of refreshment.

Second, the immunity of the people of God: go, my people; enter into your chambers, tombs, or literally, the fortifications in which they sometimes carefully kept themselves, below: in a moment of indignation have I hid my face a little while from you, but with everlasting kindness have I had mercy on you (Isa 54:8); and it was said to them that they should rest for a little time till the number of their brethren should be filled up (Rev 6:11).

26:21.t: And what follows, For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring his wrath, signifies this: that the wrath of God begins from the saints, or that all his vengeance is just and holy, not coming down from disturbance of mind, as is usual among men, but from zeal to correct. And I consider the earth of the inhabitants to be that of which it is written: Let the earth hear the words of my mouth (Deut 32:1). And: Give ear, O earth (Isa 1:2). And again: Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord (Jer 22:29). For as those who dwell on the earth, so those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8). And earth in this place signifies the soul that lives carnally. […]

Third, he sets out the order of destruction, for it comes through judgment; hence he sets out the coming of the judge: for behold the Lord will come: behold the Lord will come forth (Mic 1:3), and all the angels with him; and the revealing of their crimes: and the earth shall disclose her blood: O earth, cover not you my blood, neither let my cry find a hiding place in you (Job 16:19).

27:1.t: In the same way the serpent, which is the author of sin, is called crooked, and the sword of God is drawn against the dragon, the crooked serpent, which makes many twists and turns in its progress. As the coiling movement of the serpent trails along, it is traced unevenly on the ground, since, if it were otherwise, the first parts would hasten along, the next follow transversely and the tail bend aside in the opposite direction. Therefore, he who follows the serpent shows that his life is crooked, uneven, and filled with contrarieties; but, he who follows after the Lord makes his paths straight and his footprints right.

In that day the Lord will visit with his hard and great and strong sword upon Leviathan the bar serpent, and upon Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the whale that is in the sea. LXX: In that day God will bring the holy and great and strong sword upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. The Hebrews hand down that the devil, that is, the slanderer, which is a Greek name, is called in Hebrew SATAN (שטן), that is, adversary. Hence in Zechariah too it is said: Satan, that is, the adversary, stood at his right hand to oppose him (Zech 3:1). And he is also called BELIAL (בליעל), that is, apostate, transgressor, and without yoke. […]

For "Leviathan" is interpreted to be "their addition." Whose "addition," then, but the "addition" of people? And it is properly styled "their addition," for since by his evil suggestion he brought into the world the first sin, he never ceases to add to it day by day by prompting to worse things.Or indeed it is in reproach that he is called Leviathan, that is, styled "the addition of men." For he found them immortal in Paradise, but by promising the divine nature to immortal beings, he as it were pledged himself to add somewhat to them beyond what they were. But while with flattering lips he declared that he would give what they did not have, he robbed them cunningly even of what they had. […]
27:1.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 4, Sections 15-16

27:1.t: For who is described by the designation of the "serpent" but our old enemy, at once slippery and crooked, who for the deceiving of humankind spoke with the mouth of a serpent? Of whom it is said by the prophet, "Leviathan the serpent, the crooked one"; who was for this reason allowed to speak with the mouth of a serpent, that by Leviathan's vessel humanity might learn what he was that dwelt within. For a serpent is not only crooked but slippery as well; and so because he stood not in the uprightness of truth, he entered into a crooked animal.… He spoke to man by means of a slippery animal because if one does not resist him, he secretly slips into the interior of the heart. Now "the dens" of this serpent were the hearts of wicked people.
27:1.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 17, Section 51

27:1.t:
620. In that day. In this part he recalls divine and paternal correction, and first, by foreign scourges, second, by their own scourges: in that day (Isa 27:2); hence it said in Wisdom 11:11: for you didst admonish and try them as a father.

Concerning the first, he sets out the scourge of Babylon: with his sword, namely, vengeance; Leviathan, namely, Nabuchodonosor, because of the addition to his kingdom that he subjugated to himself; the serpent, because of his poisonous tyranny; bar, because of the correction of the people by God, above: woe to the Assyrian, he is the rod of my anger (Isa 10:5); crooked, because of their infidelity: behold, he will drink up a river, and not wonder (Job 40:18); the whale: I sit in the heart of the sea (Ezek 28:2).

630. […]

27:2.t: In that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him. I the Lord, who keep it, will suddenly give it to drink: lest perhaps it be visited, I keep it night and day. LXX: In that day the good vineyard is his desire, that he may be its prince. I am a strong city, a city which is besieged: in vain will I give it drink. For they will be taken by night, and by day the wall will fall. The Hebrew in this place differs much from the edition of the Seventy; therefore let us discuss the particulars as we have set them out. The vineyard of which Isaiah speaks above, A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place: how it ought to be understood, let us learn from his own teaching: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:1); […]

621. In that day. Here correction by their own scourges is set out. Hence he first describes the chastisement; second, the consolation: and it shall come to pass, that in that day (Isa 27:13). Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he foretells the chastisement; second, the manner is examined: there is no indignation in me (Isa 27:4). Concerning the first, he does three things. First, he foretells the song of sorrow: the vineyard, formerly, in the prophets and patriarchs, of pure wine, above: for the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa 5:7).

27:3.t: It is the soul, too, that says, "I am a strong city, a city besieged." The city is besieged through Christ, the city is that heavenly Jerusalem, in which there are interpreters of God's law and men skilled in doctrine in great abundance; through them one seeks the Word of God.

Therefore let us flee these evils and elevate our soul to the image and likeness of God. The flight from evils is the likeness of God, and the image of God is gained through the virtues. And so, like a painter, he has painted us with the colors of the virtues. "See, I have painted your walls, Jerusalem." Let us not wipe away with the brush of neglect the props of the painted walls of our soul. And so "I have painted the walls," with which we can turn away the enemy. The soul has its walls; from them it stands forth and concerning them it says, "I am a strong city, a city besieged." By these walls it is guarded, and by them it is protected under siege. And truly the soul is a wall, which stretches forth over the camp. […]

Second, he sets out the intention of the one who punishes: I am the Lord that keep it, below: you have drunk at the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath (Isa 51:17). Third, he sets out the benefit, for which they were ungrateful: lest any hurt come to it, I keep it night and day: your word, O Lord, which heals all things (Wis 16:12).

27:4.t: Indignation is not in me: who will make me a thorn and a brier in battle? I will march upon it; I will burn it up together. Or rather shall I hold fast my strength? It will make peace for me, peace it will make for me. LXX: There is none that has not laid hold of it. Who will set me as keeper of stubble in a field? Because of this adversary I have driven it back. Therefore the Lord has done all that he arranged: I have been burned; its inhabitants will say, we will make peace with him, we will make peace with him. […]

622. There is no indignation in me. Here he examines the manner of punishment, and first, the deliberation of the judge is set out; second, the execution of the result of deliberation: for the strong city shall be desolate (Isa 27:10). Concerning the first, he does three things. First, he sets out severe judgment, setting out the wrath of rage: there is no indignation in me, as if to say: indeed, I am justly indignant, for they are ungrateful for my benefits, below: full of the indignation of the Lord (Isa 51:20); and out of wrath he determines a severe punishment: who shall give to me a thorn and a brier, as to the preceding difficulties that arose together among them, above: briers and thorns shall come up over it (Isa 5:6); […]

27:5.t: 623. Second, he sets out the moderation of the sentence: or rather shall I take hold of my strength? As if to say: I will restrain my wrath; by way of contrast: the Lord will not turn away the wrath of his indignation (Jer 30:24). And he sets out the fruit of the moderation of the sentence as to the good, which all will bear in relation to God: shall it make peace with me, as if to say: will he make peace with me by good works? Below: the work of justice shall be peace (Isa 32:17).

27:6.t: Those who come forth from the root of Jacob, Israel will blossom and bud, and they will fill the face of the world with seed. LXX: Those who come are the sons of Jacob: Israel will bud and blossom, and its fruit will fill the world. After the Apostles, preaching the Gospel in the whole world, have said, We will make peace with Christ, we will make peace with him, those who were of the seed of Jacob on high, and have attained to the apostolic dignity, will be called sons of Jacob. Then Israel will bud and blossom, seeing that the whole world has been filled with the teaching of its sons and has borne most abundant fruits, which while it remained in Judea it had not borne.

In relation to himself, Israel shall blossom, in faith, or in good intention, and bud, in completion of the work, below: Jerusalem shall flourish like the lily (Isa 35:1); and in relation to his neighbor: they shall fill the face of the world with seed, who shall rush in, namely, the Apostles, above: the law shall come forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa 2:3); their sound has gone forth into all the earth: and their words unto the ends of the world (Ps 18:5[19:4]).

27:7.t: Has he struck him according to the stroke of him who struck him? Or as he killed his slain, so was he killed? This place is understood in two ways: either against Jerusalem, so as to say that it was not struck by God as it itself struck Christ and his Apostles; or against the multitude of the nations, in that, while they persecuted and shed Christian blood, the Apostles and apostolic men nonetheless took care of their salvation and reconciled them to God.

624. And he sets out the supplementing of the punishment as to the ungrateful: has he struck him according to the stroke of him that struck him? Here he reproaches the benefit of the moderated punishment: he has not dealt with us according to our sins (Ps 102[103]:10).

27:8.t: In measure against measure, when it has been cast off, you will judge it. LXX: Quarreling and reproaching, he will send them away. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: As Jerusalem did, so will it receive, and according to the measure with which it measured, it will be measured back to it. And it will receive the measure heaped up when the time of judgment has come and God has cast it off. According to the Seventy, what is said depends on what precedes. For Israel will not be struck as it struck, nor killed as it killed: Israel, which quarreled against the Apostles, and reproached its teachers, and commanded them not to speak in the name of Christ. Therefore the Lord will cast them off and drive them out of his flock. […]

In measure: here he threatens judgment adequate to their sin; when it shall be cast off, from the worship of God through faithlessness, not believing in Christ: according to the measure of the sin shall the measure also of the stripes be (Deut 25:2); he has meditated: here he shows the support of the sentence, with his severe spirit, because it cannot be placated, above: cease therefore from the man, whose breath is in his nostrils (Isa 2:22).

27:9.t: Therefore by these things iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and this is all the fruit, that his sin may be taken away: because he has made all the stones of the altar like stones of ash dashed to pieces; the groves and the shrines will not stand. LXX: Therefore the iniquity of Jacob will be taken away, and this will be his blessing, when I have taken away his sin, when he has made all the stones of the altars crushed like ash ground small, and their trees will not endure, nor the idols. He gives the reasons why, after the Jews have laid hands on the Lord, they may obtain pardon if they are willing to do penance, so that the prayer of the Savior may be fulfilled: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34). […]

625. Third, he explains the motive for moderating the punishment, so that he would not destroy them entirely at that time, namely, because Christ and the Apostles were to descend from that people, and through their preaching the worship of idols was to be abandoned; and this is what is meant by, when he shall have made all the stones of the altar, as burnt stones broken in pieces, above: man shall bow down himself to his Maker, and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel (Isa 17:7).

27:10.t: For the fortified city will be desolate; the beautiful one will be left, and abandoned as a desert. There the calf will feed, and there he will lie down and consume its topmost shoots. LXX: Their idols will be cut down like a grove, and the flock dwelling far off will be abandoned like a forsaken flock, and it will be for a long time for pasture, and there the flocks will rest, and after a long time there will not be in it anything green, because it has been dried up. Jerusalem, the city once firm and fortified, because it did not receive the son of the householder, but said, Come, let us kill him, for this is the heir, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt 21:38), will be desolate. […]

626. The strong city, namely, Jerusalem: how doth the city sit solitary that was full of people? (Lam 1:1); as to the power of the enemy: there the calf, the army of the enemy, shall feed, as though resting without fear; branches, metaphorically, that is, ears of wheat, which signify princes, above: wild beasts shall rest there (Isa 13:21); or literally, it may be a sign of desolation: they saw the chambers joining to the temple thrown down (1 Macc 4:38).

27:11.t: The women, returning from the sepulcher and from this vision of the angels, were foreseen by Isaiah, when he says, "Come, you women, who return from the vision," that is, "come" to report the resurrection of the Lord. It was well, however, that the unbelief of the disciples was so persistent, in order that to the last we might consistently maintain that Jesus revealed himself to the disciples as none other than the Christ of the prophets.

And there were many women there, watching from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him; among whom was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee (27, 55. 56). They report that Isaiah prophesied concerning these women when he said: Women coming to the spectacle, come; for it is not a people having wisdom. For he calls women those who had been from afar and from afar were watching Jesus; he calls them to the word, that they may indeed forsake the senseless and forsaken people and come to the new covenant. And I judge those women to be blessed who are built up unto blessedness by the spectacle of the word and by the death of the body of Jesus; […]

In the drought of its harvest the women coming and teaching it will be crushed. For it is not a wise people: therefore he who made it will not have mercy on it, and he who formed it will not spare it. LXX: Women coming from the spectacle, come: for it is not a people having understanding; therefore he who made them will not have mercy on them, and he who formed them will not spare. What is said, In the drought of its harvest they will be crushed, for which the Seventy translated, there will not be in it anything green, because it has dried up, according to the Hebrew is coupled with what follows, according to the Seventy with the preceding sense. Let us speak first, then, according to the Hebrew. […]

And the destruction of men: its harvest shall be destroyed with drought; this is a metaphor: that is, as ears of wheat are crushed in the drought of summer; women shall come and teach it, by whom the people were thrown greatly into sin, above: as for my people, their oppressors have stripped them, and women have ruled over them (Isa 3:12); or because the women themselves taught them, as Deborah (Judg 4), and Holda (2 Kgs 22:14).

627. Second, he sets out the fairness of the punishment in relation to their guilt: for it is not a wise people, above: therefore is my people led away captive, because they had not knowledge (Isa 5:13).

27:12.t: And it will be in that day: the Lord will strike from the channel of the river to the torrent of Egypt. LXX: And it will be in that day: the Lord will shut in from the trench of the river to Rhinocorura. Had he not added, in that day, by which we are taught that what he is about to say is to be coupled with what precedes, we could have expounded a sense proper to this passage; but now everything is to be referred to what precedes. Since the fortified city will be desolate, and the once beautiful one will be left as a desert, and there the calf will lie down and consume the shoots of the vineyard, and all things will be dried up, since it is not a people having understanding, and because of its folly it has obtained no mercy from its Creator: therefore the Lord will strike, or shut […]

628. Third, the magnitude of the destruction, both as to universality of place: and it shall come to pass, that in that day the Lord will strike from the channel of the river even to the torrent of Egypt, that is, from one end to the other, above: from the sole of the foot unto the top of the head, there is no soundness therein (Isa 1:6); and as to the small number of men who will remain: and you shall be gathered together one by one: you shall remain few in number (Deut 28:62).

27:13.t: And it will be in that day: a blast will be sounded on a great trumpet; and those who had been lost from the land of the Assyrians, and those who had been cast out into the land of Egypt, will come, and they will worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem. LXX: And it will be in that day: they will sound with a great trumpet; and those who had perished in the region of the Assyrians, and those who had perished in Egypt, will come, and they will worship the Lord upon the holy mountain in Jerusalem. […]

629. And it shall come to pass. Here he sets out the consolation, through return to their land. A great trumpet, the precept of the king, above: he shall set up a sign unto the nations, and shall assemble the fugitives of Israel (Isa 11:12).

28:1.t: Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the falling flower of the glory of its exultation, who were on the summit of the most fertile valley, going astray from wine. Behold, the strong and mighty one of the Lord, like the onrush of hail, a whirlwind that shatters; like the onrush of many waters overflowing and sent forth upon a spacious land. With feet shall the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim be trodden down. And the falling flower of the glory of its exultation, which is upon the summit of the valley of the fat, shall be like an early fruit before the ripeness of autumn, which, when the beholder has looked upon it, as soon as he has taken it in his hand, he will devour it. […]

633. Woe to the crown. In this part, he threatens against those who disdain the predictions of the prophets, and first, against those who disdain in the present, second, against those to come in the time of Jeremiah, woe to you, apostate children (ch. 30). The first of these is divided into two parts. In the first, against those from the ten tribes; in the second, against those from the two tribes: but these also (Isa 28:7).

634. Concerning the first, he does three things. First, he denounces the sin of pride: woe to the crown, for they were proud of their multitude, which is the crown or glory of a king (Prov 14:28); […]

28:2.t: 635. Second, he threatens punishment: behold the Lord is mighty; and concerning this, he does two things. First, he sets out the strength of the enemy: behold, mighty, as to the strength of the enemy, whom he will send in; as a storm of hail, as to their multitude, above: nations shall make a noise like the noise of waters (Isa 17:13).

28:3.t:
" 3. The crown of pride, the hirelings of Ephraim shall be beaten down. 4. And the fading flower of glorious hope on the top of the high mountain shall be as the early fig: he that sees it will desire to swallow it, before he takes it into his hand. 5. In that day the Lord shall be the crown of hope, the garland of glory to the remnant of his people; for they shall be left in the spirit of judgment."

And here he prophesies that the Lord will be "a crown of hope and glory" to the remnant of his people, not to all their nation, but to those only signified by the remnant, and names the others in contrast to the remnant of his people "a crown of shame and hirelings of Ephraim."
28:3.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 2, Chapter 3

28:3.t: Second, he sets out the inflicting of the punishment, namely, the casting down of pride: the crown of pride shall be trodden under feet: in your anger you will tread the earth under foot (Hab 3:12).

28:4.t: And the emptying of glory, and the flower shall be as a hasty fruit, that is, ripe or early fruit, above: for before the harvest it was all flourishing (Isa 18:5); all your strong holds shall be like fig trees with their green figs (Nah 3:12).

28:5.t: In that day the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory and a garland of exultation to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of judgment to him who sits upon judgment, and strength to those returning from war to the gate. But these also have not known because of wine, and have gone astray because of drunkenness; the priest and the prophet have not known: they are swallowed up by wine because of drunkenness, they have gone astray in drunkenness: they have not known the seer, they have been ignorant of judgment, or wonderfully. For all the tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there was no more room. LXX: In that day the Lord Sabaoth shall be a crown of hope, which is woven of glory, for the remnant of the people. […]

The prophet expounds on the destiny of those in Israel who believed in Christ, because Israel did not perish completely, as the remnant of Israel was saved, according to the prophecy. Quite a number of people believed in Christ, and his apostles were, so to speak, the first fruit. Therefore at that time the Lord of hosts will be as a crown of hope and a diadem of glory to the remnant of his people. The Lord of hosts will crown the believers with hope and glory, that is, with hope of future blessings and with glory because they will reign with him. They will become the recipients of the highest honor and will be worthy of adoration and glory. What glory can be compared with that received in the kingdom of Christ? […]

636. Third, he sets out the glory of the just, namely, of the just of the two tribes: in that day, namely, in the time of Ezechias, when the ten tribes had been destroyed; as to three things. As to the joy of the people, a crown, which is of gold or silver, in contrast to the crown of pride; a garland, of flowers, in contrast to the fading flower, below: and I will give them a crown for ashes (Isa 61:3).

28:6.t: As to the justice of the king: and he, the Lord himself, shall be a spirit of judgment: a king shall reign, and shall be wise: and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth (Jer 23:5). As to the might of their soldiers: and strength, for the Lord will fight for them, above: because you have been my strength (Isa 25:4).

28:7.t:
637. But these also. Here he threatens against those among the two tribes who disdain the predictions of the prophets; and first, against the princes, second, against the city or against the people, woe to Ariel (ch. 29). The first of these is divided into two parts. First, he sets out the threat; second, the consolation: give ear (Isa 28:23). Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he denounces the sin and threatens destruction at the same time; second, he excludes remedy: wherefore hear the word of the Lord (Isa 28:14). Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he denounces their lack of knowledge; second, their contempt of teaching: for command (Isa 28:10).

638. Concerning the first of these, he does two things. […]

28:8.t: According to the anagogy, that Hebrew text in which we said: For all their tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no more room, can be referred to the heretics, and to the scribes and Pharisees, in this way: that we say all their teaching and all their mysteries are full of vomit and filth, since they do not digest the food of the holy Scriptures nor make it life-giving to the whole body, but void it unripe and stinking, so that God finds no place in them. […]

Third, he sets out the manner of their ignorance: for all the tables were full of vomit, for they gorged themselves in their temples until they vomited, as if they were devoted entirely to idols; and filth, namely, of all their shameful vices: as a dog that returns to his vomit (Prov 26:11), and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.

28:9.t: Whom shall he teach knowledge, and whom shall he make to understand what is heard? Those weaned from the milk, those drawn from the breasts: for command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there. For with speech of lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people, to whom he said: This is my rest; refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment, and they would not hear.
