Not that they did not ask, but that they would not hear the counsel of the prophet, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having confidence in the protection, or shadow, of Egypt. For the strength of Pharaoh, which is put twice in this place, the Hebrew has written MAOZ (מעוז). We have noted this so that, where we read in the last vision of Daniel (Dan 11) the God MAOZIM (מעוזים), we may understand not, as Porphyry dreams, the God of the village of Modim, but the mighty and strong God. Pharaoh among the Egyptians is the name of the royal power; and each is called by a particular name as well, as Pharaoh Neco and Pharaoh Hophra: as if we were to set Caesars and Augusti before the proper names of kings. […]

Scripture is the mouth of God. Hence Isaiah: "Woe to you who walk to go down into Egypt," that is, to secular sciences, "and have not asked at My mouth," that is, Sacred Scripture. We need not go down to other sciences in order to gain certainty before having had the witness on the mountain, that is, of Christ, Elias and Moses, meaning of the New Testament, of the Prophets and of the Law.

669. Second, he sets out the execution of this counsel as to walking the way: who walk, which is deformed by contempt of divine counsel; who have not asked at my mouth, the prophet: if you will separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth (Jer 15:19), because you would not do what he said; and by trusting in human help, trusting in the shadow of Egypt: cursed be the man that trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm (Jer 17:5).

30:3.t: And he sets out the effect: and the strength of Pharaoh shall be to your confusion: I will change their glory into shame (Hos 4:7).

30:4.t: And what follows: For your princes shall be in Tanis, and your messengers have come as far as Hanes, is to be read with mockery and ἐμφατικῶς: that, despising the counsel of God, they sent their princes to Tanis, a city of Egypt, in which was the royal house of Pharaoh, and where under Moses very many signs and portents were performed, as the Psalmist says: Who did wonders in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis (Ps 77 [78]:43). And the same Isaiah says against Egypt: Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you and say what the Lord Sabaoth has purposed against Egypt. The princes of Tanis have failed (Isa 19:12-13); and he records that they failed at that time when the Lord entered Egypt upon a light cloud. We do not read of Hanes, a city of Egypt, anywhere else; […]

Hence, as to the end of the way: for your princes went into Taphnis, which is only in the other part of Egypt, as if they feared to remain in the first borders: what have you to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the troubled water? (Jer 2:18).

30:5.t: And he shows their lack of hope: they were all confounded: put not your trust in princes: in the children of men, in whom there is no salvation (Ps 145:2–3[146:3]).

30:6.t: It is written in Isaiah: "the vision of the quadrupeds in tribulation and distress", and the rest, up to the place where he says: "the riches of the asps will not profit them". Let each one of us consider how great wealth of asps he has borne before this, how great riches of beasts, and how a rational man never sat upon our donkey — not the word of Moses, not of Isaiah, not of Jeremiah, nor of all the rest of the prophets — and he will see that the word of God and reason then sat upon us, when the Lord Jesus came and commanded his disciples that, going, they should untie "the colt of a donkey", which before had been tied up, so that it might walk free.
30:6.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

30:6.t: But if you wish to learn yet more beasts, the prophet Isaiah will teach you, who, under "the vision" which he entitled "of the quadrupeds in the desert", speaks by the prophetic spirit certain such things concerning beasts: "in tribulation", he says, "and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp; thence also the offspring of flying asps, who carried upon asses and camels their riches to a nation which shall not profit them". Can these things in any way be seen as said of bodily beasts, even by those who are exceedingly friends of the letter? For how can "the lion and the lion's whelp" or "the flying asps" "carry upon camels and asses their riches"? […]

The burden of the beasts of the South. For this the Hebrew says MASSA BEEMOTH NEGEB (משא בהמות נגב), which the Seventy translated: The vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert. The foregoing exposition, which we have woven with a very full unfolding of the history, is the interpretation of this place: that, according to prophetic custom, the burden, that is, the weight and load of torments and punishments, came not only upon Babylon and Philistia, and Moab, and Damascus, and Egypt, and the desert of the sea, and also Edom and Arabia, and the valley of Zion, and lastly Tyre, but also upon the beasts of the South, which the Seventy translated four-footed beasts in the desert. He means the tribe of Judah, which, situated in the southern part, borders on the wilderness; […]

In a land of tribulation and anguish, the lioness and the lion: from them the viper and the flying basilisk: carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts of burden, and their treasures on the hump of camels, to a people that will not be able to profit them: Egypt shall help in vain and to no purpose. LXX: In tribulation and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp: thence asps and the offspring of flying asps: who carried their riches on asses and camels to a nation that will not profit them: the Egyptians will profit you emptily and vainly. For lion the Hebrew has written LEIS (ליש); and for flying basilisk, which the Seventy translated offspring of flying asps, in the Hebrew it is called ἐμπρηστὴς and flying, which we can call the burner, and in Hebrew it is named SARAPH (שרף). […]

670. Third, he describes the carrying away of goods: the burden of the beasts;

he threatens first the destruction of Egypt. The burden, of the sons of Judah, beasts, because of their stupidity or because they bore their goods like beasts; of the south, because they fled to the south or because their dwelling was in the southern part. In a land of trouble, in Egypt, which in Hebrew is called "Meyrey," which is translated "trouble" or "distress": the sword which you fear, shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt (Jer 42:16). […]

30:7.t: Therefore I have cried out concerning this: it is only pride: be still. For which the Seventy translators, meaning I know not what, translated: Announce these things, since this consolation of yours is vain. Further, Symmachus translated ταραχαί εἰσιν κατοικεῖν, that is, there are tumults, that they may dwell. The Hebrew word REEB (רהב) Aquila translated ὅρμημα, that is, onset and pride; Symmachus disturbance; the Seventy vanity; Theodotion breadth; it is written with three letters, RES and HE and BETH, and it is the very word read in the Psalms: I will be mindful of Rahab and of Babylon, who know me (Ps 86 [87]:4). […]

30:8.t: The box-wood tree, because of its light material, trains the child’s hand when it is used for forming the outlines of the letters of the alphabet. Hence Scripture says: ‘Write upon box,’ in order that you may be admonished by the wood itself (which is an evergreen and is never devoid of foliage) never to be deprived of the support of your hope, but rather that the hope of salvation may be generated by faith.

Now go in and write for them on boxwood, and inscribe it carefully in a book: and it shall be in the last day for a testimony forever. The Hebrews say that, since in the prophets there is one spirit, and all times are joined together with the Lord, Jeremiah is commanded, and it is God's charge, that, having entered Egypt, he should write for them on boxwood, which is a wood that does not rot; or, as Symmachus translated, ἐπὶ πτυχὶ, that is, on a very broad tablet. For them, doubtless for the Jews: and that he should set it out carefully in a book, so that there may be no difficulty in reading it, so that when the prophecy has been fulfilled in fact, they may then understand that the word of the prophets is true. We run over the plain things so that we may linger on the more obscure.

Second, he sets out the confirmation of the command. Now therefore, you, Isaiah, go in, by prophetic vision, or you, Jeremiah, go in, into Egypt with the people, as it says in Jeremiah 43;

third, he assigns the fruit of this confirmation: and it shall be in that day for a testimony for ever: write this for a memorial (Exod 17:14).

30:9.t: For it is a people provoking to anger, and lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God. Who say to the seers: Do not see; and to those who look: Do not look out for us the things that are right: speak to us pleasing things; see errors for us. Take the way away from me: turn the path aside from me: let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face. It is plain that they provoked the Lord to anger, unwilling to hear the words of Jeremiah (Jer 43). They said to him: Do not see for us what we do not want: do not forbid us the way of Egypt, nor preach the things that are right; but say what pleases us, that we may go on into Egypt, which heaps sins upon sins. Why do you press upon us what we do not willingly hear? why do you show the way by which we do not wish to go? […]

673. For it is a people. Here he sets out the contempt of the people,

and first, the contempt by which they despised God: that provokes to wrath, as to sin of transgression: do not you provoke me, as the house of Israel provokes me (Ezek 2:8); and lying children, as to sin of speech, for they promised obedience to Jeremiah, a promise which they would not keep, as it says in Jeremiah 42. The children that are strangers have lied to me (Ps 17:46[18:45]): that will not, as to sin of omission: he that stops his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination (Prov 28:9).

30:10.t: The chief priests and the Pharisees, through the agency of Pilate, sealed the tomb; but the women saw him who was risen.… The chief priests lacked understanding, but the women beheld with their own eyes. When the soldiers came into the city and told the chief priests what had happened, they said to the soldiers, "Say, his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping." Well did Isaiah foretell this also, in their persons: "But tell us, and relate another error." Christ has risen and come back from the dead, and by a bribe they persuade the soldiers.

Say, when is a person most insulted—when he is silent, and one makes no answer, or, when he does speak (and is unheeded)? So that the insult is greater in the present case, when He does speak and thou wilt not hear: greater the contempt. "Speak not to us," we read, they said of old to the Prophets: but ye do worse, saying, Speak: we will not do. For there they turned them away that they should not even speak, as feeling that from the voice itself they got some sort of awe and obligation; whereas you, in the excess of your contempt, do not even this. Believe me, if you stopped our mouths by putting your hands over them, the insult would not be so great as it is now. […]
30:10.s: HOMILIES ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES 19

30:10.t: Second, he sets out their contempt of the prophets: who say to the seers, according to which they prohibited them from carrying out their proper office: you seer, go, flee away (Amos 7:12); inasmuch as they induced them to lie: speak unto us pleasant things: behold the words of the prophets with one mouth declare good things to the king (1 Kgs 22:13).

30:11.t: Turn away, inasmuch as they prohibited the word of divine knowledge: who have said to God: depart from us, we desire not the knowledge of your ways (Job 21:14).

30:12.t: Therefore thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel: Because you have rejected this word, and have hoped in false accusation and tumult, and have leaned upon it: therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach that falls, and is sought for in a high wall: since suddenly, when it is not hoped for, its crushing shall come. And it shall be broken in pieces as a potter's jar is shattered with a very mighty crushing: and there shall not be found among its fragments a sherd in which a little fire may be carried from the burning, or a little water drawn from the pit. […]

674. Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel. Here he threatens destruction to them, resuming the subject of their guilt that the punishment may appear more just: because you have rejected this word.

30:13.t: And he adds the punishment, where it says, therefore shall this iniquity be to you, signifying sudden punishment by the likeness of ruin, which lies hidden for a long time in a wall that falls suddenly in the end: for the destruction thereof shall come on a sudden: for when they shall say: peace and security; then shall sudden destruction come upon them (1 Thess 5:3).

30:14.t: And he shows the strong punishment: and it shall be broken small, under the likeness of the breaking of a vessel, of which no fragment remains whole for any use, namely, for carrying fire and drawing water, above: with breaking shall the earth be broken (Isa 24:19).

30:15.t: Would you know the power of repentance? Would you understand this strong weapon of salvation and the might of confession? By confession Hezekiah routed 185,000 of the enemy. That was important, but it was little compared to what shall be told. The same king's repentance won the repeal of the sentence God had passed on him. For when he was sick, Isaiah said to him, "Give charge concerning your house, for you shall die, and not live." What expectation was left? What hope of recovery was there when the prophet said, "For you shall die"? But Hezekiah did not cease from penitence, for he remembered what was written: "In the hour that you turn and lament, you shall be saved." […]

It is never too late to repent. You may have gone down from Jerusalem and may have been wounded on the way; yet the Samaritan will set you upon his beast and will bring you to the inn and will take care of you. Even if you are lying in your grave, the Lord will raise you though your flesh may stink. At least imitate those blind men for whose sake the Savior left his home and heritage and came to Jericho. They were sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death when the light shone upon them. For when they learned that it was the Lord who was passing by, they began to cry out, saying, "You son of David, have mercy on us." You too will have your sight restored, if you cry to him and cast away your filthy garments at his call. […]

For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: If you return and are quiet, you shall be saved: in silence and in hope shall be your strength; and you would not, and you said: By no means; but we will flee to horses: therefore you shall flee; and we will mount upon swift ones: therefore swift shall they be who pursue you. A thousand men from before the terror of one: and from before the terror of five you shall flee. LXX: Thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: When you have returned and groaned, then you shall be saved, and you shall know where you were: because you trusted in vain things, your strength has become vain; and you would not hear, but you said: We will flee upon horses: therefore you shall flee; […]

676. For thus says the Lord. Here he denounces their contempt of divine counsel, and concerning this, he sets out three things.

First, the counsel: if you return, below: be converted to me, and you shall be saved (Isa 45:22).

30:16.t: Second, their contempt: but have said: no. Therefore shall you flee: these are the words of the Lord. One way may we go out (Deut 28:25); and we will mount upon swift ones: the voice of the rebellious people; therefore shall they be swifter: the voice of the Lord: our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of the air (Lam 4:19).

30:17.t: When Moses fought against Amalek, it was not with the sword but with prayer that he prevailed. Therefore, if we wish to be lifted up, we must first prostrate ourselves.… We do not understand the prophet's words: "One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one." We do not cut away the causes of the disease, as we must do to remove the disease itself. Else we should soon see the enemies' arrows give way to our javelins, their caps to our helmets, their saddle horses to our chargers.

Until you are left like the mast of a ship on the top of a mountain, and like a signal upon a hill. Jeremiah too writes that, when those who had fled into Egypt had been slain by sword and famine, a few remained who returned to Judea (Jer 44). And as, when a ship has been broken and its framework dissolved, only the tree that is called the mast remains, and is set up as a signal on the summit of a mountain or on a lofty hill, so, as a signal and a trace, scarcely one or two would remain, to show the power of God. And then, he says, all the remnant of Judah, who now are entering the land of Egypt to dwell there, will know, when they have returned to the land of Judea, whose word is fulfilled, mine or theirs.

Third, he threatens destruction: a thousand men, Egyptians, shall flee for fear of one, Chaldean, and for fear of five, Chaldeans, you, all you Jews, shall flee: how should one pursue after a thousand, and two chase ten thousand? (Deut 32:30); till you be left as the mast, as a sign to evade shipwreck, above: there shall be made a show as a turpentine tree, and as an oak that spreads its branches (Isa 6:13).

30:18.t: Therefore the Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you, and therefore he shall be exalted in sparing you, because the Lord is a God of judgment: blessed are all who wait for him. Great is the clemency of God, that he waits for our repentance, and, until we are converted from our vices, holds back his mighty hand, so as not to be compelled to strike. And he has mercy and spares for this reason, that his mercy may be exalted, and the goodness of the Creator made known to all. Or certainly, according to what he says in the Gospel (John 12:32): When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself, he is exalted on the cross for this reason, that he may spare all. For he is the God of judgment; and blessed are all who wait for the Lord, who waits for their conversion. […]

30:19.t: For the people of Zion shall dwell in Jerusalem. The Jews refer this to the times of Cyrus, when the people returned from Babylon to Judea under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the high priest. But we, as we have often said already, refer all the promises that exceed the modest measure of that time to the coming of Christ, at which the people once captive, set free by the passion of the Lord, dwelt in Zion and Jerusalem, that is, in the watchtower and the vision of peace, that is, in the Church. Further, as to the word of holiness added in the Seventy, who said: for a holy people dwells in Zion, we can interpret it thus: we say that no one dwells in Zion except one who is holy, and who hears the Lord saying: Be holy, for I too am holy (Lev 11:44).

Weeping, you shall by no means weep; showing mercy, he will have mercy on you: at the voice of your cry, as soon as he hears, he will answer you. When you have returned to Zion and dwelt in Jerusalem, you shall by no means weep as you had wept before, but your weeping shall be turned into joy: For blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh (Luke 6:21). And after you have cried out and said to the Lord: I cried with my whole heart, hear me, O Lord (Ps 118 [119]:145); and again: I cried, have mercy on me, and I will keep your commandments (Ps 85 [86]); and elsewhere: I waited in the morning and cried out (Ps 118 [119]:147); […]

The Divine protection then is inseparably present with us, and so great is the kindness of the Creator towards His creatures, that His Providence not only accompanies it, but actually constantly precedes it, as the prophet experienced and plainly confessed, saying: "My God will prevent me with His mercy." And when He sees in us some beginnings of a good will, He at once enlightens it and strengthens it and urges it on towards salvation, increasing that which He Himself implanted or which He sees to have arisen from our own efforts. For He says "Before they cry, I will hear them: While they are still speaking I will hear them;" and again: "As soon as He hears the voice of thy crying, He will answer thee." […]
30:19.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 8

30:19.t: These two then; viz., the grace of God and free will seem opposed to each other, but really are in harmony, and we gather from the system of goodness that we ought to have both alike, lest if we withdraw one of them from man, we may seem to have broken the rule of the Church's faith: for when God sees us inclined to will what is good, He meets, guides, and strengthens us: for "At the voice of thy cry, as soon as He shall hear, He will answer thee;" and: "Call upon Me," He says, "in the day of tribulation and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify Me." And again, if He finds that we are unwilling or have grown cold, He stirs our hearts with salutary exhortations, by which a good will is either renewed or formed in us.
30:19.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 11

30:19.t:
678. For the people. Here he describes the benefit of mercy,

and first, in their exaltation,

second, in the oppression of their enemies: behold the name (Isa 30:27).

Concerning the first, he sets out two things.

First, the removal of evils against the captivity of exile: for the people of Zion shall dwell in Jerusalem, in the time of Zorobabel; or rather, all, mystically: he shall not be moved for ever that dwells in Jerusalem (Ps 124[125]:1–2); against the anxiety of sadness: weeping, before, you shall not weep, forever, but when you will be freed, above: the Lord God shall wipe away tears from every face (Isa 25:8); against the indignation of God: he will surely have pity: he shall call upon me, and I will hear him (Ps 90[91]:15).

30:20.t: And the Lord will give you scant bread and short water. If we refer these things to the times of Zerubbabel, the interpretation is easy: that under him there was no perfect joy, as David says: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted: so that they received not full and perfect comfort, but a likeness of comfort. But if to the coming of the Savior, then by the scant bread and short water, according to the Apostle Paul and this same prophet Isaiah, the word of the Gospel is foretold, which, in place of the long-drawn observances and commandments of the Law, summed up all things in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. For the Lord has made a word completed and cut short upon the earth (Gal 5).

And he will no longer make your teacher fly away from you, and your eyes shall see your instructor, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing behind your back: This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left. LXX: And those who deceive you shall no longer come near you, because your eyes shall see those who led you astray, and your ears shall hear behind you the words of those who deceive, who said: This is the way, let us walk in it, whether to the right or to the left. In this place the Seventy's edition and the Hebrew disagree greatly. First, then, we shall treat of the common edition, and afterward follow the order of the truth. […]

He has seen us sinning and has borne with it. He who forbade us to sin before we did it does not stop waiting to pardon us even after we have sinned. The one we have rejected is calling us. We have turned away from him, but he has not turned away. Hence Isaiah said, "Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of a counselor behind you." A person is counseled to his face, so to speak, when he is created for righteousness and receives the precepts of rectitude. When he despises these precepts, it is as if he is turning his back to his Creator's face. But he still follows behind us and counsels us that we have despised him, but he still does not cease to call us. […]

Against poverty: and the Lord will give you spare bread, and this is the sense: they will be content with little food: the chief thing for man's life is water and bread (Sir 29:28[21]); or because in the return from Babylon they suffered scarcity. This should be understood mystically, according to the Gloss.

679. Second, he sets out the gathering of goods; hence he says, and will not cause.

And first, of spiritual goods, as to chosen teaching, describing the teacher: to flee, that is, to withdraw; your teacher, Esdras, whose teaching they still use, or Christ.

30:21.t: God opens the bosom of his loving kindness to us if we return to him after sinning, for he says by the prophet, "If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him and marries another man, shall he return to her any more? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have prostituted yourself to many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord." Note how the plea of justice is proposed in regard to the wife who commits fornication and is deserted, and yet, for us who return after our fall, it is not justice but loving kindness that is shown. […]

We are truly repentant if we weep bitterly over the actions we have committed. Let us consider the riches of our Creator's attitude toward us. He has seen us sinning, and has borne with it. He who forbade us to sin before we did it, does not stop waiting to pardon us even after we have sinned. The one we have rejected is calling us. We have turned away from him, but he has not turned away. Hence Isaiah said, "Your eyes shall see your Teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of a Counselor behind you." A person is counseled to his face, so to speak, when he is created for righteousness and receives the precepts of rectitude. When he despises these precepts, it is as if he is turning his back to his Creator's face. […]

Behind your back, like someone fleeing when called back by his pursuer: he has given you a teacher of justice (Joel 2:23); and he sets out the teaching: this is the way: we will go the king's highway (Num 21:22).

30:22.t: And you shall defile the plates of your graven images of silver, and the garment of your molten image of gold, and you shall scatter them like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman: Go out, you shall say to it. LXX: And you shall defile the silvered and gilded idols: you shall break them in pieces and scatter them like the water of a menstruous woman, and you shall cast them away like dung. When you have understood the truth, and the deceivers have not come near you, but your eyes have seen your instructor and your ears have always heard: This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left: then you will break in pieces and scatter all the errors and idols and likenesses of the truth which an artful tongue had composed in the splendor of eloquence, which is what […]

And also as to due worship of God: and you shall defile the plates of your graven things of silver, reducing them to common use: he defiled the high places, and demolished them (2 Kgs 23:8); the garment, every adornment of an idol.

Second, as to temporal goods; hence he says, get you hence, namely, from spiritual goods to temporal goods.

30:23.t: And rain shall be given to your seed wherever you sow in the land, and the bread of the fruits of the land shall be most abundant and rich. LXX: Then there shall be rain for the seed of your land, and the bread of the fruits of your land shall be plentiful and rich. It is written in the volume of Kings (1 Kgs 18) that after the false prophets had been slain by Elijah, rain was given to the land of Israel; and that the bread of Elisha, and afterward of the Savior, was most abundant and most rich, and had such fullness that many thousands of men were filled from it (2 Kgs 4; John 6). […]

In that day the lamb shall feed in your possession at large. And your bulls and the foals of asses that work the ground shall eat mingled mash, as on the threshing floor it has been winnowed. LXX: And in that day your cattle shall feed in a rich and spacious place. Your bulls and your oxen that work the ground shall eat chaff mixed with winnowed barley. In the abundance of all things, when the heavenly rain comes down, and that bread which came down from heaven, which whoever eats will never hunger, the lambs shall feed in a most spacious place, those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes and who are always on the right hand. The bulls are the leaders of the flock, of whom we read: The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples (Ps 67 [68]:31); […]

But that we must attain to spiritual knowledge in the order of which we have already spoken, we are taught also by the blessed Apostle. For when he wanted not merely to draw up a list of all his own virtues, but rather to describe their order, that he might explain which follows what, and which gives birth to what, after some others he proceeds as follows: "In watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long suffering, in gentleness, in the Holy Ghost, in love unfeigned." […]
30:23.s: The First Conference of Abbot Nesteros, Chapter 16

30:23.t:
680. And first, he promises fertility of the land, promising the cause: and rain shall be given: he will make the early and the latter rain to come down to you (Joel 2:23); and the effect, as to the food of men: and the bread of the corn of the land shall be most plentiful, and fat: Aser, his bread shall be fat (Gen 49:20); he fills you with the fat of corn (Ps 147:14); as to the pasture of herds: the lamb in that day shall feed, as to sheep.

683. Note on the words, and the bread of the corn (Isa 30:23), that the word of God is bread that is,

first, strait because of the difficulty of observing it: strait is the way that leads to life (Matt 7:14); […]

30:24.t: And your oxen, as to cattle; and in both, he notes their fecundity, setting out their young, and the ass colts; and as to provisions for beasts of burden: mingled provender, pure barley with husks, which they ate mingled before.

30:25.t: HOW THE PROPHECY AGREES WITH THE GOSPEL, CONCERNING THE DARKENING OF THE SUN AND CERTAIN OTHER THINGS. — Since at the Lord’s first coming it was foretold that the sun would be darkened at his passion, at the very hour when it is proved to have happened, that is, at midday, for therefore it is written in the prophet Amos: “And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day” (Amos 8:9). On that day, therefore, from the sixth hour the sun was darkened until the ninth hour, and therefore the prophecy of the aforementioned prophet was fulfilled. The image of this event, which is to occur at the Lord’s second coming, was shown in the Lord’s passion; […]
30:25.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 105: ON THE DARKENING OF THE SUN

30:25.t: And there shall be upon every high mountain and upon every lifted-up hill streams of running waters in the day of the slaughter of many, when the towers have fallen. In this place the Jews refer the many slain and the falling towers to the power of the Roman empire, of which the Apostle too speaks (2 Thess 2:7): Only let him who holds now hold, until he be taken out of the way: namely, that at that time the blessedness of the people of Israel will be so great that not only the valleys and plains but all the mountains and hills will be watered with flowing waters. But let us understand by the mountains and hills those who are lifted on high by virtues, who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5), whom the Lord invites to drink. […]

For the flocks of the believers have, as it were, a pasture full of divers plants and flowers, in the holy Scriptures, which are their wise guides: and filled with spiritual joy at the glorious doctrines and instructions which they contain, they frequent the sacred courts. And this it is which long ago was proclaimed in the words of Isaiah: "And there shall be upon every high mountain, and upon every high hill, running waters upon that day." And again; "And the mountains shall drop sweetness: and the hills flow with milk." […]
30:25.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

30:25.t: 681. Second, he promises abundance of water: and there shall be. The Jews say that these things are to be fulfilled literally at the end of the world; the slaughter of many, the Romans, according to them, which is preposterous. Or it may be metaphorical speech, so that the water signifies the consolation which they had after the return from captivity and the destruction of Babylon. Or, mystically, it may signify the teaching of Christ, below: I will open rivers in the high hills, and fountains in the midst of the plains (Isa 41:18).

30:26.t: And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of its blow. LXX: And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, in the day when the Lord heals the crushing of his people and cures the pain of your blow. I wonder how in the present place the same Seventy translated moon and sun, following the Hebrew, when above they translated the Hebrew words LABANA (לבנה) and HAMMA (חמה), which Aquila renders white and heat, and by which he signifies the moon and the sun, as brick and wall, in the place where it is written: And the moon shall blush, and the sun shall be confounded; […]

Moreover, when the day of judgment has been completed and the glory of the future life has become evident with the new heaven and the new earth, then will come to pass what the same prophet announced elsewhere: "The light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be increased sevenfold, like the light of seven days."

682. Third, the radiance of heaven: and the light of the sun shall be as the light of seven days, that is, as much light in one day as there is now in seven days, as if sevenfold; or as it was in the first week of seven days. The Jews preposterously say that these things are fulfilled literally in the golden age of Jerusalem; but it is better understood as referring to the future glory of the saints, after the renewal of the world; or metaphorically and hyperbolically, it may refer to the state of the people: who heals the broken of heart, and binds up their bruises (Ps 146[147]:3).

30:27.t: But in both editions it must be noted that it is not the Lord, but the name of the Lord, that comes after a long time, of which it is said in the Psalms: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us (Ps 117 [118]:26). And he himself says in the Gospel: I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me (John 5:43). And it is well said that he comes after a long time, since human impatience says: How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end? How long do you turn your face away from me? (Ps 12 [13]:1). His burning fury also comes with glory, so that him whom we despised in humility we may fear in majesty. This very thing is written in the psalms too: God manifestly will come, our God, and will not keep silence. […]

Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar: his fury is burning and heavy to bear. His lips are filled with indignation, and his tongue is like a devouring fire. His spirit is like an overflowing torrent reaching to the middle of the neck, to destroy the nations unto nothing, and the bridle of error that was in the jaws of the peoples. You shall have a song, like the night of a hallowed solemnity, and gladness of heart, like one who goes with the pipe to enter into the mountain of the Lord, to the Mighty One of Israel. LXX: Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time: his fury burning with glory, the utterance of his lips, an utterance full of wrath, and the wrath of his fury shall devour like fire; […]

30:28.t: His spirit too, like water in a valley, dragging, will come up to the neck, to make punishments overflow upon sinners. It will be divided according to the quality of their deserts, to destroy and confound the nations which vain error had led astray, so that they may understand that they have been overthrown.

He also sets out wrath in his work: his breath, that is, his indignation, overflowing even to the midst of the neck, that is, it will lead to their extinction, above: there shall pass through Judah, overflowing wrath (Isa 8:8).

686. Third, he sets out the effect of his indignation on the wicked, the destruction of the nations: to destroy the nations: Lord, in your city you shall bring their image to nothing (Ps 72:20[73:21]); and the cessation of tyrants: and the bridle of error: he has put a bridle into my mouth (Job 30:11).

30:29.t: Hence it is said to men of this kind, who prevailed in the power of this world and took delight in their own error, that they will not always be doing this. And some of our writers think that this passage especially, and the whole tenor of the chapter, is spoken against the heretics and all the doctrines that are contrary to the truth: that when the time of judgment has come, they shall by no means enter his holy places and his mountain, that is, the Church of the Lord, lest under the name of religion they gather riches and abandon themselves to luxury, as though celebrating the feasts of the Lord. […]

He also sets out the effect on the good in praise of the mouth: you shall have a song as in the night of the sanctified solemnity, for on three solemnities they went to Jerusalem with joy (Lev 23), below: the city of our solemnity: your eyes shall see (Isa 33:20); and in delight of heart: and joy of heart, below: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and mourning shall flee away (Isa 35:10); and the people of the Lord were joyful (Jdt 16:24).

30:30.t: And the Lord will make the glory of his voice heard, and will show the terror of his arm in the threatening of his fury and in the flame of devouring fire: he will dash them down with whirlwind and with hailstone. For at the voice of the Lord Assyria, struck with the rod, will tremble, and the passing of the rod will be founded, which the Lord will make to rest upon him with timbrels and with harps, and in chief battles he will overthrow them. For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and wide; its fuel is fire and much wood: the breath of the Lord like a torrent of sulphur kindling it. […]

687. And the Lord shall make the glory of his voice to be heard. Here he describes the manner of punishment; and concerning this, he does three things.

First, he describes the manner of punishment as to the act of the one who punishes: his voice, through which he will appear glorious, and the terror of his arm, through likeness to an angry man, who threatens in this manner: have you an arm like God? (Job 40:4); and as to the instrument: and the flame of devouring fire . . . with whirlwind, and hailstones, for, literally, the Assyrians were burned up, and perhaps there was some storm. Or the different punishments of the day of judgment are signified: fire and brimstone, and storms of winds, shall be the portion of their cup (Ps 10:7[11:6]).

30:31.t: At the command of his voice Assyria, struck with the rod, will tremble: every impious man, every imitator of the hostile nation; not that on the day of judgment the Assyrian alone is to be struck, but that by the Assyrian we should understand the devil.

Further, what is said according to the Seventy: At the voice of the Lord the Assyrians will be overcome by the stroke, when he has struck them, and there will be round about him that from which he had the hope of help, in which he trusted; they themselves with timbrels and harp will fight against him by a change, signifies that those who were once subject to the devil rise up against him, and fight against him with joy and gladness by a sudden change, when, understanding their error, they destroy him by whom they had been deceived. And it is said to him that from the beginning he deceived himself, thinking his kingdom everlasting, he for whom Gehenna and eternal punishments are prepared.
Second, he places the infliction of the punishment, showing the Assyrian's horror: for at the voice of the Lord the Assyrian shall fear.

30:32.t: Then there follows: And the passing of the rod will be founded, which the Lord will make to rest upon him. And the sense is: the rod will not strike him and then be lifted again, and, in the manner of those who flog, make an end of beating; but he will make it remain in his punishments as if founded and fixed with a deep root. And if it is understood in this way, where will the repentance of the devil be? Especially since it is said to sinners: Go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). With timbrels and with harps, and in chief battles, he will overthrow them: that is, the Lord will overthrow the demons and all the impious, to the joy of all.

And the duration of the punishment: and the passage of the rod shall be strongly grounded, that is, strengthened.

Third, the exultation of the saints: with harps, and in great battles, which are waged by divine power alone: the just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge (Ps 57:11[58:10]).

30:33.t: For from yesterday, that is, from time past, Topheth, that is, a broad and spacious Gehenna, has been prepared by the king, the Lord, to burn them with eternal fires. Its nourishment and kindling is fire and much wood, that is, perpetual flame and the punishments of sinners. And since the prophetic word had foretold this as of a furnace and an oven of burning fire, it keeps the metaphor, so that we may know that it is kindled by the breath and spirit and will of the Lord, with sulphur mixed in, which rouses the flames, to make the torments more bitter.

688. For Topheth is prepared. Here he describes the place of punishment.

And first, its disposition: Topheth, the valley of the son of Ennom, Gehenna, for the fire for sacrifices was kept there on stones of tufa (Tophis); this is the same as the valley of Gethsemane, where the army of Sennacherib was destroyed. Or it signifies hell; hence the Jews conjecture that hell is there, because smoke is always emitted from two palm trees which are there. From yesterday, that is, from the beginning; or, according to the Jews, from the second day, which had only yesterday, and no day before. Jeremiah 7 and 19 discuss this valley. Prepared by the king, God, deep, and wide, above: therefore has hell enlarged her soul (Isa 5:14). […]

31:1.t: Let our course take us to regions above, because it is better to ascend. Finally, as was read today, "Woe to them that go down to Egypt." Surely it is not wrong to go to Egypt, but to change to the ways of the Egyptians, to change to the violence of their treachery and to the ugliness of their wantonness—this is wrong. He that changes in this way descends, and one who descends falls. Let us keep away, then, from the Egyptian who is a man, but [let us] not [keep away] from God. Even the king of Egypt himself fell under the dominion of his own vices and in comparison with him Moses was accounted a god, ruling over kingdoms and subjecting powers to himself. So we read that it was said to Moses: "I shall make you a god to Pharaoh."

Woe to those who go down into Egypt for help, hoping in horses, and having confidence in chariots, because they are many, and in horsemen, because they are exceedingly strong, and have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, and have not sought the Lord. But he, being wise, has brought evil, and has not taken away his words; and he will rise up against the house of the most wicked, and against the help of those who work iniquity. Egypt is man and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit: and the Lord will incline his hand, and the helper will collapse, and he to whom help is given will fall, and all of them together will be consumed. […]

These things, indeed, we can also understand of those who, in a time of persecution and of tribulation and distress, do not trust in the Lord, but in the help of the Egyptians, that is, of worldly men; not knowing that Abraham was endangered in Egypt, and that the people of God served with clay and bricks in that region, which is spiritually called the iron furnace. Hence in the Apocalypse of John too we read: The place in which the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt (Rev 11:8).

693. Woe to them that go down. In this part, he threatens both at the same time, namely, the Egyptians and the Jews, and concerning this, he does two things:

first, he sets out the threatening;

second, the consolation, where it says, for thus says the Lord to me (Isa 31:4).

Concerning the first, he sets out two things.

First, he sets out their guilt from trust in human help: trusting in horses: vain is the horse for safety: neither shall he be saved by the abundance of his strength (Ps 32[33]:17); and from contempt of divine help: and have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, against what it says in Psalm 19:8[20:7]: some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will hope in the name of the Lord, our God.

31:2.t: But he, being wise, that is, the Lord, brought evil upon them, and the worst, namely Nebuchadnezzar; or evil in the absolute sense, signifying a thing, not a person; and he did not take away his words, which he had spoken through the prophets. Wherefore he will rise up against the tribe of Judah, the house of the most wicked, and against the help of the Egyptians, who work iniquity.

694. Second, he threatens the punishment: but he.

And first, against their contempt of divine help he sets out the wisdom of God, and the firmness of the sentence: the wise one has brought evil, and has not removed his words, that is, he has not made void what he threatened through the prophets: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor as the son of man, that he should be changed (Num 23:19); and he adds the punishment: and he will rise up.

31:3.t: For Egypt, or the Egyptian, as the Seventy translated, is man and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit. Hence it is also written in Jeremiah: Cursed is the man who has his hope in man, and has made firm the flesh of his arm, and whose heart has departed from the Lord. And he will be like a tamarisk in the desert, which will not see when good things come (Jer 17:5, 6). And in another place it is written: Vain is the salvation of man (Ps 59 [60]:13), or, as it stands better in the Hebrew, in man. And when the Lord stretches out his hand to punish, or inclines it, under the metaphor of a charioteer, and slackens the reins of the running horses, the Egyptian helper will collapse, and Israel, to whom help was being given.

Second, against trust in human help, he sets out their weakness: Egypt is man: whereas you are a man, and not God, in the hand of them that slay you (Ezek 28:9–10); and he adds the punishment: and the helper shall fall: they that dwell in houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation (Job 4:19).

31:4.t: For thus says the Lord to me: as when a lion roars, and a lion's whelp, over its prey, and a multitude of shepherds comes against it, it will not dread their voice, nor be afraid at their multitude: so will the Lord of hosts come down to fight upon Mount Zion and upon its hill. Like birds flying, so will the Lord of hosts protect Jerusalem, protecting and delivering, passing over and saving. In plain passages we set down one edition, especially where there is no difference of sense. When the Israelites, and the Egyptians in whose help they trusted, have been slain in Egypt, the captives will return to Jerusalem in the reign of Cyrus. And by two likenesses the strength of the Lord, who had promised that he would be their helper, is shown. […]

695. For thus says the Lord. Here he sets out the consolation, promising liberation by God from their enemies, from whom they could not be liberated by the Egyptians. And concerning this, he does three things.

First, he sets out the defense of the Jews under the likeness of a defending lion, saying: you and the Egyptians in whom you trusted in contempt of me will perish: for thus says the Lord, who alone saves; so shall the Lord of hosts come down to fight, as a defender against those who hindered the building of the temple after the return from captivity; or against the Assyrians: and I will be to them as a lioness, as a leopard in the way of the Assyrians (Hos 13:7).

31:5.t: Let us state the other comparison as well: as birds, to defend their young, fly over their nests, and if they see a serpent or a man, or other birds approaching their chicks, forget their own weakness and fight with beak and claws, and redouble the grief of their breast with chattering cries: so the Lord will protect Jerusalem, and will deliver it, passing over, and will save it. For passing over, in the Hebrew it is PHASE; in the three translators, besides the Seventy, ὑπερβαίνων is set down. From this it is plain that Pascha, that is, the Phase of the Lord, signifies not passion but passage. […]

And under the likeness of a protecting bird: as birds: how often would I have gathered together your children, as the hen doth gather her chickens under her wings, and you wouldst not? (Matt 23:37); as the eagle enticing her young to fly, and hovering over them (Deut 32:11).

31:6.t: In place of the last clause ["But you have played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, says the Lord."] the true Hebrew text (which is not preserved in the Greek and Latin versions) gives the following: "you have forsaken me, yet return, and I will receive you, says the Lord." Isaiah also speaking in the same sense uses almost the same words: "Return," he cries, "O children of Israel, you who devise a deep and sinful counsel. Return to me, and I will redeem you. I am God, and there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Savior; there is nothing beside me. Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth." Remember this and show yourselves men: bring it again to mind, O you transgressors. […]

Turn back, as you had withdrawn into the depth, sons of Israel. For in that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands have made for you for sin. And Assyria will fall by a sword not of a man, and a sword not of a human being will devour him: and he will flee, not from the face of the sword, and his young men will be tributaries. And his strength will pass away from terror, and his princes will flee in fear, said the Lord, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem. LXX: Turn back, as you had withdrawn into the depth, sons of Israel. For in that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands have made for you for sin. […]

696. Second, he sets out the destruction of their enemies, promising counsel for meriting this: return, to me: the wicked man, when he is come into the depths of sins, contemns (Prov 18:3); as you have yielded your members to serve iniquity, unto iniquity: so now yield your members to serve cleanness, unto sanctification (Rom 6:19).

31:7.t: And he sets out the completion of the counsel: in that day, above: in that day a man shall cast away his idols (Isa 2:20).

31:8.t: And he sets out the fruit, namely, the destruction itself as to the death of the slain: by the sword: my sword shall devour flesh (Deut 32:42); and as to the removal of the survivors in flight, fear, and servitude, for his young men shall be tributaries, afterwards, to the Babylonians.

31:9.t: Fire and light are written in Hebrew with the same letters, ALEPH, VAU, RES; if it is read UR, it means fire; if OR, light. This is said because for fire, which Symmachus alone translated, Aquila and Theodotion translated light. But what is meant by what we read in the Septuagint: They will be surrounded by rock as by a rampart, and will be conquered: and whoever flees will be taken, I am unable to know. Unless perhaps we can say this: that the young men of the Assyrian king, who are to be conquered and taken, are surrounded by rock, that is, by the strength of the Lord, as a city is surrounded by a rampart. […]

Of this love that is begun here to be perfected from the sight of the Lord in the eternal kingdom Isaiah rightly speaks, saying, "The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem." It is, however, greater to be a furnace than a fire because a fire can also be small, but a larger flame is kindled in a furnace. Zion truly is said to be speculation but Jerusalem the vision of peace. Truly we sometimes catch a glimpse of our peace here in order there later to see it fully. Therefore through the Lord's love the fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem because here we burn in some measure with the flames of his love when we glimpse him, but there we shall burn totally when we shall fully see him whom we love.

If the breads of the furnace that were baked in secret signify the interior devotion of the mind of the faithful confirmed by the fire of charity, breads which were also commanded by the law to be offered in the sacrifice of the Lord, it is most fitting that the hearts which were made to burn constantly with the flame of intimate love and virtue and to beget words are symbolized through the furnaces in which the same breads were baked. The prophet spoke beautifully about these things when he referred to "the Lord whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem." It is also written: "Did our hearts not burn within us when he spoke along the way and opened the Scriptures to us?"

The precept of the law, therefore, is to be taken in a more spiritual sense. For there is spiritual seed which is conceived through the love and fear of God in the spiritual womb, travailing and bringing forth the spirit of salvation. And in this sense must be understood this verse: Blessed is he who hath seed in Zion and posterity in Jerusalem. For does it mean that, although he be a whoremonger and a drunkard and an idolater, he is still blessed if only he hath seed in Sion and posterity in Jerusalem? No one in his senses will say this.
31:9.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 24

31:9.t: But if you ask how these things come about, ask grace, not doctrine; desire, not understanding; the groaning of prayer, not the study of reading; the Bridegroom, not the master; God, not man; darkness, not clarity; not light, but the fire that wholly inflames and carries into God through ecstatic anointings and most ardent affections. Which fire is indeed God, and his furnace is in Jerusalem, and Christ kindles this in the fervor of his most ardent passion, which only he truly perceives who says: My soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death. Whoever loves this death can see God, because it is indubitably true: No man shall see me and live. Let us die, therefore, and enter into the darkness; let us impose silence upon our cares, concupiscences, and phantasms; […]

697. Third, he sets out the strengthening of both: the Lord has said it, whose fire, burning the Assyrians, above: the light of Israel shall be as a fire, and the Holy One thereof as a flame (Isa 10:17); or the fire on the altar of incense; his furnace, on the altar of holocausts: the fire on the altar shall always burn (Lev 6:12); or the fire of charity burning imperfectly in the Church militant, but a furnace burning perfectly in the Church triumphant.

698. Note also that charity is called a fire: see the collation preceding this chapter.

32:1.t: Behold, a king will reign with righteousness, and princes will rule in judgment. And a man will be like one who is hidden from the wind and conceals himself from the tempest: like streams of waters in thirst, and the shade of a jutting rock in a desert land. The eyes of those who see will not be dimmed, and the ears of those who hear will listen diligently. And the heart of the foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of stammerers will speak quickly and plainly. He who is senseless will no longer be called a prince, nor will the deceitful man be called great. For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will work iniquity, to accomplish pretense, and to speak deceitfully to the Lord, and to empty the soul of the hungry, and to take away drink from the thirsty. […]

These things are according to the Hebrew, from which the Seventy disagree in most places not only in words but also in senses. For when the righteous king has reigned, and his princes have ruled with judgment, there will be a man hiding his words, a man who by nature is God, and he will hide his words, speaking to them in parables (Matt 20:21, 23, 24, and 25). And he will hide them as from running water, that is, from the people of the Jews, which, like water, is borne and drawn this way and that at the will of its teachers. This man, hiding his words among the unbelieving, will appear in Zion, that is, in the Church, like a glorious river running down in a thirsty land. For he will appear to the people of the Gentiles, which before suffered thirst for the truth; […]

This is the third part of the threatening, in which he describes their liberation from the enemies who were threatening them then. And first, he foretells the liberation in the manner of prophecy, second, he recounts it in the manner of history: and it came to pass (ch. 36). The first of these is divided into two parts: in the first, he foretells the prosperity of the Jews; in the second, the destruction of their enemies: woe to you that spoils (ch. 33).

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he foretells the status of the liberated, as to the equity of the king: a king shall reign, namely, Ezechias: a king shall reign, and shall be wise (Jer 23:5); as to the prosperity of the people: and princes shall rule in judgment.

32:2.t: And whoever is under his shelter will be as safe in tribulations and distresses, and in the tempest of this world, as one who, fleeing wind and whirlwind, hides himself in a safe place; and as one who finds the purest springs in the desert; and as one who, in fierce heat, when the blaze of the sun scorches everything, rests under a jutting rock. Where we said: like streams of waters in thirst, the Seventy translated: and he will appear in Zion like a running river. For the Hebrew word about which we argued above, BASAION (בציון), which means in thirst, or in dryness, and in a pathless place, the Seventy and Theodotion translated in Zion, reading SION, which is written with the same letters, for SAION, that is, thirst.
As to consolation in tribulation: and a man shall be as when one is hid from the wind, above: there shall be a tabernacle for a shade in the daytime from the heat (Isa 4:6).

32:3.t: When, therefore, Christ has reigned, and his princes have ruled in judgment, the eyes of those who believe will not be dimmed, and the ears of those who hear, which before were deaf, will attend diligently, and the heart of those once foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammering and the mute, which could not utter Christ, will confess the Lord with full and open speech.

As to amendment in spiritual matters: the eyes of them that see, namely, the prophets, shall not be dim, as before, because of the sins of the king and the people, but shall receive clear visions from the Lord; and the ears, namely, of their subjects, shall hearken, fulfilling the precepts of the Lord given by the prophets.

32:4.t: The heart of fools, who formerly erred following idols; and the tongue of stammerers, the prophets, who formerly spoke obscurely and enigmatically: wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis 10:21).

32:5.t: He who is foolish will no longer be called a prince (1 Cor 1). For God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. Nor will the deceitful and perverse teacher be called great among the peoples: namely the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Lord said: Fools and blind, which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? (Matt 23:17).

And also as to their consequent liberty, namely, from tyrants: the fool shall no more be called prince, namely, Sennacherib, to whom formerly they paid tribute, as is evident in 2 Kings 18:14. I will deliver them out of the hand of the king of the Assyrians (Ezek 24).

32:6.t: For the fool will speak foolish things, for which in the Hebrew it is written: NABAL NABALA IDABBER (נבל נבלה ידבר). We say this in order to explain the words of Abigail, who says of Nabal the Carmelite: According to his name he is foolish (1 Sam 25:25). For truly the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will accomplish iniquity: he who feared where there was no fear, and practiced folly in place of wisdom, saying: If this man were from God, he would not break the sabbath (John 9:16). This the master of the synagogues does to this day, to accomplish pretense, for which in the Hebrew is written ONEPH (חנף), that is, ὑπόκρισις. Hence it is said again and again to the Pharisees: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14). […]

What follows contains nearly the same sense as the Hebrew, and can be fitted to the heretics. For these speak a lie against the Lord, and pervert the hungry and thirsty souls, and make them go away empty; so that even if they have anything good by nature, they lose it through the fault of their teachers, whose whole counsel is to destroy the humble with unjust words and to scatter the words of the humble in judgment. In which it must likewise be noted that whoever can be deceived by them is humble, and clings to the earth.

Second, he describes the manner of liberation: for the fool. And first, he describes the affliction; second, the liberation: until the spirit be poured upon us (Isa 32:15). Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he describes the enemy who persecutes them; second, the persecution: rise up, you rich women (Isa 32:9). Concerning the first, he sets out three things. First, the wickedness of the king himself, as to the blasphemy of his mouth: the fool, namely, Sennacherib, will speak foolish things, blasphemous words, below (Isa 37:17). The mouth of fools bubbles out folly (Prov 15:2); as to the duplicity of his heart: his heart will work iniquity, promising good land to the people, to the Lord deceitfully, saying he has come by his command, below (Isa 36:10). […]

32:7.t: For all the vessels and weapons of the deceitful teacher and prince are most evil; he contrives snares to destroy the simple with the word of a lie, saying to the deceived people: Search and see, that a prophet does not arise from Galilee (John 7:52). When the poor man spoke to them judgment: he who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor 8). For truly Christ spoke judgment and righteousness to them, saying: If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me: but if I do them, even if you will not believe me, believe the works (John 10:37).

Second, the malice of his princes: the vessels, that is, the messengers and princes, of the deceitful, namely, of Sennacherib: a prince that gladly hears lying words, has all his servants wicked (Prov 29:12); and the execution of their malice: for he, namely, Rabsaces, about whom, see below (36), will frame (concinnabit), that is, compose, devices—cinnus is a kind of drink composed of different kinds of things; the poor man, the Jew: your mouth has abounded with evil, and your tongue framed deceits (Ps 49[50]:19).

32:8.t: This poor man who speaks judgment, the prince and Lord, will think the things that are worthy of a prince, saying: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And he will be anxious for the unbelieving, desiring to save those who do not believe; and he will stand over his leaders, the Apostles, to one of whom he says: But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my familiar friend (Ps 54 [55]:14).
Third, the prudence of Ezechias in his reign: the prince, for Ezechias commanded that no one should respond to Sennacherib, above: I will restore your princes as they were before (Isa 1:26).

32:9.t: After the calling of the nations, when Christ the king has ruled with righteousness, and his princes, the Apostles and apostolic men, have presided over the believers with judgment, the prophetic word will be directed to the wealthy women, whom we must take either as the cities of Judea, or as the synagogues of that time, or, as most think, as the matrons of the rich men of the former people of the Jews, to whom, as to women lying prostrate after their ruin, it is said: Rise; and they are nonetheless called confident daughters, or hoping; […]

Here he describes the persecution inflicted on them as to three things. First, as to the loss of fruits, stirring up attention: you women, who cry easily, rich, who have reason to cry from the ruin of their goods; or you women, that is, you feeble Jews: they that trust in their own strength, and glory in the multitude of their riches (Ps 48:7[49:6]).

32:10.t: And he sets out the determination of the time: after several days and one year: for tribulation is very near: for there is none to help me (Ps 21:12[22:11]). And he sets out the loss of fruits: the vintage is at an end, destroyed, the gathering, of crops, shall come no more, into our houses from the fields: the joy of the vintage is taken away (Jer 48:33).

32:11.t: Hence they are summoned to lamentation, and are commanded to bare their breasts and to gird their loins, because the country once desirable, and the fruitful vine, of which it is written: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true: how have you turned into the bitterness of a strange vine? (Jer 2:21), has been destroyed by the ravaging Roman.
Second, as to the devastation of the fields, he prescribes mourning, be astonished: I have put off the robe of peace (Bar 4:20), above: and the Lord in that day shall call to weeping (Isa 22:12).

32:12.t: And he foretells harm: upon the land, above: briers and thorns shall come up (Isa 5:6) over it.

32:13.t: Over the ground, he says, of my people thorns and briers, or grass will come up. And the sense is: if thorns and briers have filled the land of Judea, which is the land of promise, how much more the other cities, which are full of joy, and which that saying of the Gospel will overtake: Woe to you who rejoice now, for you will weep (Luke 6:25)!

What was said above according to the LXX: Over the land of my people thorns and grass will come up, can be referred both to the heretics and to all the simple among believers, who do not understand Holy Scripture as befits its majesty. Hence we have fitted each to each: that the land of the people of God brings forth thorns for the heretics, and grass for all the unskilled in the Church.

If those very persons, who amid the darkness of the present life shine bright by virtuous attainments—if they also cannot be void of contagion, with what guilt of wickedness are those bound, who still live after the flesh? If those persons cannot be free from sin who are already walking in the way of heavenly desires, what about those who still lie under the loads of sinful habits, who, abandoned to the gratifications of their fleshly part, still bear the yoke of rottenness? So Peter says, "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" And it is said by Isaiah, "Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briars; how much more upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city." […]
32:13.s: Morals on the Book of Job 17.23

32:13.t: Third, as to the desolation of their cities and houses, he sets out the desolation itself: how much more, namely, to be wept for, the city that rejoiced, namely, Jerusalem, whose lower part was handed over to the Assyrians, above: a populous city, a joyous city (Isa 22:2).

32:14.t: Wealthy women, rise and hear my voice: confident daughters, take in my speech with your ears. After days and a year you too will be troubled, you confident ones: for the vintage is ended; the gathering will come no more. Be astonished, you wealthy women; be troubled, you confident ones: strip yourselves and be confounded. For which Symmachus translated be made naked; there follows: Gird your loins, lament upon your breasts, over the desirable country, over the fruitful vine: thorns and briers will come up over the ground of my people: how much more over all the houses of joy of the exulting city? For the house has been forsaken; the multitude of the city has been left; darkness and groping have come upon the caves for ever: the joy of wild asses, pastures of flocks. […]

For the Lord, that is, my temple, has been forsaken, as I said to the Apostles: Rise, let us go hence (John 14:31); and to the unbelieving: Your house will be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35). Palpable darkness has taken possession of the inner sanctuaries of the Temple and its secret mysteries, and they have become no longer storerooms for the vessels of the Lord, but caves for ever. For they had heard from the Lord Savior (Matt 21:13): The house of my Father shall be called a house of prayer: but you have made it a den of robbers. The joy, he says, of wild asses, pastures of flocks. This is to be understood either according to the letter, in that all things are deserted; […]

And the magnitude of the desolation as to the houses, for they were reduced to perpetual darkness, as happens to ruined buildings: and darkness: they shall grope in the dark, and not in the light (Job 12:25); and as to their fields: a joy of wild asses, which dwell in great wildernesses: a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness (Jer 2:24).

32:15.t: And this is to be until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high, which the Savior, ascending to the Father, promised to believers, saying: Behold, I go, and I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth (John 16). And again: Until you receive power from on high (Luke 24:49). And what he had said above: Yet a little while, and Lebanon will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest: and in that day the deaf will hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see (above, Isa 29), he now repeats in other words: that the wilderness of the nations is turned into the riches of Israel, and Israel is counted among the nations: at which time judgment will have dwelt in the desert, the Lord and Savior, to whom the Father has given […]

Here he describes their liberation. And first, he sets out the consolation of the Jews; second, the destruction of their enemies: but hail (Isa 32:19); third, the prophet's congratulation: blessed are you that sow (Isa 32:20). Concerning the first, he sets out three things. First, divine consolation: these things, I say, will happen, when Sennacherib lays waste the land, until the spirit, divine consolation, be poured upon us: you shall know that I am the Lord, for I will send spirit into you, and you shall live (Ezek 37:5–6).

Second, the manner and order of the consolation, as to the fertility of the land: and the desert shall be as Carmel, and Carmel shall be counted for a forest; […]

32:16.t: As the observation of justice: and judgment shall dwell, above: Zion shall be redeemed in judgment (Isa 1:27).

32:17.t: The work of righteousness too will be peace, which, according to the Apostle, surpasses all understanding (Phil 4). And the service of righteousness silence, so that they may worship the Lord not with the much speaking of the Jews but with the brevity of faith; and may rest secure in eternal peace, and in their tabernacles may be the riches of which the Apostle spoke (1 Cor 1:5): I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ, because in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge.

He that suffers from a flux of seed is pronounced unclean, because, being addicted to much speaking, he defiles himself by that which, had it been orderly issued, might have produced the offspring of right thought in the hearts of hearers; and, while he incautiously spends himself in loquacity, he sheds his seed not so as to serve for generation, but unto uncleanness.
32:17.s: The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

32:17.t: It is the practice of the impertinent ever to answer by the opposite what is said aright, lest, if they assent to the things asserted, they should seem inferior. And to these the words of the righteous, however small in number they have been heard, are 'much,' in that as they cut their evil habits to the quick, they fall heavy upon the hearing, whence that is even wrested to a crime, which by a right declaration is pronounced against crimes. For the very person, who had delivered strong sentences on grounds of truth, Zophar rebukes and calls full of words, in that, whereas wisdom reprimands sins by the mouth of the righteous, it sounds like superfluity of talkativeness to the ears of the foolish. […]
32:17.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 10, Section 2

32:17.t: And as to the tranquility of peace: and the work, that is, the effect, of justice shall be peace, and the service of justice quietness, for it will be without the tumult of contentions and wars, above: Lord, you will give us peace (Isa 26:12).

Note on the words, the work of justice shall be peace, that the peace of the saints in heaven will be beautiful, first, because it will not be false (Wis 15); second, because it will not be interrupted, above: and there shall be no end of peace (Isa 9:7); third, because it will be full: he has placed peace in your borders (Ps 147:14).

Note also on the peace to come that three things make it desirable: first, the strength of divine power: they that trust in the Lord shall be as mount Zion: he shall not be moved for ever that dwells in Jerusalem (Ps 124[125]:1–2); second, the purity of one's own conscience: you shall walk confidently in your way, and your foot shall not stumble (Prov 3:23); third, the removal of hostile wickedness: have confidence. […]

32:18.t: And when the Christian people sits, or dwells, in beauty, or, as the Seventy translated, in the city of peace, which is without doubt in the Church, then hail and tempest and the raging wrath of the Lord will come down upon the forest, of which it was said above: And Carmel will be counted as a forest; and the city of Jerusalem will be brought low, and, according to another Scripture, will speak from the earth.

Third, he sets out the pleasant enjoyment of divine consolation: and my people shall sit in the beauty of peace: but he that shall hear me, shall rest without terror, and shall enjoy abundance (Prov 1:33).

32:19.t: Hail, namely, of tribulation, in the descent of the forest, that is, it shall descend from the Lord upon your enemies; the city, Ninive, above: the high city he shall lay low (Isa 26:5).

32:20.t: The prophet says, "Blessed is he that sows into all waters, whose ox and donkey tread," [that is] the people, from the law and from the Gentiles, gathered into one faith.

Blessed is he from whom Jesus asks drink, as He did from that Samaritan woman, and gives a well of water springing up unto eternal life. Blessed is he that soweth beside all waters, and upon every soul, tomorrow to be ploughed and watered, which today the ox and the ass tread, while it is dry and without water, and oppressed with unreason. And blessed is he who, though he be a "valley of rushes," is watered out of the House of the Lord; for he is made fruitbearing instead of rushbearing, and produces that which is for the food of man, not that which is rough and unprofitable. And for the sake of this we must be very careful not to miss the Grace.

Accordingly, like a perfect man learned in the law and made firm in the gospel, accept the faith of both Testaments, for, as we read today, "Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread," that is, who sows upon the people who follow the teaching of both Testaments. This is the ploughman's ox, wearing the yoke of the law, of which the law says, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out your corn," for this ox has the horns of holy Scripture. But in the Gospel the Lord, representing the people of the Gentiles, mounts the colt of a donkey.

Let them take as much pleasure as they please in their Gallican geldings; we will be satisfied with the simple "donkey" of Zechariah, loosed from its halter and made ready for the Savior's service, which received the Lord on its back and so fulfilled Isaiah's prediction: "Blessed is he that sows beside all waters, where the ox and the donkey tread under foot."

Do we ask where we have read of the ox and the ass together? In Deuteronomy it is written: You shall not plough with a calf and an ass together (Deut 22:10). And in this same Isaiah: Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread (Isa 32:20). Ebion ploughs with the ox and the ass together, worthy, for the lowliness of his understanding, of the poverty of his name; for he so receives the Gospel as not to abandon the ceremonies of the Jewish superstitions, which went before in shadow and image. But blessed is he who sows in the words of the Scriptures, of the old as well as of the new Instrument, and treads the waters of the letter that kills, so as to reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit.
At the end of the section too they translated thus: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread.

Since these things are so, and we have learned from the prophetic oracle how great the goods are that the Church will possess, and how great the evils that Jerusalem will suffer: blessed are you, Apostles, and you other teachers, who sow upon all the waters of Holy Scripture, in which the ox and the ass tread. The ox is a clean animal, on account of the election of the fathers; the ass unclean, on account of the former idolatry of the Gentiles; so that the Church of the Lord may be gathered both from the Circumcision and from the Uncircumcision.

Something of the same kind, I think, is said in Isaiah too: Blessed is he who sows upon the water, where the ox and the ass tread. That is, that teacher is held worthy of blessedness who sows upon the well-watered breast of his hearers, a people gathered from the Jews as well as from the Gentiles.

By water peoples are denoted, as it is said by John, "Now the waters are peoples." By water likewise not only the tide of peoples drifting away, but also the minds of good men that follow the preachings of faith, are denoted, as the Prophet saith, "Blessed are ye that sow upon all waters." And it is said by the Psalmist; "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters."
32:20.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 19

32:20.t: What else is meant by 'seed,' but the word of preaching? As the Truth says in the Gospel, "A sower went forth to sow"; and as the Prophet says; "Blessed are ye who sow upon all waters." What else but the Church, ought to be understood by the threshing floor? Of which it is said by the voice of the Forerunner; "And He will throughly purge His floor."
32:20.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 31
