What we have set down, I have helped you: do not fear, worm Jacob, is not found in the Seventy. Now the worm, which in Hebrew is called THOLATH (תולעת), is the name given, for its lowliness and contempt, to the choir of the Apostles, imitating the Savior, who speaks in the psalm: I am a worm, and no man, a reproach of men, and the outcast of the people (Ps 21 [22]:7). For as a worm penetrates the earth, so the apostolic word penetrated the cities of the nations, and entered first into the hardest hearts. […]

There are many who think of the holy mysteries and the saving message in disrespectful ways, but they amount to nothing, and such impious adversaries will perish. For those who oppose the divine agents of preaching are doing no less than fighting against the teachings of godliness.… For thousands will make war against God's ministers, but these will end up as though they never existed and will clearly be brought low, falling under the machinery of the wrath of God. [Isaiah] tells them to quit relying on human strength and their own foolhardiness, saying, "I am your God who strengthens your arm," that is, I am the one who supports you and makes you prevail in any test. I say to you, "Do not be afraid, O little Israel."
He also shows the reason for their destruction: for I am the Lord your God: put forth your hand from on high (Ps 143:7[144:6]).

41:14.t: 807. Second, as to abundance of goods; and first, against slavery, he sets out the very yoke of slavery: fear not, you worm, as if to say: you who were thought vile and trampled on as a worm, and were reckoned for dead: I am a worm, and no man (Ps 21:7[22:6]); he also sets out divine help, below: I have helped you (50).

41:15.t: And what follows, I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sawing teeth, signifies this: that the preaching of the Gospel crushes the adverse powers and the spiritual wickedness that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, which, according to the variety of their pride, are called mountains and hills; and when these are carried off and scattered after the manner of a whirlwind, let Israel exult and rejoice in the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. We can also say that the churchman, having the sawing teeth of the Gospel preaching on a new wagon, which works not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit, crushes the hardest hearts of unbelievers, separating the wheat from the chaff and crushing the mountains and hills, that is, all the chiefs of the […]

He also sets out the benefit of exaltation as to the subjugation of enemies: I have made you as a new thrashing wain, above: Moab shall be trodden down under him, as straw is broken in pieces with the wain (Isa 25:10); which perhaps was fulfilled in the time of the Maccabees.

41:16.t: And as to their exaltation: and you shall exult: we will exult and rejoice in you (Song 1:3[4]).

41:17.t: The needy and the poor seek water, and there is none; their tongue is parched with thirst. I the Lord will hear them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the sloping hills, and fountains in the midst of the plains. I will make the desert into a pool of waters, and the trackless land into streams of waters. I will put in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, and the myrtle, and the olive tree. I will set in the desert the fir, the elm and the box together, that they may see and know and consider and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done this, and the Holy One of Israel has created it. LXX: And the poor and the needy will exult; for they will seek water, and there will be none; their tongue has dried up for thirst. […]

Second, against poverty, he first sets out the disadvantage of poverty: the needy and the poor, above: their nobles have perished with famine (Isa 5:13); second, the divine intention: I the Lord will hear them: he shall call upon me and I will hear him (Ps 90:15).

41:18.t: God is not offering his services as a water manager or a farmer when he says, "I will open rivers in a dry land; I will plant in the wilderness the cedar and the box tree."

Therefore the Lord, the God of Israel, did not wholly forsake them, nor let them perish for ever, but opened rivers on the sloping hills, or on the mountains, and fountains in the midst of the plains. These rivers took their beginning from that river which is read of in the Psalms: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4); and in another place: The river of God is filled with waters. These waters and fountains flowed from that fountain who speaks through Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water (Jer 2:13). And above in this same Prophet it is said: They will drink waters from the fountains of the Savior. Of these also it is sung in the Psalms: Bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). […]

808. Third, he sets out the benefit as to abundance of waters in mountainous places: I will open rivers in the high hills, above: there shall be upon every high mountain rivers of running waters (Isa 30:25); and in desert places: I will turn the desert, that is, your land formerly desert: he has turned a wilderness into pools of waters (Ps 106[107]:35).

816. There is the water, of tears poured out: who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes? (Jer 9:1); of baptismal purity: unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God (John 3:5); of spiritual grace: he that believes in me: out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:38); of divine wisdom: I, wisdom, have poured out rivers (Sir 24:40); of internal joy: drink water out of your own cistern (Prov 5:15).

41:19.t: Since, then, the multitude of the Church, once a desert, had been watered with life-giving waters, therefore, according to the Seventy, there spring up in it the cedar, and the box, and the myrtle, and the cypress, and the poplar; according to the Hebrew and the other translators, the cedar, the setta, and the myrtle, and the olive tree, and the fir, and the elm, and the box together. These varieties of trees signify the diversity of spiritual grace. And because the nature of the others is known to all, let us discuss only the Hebrew SETTA (שטה), which Theodotion translated thorn. […]

The water was not life-giving. For they were not able to satisfy those who longed for truth from their teachings. Their tongues remained parched from thirst. But I will hear them, says the God of Israel, and I will not abandon them. For he had mercy on the mass of those who strayed and did not leave them without gifts from above, but rather he gave to them in fullness, and this in such a way as is finely described in the verses that follow.… The desert and the land short of water is the region of the Gentiles. The desert that will run dry and barren of any flowering growth, meaning spiritual growth, is the way of shriveling, where the wild trees are those useful only for burning in fire. The water allows the nations to bear fruit. […]
And as to the beauty of the trees: I will plant in the wilderness: his branches were multiplied (Ezek 31:5).

41:20.t: 809. Fourth, he sets out the fruit of the benefit: that they may see: that they may know that there is no God beside you, and that they may show forth your wonders (Sir 36:2).

41:21.t: Bring your judgment near, says the Lord; bring forward whatever you may have, said the king of Jacob. Let them approach and tell us whatever things are to come; tell the former things that have been, and we will set our heart on them and we will know their last end; and show us the things that are to come. Declare the things that are to come hereafter, and we will know that you are gods. Do good also, or evil, if you can, and let us speak and see together. Behold, you are of nothing: and your work is of that which is not; an abomination is he who has chosen you. LXX: Your judgment is near, says the Lord God; your counsels have come and drawn near, says the king of Jacob. Let them draw near and declare to us the things that are to come; […]

810. Bring your cause near. Here he sets out the disputation against the idols themselves; and first, he sets out the disputation; second, the determination of the sentence: and I saw, and there was no one (Isa 41:28).

Concerning the first, he does two things: first, he disputes against the idols with universal reasons; second, by a reason taken from a particular fact: I have raised up (Isa 41:25).

Concerning the first, he does three things.

First, he calls them to judgment: bring your cause near, that is, come near to me that we may be judged together; you, idols or idolaters, bring hither, that is, allege, if you have any thing, that you might prove that you are gods: God has stood in the congregation of gods: and being in the midst of them he judges gods (Ps 81[82]:1).

41:22.t: And at the same time an apostrophe is made to the idols themselves, which are without sense and possess the faculty neither of hearing nor of answering. Tell us, he says, either things past or things to come, and show your power by the outcome of events. Now this signifies that after the coming of Christ all the idols fell silent. Where is Delphic Apollo, and Loxias, and the Delian, and the Clarian, and the other idols that promised knowledge of the future, which deceived the most powerful kings? Why could they foretell nothing of Christ, nothing of his Apostles, nothing of the ruin and abolition of their temples? If, then, they could not foretell their own destruction, how could they announce what concerned others, whether evil or good? […]

Second, he sets out a twofold argument: one is taken from divine knowledge, which knew all things fully, past and future, and which the idols do not have: tell us the former things what they were: for all things were known to the Lord God, before they were created (Sir 23:29[20]).

41:23.t: Or else it must be said that mute images of men, without sense, can do neither good nor evil, nor know things past nor things to come, because they are of nothing and of that which is not, and it is not so much they as he who worships them that is worthy of abomination. For the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of men's hands. They have a mouth, and will not speak (Ps 113 [115]:13). How then can they know and announce things to come, or relate things past, and do good or evil, when they have neither the sense of men nor that of brute animals? Nor does it matter of what material they seem to be made, since all are earthly.

The other is taken from divine power, which can punish and impart benefits: do also good or evil, if you can: and whether it be evil that one doth unto them, or good, they are not able to recompense it (Bar 6:33).

41:24.t: Third, he deduces their defect as to material cause: behold, you, idols, are of nothing, created out of matter; as to formal cause, your work, that is, the artificial form, which fashioned in you a divinity, which does not exist; and as to efficient cause: an abomination, that is, abominable. Or: you, artists, your work, namely, the idols, he that has chosen you, worshippers: we know that an idol is nothing (1 Cor 8:4); every artist is confounded in his graven idol (Jer 10:14).

41:25.t: I have raised up from the North, and he will come from the rising of the sun; he will call upon my name, and he will bring on rulers as mud, and as a potter treading the ground. Who has announced it from the beginning, that we may know; and from the first, that we may say: You are righteous? There is none announcing, nor foretelling, nor hearing your words. The first will say to Zion: Behold, they are here; and to Jerusalem I will give a bearer of good tidings. And I looked, and there was not even any of these who would enter into counsel, and, when asked, would answer a word. Behold, all are unrighteous, and their works are vain; their images are wind and emptiness. LXX: But I have raised up him who is from the North, and him who is from the rising of the sun; […]

The Hebrews interpret the one raised up from the North and coming from the rising of the sun as the Assyrian and the Persian, who came to Jerusalem and trod down all its princes; and none of the idols which they worshiped knew that this would come, but the Lord alone, who punished them for their sins.

811. I have raised up. Here he takes up a certain particular fact to argue against idols.

And first, he foretells something to come: from the north, Chaldea; from the rising of the sun, Persia, which subjugated to itself various lands and princes, potter (plastes)—plasma, a thing produced; mystically: he who comes from the north signifies the gentile; he who comes from the rising of the sun, Christ: I shall bring them to naught, like the dirt in the streets (Ps 17:43[18:42]).

41:26.t: These things, which, according to prophetic custom, I say that I have done as though they were already past, or, according to Symmachus, which I promise as future, none of the demons and idols can foretell. Hence all the oracles fell silent, because there is no one who announces, no one who hears, while the once brutish hearts of the Gentiles have understood their error and forsaken false prophecies.

Second, from this, he sets out an argument under the form of a question: that he who can foretell this is justly called God; and he who cannot, is not: who has declared, below: assemble yourselves together, all you, and hear (Isa 48:14).

Third, he excludes proof of divinity from the idols: there is none, any of you gods, that shows nor, any of your worshippers, that hears, etc., they have eyes and see not; they have ears and hear not (Ps 113:13–15[115:5–6]).

41:27.t: And the Lord will speak first to Zion, that is, to his Church, and will say to her: Behold, here are your sons, whom I have given to you through faith in me. And he means the Apostles, who preached the Gospel in the whole world. Zion and Jerusalem differ in name; but as there is one city, so also there is one Church.

"I will give a leader to Zion, and I will console Jerusalem as I go." … Again the multitude of those going astray is promised the revealing of the Savior, through whom each one under heaven has been saved and is summoned to the recognition of the truth. So that we could have a guide who would be able and skilled to lead us along the path of salvation, the only-begotten Son of God became a human being. And though he was King by nature in that he is considered to be God and from God the Father and ruler of all things with all creation under his feet, he is said to be elected king among us.

Fourth, he shows the sign of divinity in the true God: the first, that is, the only one, our God; behold I am here to help, evangelists, announcing things to come: verily, your God is the God of gods (Dan 2:47); or: the first, prophet of the Lord, in the person of God; or the first, the firstborn Son of God: he gave some apostles, and some prophets, and other some evangelists (Eph 4:11).

41:28.t: Let all the nations, therefore, which follow the error of idols, be questioned by us, so that they may answer whence they are. And this will be the answer of them all: that all follow vanity and the winds, and worship the works of their own hands. Whatever we have said of the idols and the nations, let us refer to the doctrines of perversity, and to their chiefs, the heresiarchs: that while Christ announces the peace of the Church and shows them the way of truth, they follow error and are likened to wind and whirlwind.
812. And I saw. Here from the disputation set out above, he deduces the determination of the sentence, and it is self-evident: they are vain things, and a ridiculous work (Jer 10:15 and 51:18).

42:1.t:
[Passage quoted, Isa. xlii. 1-7.]

THE Evangelist alludes to this passage, when the Pharisees went out and took counsel against our Saviour to put Him to death, when He healed the sick on the Sabbath day. But Jesus, knowing, as He says, this conspiracy against Him, departed thence, and great multitudes followed Him, and He healed them all, and He straitly charged them that they should not make Him known. And He adds to this the words, "All this was done" (that is to say His departure, and His yielding to those that plotted, and His effort to escape notice in the miracles that He did, and His pledging those that were healed not to make Him known), in order that what was said by the prophet might be fulfilled, when He said:

"Behold, my son, in whom I am well pleased, my beloved in […]
42:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 15

42:1.t:
And the same Isaiah, continuing, prophesies these things about Christ:

"Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased, he shall bring judgment to the nations."

And he adds: "Till he place judgment upon the earth, and in his name shall the Gentiles trust."

Here, then, the second time the prophet states that the Gentiles will hope in Christ, having said above "In Him shall the Gentiles trust." Though here it is "In His name shall the Gentiles trust."
42:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 3, Chapter 2

42:1.t: It is possible, with the help of God, easily to distinguish the presence of the good and the bad; a vision of the holy ones is not agitated. "He shall not protest and cry out; none will hear his voice." It occurs so quietly and gently that joy and gladness and confidence are at once born in the soul.… The soul's thoughts remain untroubled and calm, so that, enlightened of itself, it contemplates those who appear. LIFE OF ST.

Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in him my soul is well pleased. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he accept a person, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench; in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad nor troubled, until he sets judgment in the earth; and the islands will wait for his law. LXX: Jacob my child, I will take him up; Israel my chosen one, my soul has received him. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations; he will not cry out, nor will he let go, nor will his voice be heard outside. A broken reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench; […]

Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, and the rest. This is said through the prophet Isaiah in the person of the Father: I will put my Spirit upon him. The Spirit is put not upon the Word of God and upon the Only-begotten who came forth from the bosom of the Father, but upon him of whom it was said: Behold my servant.

What does it mean that it is written in Matthew: 'A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench' (Matthew 12:20). For the explanation of this passage, the whole testimony that Matthew takes from the Prophet Isaiah must be set forth, even the words of Isaiah (Isaiah 42): according to the Septuagint interpreters and the Hebrew itself, to which Theodotus, Aquila, and Symmachus agree. Thus of the four Evangelists, only Matthew relates: "And Jesus knowing it, retired from thence: and many followed him, and he healed them all. And he charged them that they should not make him known. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaias the prophet, saying: Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul hath been well pleased. […]

The passage reads, "Jacob, my son, I will uphold him; Israel, my elect, my soul has assumed him." … It is true, indeed, that the Vulgate text has "my servant" in place of "Jacob" and "Israel," but the Septuagint translators preferred to make the meaning more explicit, namely, that the prophecy concerns the "Highest" insofar as he became the "lowliest," in the form of a servant. Hence they placed the name of that man from whose stock the "form of a servant" was assumed. It was to him that the Holy Spirit was given.

42:2.t: He will not cry out: for he will be gentle and meek; and he will not accept a person in judgment, or he will not lift up (it is understood) his voice on high. Or, according to Symmachus, he will not be deceived, understanding all the snares of the devil; or, according to the Seventy, he will not let go, namely the people of the Jews, calling them to repentance. Nor will his voice be heard outside: for he did not preach the Gospel outside Galilee and Judea among the other nations. And if we read that he was in the borders of Tyre and Sidon (Matt 15), or in the region of Caesarea Philippi, which is now called Paneas, still it must be known that it is not written that he entered those cities themselves.

Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. Wide indeed and spacious is the way that leads to perdition, and many enter by it. Who are the many? Those who do not hear the voice of the Savior, because they are not on the narrow way but on the spacious one.

To which he joins his meekness: he shall not cry: the words of the wise are heard in silence, more than the cry of a prince among fools (Eccl 9:17).

Second, he shows the equality of the judge: nor have respect to person: God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34); to which he joins his piety in coming to help: neither shall his voice, the voice of his preaching, be heard abroad, outside Judea, so that he should first come to the aid of those to whom he was sent (Matt 15:24): to day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts (Ps 94[95]:8).

828. There is the cry (see 42:2),

of devout prayer: with a strong cry and tears (Heb 5:7);

of attentive preaching: and on the last festival day, Jesus cried (John 7:37); […]

42:3.t: The prophets, therefore, did not openly behold the actual face of God, but [they saw] the dispensations and the mysteries through which man should afterwards see God. As was also said to Elias: "Thou shalt go forth tomorrow, and stand in the presence of the Lord; and, behold, a wind great and strong, which shall rend the mountains, and break the rocks in pieces before the Lord. And the Lord [was] not in the wind; and after the wind an earthquake, but the Lord [was] not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord [was] not in the fire; and after the fire a scarcely audible voice" (vox aurae tenuis). […]

And therefore it was prophesied of Christ, because he was not to be bent down to earthly things: A bruised reed he will not break, since the flesh which sins had bruised he made solid by the power of the resurrection. A good reed is the flesh of Christ, which fixed the head of the serpent devil and the allurements of worldly desire to the gibbet of the cross.

It appears that Matthew the Evangelist did not by preferring the authority of the old interpretation ignore the truth of the Hebrew text. Rather, as a Hebrew among Hebrews and deeply taught in the law of the Lord, Matthew distributed his Hebrew learning to the nations. For if the Septuagint translators are accepted when they write, "Jacob my son, I will lift him up; Israel my chosen, my soul has lifted him up," then how can we understand the text fulfilled in Jesus, since it was obviously written about Jacob and Israel? We read that the blessed Matthew, not only in this verse but in another, has done this: "Out of Egypt I have called my son," while the Septuagint translated, "Out of Egypt he has called his sons.

For after the coming of the Lord and Savior, who gave the spirit of the gospel interpretation, [Christ] rested in the death of the Jewish letter, with which all works are bruised. Christ did not snuff out the smoking wick, reducing it to ashes. Instead, he ignited a great flame from this little spark, a spark that had almost gone out. The result is that the whole earth was ablaze with the fire of the Lord and Savior.

A bruised reed, or a broken one, he will not break. For he will be easy to appease toward all, and will give pardon to sinners, saying to the woman: Take heart, daughter, your sins are forgiven you (Luke 7:48). And smoking flax, or, as the others translated, dim and dark, he will not quench: those who were near to being quenched were preserved by the clemency of the Lord (which we have discussed in the works mentioned above concerning the Jews and the nations); but he will judge all things with truth, in no way fearing the scribes and Pharisees, whom he boldly called hypocrites (Matt 7, 15, 22, 23 throughout, and Luke 6, 12).

A battered reed he will not break, and smoldering flax he will not put out. He who does not hold out a hand to a sinner and does not carry the burden of his brother, he breaks the battered reed. And he who despises the small spark of faith in little ones, he puts out the smoldering flax. Christ did neither of these things; for he had come for this, to save what had perished.

And in dissembling: the bruised reed, namely, the kingdom of the Jews, smoking flax, of the priests: that which was broken you have not bound up (Ezek 34:4).

Third, he shows the truth of his judgment: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth: he shall judge the world with justice, and the people with his truth (Ps 95[96]:13).

42:4.t: The words, "And in his name shall the Gentiles trust," have also been exactly fulfilled. For the nations of Christians trust only in the Name of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and are marked with His Name as that of the Father of the religion with which they are associated. For it was foretold that He should be given for a Light to none but the Gentiles. And by Him in accordance with the prediction, the eyes of the blind—those that had long been impaired in understanding, and not only of these but of those who had lost their very bodies, and those who before were involved, bound and chained in sin, in darkness and ignorance of true religion, by Him freed from their sins— were accounted worthy of the light of knowledge and of the freedom of God. […]
42:4.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 9, Chapter 15

42:4.t: But what follows, He will shine and will not be broken, until he sets judgment upon the earth, the Evangelist Matthew did not set down (Matt 12); or else the words in the middle, between judgment and judgment, were removed by a scribe's error. And it signifies that, rising from the dead, he enlightened all, and was not broken by death, until he set judgment upon the earth, he who said in the Gospel: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9:39). For this we translated: He will not be sad, nor troubled, but he will keep an evenness of countenance at all times: what the philosophers falsely boast of Socrates, that he was never sadder or happier than usual. […]

To which he joins his pleasantness: he shall not be sad, in his heart, nor troublesome, in his face, for he was always cheerful and pleasant, keeping evenness of mind, even if, as to the sensible part, there was the suffering of sadness, not indeed of necessity, but of will; thus, my soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38); the joyfulness of the heart (Sir 30:23[22]).

820. Third, he shows the power of the Lord: till he set the final judgment, or his precept, by the preaching of the Apostles; his law, the Gospel: he shall be the expectation of nations (Gen 49:10), below: for, the islands wait for me (Isa 60:9). Others explain these things of Darius the king of the Persians, who was meek, just and peaceful, and whom the Lord chose to liberate the Jews.

42:5.t: For the breath of life, which also rendered man an animated being, is one thing, and the vivifying Spirit another, which also caused him to become spiritual. And for this reason Isaiah said, "Thus saith the Lord, who made heaven and established it, who founded the earth and the things therein, and gave breath to the people upon it, and Spirit to those walking upon it;" thus telling us that breath is indeed given in common to all people upon earth, but that the Spirit is theirs alone who tread down earthly desires. And therefore Isaiah himself, distinguishing the things already mentioned, again exclaims, "For the Spirit shall go forth from Me, and I have made every breath." […]

And again, "who gave breath to the people on the earth and spirit to those walking on it." For at first the soul, that is, "breath," was given to the people who go around on the earth, that is, to those acting in flesh in a fleshly manner; then later the Spirit was given to those who walk on the earth, that is, those who subdue the works of the flesh, as the apostle affirms, "Not that which is spiritual first, but that which is animal and then that which is spiritual." For although Adam from the beginning prophesied that great mystery in Christ and the church, "this is now bone of my bone and flesh of my flesh, on which account a man will leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife and they two will become one flesh," he was subject to a falling of the spirit.

It says, "He who gives spirit to the people who are on the earth, and spirit to them who walk on it." For undoubtedly every one who walks on the earth, that is, every earthly and corporeal being, is a partaker of the Holy Spirit that he receives from God.

And so says Isaiah;—"He that spread forth the earth and that which cometh out of it; he that giveth breath unto the people upon it, and Spirit to them that trample on it"; for they that trample down earthly things and rise above them are borne witness to as worthy of the gift of the Holy Ghost. What then ought to be thought of Him whom the world cannot receive, and Whom saints alone can contemplate through pureness of heart? What kind of honours can be deemed adequate to Him?
The Son is both sent and given, and the Spirit also is both sent and given; they have assuredly a oneness of Godhead who have a oneness of action.

Thus says the Lord God, who creates the heavens and stretches them out, who makes firm the earth and the things that spring from it, who gives breath to the people that is upon it, and spirit to those who tread on it: I the Lord have called you in righteousness, and have taken hold of your hand, and have kept you, and have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind, and bring the bound out of confinement, out of the prison house those who sit in darkness. I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another, nor my praise to graven images. The former things, behold, they have come; new things too I declare; […]

Isaiah again says: Thus saith the Lord, he that made the heaven and pitched it; and the Apostle in like manner says: Of the true Tabernacle which the Lord pitched and not man. They both speak of the heaven as standing on and fixed on the earth, and not as revolving round it.

821. Thus says the Lord God. Here he foretells the sending.

And first, he sets out the power of the one who sends as to the creation of heavenly things: that created the heavens; as to the disposition of earthly things: that established the earth; as to the animation of living things: that gives breath, of natural life, and spirit, freely: the Lord, who stretches forth the heavens, and lays the foundations of the earth, and forms the spirit of man in him (Zech 12:1).

42:6.t: Moses then received it, but they proved themselves unworthy. Learn now how we have received it. Moses, as a servant, received it; but the Lord himself, having suffered in our behalf, hath given it to us, that we should be the people of inheritance. But He was manifested, in order that they might be perfected in their iniquities, and that we, being constituted heirs through Him, might receive the testament of the Lord Jesus, who was prepared for this end, that by His personal manifestation, redeeming our hearts (which were already wasted by death, and given over to the iniquity of error) from darkness, He might by His word enter into a covenant with us. For it is written how the Father, about to redeem us from darkness, commanded Him to prepare a holy people for Himself. […]
42:6.s: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XIV

42:6.t: He, then, whose praises are so great, spoke these things to him whose law the islands and the nations await: I the Lord have called you in righteousness: of whom he himself speaks in the Gospel: Righteous Father, the world does not know you (John 17:25); so that he might be the God not only of the Jews but also of the nations. And I have taken hold of your hand, because whatever the Son works, the Father works. And I have kept you, you who yourself preserve all things. And I have given you as a covenant of the people of Israel, to whom I had promised beforehand that you would come. And as a light of the nations, which sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, that you might open the eyes of the blind, who before did not see God. And bring the bound out of confinement (Prov 5); […]

Those also whose heart was of old obscured by the darkness of the devil, He has illuminated by rising as some Sun of Righteousness, and making them the children no longer of night and darkness, but of light and day, according to Paul's word, And those who were blind,—for the Apostate had blinded their hearts,—have recovered their sight, and acknowledged the truth; and, as Isaiah says, "Their darkness has become light:" that is, the ignorant have become wise: those that once were in error, have known the paths of righteousness. […]
42:6.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

42:6.t: Second, he foretells the sending, setting out the exaltation of the one sent: I the Lord have called you, my Son, from eternity predestining to the unity of the divine person, in justice, that is, that I may be just, fulfilling my promise: who was predestined the Son of God (Rom 1:4); and taken you by the hand, as to his working: the Father who abides in me, he doth the works (John 14:10), and preserved you, lest you be detained by death: nor will you give your holy one to see corruption (Ps 15[16]:10), below: I have called him and brought him (Isa 48:15). […]

42:7.t: "The opened eyes of the blind" means [Christ] provided clear knowledge of the Father through the Son.

He also shows the use of his office against faithlessness: that you might open the eyes of the blind: for judgment I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind (John 9:39); against the slavery of sin: and bring forth the prisoner out of prison: you also by the blood of your testament have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit (Zech 9:11).

42:8.t: Who says by the prophet, "I am God, and there is none beside me." Who says by the same prophet, "Because I will not give my majesty to another," that He may exclude all heathens and heretics with their figments; proving that that is not God who is made by the hand of the workman, nor that which is feigned by the intellect of a heretic. For he is not God for whose existence the workman must be asked.

[Eunomius says:] "…receiving glory from the Father, not sharing His glory with the Father, for the glory of the Almighty is incommunicable, as He hath said, 'My glory will I not give to another.'" Who is that "other" to whom God has said that He will not give His glory? The prophet speaks of the adversary of God, and Eunomius refers the prophecy to the only begotten God Himself! For when the prophet, speaking in the person of God, had said, "My glory will I not give to another," he added, "neither My praise to graven images." […]

And what he adds, I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another, does not exclude the Son; for when he says in the Gospel, Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was (John 17:5), the Father himself answered: I have both glorified it, and will glorify it. For he did not say: My glory I will give to no one, for if he had said that, he would have excluded the Son too; but my glory I will not give to another, besides you, to whom I have given it, to whom I will give it. Hence I greatly admire the propriety of holy Scripture, in that all the translators, who are accustomed to disagree in many other places, translated the word AHER (אחר) with one voice another. […]

Since he is the only God, in a proper and true sense, he is the Creator of all, and so he is confessed to be by us; as the most wise Paul says: "Even though there may be many so-called gods and lords in heaven or on earth, yet for us there is one God and Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and through whom we exist." And since he presented himself to us as the author of great and marvelous things, he says that his glory, which is the virtues proper to God, is not to be given to lifeless idols or to any other created thing, but to be retained for himself alone. […]

Third, from the sending he deduces the singularity of the divine majesty as to power: I the Lord: make a way for him who ascends upon the west: the Lord is his name (Ps 67:5[68:4]); my name Adonai (Exod 6:3); my glory, by which I am called Lord: glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:14).

42:9.t: There follows: The former things, behold, they have come. And the sense is: What I have spoken, what I have promised through Moses and the Prophets, all has been fulfilled. But now I announce to you the Gospel, the calling of the nations, the passion of Christ, the newness of faith: so that as you see the former things fulfilled in fact, so you may also believe that the things I now promise will come,

When the prophet says, "See, the former things have come to pass, and new things I now declare; before they spring forth, I tell you of them," he does not allow for us to disbelieve the word of the Savior in any respect. In fact, he is saying that, just as what was said from the beginning about his coming has been fulfilled, so also what he calls the "new things" will be shown to be true and will be revealed before they are made manifest. And what are these things? Our Lord Jesus Christ promised life in the age to come, namely, the life of incorruption, and holiness, and righteousness, the kingdom of heaven, the glorious participation in the spiritual goods, the fruits of gentleness, the reward of piety, the crown of love for him. […]
And as to knowledge: the things that were first, etc., below: I foretold you of old (Isa 48:5). They also refer this to Darius.

42:10.t: Well, in as much as the Word was from the first, He was and is the divine source of all things; but in as much as He has now assumed the name Christ, consecrated of old, and worthy of power, he has been called by me the New Song. This Word, then, the Christ, the cause of both our being at first (for He was in God) and of our well-being, this very Word has now appeared as man, He alone being both, both God and man-the Author of all blessings to us; by whom we, being taught to live well, are sent on our way to life eternal. This is the New Song, the manifestation of the Word that was in the beginning, and before the beginning. The Saviour, who existed before, has in recent days appeared.

These indeed try to pursue, but you go down into the water and come out unharmed, and, the filth of your sins being washed away, you ascend "a new man" ready "to sing a new song." But the Egyptians, pursuing after you, are drowned in the abyss, even though they seem to beg Jesus not to send them meanwhile into the abyss.

Sing to God a new song, his praise from the ends of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and its fullness, the islands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its cities lift up; Kedar will dwell in houses; give praise, you inhabitants of Petra; from the top of the mountains they will cry out. They will give glory to the Lord, and will declare his praise in the islands. The Lord will go forth as a mighty one, as a man of war he will stir up zeal; he will shout and cry aloud; he will prevail over his enemies. I have always held my peace, I have kept silent, I have been patient; like a woman giving birth I will speak; I will scatter and swallow up at once. I will make the mountains and hills desolate, and I will dry up all their grass; […]

The word of the holy apostles and Evangelists about the Savior made visible the message of the glory of the Savior. At that time they wrote words concerning his ineffable divinity, and they hymned his transcendent virtue, not placing him among the things that are born but above those things that have been called into being and in such a nature he was placed beside God the Father. At that time their words set forth the divine signs that are beyond wonder and its explanation.

822. Sing to the Lord. Here he invites to thanksgiving.

And first, he enjoins praise, and especially upon the rustic, whether because of the distance of their habitation: from the ends of the earth, above: from the ends of the earth we have heard praises (Isa 24:16); or because of they are confined by the sea: you that go down to the sea, namely, sailors, and the fullness thereof, namely, of the sea, that is, let everything with which it is filled praise God: they that go down to the sea in ships (Ps 106[107]:23-24).

42:11.t: Let, he says, the desert and its cities lift up their voice, of which we have also spoken above. Or let the desert rejoice, and its villages, and Kedar, which was once an uninhabitable region beyond Arabia, of the Saracens; and the inhabitants of Petra, which itself is also a city of Palestine. And this signifies that the people of the nations, formerly a desert as regards the knowledge of God and bound by the errors of idolatry, is turned to the praises of the Lord. Or, because Kedar means darkness, and, according to the Apostle (1 Cor 10), the rock is Christ, all believers are commanded that those who were before in darkness, and now believe in the Lord the Savior, should cry aloud from the top of the mountains and openly preach Christ, those to whom it was said also above (cf. […]

Or because their way of life is in the desert: let the desert, that is, its inhabitants, especially as to the Ishmaelites, raise, its voice in praise of God; Cedar, the son of Ishmael, shall dwell in houses, according to the custom of other nations, for they were formerly wanderers through the desert, above: the land that was desolate and impassable shall be glad, and the wilderness shall rejoice (Isa 35:1); or because their habitation is in the mountains: give praise, you inhabitants of Petra, the city in Palestine, which is built in the rocks; or any mountain, below: the mountains and the hills shall sing praise (Isa 55:12); and he invites these who seem less likely to be turned to praising God.

42:12.t: Second, he foretells the spreading of divine praise: they shall give glory to the Lord, in others, not only in themselves, below: I will send of them that shall be saved, to the Gentiles (Isa 66:19). Mystically, all this refers to the conversion of the gentiles to the faith.

42:13.t: And the prophetic word describes the glorious coming of the Savior, of which the Apostle Paul also speaks: According to the illumination of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4; 2 Tim 1:10); and compares him to a most mighty man, who is about to fight against his adversaries and to stir up zeal. Of this it was prophesied also in the Song of Deuteronomy: They have moved me to jealousy with that which was not God, and have provoked me with their idols; and I will move them to jealousy with a nation that is not, and with a most foolish nation I will provoke them (Deut 32:21).

42:14.t: It is sufficiently discovered that He suffered shame for man's sake, to set him free from death; and that He exclaimed, as in the words of the prophet, "I have endured as a travailing woman." In very deed did He endure for our sakes sorrow, ignominy, torment, even death itself, and burial. For thus He says Himself by the prophet: "I went down into the deep." Who made Him thus to go down? The impious people. Behold, ye sons of men, behold what recompense Israel made unto Him! She slew her Benefactor, returning evil for good, affliction for joy, death for life. They slew by nailing to the tree Him who had brought to life their dead, had healed their maimed, had made their lepers clean, had given light to their blind. Behold, ye sons of men! behold, all ye people, these new wonders! […]

“I have long time holden my peace. Am I to hold my peace for ever? Shall I still further endure to enforce against myself the hardest punishment of silence, by neither writing myself, nor receiving any statement from another? By holding fast to this stern determination up to the present time I am able to apply to myself the prophet’s words, “I endure patiently like travailing woman.” Yet I am ever longing for communication either in person or by letter, and ever, for my own sins’ sake, missing it.

Nevertheless I thought that I ought to bear my troubles in silence, waiting for some indication to come out of them. I did not even think that what was said against me proceeded from ill will; I thought it was the result of ignorance of the truth. But now I see that hostility increases with time, and that my slanderers are not sorry for what they said at the beginning, and do not take any trouble to make amends for the past, but go on and on and rally themselves together to attain their original object. This was to make my life miserable and to devise means for sullying my reputation among the brethren. I, therefore, no longer see safety in silence. I have bethought me of the words of Isaiah: “I have long time holden my peace, shall I always be still and refrain myself? […]

WHAT IS GOD? — [God is] good, just, merciful. Good, because He brought into existence things that were not; just, because whatever He made to advance He left to the free judgment of their own liberty; yet because they are not so perfect that they cannot fall, He decreed that seeds of law should naturally exist in them, adding the help of revealed law, so that His authority might be complete for humankind; merciful, because He does not quickly repay those who sin, but bears with them so that He may forgive the repentant. He is also severe, so that, through fear, the things well created by Him may be preserved, lest negligence give rise to the downfall of life. […]
42:14.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 1: WHAT IS GOD?

42:14.t: He will also shout and cry aloud against his enemies, openly rebuking their unbelief and declaring with a loud cry: I have held my peace, I have always kept silent, I have been patient, or, as the Seventy translated: I have held my peace; shall I always hold my peace (Eccl 3:7)? So that what is said through Solomon may be fulfilled: A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And the sense is: For a long time I have often borne you when you sinned; but because I had kept silent before, I will no longer keep silent. And as a woman giving birth pours forth the infant into the light, and makes open what was before held shut in her womb, so I will now bring forth my pain and the forbearance which I always had over your crimes, and I will scatter your counsels; […]

The one who speaks is now keeping quiet. He speaks in commandments; he keeps quiet in judgment.… How has he kept quiet, seeing that he spoke to say this very thing? He says, "I have kept quiet," and yet he does not keep quiet, because just by saying "I have kept quiet," God has not kept quiet. So then, Lord, I hear you speaking in so many commandments, as many sacred signs, so many pages, so many books. And then I hear you saying this, "I have kept quiet, will I keep quiet always?" So how have you kept quiet? Because I am not yet saying, "Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom." And I am not yet saying to the others, "Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels." […]

Which same truth he conveys by the Prophet in few words, saying, "I have long time holden my peace, I have been still and refrained myself; now will I cry like a travailing woman." For as we have already before said, a woman in travail with pain gives forth that which she bore for long in her inner parts, He then that for long time held his peace, 'crieth like a travailing woman,' in that the Judge that shall come, who for long bore with the deeds of men without taking vengeance, sooner or later brings to light with hotness of examination, as if with pain of mind, the sentence of direful visiting which He kept within. Therefore let none despise this Lamp, when it is out of sight, lest He burn up His despisers when He shineth from heaven. […]
42:14.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 10:31

42:14.t: Third, he sets out justice, for it is just that when he has long waited for the impenitent, he should swallow them all up at once: I have always held my peace: have I not dissembled? Have I not kept silence? (Job 3:26), I have been patient, above: therefore the Lord waits that he may have mercy on you (Isa 30:18); as a woman in labor, I will bring forth hidden pain, as a woman brings forth the infant she has conceived, or because as a woman in labor, I will be pained at such a grave penalty.

42:15.t: Fourth, he sets out the punishment as to men: I will lay waste the mountains, the great, hills, the middle ranks, grass, the common people: and I will make mount Seir waste and desolate (Ezek 35:7); and as to the removal of every teaching or consolation, I will turn rivers into islands: he has turned rivers into a wilderness: and the sources of waters into dry ground (Ps 106[107]:33). This can also be referred to the destruction of the enemies of the Jews by Darius.

42:16.t: And I will lead the blind by the way which before they did not know, of whom we also read above: I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind. These will be led by the way of which Christ speaks: I am the way, or by the way of the knowledge of God; and I will make them walk by the paths of the Prophets. Then their darkness will be changed into light, and crooked things will be turned into straight, so that they may understand what they read, and with the eyes of the heart behold the clear light of Christ in the Old Testament. And at the same time he adds: These words which I have done, or I will do for them: no longer promising things to come, but rendering what I had promised before.

If, dearly beloved, we comprehend faithfully and wisely the beginning of our creation, we shall find that man was made in God’s image, to the end that he might imitate his Creator, and that our race attains its highest natural dignity, by the form of the Divine goodness being reflected in us, as in a mirror. And assuredly to this form the Saviour’s grace is daily restoring us, so long as that which, in the first Adam fell, is raised up again in the second. And the cause of our restoration is naught else but the mercy of God, Whom we should not have loved, unless He had first loved us, and dispelled the darkness of our ignorance by the light of His truth. […]

42:17.t: But while I say these things, the people of the Jews has turned back, so as not to believe him who promises, and to be confounded in its errors, and to neglect the pledge of God, having before believed in idols. Or, when the fullness of the nations has come in, then the people of Israel too will be converted (Rom 11), and will repent of its error, through which it had before served idols. Or certainly, after the calling of the nations, he returns to the beginning, so as to say that all the nations which refused to believe the Gospel are to be confounded in their idols.

42:18.t: Now the blind see when they see the world, and from the exceedingly great beauty of things that have been created they contemplate the Creator corresponding in greatness and beauty to them. And when they see clearly "the invisible things of God from the creation of the world, which are perceived through the things that are made," [then] they see and understand with attentiveness and clarity.

And since the keenness of the inner hearing is in our power, the prophet says: "Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see. Who is so deaf as My servants, and who is so blind as those who rule over them?" Even the servants of God are blinded.

You deaf, hear, and you blind, look, that you may see. Who is blind but my servant? and deaf but he to whom I have sent my messengers? Who is blind but he who has been sold? and who is blind but the servant of the Lord? You who see many things, will you not keep them? you who have open ears, will you not hear? And the Lord willed to sanctify him, and to magnify the law and exalt it. But this is a people plundered and laid waste; all are the snare of young men, and they are hidden in prison houses; they have become a prey, and there is none to rescue; a plunder, and there is none to say: Give back. Who is there among you who will hear this, who will attend and listen for the time to come? Who gave Jacob up to plunder, and Israel to those who lay waste? […]

826. Hear, you deaf. Here he shows that they are hard-hearted or disobedient toward his precepts.

And first, he shows their hard-heartedness, calling them deaf and blind unitedly: for their own malice blinded them (Wis 2:21), though they may have the eyes and ears of the body, which shows that those who see take heed and those who have the ears of their hearts open obey.

42:19.t: He that is sold, as a slave of sin for love of temporal good: you are sold, to do evil in the sight of the Lord (1 Kgs 21:20).

42:20.t: To him it is said: O Israel, you who see many things, and have very many Prophets through whom to know the commandments of God, will you not keep what has been commanded you? You who have open ears, will you not hear what is said? Of whom we also read above: Hearing you will hear, and will not understand; and seeing you will look, and will not see; for the heart of this people has been made fat (Isa 6:9).

You that have ears open: hear, O foolish people, and without understanding: who have eyes, and see not: and ears, and hear not (Jer 5:21); above: blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy (Isa 6:10).

42:21.t: The Lord, he says, willed to sanctify him, and to magnify his Law, and to exalt and raise up the people lying prostrate.

Second, he shows the foolishness of the hard-hearted, because the Lord intended what is found in the precepts for their own advantage. Hence he sets out the intention of the Lord: and the Lord was willing to sanctify him, the people, both that the people themselves should magnify the law of God in their hearts by keeping it, and that the Lord should exalt the people: for this is the will of God, your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3).

42:22.t: But he refused to do the will of God, and therefore he was plundered and laid waste by his adversaries, whom we ought to understand either as demons or as enemies. All are the snare of young men, and they are hidden in prison houses. Or, as the Seventy translated, There is a snare in the chambers everywhere, and in the houses together, in which they hid them: signifying the scribes and Pharisees, who deceived the wretched common people and everywhere laid snares against the Lord the Savior and his Apostles (Luke 11), having the key of knowledge, neither entering themselves, and forbidding others who wished to enter. And beautifully he called their breasts, in which the worst thoughts dwelt, prisons. […]

And he also shows their contradiction, because they sinned against themselves: but this is a people that is robbed, by demons through various sins, and therefore they are wasted, by enemies, above: from a people rent and torn in pieces (Isa 18:7); also by others who furnished the occasion of sin: the snare, that is, the occasion of sin, of young men, the foolish: you have been a snare to them (Hos 5:1); and because they hid their sins in the houses of prisons, that is, in the secret of their hearts: with a double heart have they spoken (Ps 11:3[12:2]). […]

42:23.t: And at the same time the Prophet exhorts them that, if all cannot hear, at least a few may know the things to come and understand from whom they have suffered these things, and may recognize the causes of their devastation, they who would neither hear nor do what had been commanded in the Law.

827. Who is there among you. Here he shows that they cannot be corrected by scourges, because they do not even recognize the cause of the scourges; and concerning this, he does three things.

First, he seeks those who perceive rightly, intimating their scarcity; things to come, which I foretell concerning your punishments: who is wise, and he shall understand these things? (Hos 14:10).

42:24.t: In this part of the Lord's Prayer, [Christ] shows that the enemy is powerless against us without God's prior permission. During temptation, consequently, all our fear and devotion and attention should be focused on God, since evil has only such force as he himself permits. … Moreover, evil is given power over us according to our [willful] sins. As Isaiah writes, "Who gave Jacob up to the looters and Israel to the ponderers." It was the Lord, against whom we sinned, in whose ways we would not walk and whose law we refused to obey. So he unleashed the fury of his anger against us. And again, when Solomon strayed from the precepts and paths of the Lord, it was recorded, "The Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon himself."
42:24.s: Treatise IV. On the Lord's Prayer 25

42:24.t: Second, he determines the truth as to the doer of the punishment: who has given Jacob for a spoil, the Lord kills and makes alive (1 Sam 2:6); as to the fault: has not the Lord himself, against whom we have sinned: and they have not known his justices, nor walked by the ways of God's commandments (Bar 4:13).

42:25.t: Therefore the Lord poured out upon them all his anger and an indignation full of fury, so that he who before had kept silent would no longer hold his peace, and would chastise them not with words but with punishments and torments; and a most mighty war would seize them, which they could in no way escape, showing the ferocity of the Romans. And though he has been burned on every side and has no soundness in him, yet he does not understand the cause of his punishment: that he has been punished because he did not receive the Son of God.

And as to the punishment, and he has poured out: pour out your indignation upon them (Ps 68:25[69:24]), "pouring out" signifies its abundance.

Third, he excludes knowledge of the truth: and has burnt him, namely, with material fire through the wasting by their enemies, and he knew not, that he was punished by God for his sins: they have not known nor understood (Ps 81[82]:5).

43:1.t: And now thus says the Lord who creates you, Jacob, and forms you, Israel: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you, and I have called you by your name: you are mine. When you pass through the water , I will be with you, and the rivers will not cover you. When you walk into the fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not burn in you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I have given Egypt as your propitiation, Ethiopia and Saba for you. Since you have become honorable in my eyes and glorious, I have loved you, and I will give men for you, and peoples for your life. Do not fear, for I am with you; from the East I will bring your seed, and from the West I will gather you. I will say to the North: Give; and to the South: Do not hold back; […]

And now thus says the Lord. Here he shows them divine love through the remedies which he granted them among their difficulties. And it is divided into three parts: in the first, he promises future remedies to show them his love; in the second, he recalls past benefits to confirm the promise: thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea (Isa 43:16); in the third, he excludes their merits to take away their presumption: but you have not called upon me (Isa 43:22).

Concerning the first, he does three things: first, he shows the privilege of divine love toward them; second, he excludes the sharing of divine power from the promised remedies: all the nations are assembled together (Isa 43:9); in the third, he sets out the sign of his love: thus says the Lord your redeemer (Isa 43:14). […]

43:2.t: "Even if we cross over, they shall not slip, says the Lord." We shall not slip into corruption, we who are crossing over into incorruption, because he himself will support us. For so he himself has said and so he has willed.

There is a way to the tree of life, so that it may come to pass: "If you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you." What fire? "He stationed the Cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way of the tree of life." So for this reason the blessed ones waited there, carrying out a dispensation and not being able to come where the tree of life is, where the paradise of God is, where God is husbandman, where the blessed and chosen and holy ones of God are.

It happened one day, that a man, who is called wise amongst the Jews, questioned me, saying:—Jesus, Who is called your Teacher, wrote for you, that If there shall be in you faith like one grain of mustard, ye shall say to this mountain, Remove, and it shall remove from before you; and (ye shall say) even, Be lifted up and fall into the sea, and it shall obey you. So apparently there is in all your people not one wise man, whose prayer is heard, and who asks of God that your persecutors should cease from you. For clearly it is written for you in that passage, There is nothing which ye shall not be able to do. […]

We are wayfarers in this life; many walk, but it is needful that we walk aright, for then is the Lord Jesus with us, as we read, When thou passest through the waters I will be with thee, and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee; when thou walkest through the fire thou shalt not be burned. But if a man take fire in his bosom, the fire of lust, the fire of immoderate desire he walketh not through, but burns this clothing of his soul. A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour than silver and gold! Faith is sufficient for itself, and in its own possession is rich enough. And to the wise man nothing is foreign, but what is contrary to virtue; wherever he goes, he finds all things to be his own. […]

And what he adds, waters and rivers, and fire and flames, describes the onslaught and fury of the persecutors, who begrudge the salvation of the nations and do not want the word of the Gospel to be preached. The Jews, however, would have the Egyptians understood by the waters, the Babylonians by the rivers, the Macedonians by the fire, the Romans by the flame.

And through the prophet the Lord promises saying, "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee, and the rivers shall not overflow thee." For the rivers overflow those whom the active business of this world confounds with perturbation of mind. But he who is sustained in mind by the grace of the Holy Spirit passes through the waters, and yet is not overflowed by the rivers, because in the midst of crowds of peoples he so proceeds along his way as not to sink the head of his mind beneath the active business of the world.

Knowledge is not able to make anything without materials. Knowledge does not venture to step over unto the domain which lies outside nature. How then? That the dissolved nature of water does not suffer the footsteps of flesh on its back, that he who excites fire is burnt by it, and that it is dangerous to act contrary to these [rules]. Such lore is cautiously guarded by knowledge. And it is absolutely impossible to persuade it to order an advance into this domain.

Faith on the other hand commands this with authority, saying: If thou tread on fire it will not burn thee; and floods ‘will not drag thee along. And faith has done these things many times before the eyes of all creatures. […]

He sets out the promise: when you shall pass through the waters, the Egyptians; the rivers, the Chaldeans; the fire, the Greeks; the flames, the Romans: for they were not entirely consumed: we have passed through fire and water (Ps 66:12).

The Lord liberates his saints from the fire, of carnal temptation: it is a fire that devours even to consumption (Job 31:12); of temporal tribulation: you have tried me by fire (Ps 17:3); of eternal damnation: go, you cursed, into everlasting fire (Matt 25:41); of divine wrath: a fire is kindled in my wrath (Deut 32:22); in which are burned the lascivious: for it is better to marry than to be burnt (1 Cor 7:9); the impatient, above: their countenances shall be as faces burnt (Isa 13:8); the impenitent: the flame burned the wicked (Ps 106:18); […]

43:3.t: And he commands them not to fear for this reason, that the Lord God, their Savior and the Holy One of Israel, is with them, who has made them preach to Egypt, Ethiopia and Syene, and to the furthest bounds of the world. For Syene the other translators put SABA (סבא), whence came the queen of the South, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kgs 10).

And he assigns the reason for this: for I am the Lord, above: for God himself is my savior (Isa 12:2).

Second, he promises the commutation of their punishments, namely, that he would punish others in their place; and he sets out the commutation: I have given Egypt for your atonement, that is, that I may be propitiated toward you, as though by the punishments of those who provoked you to sin by hoping in their help: Saba, a city of Ethiopia: the just is delivered out of distress: and the wicked shall be given up for him (Prov 11:8).

43:4.t: Therefore the choir of the Apostles has become honorable in the sight of God and beloved by him; and the salvation of all the men and peoples who have been called through them to the Gospel will also be reckoned to the salvation of their own souls.

And he assigns the reason, namely, the love of God itself: since you became honorable, that is, I made and reckoned you honorable; I will give men for you, for your liberation: surely Ephraim is an honorable son to me (Jer 31:20).

43:5.t: Hence he adds and says: Do not fear, I am with you, I who say to you in the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt 28:20). For from the East and from the West I will bring your sons, to rest in the bosom of Abraham; and from all parts of the world a people of my sons and daughters will be gathered, who either call upon my name or are called by my name, so that they are called Christians, to the glory of their founder.

Third, he promises them every kind of liberation from tribulation. First, he promises the benefit of liberation: fear not; from the east, for they had been dispersed in every direction, above: he shall assemble the fugitives of Israel (Isa 11:12); behold I will bring them from the north country (Jer 31:8).

43:6.t: The same thing is signified also by that which is written: I will say to the north wind: Bring; and to the south-west wind: Do not hold back. For the south wind and the east wind are never commanded to bring, because those who are afterwards to be led to the east and the south must be in other regions. The north wind, therefore, brings its inhabitants to the south, and the south-west wind brings its own to the east. For they cannot make progress if they remain in their former seats.

43:7.t: Thou, Master almighty, didst create all things for Thy name's sake; Thou gavest food and drink to men for enjoyment, that they might give thanks to Thee; but to us Thou didst freely give spiritual food and drink and life eternal through Thy Servant. Before all things we thank Thee that Thou art mighty; to Thee be the glory for ever.

Second, he sets out their fitness for liberation: and every one that calls upon my name, I will lead into my glory, that he might glorify me, and that I might appear glorious in him: every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved (Joel 2:32).

43:8.t: And what follows, Bring forth the people that is blind and has eyes, that is deaf and has ears, many think is said of the people of the nations, who through the teaching of the Apostles began to hear and to see. But let us understand this too of scattered Israel, which was called through the Apostles and believed first; to whom Paul also says: It was necessary that the word of God be preached first to you (Acts 13:46). And the Lord himself in the Gospel: Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:6). Then follows: All the nations are gathered together, and the tribes are assembled, that is, together with the people that believed from among the Jews, so that the calling may be twofold, of the circumcision and of the uncircumcision. […]

And with the same meaning the Lord rebukes by the prophet the unnatural but freely chosen blindness of the Jews, which they by their obstinacy brought upon themselves, saying: "Hear ye deaf, and ye blind, behold that you may see. Who is deaf but My servant? and blind, but he to whom I have sent My messengers?" And that no one might ascribe this blindness of theirs to nature instead of to their own will, elsewhere He says: "Bring forth the people that are blind and have eyes: that are deaf and have ears;" and again: "having eyes, but ye see not; and ears, but ye hear not." The Lord also says in the gospel: "Because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not neither do they understand." […]
43:8.s: The Third Conference of Abbot Chaeremon, Chapter 12

43:8.t: Third, he promulgates the command of liberation: bring, O Cyrus, forth, out of the land of their captivity, the people, namely, of the Jews: hear, O foolish people, and without understanding: who have eyes, and see not: and ears, and hear not (Jer 5:21).

43:9.t:
All the nations. Here he excludes the sharing of divinity. And first, he shows the falsehood of other gods by the manner of a judgment, setting out the consensus of the nations in idolatry: assembled together, in one error: they are all gone aside (Ps 14:3); seeking a sign of divinity: who among you, that is, which of your gods; or this is said to the idols; and he seeks testimony: let them bring forth their witnesses, let them be justified, that is, let them justly be called gods; and let the witnesses hear, future things from them, and say, testimony for you, above: there is none that shows, nor that foretells (Isa 41:26).

Second, he shows the truth of his own divinity, and first, as to knowledge, second, as to power: you are my witnesses (Isa 43:12).

43:10.t: What then do the divine Scriptures intend to say, for example, here: "Before Me there was no God, and after Me there shall be none," and "I am, and there is no God besides Me"? Do not suppose that in these utterances the unity is applied to the God of the universe … apart from Christ, and, of course, not to Christ alone apart from God. But let us speak of this as Jesus Himself taught: "I and the Father are one."

Still I should like to ask our objectors, what means that which is said by the Prophet, "Before Me there was no God formed, nor is there any after Me"? For if the Son is younger than the Father, how, says He, "Nor is there any after me"? Will you take away the being of the Only-Begotten Himself? You either must dare this, or admit one Godhead with distinct Persons of the Father and Son.
43:10.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 4

43:10.t: Or else God himself is the witness and performer of his own words, and so is his child and servant whom he has chosen. There is no doubt that he means Christ, to whom he says also above: It is a great thing for you to be called my child. And all these things will take place so that the truth may be preached to the world, and that those whose mind was before brutish and senseless may know and believe and understand that besides the one God there is no other God, neither before nor after. For the founder of the times never has a beginning, since this very word, ever, belongs to time. And as he has now said, I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the child whom I have chosen, the Lord saying this same thing in the Gospel: The testimony of two men is true. […]

And according to what he commands in another place: Be my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I have chosen, the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit is a witness for us, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. And it seems to me that the sentence stands rather in this way, and that the truth is confirmed under these three witnesses, rather than through the letter. For there were two witnesses against Susanna, and against the Lord Savior himself, and yet the word did not stand in their mouth. Against Naboth, too, almost the whole city bore witness, and the agreement of most wicked witnesses had not the firmness of truth but the conspiracy of a crime.

He gives testimony, assigning men to give testimony: you are my witnesses, my servant, the people of Jacob, or Christ: you shall be witnesses (Acts 1:8); setting out the manner of knowing: that you may know, as to those things which can be known about God by natural reason, and believe, as to those things which are above reason, and thus, understand, for unless you believe, you will not understand, above (Isa 7:9), according to another reading; and setting out what is said by the witnesses, that he alone is God: that I, alone, am, God; there was no God who forms, or formed, namely, no idol: see that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me (Deut 32:39).

43:11.t: And what follows, And besides me there is no Savior, shows that the Son saves all things in the Father. Of him the same prophet testifies: And the Lord will send them a Savior, who will save them (Isa 19). For God, who is wise and strong, cannot be without his own wisdom and power.
And that he alone is Lord: I am, singularly, I am, preeminently: neither is there salvation in any other (Acts 4:12).

43:12.t: Since, then, I foretold from the beginning that these things would come, there will be no one who can refuse my will, nor indeed make void what I shall have done. These things are said indeed to Jacob and Israel, but they refer to the apostolic choir and to all of the people of the Jews who have been willing to believe in Christ.

Second, he gives a sign of his divinity: I have declared, there was no strange one among you, by which you could know: O Israel, if you will hearken to me, there shall be no new god in you: neither shall you adore a strange god (Ps 81:8–9).

Here he shows the truth of his divinity as to power. And first, he gives the testimony: you are my witnesses: I am the beginning (John 8:25).

43:13.t: "I will act, and who will hinder it?" For I have accomplished the calling of the nations, he says, that is, I have saved those who were led astray. And who can alter this, or who could change things so that they did not happen? The Savior himself assures us that no one can snatch those who are being saved from the hand of God. "For my sheep hear my voice, and I know them; and they follow me, and I give them eternal life."

He gives a sign of his power in punishing: and there is none that can deliver out of my hand, as in Deuteronomy 32:39 and Job 10:7; and in working: I will work, above: the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who can disannul it? (Isa 14:27).

43:14.t: Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and I have pulled down all the bars, and the Chaldeans glorying in their ships. I am the Lord, your Holy One, the Creator, Israel, your King. LXX: Thus says the Lord God, who redeemed you, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I will send to Babylon, and I will rouse up all the fugitives, and the Chaldeans will be bound in ships. I am the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who have shown Israel your king. […]

Thus says the Lord. Here he sets out the sign of his love, that he destroyed for them the Babylonians, who gloried in their ships because of the multitude of their waters: I sent, namely, my wrath: the Lord has both purposed, and done all that he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon (Jer 51:12).

43:16.t: Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea, and a path in the rushing waters; who brought forth the chariot and the horse, the army and the strong man: together they have fallen asleep, and they will not rise again; they are crushed like flax, they are quenched. Do not remember the former things, and do not look upon the things of old. Behold, I am doing new things; now they will spring forth; surely you will know them. I will make a way in the desert, and rivers in the trackless land. The beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches; for I have given waters in the desert, rivers in the trackless land, to give drink to my people, my chosen one. This people I have formed for myself; they will tell my praise. […]

Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea. Here he recalls his past benefits to confirm their hope for future benefits. And concerning this, he does two things. First, he recalls his past benefits in directing them when they came out of Egypt: in the Red sea (Exod 14); in the mighty waters, in the Arnon (Num 21), in the Jordan (Josh 3).

43:17.t: And as to the destruction of their enemies, who brought forth the chariot, the chariots of Pharaoh: his chosen captains are drowned in the Red Sea (Exod 15:4); as flax, cut down in a moment.

43:18.t: Therefore I command you this: that among my signs and wonders, by which Babylon, the mightiest city, was overthrown, and by which a way was opened for my people in the Red Sea and in the Jordan, you should in no way remember the old things, since in the Gospel I am going to do far greater things, in comparison with which past things ought to be passed over in silence. For no longer will I find a way in the Red Sea, but in the desert of the whole world. Nor will one river or fountain burst forth from the rock, but many rivers, to refresh not bodies, as before, but thirsting souls; and that will be fulfilled which we read above: You will drink waters from the fountains of the Savior (cf. Isa 12:3).

Second, he promises much greater future benefits. First, he shows the greatness of his future benefits by comparison to the former ones: remember not former things, as if to say: they are not worthy to be kept in memory in comparison with future things: forgetting the things that are behind (Phil 3:13).

43:19.t: The Word says, "Look, I am doing something new, which no eye has seen, no ear heard, no human heart felt." These are to be seen, heard and grasped by a new eye, a new hearing and a new heart when the Lord's disciples speak, listen and act in the Spirit.

For of this number I find figurative hints up and down the Creator's dispensation in the twelve streams of Elim. … Now the same number of apostles was thus portended, as if they were to be fountains and rivers that should water the Gentile world, which was formerly dry and destitute of knowledge, as he says by Isaiah, "I will put streams in the unwatered ground."

But as often as water is named alone in the holy Scriptures, baptism is referred to, as we see intimated in Isaiah: "Remember not," says he, "the former things, and consider not the things of old.
